I shall declare their supreme essence by which one becomes composed of Brahman.
The recitation of the Pārāyaṇa is that meditation on Brahman which is performed correctly;
the meditation here upon that very same Brahman with attributes (saguṇa) constitutes the "ghaṭikā-japa."
O Goddess, this recitation (japa) is of two kinds: with attributes (saguṇa) and likewise without attributes (nirguṇa).
Recollecting that it is either accomplished (siddha) or to be accomplished (sādhya), one should perform the recitation of the mantra through its complete course (pārāyaṇa).
On the day the Kali age began, the Sun rose within the seed-syllable *hṛllekhā* (hrīm).
From that time onward, the Sun moves one syllable every day at the measure of a single *ghaṭikā*.

The seeker of liberation, having divided the nine-syllable mantra string into three parts— at midday, in the evening, and at dawn— and likewise placing them at the beginning, the end, and the middle of the day, should perform the recitation of the mantra.
By joining the nine syllables of the mantra with rows of letters from one up to fifty,
the letters of the Kulamātṛkā become equal in measure to the ghaṭīs for the sake of attaining the success of the King of Mantras.
O Śivā, having adorned the Mātṛkā with the vowel *ā* and embellished it with the *haṃsa*,
the practitioner of mantra should recite the root-vidyā, which consists of Śiva and Śakti.
Having abandoned the five types of noise, he who recites the sixteen-syllable [mantra] becomes composed of the five sounds, which are the roots of the sixty-five syllables. || 24 ||

O Goddess, one should abandon the Vidyā at the beginning of the Vidyā, in the middle of the Vidyā, and after it; even at the end of the Vidyā, one should abandon the Vidyā which is the form of Śiva, and one shall become Śiva.
Then Viśvarūpa, though the Sun, arose within the syllable *a*;
from that time forward, Ravi moved through the Mātṛkās in this world. (26)
By the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), the three-eyed one becomes composed of fiery splendor;
having attained Lakṣmī, the practitioner of mantra becomes Śiva, culminating in good fortune, in due order. (27)

O Goddess, the mantra practitioner should always recite the Vidyā, which has been gradually made to sprout by the water of the clouds [of the Mātṛkā], ending with the Haṃsa, together with the Mātṛkā. (28) p. 42)
This recitation known as the Pārāyaṇa bestows success in the Kali age;
it is the supreme Mahāśrīṣoḍaśī-vidyā, consisting of the eightfold prosperity.
One who takes refuge in the Kula should recite [the mantra] beginning with the Vedas along with the Mātṛkās.
This supreme secret, consisting of the recitation of the Pārāyaṇa, which arises from the awakening of the seat of Brahma-knowledge, must not be disclosed by those who discourse on Brahman. || 30 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Recitation of Pārāyaṇa," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrī Devī Rahasya*.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Now I shall declare the transmission of the *saṃpuṭa* for all mantras;
by knowing which, O Goddess, the wise one becomes possessed of all happiness. (1)
O Maheśvarī, one should first place the seed-syllable of Śakti for Bālā;
this mantra of Bālā Tripurasundarī is known as the "encased" (saṃpuṭa) mantra. || 2 ||
O Maheśvarī, one should recite the three *māyās* at the end of the *trikūṭā*;
this mantra of Tripurabhairavī is known as the *saṃpuṭa*. || 3 ||
One should place the *kūṭa* of Śakti and the others at the beginning of the mantra and then recite the mantra;
this is the mantra of Mahātripurasundarī known as *saṃpuṭa*.
O Śivā, there is the twenty-two-syllable mantra of Dakṣiṇākālī known as Śyāmā;
it is free from all defects, as I have previously declared. (5)
O Maheśvarī, having placed [the name] within the *amaṃcala* (the beginning and end), one should recite the root mantra;
O beautiful one, this is the mantra of Bhadrakālī known as *saṃpuṭa*. (6)
O Goddess, at the end one should mutter the *tāra* (om); the wise one should utter it three times.
This mantra of the goddess Rājamātaṅginī is known as the *saṃpuṭa*. (7)
O Śivā, one should recite the seed-syllable of Parā ten times at the end of the entire [mantra];
this mantra of Bhuvaneśvarī, known as *saṃpuṭa*, bestows excellent accomplishment.
O Pārvatī, the practitioner should recite the horse-mantra at the beginning of the root-mantra;
this mantra of Ugratārā is known as the Śrī-sampuṭa.
O Sovereign of Sādhakas, at the end, the practitioner should recite the two *māyās*.
This mantra of Chinnamastā, known as *saṃpuṭa*, is extremely rare. (10)
O Maheśvarī, one should recite the three *padmas* at the beginning and the *māyā* at the end;
this mantra of the goddess Ucchiṣṭamātaṅgī is known as the *saṃpuṭa*.
O Goddess, the best of practitioners should recite the Vāgbhava syllable at the end of the mantra of Sarasvatī; this is known as the "encased" (saṃpuṭa) mantra.
O Pārvatī, the practitioner should place the syllable *tāram* (oṃ) at the beginning and the word *kāmaṃ* (kāmam) at the end of the mantra;
this is the mantra of Annapūrṇā known as *saṃpuṭa*. (13)
One should place the Vāgbhava at the beginning and the Manmatha at the end;
this is the mantra known as Saṃpuṭa for the deity Mahālakṣmī. || 14 ||
O Maheśvarī, the practitioner should offer sindhura at the end of the mantra;
that mantra of the root-mantra of Śārikā is known as the *saṃpuṭaka*.
The most excellent practitioner should recite "Tāram" (Om) at the beginning and "Kāmam" (Hrīṃ) at the end of the mantra;
this is the mantra of Śāradā Sarasvatī known as "saṃpuṭa. || 16 ||
O Maheśvarī, the practitioner of mantra should recite the *śakti* at the beginning and the *vāṇī* at the end;
this is the mantra known as *saṃpuṭa*, belonging to Indrākṣī who holds a thunderbolt in her hand. (17)
The wise practitioner should recite the seed-syllable of earth (*mṛttikā-bīja*) at the end of the mantra of *Manu*.
This is known as the "encasement" (*saṃpuṭaka*) of the mantra of the illustrious goddess Bagalāmukhī. (18)
O Pārvatī, at the end of the mantra, the practitioner should utter the syllable *tāram*;
this is known as the "encasement" (*saṃpuṭa*) of the great fourth [syllable] of the mantra, which bestows accomplishment. || 19 ||
O Pārvatī, the practitioner should recite "vahniṃ vāṇīm" at the end and then perform the japa;
this mantra of the Mahārājñī-mantra is known as the *saṃpuṭa*.
O Maheśvarī, one should recite the *kūrca* at the beginning and *hara* at the end of the root mantra;
O Pārvatī, this is the mantra of Jvālāmukhī known as the "encased" (*saṃpuṭa*).
One should first recite the syllable *tāra* (om), followed by *śakti* (hrīṃ), and at the end of the mantra, the two syllables *ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*.
This is known as the *saṃpuṭa* mantra of Bhīḍā, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
One should first recite the seed-syllable of Kuru and at the end of the Viśva-mantra recite the Praṇava;
this is the method for forming the "encasement" (saṃpuṭa) of the Kālarātri-mantra.
O Maheśvarī, one should recite "Ramā" at the end and "Kūrca" at the beginning;
this, I have declared, is the "encasement" (saṃpuṭa) for the root mantra of Bhavānī.
O Dear One, one should place the *tāra* (om) at the beginning and recite the *tāra* at the end;
O Goddess, this "encasement" (*saṃpuṭa*) has been described for the mantra of Śrī Vajrayoginī. 25.
One should first recite the seed-syllable of Maṭha and then recite the lotus at the end of the mantra;
this mantra of Dhūmravārāhī, known as Saṃpuṭa, has been proclaimed by me. (26)
One should first recite the Kāmarāja mantra and at the end recite the Vāgbhava mantra;
this "encasement" (saṃpuṭa) for the Siddhalakṣmī mantra has been described by me.
O Goddess, one should first recite *spṛhām* and then recite *paṅkajam* at the edge of the forest;
this mantra is known as *saṃpuṭa* for the mantra of Kulavāgīśvarī. (28)
One should first recite the Kāmarāja [mantra] and then recite the entire Padmāvatī-mantra at the end of the forest; this is known as the Saṃpuṭa [method]. || 29 ||
One should recite the *praṇava* at the beginning and the lotus (*paṅkaja*) at the end of the snare;
this is the mantra known as "encapsulation" (*saṃpuṭa*) for the root-mantra of Kubjikā. (30)
O Great Goddess, one should recite "maṭha" at the beginning and "śiva" between the two "ṭha"s;
this is described by me as the "encased" (saṃpuṭa) mantra of Gaurī.
One should recite the *kūṭa* at the end of the *viśva*, and recite the *śara* at the beginning of the *kūṭa*;
this is the mantra known as *saṃpuṭa* for the root-mantra of Khecarī. (32)
One should recite the *kūrca* mantra at the beginning of the *mantra*, and recite the horse (*turaga*) at the end of the forest (*vana*).
This encapsulation (*saṃpuṭa*) of the *mantra* of Nīlasarasvatī has been described by me. (33)
O Goddess, the first is Vāgbhava, followed by the Praṇava at the edge of the two Ṭha-s;
this is the mantra of the Parāśakti-mantra that serves as the cause for encapsulation (saṃpuṭa).
O Goddess worshipped by the Kula, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, I shall now describe the *saṃpuṭa*—common to all—the mantras of Śiva which are unbarred. (35)
One should recite the two *tāra*s (oṃ) at the beginning, the name in the middle, and *parā* at the end;
this mantra is known as the "enclosure" (*saṃpuṭa*) for all Śaiva mantras. (36)
One should recite "Tāram" (Om) in the middle and "Hṛjjaṃ" (Namaḥ) at the end, with the two words "Pālaya" placed at the beginning;
this is described by me as the "encased" (saṃpuṭa) form of the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra.
O Great Goddess, the wise one should recite "Viśva" at the beginning and "Śakti" at the end;
this mantra is known as the "encasement" (saṃpuṭa) of the Amṛteśvara mantra. (38)
Place the *praṇava* (oṃ) at the beginning of the two parts and place the pair again at the end;
O Śivā, this mantra of Vaṭuka is declared by me to be known as "encased" (*saṃpuṭa*).
Having twice uttered the syllable "hari," followed by the name in the middle and then the final syllable;
this mantra of Nīlakaṇṭha, called "encased" (saṃpuṭa), has been proclaimed by me.
The best of practitioners should recite "tāra" at the end and "parā" at the beginning;
this is known as the *saṃpuṭa* method for the Sadyojāta mantra. (41)
Three *parā*s at the end of *śiva* and three *śiva*s at the end of the *praṇava*—
this is the mantra of Mahāgaṇapati that functions as a *saṃpuṭa*. (42)
O Dear One, one should recite the seed-syllable of the universe at the beginning and recite the universe at the end;
this is the mantra of the god Aghora known as the "encased" (saṃpuṭa). 43.
O Great Goddess, one should recite the *kūṭa* at the beginning and the *vāgbhava* at the end;
this is the mantra known as *saṃpuṭa* for the Śrī Kāmeśvara mantra. (44)
O Kulanāyikā, among these Śaiva mantras as well,
the mantra of Mahākāla is free from obstacles and devoid of defects.
Now, O Supreme Goddess, out of a desire for the welfare of practitioners, I shall declare the *saṃpuṭa* mantras of those Vaiṣṇava mantras. (46)
One should recite "Kamalā" at the end of the name and the Praṇava at the end of "Viśva";
this is the mantra of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa known as Saṃpuṭa.
O Great Goddess, one should recite "Hara" at the beginning and the two instances of "Ṭha" at the end, followed by "Ramā";
this is the mantra known as *saṃpuṭa* for the Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa mantra. (48)
O Goddess worshipped by the universe, one should first recite "Tāra" at the end;
this mantra of the root-mantra of Śrī Viṣṇu is known as "saṃpuṭa. (49)
O Goddess, one should first recite the seed-syllable of Smara (Klīm) and likewise at the end;
this mantra of the Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha mantra is known as "saṃpuṭa" (encased).
O Goddess, one should first recite "viśvam" before the name of Manu and then recite the entire mantra of Lakṣmī-Varāha; this is known as the *saṃpuṭa* (encasement) method.
O Goddess, one should first recite "sarojam" and at the end of the forest [of the mantra] recite "ramām";
this is the mantra for Jāmadagnya Manu that acts as an encapsulator (saṃpuṭakāraka). || 52 ||
The best of practitioners should recite the *tāra* at the end and the *vana* at the beginning;
this is known as the *saṃpuṭa* method for the mantra of Śrī Sītārāma.
O Goddess of the gods, at the end of *viśva*, one should first recite the *māyā-yuga*.
(p. 47) This mantra of the *Śrī-Janārdana-mantra* is known as the *saṃpuṭa*. 54.
The leader of practitioners should recite [the mantra] at the beginning and at the end with *parā*;
this is the mantra that forms the *saṃpuṭa* for the Viśvaksena-mantra. (55)
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, one should recite the mantra of Vāṇī at the beginning and that of Lakṣmī at the end;
this is known as the *saṃpuṭa* (encasement) of the Śrī-Vāsudeva mantra.
Thus, this entire essence of mantra, the secret, the supreme reality, has been determined out of affection for you; it must be guarded by those who seek liberation.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Exposition of the Method of the *Saṃpuṭa*, in the *Śrīrudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrīdevīrahasya*.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, O Goddess, I shall describe the practice of *puraścaraṇa*,
by the mere accomplishment of which a mantra becomes a bestower of success (*siddhi*).
Just as a living being deprived of life is incapable of performing any action, so too a mantra devoid of *puraścaraṇa* does not bestow success. || 2 ||
O Maheśvarī, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, or half of that;
one should perform it up to the limit of one hundred thousand, but never less than that.
In a banyan tree, a forest, a cremation ground, an empty house, or at a crossroads;
even at midnight or at midday, one should begin the *puraścaraṇa* rite. (4)
O Maheśvarī, on an auspicious day, under a favorable constellation, and at a propitious moment,
one should first worship one’s own guru and then commence the *puraścaryā*.
Having received the command of the Guru and bathed, the wise one should prepare the altar;
it should be square, extending one cubit on each side, located in the northeast direction.
There, O Great Goddess, having smeared it with vermilion and the eight fragrant substances,
one should first draw a circle consisting of a dot, a triangle, and a hexagon.
O Daughter of the Mountain,
I have described this yantra for the preliminary rites (puraścaryā), which possesses eight petals, is enriched by twelve [spokes], and is adorned with nine chambers.
It is common to all and should be worshipped by practitioners who perceive reality:
Indra, Agni, Yama, Māṃsāda, Varuṇa, Anila, and Vittada.

O Goddess, those who possess their lords, along with the seed-syllables of La, Ra, Ya, Ṭa, Kṣa, Bha, Ya, Sa, and Ha, together with their respective weapons, are to be worshipped in the circle of the abode of the Earth. 10.
O Goddess, Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, Raudrī, Kaumārī, Nārasiṃhikā, Vārāhī, Caṇḍikā, and Aparājitā are to be worshipped. 11.
Together with Bhairava, they reside on the eight petals in counter-clockwise order for those seeking liberation:
Pārvatī, Kubjikā, Durgā, Cāmuṇḍā, and Nīlatāriṇī. (12)
Kātyāyanī is to be worshipped by the most eminent in the hexagons;
and the goddess Gaṅgā and Yamunā, as well as Sarasvatī, are to be worshipped in the triangles.
And within the Bindu, the practitioner’s chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), together with Śiva,
should be worshipped by the practitioners with the root mantra, using perfumes, water for honor (arghya), flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth.
There, O Maheśvarī, the practitioner of mantra should place the yantra of his chosen deity within that drop (bindu),
having established four water-pots at the corners of the altar.
O Goddess, having consecrated barley grains with the root mantra, the practitioner should sow them;
he should worship them in this manner according to the sequence of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśa. (16)
O Goddess of the Gods, one should likewise perform the daily worship of Gaṇeśa, Bhāratī, Durgā, and Kṣetrapāla within the jars using their respective root mantras.
O Goddess, one should perform the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) in front of that;
having first worshipped the Śrīcakra, the wise practitioner should then perform the recitation (japa). || 18 ||
For the sake of attaining success in the mantra, one who is tranquil should abandon hypocrisy as well as greed;
the practitioner of the mantra, observing the vow of celibacy, should meditate upon the Goddess who bestows boons. (19)

O Great Goddess, one who has attained self-control should recite the root mantra one hundred thousand times with discipline and concentration, subsisting on sacrificial food; thereafter, his mantra will become perfected.
Having recited the king of mantras, O Goddess, the practitioner of mantra should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with one-tenth of that number;
he should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with one-tenth of that, and the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) with one-tenth of that.
One should feed [the brahmins] with a tenth part of that [number]; then the perfection of the mantra will certainly occur.
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired in another manner.
O Śivā, at night, the practitioner of mantra should bring another’s wife— whether she be young, dark-complexioned, or afflicted by passion— and worship her according to the prescribed ritual.
Naked, with disheveled hair, steadfast, and intent upon drinking honey-wine,
he should, while closely embracing the Śakti at her chest, recite the root mantra according to the prescribed rule.
When one hundred thousand recitations have been consecrated by means of a tenth-part of fire-oblations and libations,
the accomplishment of the mantra will be attained for him, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Alternatively, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is desired in another manner:
on the day of the festival celebrating the birth of a son, in the house of the maternity chamber.
The practitioner of mantras should recite his own root-mantra for a period of ten days;
having consecrated the mantra with its tenth part, the mantra will become perfected. (27)
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired in another manner:
on the first day of impurity following a death, the practitioner should perform the recitation (*japa*). (28)
On the eleventh day, the wise one, having become self-controlled by day and a hero by night in accordance with reality, should perform the consecrated mantra.
Through action, mind, or speech, the mantra becomes a wish-fulfilling tree;
or else, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired in another manner.
Beginning from sunrise until the next sunrise, by reciting [the mantra] for that duration, the mantra becomes free from obstacles and like a wish-fulfilling tree. || 31 ||
Alternatively, another method for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is desired:
O Maheśvarī, one should recite the mantra at the time of a solar eclipse.
Having performed the recitation and the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites, the perfection of the mantra will certainly be attained;
or else, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is desired by another method.
O Goddess of the gods, during a lunar eclipse, one should recite the root mantra according to the prescribed rite;
thus consecrated by its tenth part, the mantra becomes a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) in an instant.

He who lacks the capacity for recitation should instead recite the Pañcaratneśvarī; that practitioner obtains the fruit of the preliminary rite consisting of one hundred thousand recitations of each syllable. || 35 ||
This is indeed the reality of mantras—the essence of essences, higher than the highest;
it is ineffable, secret, O Īśānī, and must be guarded by those seeking liberation. (36)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for Puraścaryā," in the Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra, within the Śrī Devī Rahasya.
p. 51) Now begins the eleventh chapter.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, O Goddess, I shall declare the supreme fruit of *puraścaryā*,
by attaining which, O Goddess, even a mortal practitioner may obtain immortality.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, you are the knower of reality and have reached the further shore of all the Agamas;
O All-pervading Lord, tell me today the procedure for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) of the fire-oblation (homa).
Śrī Bhairava said:

Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, O Goddess, the practitioner who seeks to master the mantra should go to a secluded place and perform a fire sacrifice (homa) consisting of one-tenth that number.
On an auspicious day and under a favorable lunar mansion, the practitioner, having gathered the materials for the fire sacrifice, should proceed to the worship of Bhairava with a disciplined mind.
There, O Goddess of the Gods, having established the cremation ground on one side, both in front and behind, one should draw the supreme Śrīcakra in the northeastern direction.
Having worshipped that Śrīcakra according to the prescribed rite with the root mantra,
one should then recite the perfected mantra one hundred and eight times.
In the eastern direction, one should dig a triangular pit from a mechanical device;
it should be one cubit in width and one cubit in depth.
In this pit, one should draw a diagram consisting of a triangle adorned with a central point,
a hexagon, an eight-petaled lotus, three concentric circles, and marked by an enclosure of the earth.
Thereafter, O Goddess Pārvatī, one should perform the worship of the Kuṇḍacakra according to the prescribed rule,
by which the practitioner becomes initiated.
Gaṇeśa, Dharma, Varuṇa, and likewise Kubera—
these four gatekeepers are to be worshipped at the four doors. (10)
Māyā, Mohinī, Mattā, Mādhavī, Vahnivallabhā,
Vartulī, Vīrasū, and Vāmā— these are to be worshipped, residing upon the eight petals.
Ambālikā, Ambā, Bagalā, Chinnashirshāmbikā, and Bhagā—
these are to be worshipped in the center of the hexagon within the Kuṇḍacakra, O Maheśvarī.
O Śivā, one should worship the fire Vaiśvānara and the fire Agni within the triangle;
one should worship the goddess Svāhā in the bindu and Jātavedas [therein].
O Goddess of the gods, [one should worship] Agni with the root mantra; then the ten kalās of fire.
O Maheśvarī, [the mantra for these is]: Tāra (Om), Vahni (Ra), Śiva (H), Abdhi (La), Hṛjja (Ha), and Śakti (Kṣa).
One should speak of Agni Vaiśvānara; one should address him as Jaṭābhāra; as Bhāsvara; as Trinetra; and one should utter the word Jvālāmukha. (15)
One should say "prajvaleti" for the pair [of syllables], and one should speak "jātavedasi";
one should speak the two "ṭha"s at the end—this is the mantra beloved by Agni.
With this root mantra,
one should worship the fire-wheel with perfumes, unbroken grains, flowers, incense, lamps, and other offerings.
O Goddess of the Gods, having worshipped there the Śrīcakra consisting of nine triangles with offerings of food, water for sipping, and well-scented betel leaves; || 18 ||
Then one should worship the Bhūtas who are the Terrifiers of the Directions with flowers;
thereafter, O Goddess Kuleśvarī, one should churn the fire into the circle of the sacrificial pit.
O Śivā, having invoked the fire into the *bindu*, one should kindle it with the root mantra;
then, having inflamed the fire with the root mantra, one should prostrate with the *vahni-mudrā*.
Then, O Pārvatī, one should offer oblations into the fire with sixteen recitations of the root mantra,
and subsequently offer clarified butter in one hundred and eight repetitions.
O Goddess, one should offer oblations with milk-rice, grapes, agallochum, and flowers, along with candied sugar, granulated sugar, and camphor, marked with musk and realgar. (22)
Then, O Śivā, having recited the Great Vidyā, one should worship the practitioners—five, or nine, or eleven, O Goddess, O Śivā. (23)
Those who are of noble birth, righteous, pure, whether initiated or uninitiated, firm in their vows, of auspicious conduct, and likewise devoted to the Goddess. (24)
O Girijā, having duly honored there the Vaiṣṇavas and Śaivas who are devoted to their gurus, and having recognized them as being like Bhairava himself, [he should proceed]. (25)

Having worshipped them, O Great Goddess, with water for the feet, the arghya offering, honey-mixture, and the like, as well as with perfumes, unbroken grains, and beautiful flowers, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) consisting of a tenth part [of the recitation].
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Knower of Tantra, Supreme Lord, you ought to dispel my doubt regarding the worship of the Kula practitioner. (27)
In that ritual of worship, O Lord, are all the best of the twice-born to be honored?
Or rather, are Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras? Tell me in detail. (28)
The illustrious Bhairava said: When the Bhairava Tantra is active, all castes are the best of the twice-born;
when the Bhairava Tantra has ceased, all castes remain distinct from one another.
O best of the twice-born, this tradition has been declared for this Śiva-cakra at all times; there is no requirement for preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) or formal worship (arcā) therein.
But there was one virtuous Kṣatriya, a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu, firm in his vows, of auspicious conduct, well-born, and a worshiper of Śiva. || 31 ||
One who is empowered by Śakti and supremely devoted is said to belong to the Kula-cakra;
having performed the fire-oblation (homa) there, he should respectfully present the food offering (naivedya).
O Goddess, a heroic Kṣatriya endowed with devotion and faith should worship the Brāhmaṇas who belong to the family circle and are the best of practitioners. (33)

O Śivā, [one should worship] with perfumes, unbroken grains, and beautiful flowers, as well as incense, lamps, and so forth, along with offerings of food, water for rinsing the mouth, and various kinds of edibles, foods, and delicacies to be licked.
O Goddess, having gratified the practitioners while being served by supreme bliss, the practitioner [should seek] a Kṣatriya hero who is a donor and a servant of heroes. (35)
O Goddess, one should cause [the disciple] to grow with blessings and bow down to Tripurāmbikā;
those heroes who have entered the Kula-cakra and are worshippers of the Kula-cakra [should do the same]. 36.
O Great Goddess, all those who belong to the Kula go swiftly to the abode of the Kula;
even a Kṣatriya, O Great Goddess, who knows the meaning of the Kula, [attains it] along with the assemblies of the Kula.
Completely liberated from all sins and endowed with all perfections, having attained prosperity in this world and enjoyed pleasures as desired; || 38 ||

O Supreme Goddess, having performed the fire-oblation (homa) in this manner for the sake of attaining the fruit of recitation (japa), the knower of mantras shall go to the state of a goddess after death in the next world. (39)
O Goddess, he enjoys the fruit of a hundred thousand recitations of the syllables;
in this way, the Kaulika obtains the fruit of a hundred thousand recitations of the syllables. (40)
All who were present there, having bowed to Bhairava situated in the cremation ground,
dismissed the Goddess together with Śiva by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā* into the auspicious [source].
All those excellent practitioners shall become partakers of the [divine] family.
O Goddess of gods, this secret has been declared by me to you out of devotion. It is not to be revealed and must not be given away; such is the command of the Supreme Lord. 42.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for Puraścaryā and Homa," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrī Devī Rahasya*.
p. 55) Now begins the twelfth chapter.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the secret, the supreme essence of all, the chapter named "The Determination of the Śrīcakra," which is difficult even for the gods to obtain. 1.
Out of supreme affection for the goddesses, I shall describe the extraction of the yantra;
it must not be told to just anyone, but especially kept secret.
O Maheśvarī, there shall be thirty-three crores of gods,
and likewise, O Goddess, thirty-three crores of goddesses.
Among them, O Great Goddess, thirty-three deities are the principal ones;
hear now their supreme mantras, which were mentioned previously.
Now, O Maheśvarī, out of affection for you, I shall describe the Bālā-yantra,
O Goddess, which accomplishes all aims and fulfills all hopes.

This wheel of Bālā and the others, which removes all suffering and is saluted by Śiva, Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu, has been described by me to you; it consists of three earth-dwellings adorned with a drop (bindu), a triangle, a hexagon, an eight-petaled lotus, and three circles.
Now, I shall describe the extraction of the yantra of Tripurabhairavī,
which is enriched with the essence of all the Agamas and is capable of rescuing one from calamity.
A point, a triangle, a serpent-cornered [figure], a ten-spoked [wheel], adorned with a circle, an eight-petaled [lotus], and a sixteen-petaled [lotus].
The three circles and the three abodes of the earth—thus has the Śrīcakra of Bhairavī been described to you. (8)
Now, O Goddess, I shall declare the determination of the Śrīcakra of Tripurasundarī,
which brings about the subjugation of all and sets in motion all supernatural powers (siddhis).

The Tripuṭa [maṇḍala] is empty in the center, joined with the fire-corner (southeast), marked by the directions, the elephants (the eight points), and the corners; it possesses twenty spokes interspersed with mantras, adorned with sixteen auspicious petals like elephant-ears, endowed with three perfect circles, and marked by the house of the earth (the square).
In the Kali age, the Śrīcakra shines forth, bestowing desired fruits through devotion.

The Śrīcakra of the Supreme Deity is said to consist of a point, a triangle, an eight-cornered figure, two sets of ten-cornered figures, a fourteen-cornered figure, a sixteen-petaled lotus, three circles, and three abodes of the Earth.
Now I shall describe to you the extraction of the yantra of Kālikā,
which bestows the accomplishment of all aims in this world and fulfills every desire.

May this Śyāmāyantra be victorious: a void situated within a triangle, above which is a triangle joined with an autumnal (three-sided) corner, then a hexagon, O Goddess, a circle, and an eight-petaled lotus;
outside that, three circles, and it is endowed with the terrestrial realm.
The crushing of the category of the fear of death. || 13 ||
Then, O Goddess, out of compassion, I shall describe to you the extraction of the yantra of Bhadrakālī, which is dear to the gods and bestows all eloquence. 14.

May this Yantra be victorious— adorned in its center with the excellent Fourth (Turya) joined with the circle of Space (Kha), marked by twice seven (fourteen) syllables, possessing two sets of four spokes,
beautified by rows of four-petaled lotuses multiplied fourfold,
embellished by three perfect circles, and illuminated externally by three enclosures of the Earth (Ila).
It bestows desired fruits and is dear to the illustrious Bhadrakālī. || 15 ||
Now, O Goddess of gods, out of affection for you, I shall explain the yantra of Mātaṅgī as determined in the Tantra; one should not reveal it elsewhere. (16)

A bindu, a triangle, an eight-cornered figure, a circle, then a lotus with eight petals and three circles, and a square enclosure with a single line of fire—O Pārvatī, this is declared to be the Mātaṅginī yantra. (17)
Then, O Great Goddess, out of love and devotion, I shall describe to you the extraction of the yantra of Bhuvaneśvarī; it must not be disclosed even by high-souled ones.
The *bindu* is a triangle joined with six corners, adorned with a circle and embellished by eight petals;
it is marked by three circles of digits and the abode of the earth.
This Śrīcakra is beloved by Bhuvaneśvarī. || 19 ||
Now, O Goddess, I shall describe the unsurpassed extraction of the yantra of Tārā, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; O Maheśvarī, keep it secret. (20)

The dot (bindu), the triangle, the hexagon, the circle, as well as the eight-spoked [wheel], the lotus, the triple circle, and the enclosure of the earth—this is the yantra of the playful abode of Ekajaṭā as taught by me. (21)
Now, out of affection for you, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed extraction of the yantra of Chinnamastā; it must not be spoken by those seeking liberation.

The Bindu, the inner triangle, the outer triangle, the upward-pointing triangle, and the auspicious circular orb joined with the eight-petaled lotus—this is the Śrīcakra, the abode of the Earth, belonging to the Supreme Deity. || 23 ||

Now, O Maheśvarī, I shall explain to you the extraction of the yantra of the goddess Sumukhī, which is the very essence of all essences; it must not be given away by those who discourse upon Brahman. (24)
O Pārvatī, one should draw a *bindu* located in the corner above the *ananta*, a circle marked by corners shaped like arrows,
adorned with the petals of a serpent, and further marked by sixteen spokes;
it should be joined with three excellent circles and marked by a square enclosure.
May the Śrīcakra, beloved by Sumukhī and bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, be victorious! || 25 ||
Now, O Maheśvarī, I shall declare to you the reality of the extraction of the Yantra of Sarasvatī, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon the Kaulikas. (26)
First a triangle with a bindu, then a hexagon with a circle; then an eight-petaled lotus with three circles;
and finally the abode of the Earth, radiant with lines of fire—these are yours.
For I have indeed stated that this is the Sārasvata Yantra. || 27 ||
Now, O Goddess, I shall describe to you the Yantrarāja belonging to Annapūrṇā, which deludes all beings and is the sole means for attaining all enjoyments. (28)
A triangle, a hexagon, a triangle, a triangle,
a triangle, a triangle, and indeed a circle;
then [the design] adorned with serpent-leaves and a circle of fire.
And the Dharāmaṇḍira [temple] and the Annapūrṇeṣṭacakra. || 29 ||
Now, O Śivā, I shall describe the Yantra of Mahālakṣmī, which is higher than the highest;
by worshipping it, I attained that supreme state which is difficult to reach. (30)
The letter Kha, along with Va, Hni, and Āra, is stainless; it is circular and beautiful on the outside,
with serpent-petals externally, and illuminated by three circles shining with the sound of Kalā.

This supreme Śrīcakra, adorned with three earth-dwellings (bhūgeha), has been determined by me for you; it bestows the ultimate truth, is dear to Mahālakṣmī, and grants spiritual accomplishments (siddhi). || 31 ||
O Great Goddess, I shall proclaim the extraction of the yantra which brings auspiciousness to practitioners; it belongs to Śārikā and is filled with the movements of the abode of Līlā. (32)
The mandala consists of a triangle, an eight-cornered figure, a perfect circle, a shining eight-petaled lotus, a circle with sixteen petals,
and a square enclosure for the earth, adorned by the fires, the sun, and the moon.
This yantra is declared to be the abode of Śilā. || 33 ||
O Great Goddess, I shall now describe the extraction of the yantra of Śāradā;
it is a wheel that accomplishes all aims and fulfills all desires. (34)
In the center is the *bindu*, outside of which there should be a triangle; then a hexagon joined with a circle and an eight-petaled lotus;
[and finally] a circular form with sixteen spokes and three circles.
This is the Śāradāyantra, which is the "earth-house" (bhūgeha). || 35 ||
Now I shall declare to you the extraction of the yantra, which is very difficult to obtain—the entire essence of the reality of Indrākṣī, hidden throughout the three worlds. (36)

This Jayacakra is victorious; it is composed of a Bindu, a triangle, a hexagon, another hexagon joined with a six-cornered figure, a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, and a sixteen-petaled lotus, all intermingled; it has the form of a square, is colored like fire and the luster of the moon, and is most dear to the two eyes of Indra.
Now, O Goddess, I shall describe to you the extraction of the Yantra of Bagalāmukhī, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments and must be guarded with great effort. (38)
The Śrīcakra of Bagalāmukhī consists of a Bindu, a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, an octagon, a circle adorned with sixteen spokes, three circles, and three enclosures of the earth. || 39 ||
Now, out of supreme affection, I shall describe to you the unsurpassed extraction of the Great Turya Yantra, which accomplishes all desired goals. (40)
The drop (bindu), the triangle joined with nine wombs (yonis), adorned with circles, the eight-petaled lotus, and the triple circle;
this wheel, praised by the flames of fire, is taught as the abode of the Fourth (turya) within the house of earth. (41)
I shall now proclaim the extraction of the yantra, which fulfills all desires, O Maheśvarī;
it is the wheel that accomplishes all aims and likewise deludes all beings.
The point, the triangle, the hexagon, adorned with a circle and eight petals, three circles, and the abode of the Earth—this is declared to be the Śrīcakra of Rājñī. (43)
Now, O Maheśvarī, I shall describe the supreme yantra of Jvālāmukhī, which is the sole abode of all principles and the bestower of all desires. (44)
O Goddess, having drawn a void in the center and above it a triangle, one should then draw below that a trident, and outside of it a lotus with eight petals,
a circle, an octagon, and twice again a lotus, a triangle, a circle, and a square.
O Great Goddess, may this wheel of Jvālāmukhī be victorious in the world! 45.
Now, O Goddess of the Gods, I shall describe the unsurpassed Bhīḍāyantra (or Bheḍāyantra), which is rich with the secrets of all the Āgamas and bestows all eloquence. (46)
A dot, a triangle, a quadrilateral mixed with a triangle, a perfect circle, and an octagon;
outside of that, a sixteen-spoked wheel and three circles enriched with three earth-pavilions—this Bhīḍāyantra shall bestow all accomplishments. || 47 ||
Now, O Goddess of gods, I shall describe the unsurpassed extraction of the yantra of Kālarātri, which is the unique elixir for the practice of supreme bliss. (48)

O Daughter of the Mountain, this yantra— consisting of a drop (bindu), a triangle, a six-cornered figure, a well-rounded circle, a serpent-leaf (eight-petaled lotus), a large circle shining with the spokes of the digits (sixteen-petaled lotus), and three earth-pavilions— is the abode of the illustrious Kālarātri and bestows the supreme goal.
Now I shall declare to you the supreme yantra of Bhavānī,
which is rich with the secrets of the root mantra and bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
The Bindu, the triangle, the hexagon, the circle, and that which is enriched with the petals of the serpent’s digits;
three circles and three lotus-seats—this is the Śrīcakra, the station of bliss belonging to Bhavānī.
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the King of Yantras, which is very difficult to obtain, and which increases all happiness for the goddess Śrī Vajrayoginī. (52)

O Great Goddess, this is the Yantra of the Abode of Earth (Dharāgṛha), consisting of a Bindu, a triangle, and externally a hexagon, a circle, an eight-sided figure, a sun-circle (sixteen-sided figure), and another circle; it is the Yoginī marked by the word "Śrīvajra."
Now I shall describe the unsurpassed extraction of the yantra of Vārāhī, which is the most auspicious of all auspicious things and brings welfare to practitioners. (54)
A triangle with a bindu, then another triangle, and then one should form a triangle seven times;
a lotus of eight petals marked by three circles—this is the earth-abode yantra belonging to Varāheśvarī.
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the extraction of the yantra of Siddhalakṣmī, which is very difficult to obtain, which pacifies all enemies, and fulfills all desires. (56)

Adorned with a bindu, a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and an eight-petaled lotus, and featuring three circles and an enclosure of the earth—this is the yantra of Siddhalakṣmī as remembered by me. (57)
Now I shall describe the supreme yantra, which is dear to Kula-Vāgīśvarī;
it bestows the desired objects upon practitioners, is divine, and is the abode of the essence of the highest state. (58)
A triangle with a bindu, a five-pointed star, a circle, then adorned with serpent-leaves, a sixteen-spoked wheel,
three circles, the abode of Earth, and the seat of the Lotus— this well-constructed diagram is declared to belong to Vāgīśvarī. (59)
Now, O Goddess of gods, I shall describe the divine yantra beloved of Padmāvatī, which accomplishes all aims and fulfills every desire. || 60 ||

The Bindu, the Triangle, the Octagon, the Circle, the Naga-leaf, and so forth, up to the sixteen petals and the Fire-circle—this triple-layered mandala of the earth bestows all desired objects; this is the Jayacakra, most dear to Padmavati.
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the supreme Yantra of Kubjika.
And this secret of all the gods must be kept hidden, especially so.
The Bindu, the Triangle, the hexagon, then the circle, the eight-petaled lotus, and the solar circle;
this Śrī Kubjikā Yantra, which contains all secrets within its womb, has been described by me as the abode of the Earth. 63.
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the Gaurī-yantra, which is very difficult to obtain;
it bestows all sovereignty and pacifies all obstacles, O Śivā. (64)
In the center is a triangle joined with [the letters] *ka* and *kha*, followed by a hexagon, a circle, and likewise a circle with eight petals and three fires;
this excellent wheel, which is the abode of the earth and consists of the reality cherished in the Kaula lineages, has indeed been described as belonging to Gaurī.
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the supreme Khecarīyantra,
which is difficult for yogins to attain and is the cause of the bliss of yogic practice. (66)
A dot, a triangle, a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, a fire-circle (triangle), and an earth-house—this, I have described, is the supreme Khecarī Yantra. 67.
Now, O Śivā, I shall describe the extraction of the yantra of Nīlasarasvatī,
which bestows both supernatural powers and worldly enjoyments upon those established in the Mahācīna region.
From that, a Bindu; then a hexagon joined with fire-spokes; then a circle; then a circle with eight petals and fire-spokes;
and the abode of Earth (a square) with fire-fingers—this is the supreme Yantra of Nīlasarasvatī, worthy of praise. (69)
Now I shall describe the extraction of the yantra of the Goddess, the Supreme Śakti, which bestows all prosperity, is divine, and grants all sovereign powers. (70)
The drop (bindu), the triangle, the circle, the eight-petaled lotus, the fire-triangle, the circle, and the enclosure of the earth—
this is the yantra of the Supreme Power (Parā-śakti) as it has been remembered by me.
Then, O Īśānī, I shall describe the supreme yantra of Śiva, which is common to all and the sole bestower of every desired object. (72)
This triple-layered earth-mansion, consisting of a point, a triangle, an eight-cornered figure, a ten-cornered figure, a circle, an eight-cornered figure, a sixteen-petaled lotus, and a fire-circle,
is the beginningless Śaiva yantra that grants the supreme goal and is common throughout the world. (73)
Then, O Goddess, I shall describe to you the King of Yantras belonging to Viṣṇu, which is common to all in the world and bestows auspiciousness upon the Vaiṣṇavas. (74)

O Bhavānī, may this true and universal yantra, the abode of the supreme Vaiṣṇava, consisting of a point, a triangle, an eight-petaled lotus, a perfect circle, a serpent-leaf pattern, and adorned with a sixteen-petaled lotus within a circular orb, and containing the temple of the earth, be victorious! 75.
(64) O Supreme Goddess, for all mantras belonging to Śiva,
the Guru is Aghora; I shall now describe his unsurpassed yantra.
A triangle with a dot, a five-pointed star with its points, then an eight-petaled lotus with a circle and a filigree;
illuminated by four square enclosures and a single line of fire, this is the ever-shining yantra of the god Aghora.
O Maheśvarī, among all the Vaiṣṇava mantras, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is the most excellent; I shall now describe its yantra.
The bindu, the triangle, the eight-sided figure, adorned with circles and eight petals, the sixteen-spoked wheel, the sun-circle, and beautified by the enclosure of the earth. || 79 ||
This Śrīcakra of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa bestows the supreme goal;
thus, this most wonderful secret of all the gods has been declared by me to you. It must be guarded like one's own private parts. (80)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Elevation of the Yantra," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrī Devī Rahasya*.
(p. 65) Now, [the next section begins].
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the secret that fulfills all desires.
The supreme, general procedure for the worship of the Yantra-dhāraṇa.
O Maheśvarī, O Pārvatī, without the armor and without the thousand names,
there is no success for the practitioner, even for Bhairava himself.
If a practitioner recites the mantra while devoid of wearing the yantra,
that mantra, even if recited ten million times, shall become fruitless for him.
O Maheśvarī, on an auspicious day, under an auspicious lunar mansion and an auspicious weekday,
having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, one should bathe and meditate upon one’s own Guru.
Having meditated upon the deity together with Śiva in a secluded place well-perfumed with incense,
one should draw the yantra with the eight fragrances, encircled by the root mantra.
Outside of that, one should write the divine armor (kavaca) as well as the Thousand Names (nāmasahasraka) with a golden pen upon a beautiful birch-bark leaf (bhūrjapatra).
O Dear One, I shall proclaim the eightfold incense, a supreme secret; it must never be spoken to one who is not a devotee of the God, nor to anyone who is not a disciple.
Svayaṃbhūkusuma, that which arises from the kuṇḍa and the gola, rocanā, aguru, camphor, musk, liquor, and sandalwood from the Malaya mountains.
Furthermore, I shall declare to you the means of preparing perfumes that grant success,
which brings auspiciousness to the Vaiṣṇavas, the Śaivas, and the Śāktas.

Saffron from Kashmir, *gorocana*, betel nut and the like, musk, *rudraja*, *mūrvā*, *pūtāsaka*, and sandalwood—this is the "Eightfold Incense" (*gandhāṣṭaka*), beloved by Bhairava and Bhairavī. (p. 66)
Bhairavī, the beloved of Bhairava. || 10 ||

Having applied the eight perfumes with its own root mantra, the Kula practitioner, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) along with the rishi-mantra and other rites, should meditate upon the Goddess seated upon the lap of Śiva.
One should write one's own divine [form] there, and outside of that, by means of the root mantra;
the practitioner of mantra should write the Mātṛkā, and outside of that, he should write the armor (kavaca).
Likewise, having written the Thousand Names on a birch-bark leaf,
one should wrap it with white thread, followed by yellow and blue threads.
O Supreme Goddess, having wrapped it with lac of a color resembling the radiance of the meditation upon one's own chosen deity,
one should then wrap it with gold.
Then, having meditated upon the supreme, divine pill in the form of the Goddess,
one should place it within the bindu of the Śiva-yantra while holding the yantra.
I shall describe to you, O worshipper of the practitioner, the holding of the yantra; for the benefit of the Kaulikas, it must be kept especially secret. (16)
The dot, the triangle, the hexagon, the six-cornered figure, the eight-petalled lotus, the three circles, and the square—the abode of the earth—constitute the yantra for wearing the yantra. || 17 ||
O Goddess, O Śivā, one should draw the limbs of dissolution with vermilion and worship them;
by the mere act of worshipping this, the practitioner of mantra attains the state of Bhairava. (18)
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, Dharmarāja, Varuṇa, and Kubera at the four gates, these four should be honored as the gatekeepers. || 19 ||
Asitāṅga, Kālāgni, Saṃhāra, Rurubhairava, Karāla, Vikarāla, Supteśa, and Unmattabhairava. (20)
O Pārvatī, having worshipped the eight Bhairavas upon the eight petals,
one should worship Durgā, Caṇḍī, Sumukhī, Śivādūtī, Śivā, and Jayā.
Outside, on the hexagon, these should be worshipped by the practitioners with the root mantra:
Tārā, Tāriṇī, Turyā, Bagalā, and likewise Vijayā. (22)
The most excellent practitioner should worship Chinnamastā within the six corners;
O Maheśvarī, Bhavānī, Kubjikā, and Gaurī are to be worshipped in the triangle. (23)
The best of Kaulas [should worship] his chosen deity together with Śiva within the *bindu*,
using perfumes, unbroken grains, flowers, incense, lamps, and other offerings.
O Great Goddess, one should offer oblations of food, water for sipping, and well-scented betel leaves there at the Bindu, according to one's own means. (25)
For the pleasure of the deities, one should give as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) objects made of gold, silver, pearls, gems, copper, and so forth, and also to the preceptor.
There, O Kuleśvarī, the best of practitioners himself should bathe the divine pill, which has the form of the Goddess, with the five nectars and the five products of the cow.
Having established the pill, the mantra-practitioner should then place it within the [central] drop;
having offered the vital breaths, the practitioner should display the mudrās beginning with the invocation (āvāhana). || 28 ||
One should present there everything, such as water for the feet, the arghya offering, and the honey-mixture;
one should contemplate her as having the form of the deity and worship her as one would the king of yantras.
Having worshipped the divine pill,
the practitioner should recite the root mantra before it as much as possible, using a rosary made of the fingers.
One should recite the armor, the thousand names of the mantra, and the hymn consisting of mantra right there, O Goddess; one should worship the wheel of mantras.
O Goddess, together with those practitioners, one should perform the salutation to the vessel;
having gratified them with devotion, the wise one should hold the deity within the heart.
Having dismissed the Goddess together with Śiva, one should bow with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*.
Or, one should wear the boon-granting pill upon the head or on the arm. (33)
The practitioner who thus bears this yantra and recites the mantra shall become visibly liberated from the fear of worldly existence and become like Bhairava himself. || 34 ||
The perfection of recitation shall belong to him who wears the pill in this manner;
what is the use of much speaking, O Goddess? He himself becomes Bhairava.
This is the most essential truth, divine, the very essence of all, bestowing the supreme goal; it is the core of cores, to be guarded and kept secret by those seeking liberation.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for Wearing the Yantra," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrī Devī Rahasya*.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, I wish to hear the determination regarding the meters and the sages, as well as the determination regarding the seed-syllables of the deities such as Devīśvara and others. || 1 ||
O Supreme Lord, O God, if you have compassion for me, you should explain to me the determination of the ritual piercing with the *śakti*, the *kīlaka*, and the binding of the directions.
Śrī Bhairava said:
O Goddess, this is the most secret [teaching], the supreme essence of the gods,
the secret of my mantras, and the primordial deity of the goddesses.
Out of devotion to you, I shall explain the determination of the seers and meters for the king of mantras of the gods, and likewise for those of the goddesses.
For sixty thousand kalpas he performed the recitation (japa) as ordained;
likewise, for sixty hundred-thousand years and through sixty subsequent births. (5)
O Goddess, one who performs the *puraścaryā* is called a *ṛṣi*;
a mantra devoid of its *ṛṣi*, even if recited, [yields results] only in future births.
O Maheśvarī,
O Great Goddess, when a mantra is brought forth from my mouth, it brings about obstacles for practitioners in this world.
Enveloped by which the radiant one is proclaimed as *Chanda*;
these are the various *chandases* of those mantras, O Supreme Goddess. (8)
O Dear One, a mantra devoid of *chanda* is like a naked mortal;
O Goddess, when the *mantra* was recited by me with supreme devotion, [it became effective]. (9)
That goddess who was mentioned appeared before me instantly—
she by whom the origin of the queens of the king of mantras was brought about by me.
O Supreme Goddess, that is described as the seed-syllable (bīja) of mantras;
O Śivā, a mantra devoid of its seed-syllable causes the loss of spiritual accomplishment (siddhi).
Devoid of seed, the world is lost, just as a river is lost when devoid of water;
at the end of the recitation, the mind [realizes] the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world.
O Goddess of the gods, that by which I was born is sung of as Śakti;
O Great Goddess, a mantra devoid of Śakti is considered to be a cause of obstacles.
O Great Goddess, having recited and praised this mantra—which bestows great auspiciousness and arises from the seed-syllable of the Śaktis of the goddesses—he concealed it once again. 14.
O Śivā, that which is devoid of luster yet born again is declared to be a *kīlaka*;
and at the end of the recitation, O Śivā, the mantra becomes *niṣkīlita* (unfettered) through lack of faith.
O Great Goddess, at the time of recitation, Bhairava seizes the accomplishment of the king of practitioners; likewise do the Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Pretas. 16.

The ten directions flee away; that is what constitutes the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*). O Goddess, without this binding of the directions, neither recitation (*japa*) nor even the study (*pāṭha*) of the text is effective. (17)
It is always fruitless and creates obstacles; therefore, one should perform the binding of the directions (digbandhana).
A mantra devoid of these is fruitless and causes obstacles. (18)
"O Goddess, what more shall I say even regarding lowly creatures? Thus, O Supreme Sovereign, is this secret chapter concerning the meters."
"It must be kept secret by the great heroes"—this is the command of the Supreme Lord. (19)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Seers and Other [Limbs]," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrī Devī Rahasya*.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the fierce practice (*ugrasādhana*) of the cremation ground, by the mere performance of which the practitioner becomes Bhairava. (1)
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, by your devotion you have shown me this great favor;
yet I have forgotten this secret rite characterized by the worship of the cremation ground.
This supreme [teaching], unknown in all other tantras, has now been brought to my mind.
Śrī Bhairava said:
O Goddess, the powers of thirty-three crores of deities, renowned by their names, have been heard by me from you. (3)
O Goddess, O Śivā, I shall now describe to you the worship of the cremation grounds according to the rules,
by which practitioners become endowed with all supernatural powers (siddhis).
O lady of excellent hips, in the Kali age, due to the curse of Bhairava, worship, yoga, recitation, and other practices do not attain success without the ritual of the cremation ground.
There are thirty-three crores of goddesses, all of whom reside in the abode of the pretas;
he who goes there and worships them shall become equal to Bhairava.
There, O Goddess, Mahākāla was surrounded by jackals with terrible howls,
as well as by dogs, lords of the Yakṣas, serpents, and Piśācas.
Indeed, he performs worship in the cremation ground with vetālas, bhūtas, and pretas;
there, four most terrible bhūtas act as obstacles.
Those eight goddesses, who are Bhūtas and Bhairavas, wander in the cardinal and intermediate directions; when those cruel Bhūtas come face to face with one, they cause harm.
The Bhairavas are destroyers of obstacles; when facing them, they bring about auspiciousness.
I shall proclaim their ritual procedure, which is secret, the essence, and the most excellent of the excellent. (10)
This supreme worship of the cremation ground is not to be disclosed and must not be given away;
it is [effective] on Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and likewise on Saturday.
Furthermore, as the sun revolves, those eight Bhairavas are situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions:
in the east, northeast, north, northwest, southeast, south, southwest, and west,
they are Mahogra, Citrāṅgada, Caṇḍa, Bhāsval, Lolākṣa, Bhūteśa, Karāla, and Bhīma.
O Great Goddess, these Bhairavas of the directions, accompanied by spirits, constantly roam the cremation ground.
By worshipping them, one may dwell in the cremation ground; otherwise, there will be confusion of mind and disaster. (13)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for Worship in the Cremation Ground," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrī Devī Rahasya*.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Then, O Goddess, I shall respectfully declare the manual for this worship, composed in both prose and verse, which bestows the attainment of mantra-siddhi. (1)
Having risen at the end of the night and performed his daily rites, the practitioner,
accompanied by his followers, should take with him the requisites for worship in the cremation ground.
O beloved, one who possesses heroes should go to the ground of heroes at the onset of night;
O Goddess Pārvatī, listen with respect as I describe the ritual procedure there. (3)
This is a secret, the very essence, to be guarded; it must not be disclosed by those who desire spiritual accomplishment.

There, at the beginning of the night, the practitioner accompanied by his hero (vīra) shall go to the cremation ground; having stepped no further than seven paces, he must not overstep the boundary of the cremation ground. Having arranged the ritual materials there, washed his own hands and feet, performed the triple sipping of water (ācamana), and executed three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra, he should perform the sipping of water as before.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of one's own root-ṛṣi and meter, and having performed the hand and limb placements (*karāṅganyāsa*),

one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times. Having recited according to one's capacity, and having meditated upon the Goddess together with Śiva and one's own Guru, one should recite the armor (*kavaca*), the thousand names, and the hymns, and then step across a distance of seven paces.
Having circumambulated the cremation-ground mandala and entered it, one should bow to the funeral pyre:
"O you whose mouth is formidable with flames, O beloved of the fire at the end of the aeon!"
O Consciousness, which has arisen as the abode of the life-breaths of all living beings, bestow Your grace upon me. || 4 ||
Having thus bowed according to their respective positions, and having placed the auspicious and inauspicious Bhūtabhairavas in front and behind, one should begin the worship.
The Śrīdevī said:
O Blessed One, how should a practitioner of mantra sustain the Bhairavas and spirits who bestow curses and favors, whether they are facing him or behind him? (5)
The illustrious Bhairava said: O Goddess, I shall tell you this supreme secret, the sādhana of Bhūtabhairava, out of devotion for you; it must not be told to one who is evil-minded.

Bhūta is in the east when the Sun is there; Mahogra and Citrāṅgada are in the north when the Moon is there; likewise, Caṇḍa is in the northeast when Mars is there; and Bhāsvat and Bhairava are in the northwest when Mercury is there.
Lolākṣaka is situated in the southeast when Jupiter is present; Bhūteśvara is in the south when Venus is there;
Karālaka is in the southwest when Saturn is present; and furthermore, Bhīma is in the west when the Sun is there.
O Great Goddess, thus the Bhairavas of the directions and the hosts of spirits wander constantly in the cremation ground;
O Śivā, they wander in the opposite manner when the moon waxes and when it wanes.
The Śrī Devī said:
O Lord of Gods, dense with compassion, Lord of practitioners, Master of the World!
It is known that these most excellent of practitioners conceive this formidable rite within their hearts.
(74) O Goddess, how will they perform the worship of Mahogra and Bhīma on the two fortnights— the fierce and the gentle— on the two days of the Sun? 11.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Śivā, having observed the weekday on the full moon day, one should then multiply it eightfold; having multiplied the Sunday [count], one should take either the first or the second [result]. 12.
On the first Sunday, one should worship Mahogra in the east;
on the second, during the bright fortnight, one should worship Bhīma in the west.
One should worship the Bhūtas during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) in reverse order;
O Maheśvarī, I shall now proclaim the essence of their worship.
It must not be spoken to another's disciple, nor to one who wears tattered rags, nor to one of evil nature.
Mahākāla is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi) of the mantra for the cremation ground worship. || 15 ||
The meter is known as Uṣṇik; the goddess is Śmaśānakālikā;
Parā is the seed-syllable, Taṭa is the power (śakti), and Kālī is declared to be the pin (kīlaka). || 16 ||
Its application is proclaimed to be in the spheres of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Of this mantra for the worship of Śrī Śmaśānakālikā, Mahākālabhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Uṣṇik is the meter (chanda),
Śrī Śmaśānakālikā is the deity (devatā), Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Hūṃ is the power (śakti), and Krīṃ is the pin (kīlaka).

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and for worship. Salutation to the sage Mahākālabhairava on the head; salutation to the *uṣṇih* meter on the face; salutation to the deity Śmaśānakālikā on the heart;
salutation to the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* on the navel; salutation to the power (*śakti*) *hūṃ* on the secret place; salutation to the *kīlaka* *krīṃ* on the feet.

Salutation to Viniyoga on all limbs. *Oṃ krāṃ* to the heart; *oṃ krīṃ* to the head, and so forth—this is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the hands and limbs. Having thus performed the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should purify the seat. *Oṃ āṃ*:
for the mantra of seat purification, Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (*ṛṣi*).

Sutala is the metre, Kūrma is the deity; this is the application for the purification of the seat. *Prīṃ*. Salutations to the Earth. O Goddess, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu. You, O Goddess, support me; make my seat pure. *Oṃ krāṃ*, salutations to the lotus-seat of the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*). To Ananta...

Homage! Homage to the lotus! Homage to the lotus stalk! Having sat there, one should perform the triple clapping of the hands with the mantra beginning, "May those spirits depart" (apasarpantu te bhūtāḥ), etc.

Having given three claps of the hands, one should display the nārāca-mudrā. Having thus performed the purification of the seat, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). With "Oṃ Hūṃ," by means of the hook (or contraction), having led one's own life-force (jīva)—which has the form of a lamp-flame—into the path of Brahmā via the channel of Suṣumṇā, there...

Having meditated on [the self] as dissolved in Sadāśiva, one should first dry up the person of sin (pāpapuruṣa) located in the left side of the belly by reciting the seed-syllable of air, *yaṃ*, sixteen times. One should burn it by reciting the seed-syllable of fire, *raṃ*, sixty-four times. One should flood it by reciting the seed-syllable of water, *vaṃ*, thirty-two times. One should [stabilize it] by reciting the seed-syllable of earth, *laṃ*, ten times.
Having contemplated the body as a solid mass and having established one’s own *jīva* in the heart, one should offer the vital breaths (*prāṇas*).

Thus ends the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ so’haṃ haṃsaḥ*. In this manner, my vital breaths are here; likewise for "my... [and so on].

"O Jīva, remaining right here, may all my senses— my speech, mind, eyes, ears, tongue, nose, and vital breaths— come to this very place and remain happily for a long time, Svāhā! Having thus offered the vital breaths (prāṇas) and performed the Mātṛkā-nyāsa as before, [one proceeds].
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs, one should construct a square altar to the northeast of the funeral pyre.
Having visualized the *Śrīcakra* there and worshipped it according to the prescribed rite, one should worship the nine planets there—
[Oṃ Srīṃ]— and, having worshipped Vaṭuka in the east, [worship] the Bhūtabhairavas.
One should worship as follows: *Oṃ mrīṃ, obeisance to Mahogrā*. *Oṃ mrīṃ, obeisance to Madālasā* in the east.

*Oṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Citrāṅgada*. *Oṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Citriṇī* in the north. *Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍa*. *Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍī* in the northeast. *Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Bhāsvara*. *Oṃ...*
Hauṃ, obeisance to Prabhā; to Vāyu. Oṃ lāṃ, obeisance to Lolākṣa; Oṃ lāṃ, obeisance to Lolā; to Āgneya. Oṃ bhaiṃ, obeisance to Bhūteśa; Oṃ bhaiṃ, obeisance to Bhūtadhātrī;
to the South. Oṃ krīṃ, obeisance to Karāla; Oṃ krīṃ, obeisance to Karālinī; to Nairṛta. Oṃ...
"Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Bhīma; Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Bhīmarūpā in the west.

Having thus worshipped with perfumes, unbroken rice, and flowers according to the sequence of the directions, one should visualize either the Śrīcakra or the Navayonicakra upon the funeral pyre there, perform the worship of the Yogapīṭha, and arrange the ritual vessels.

Having performed the worship of the vessel (*pātrapūjā*) there, preceded by the worship of the assembly of deities (*devatāvaraṇa*), one should fully worship the Goddess together with Śiva; having recited the mantra according to one's capacity and offered that recitation (*japa*) to the Goddess, one should then perform the recitation of the armor (*kavaca*), the thousand names (*sahasranāma*), the hymn of praise (*stava*), and so forth, and having offered those as well, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the funeral pyre fire (*citāgni*) consisting of a tenth part of the recitation. Therein, [one should worship] Vaṭuka and the others.
Having satisfied even the Bhairavas of the elements, and having satisfied the nine maidens,
one should drink together in mutual succession, ending with the ninth vessel.
The Śrī Devī said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge;
tell me the procedure for drinking liquor, by which success may certainly be attained. (17)
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for the worship with the drinking [of the nectar].
By which practitioners are born in the Kali age resembling Bhairava himself. || 18 ||
O Maheśvarī, one should consume the drink in cremation grounds or at midnight;
for in the Kali age, it is certain that there is no accomplishment for practitioners without this drink.
Surā, saṃvid, and vāruṇī—these three drinks are always supreme.
Within them, the gods beginning with Brahmā are dissolved for the sake of ultimate liberation. 20.
Āsava, sweet liquor (madhura-madya), and śīdhu—these three are supreme;
there all the gods, headed by Vāsava, reside day and night. (21)
Having worshipped the Goddess together with Śiva when the adoration of Bhairava has commenced,
there the drinking of the supreme Goddess bestows great bliss.
Without the drink there is no accomplishment, nor without the worship of Śakti;
likewise, the mantra is not perfected in Śiva without the worship at the cremation ground. (23)
Therefore, having fully worshipped the cremation ground and having honored the Śakti,
the practitioner should partake of the drink of the Supreme Goddess before the Śrīcakra according to the prescribed rule.
One should practice the drinking of consciousness at night and the drinking of *śīdhu* by day;
O Śivā, the drinking of wine throughout day and night bestows both enjoyment and liberation.
Between consciousness and liquor, consciousness alone is superior.
He who goes to the cremation ground is indeed a Vaiṣṇava, he is a Śākta, and he is a Śaiva. (26)
By frequenting the cremation ground, the hero becomes like Bhairava himself.
O Goddess, one should partake of the drink until consciousness has become composed of mind.
If any modification should arise therein, that drinking is like the murder of a Brahmin.
As long as the gaze does not waver, and as long as the mind does not waver— || 28 ||
One should perform the drinking [of wine] only up to that point; beyond this is the "drinking of the sacrificial animal" (paśupāna).
He who performs the drinking, chewing, or other such acts without having performed worship, [commits an offense]. (29)

O Goddess of the Gods, he who [approaches] the five types of women beginning with the letter *m*—whether they be a *kulaṭā*, a woman of the family, or another's wife—is diseased; he is censured in the world as one who subsists on the food of others. (30)
O Sovereign Lady, one who kills a Brahmin quickly enters the jaws of death;
one should not give what is left over from oneself, nor should one eat the leavings of another.
O Śivā, if a Kaulika should consume what remains as leavings in the Vīracakra,
his attainment of siddhi will be immediately lost, and the Yoginīs will devour him.
At the time of worship and at midnight, having meditated upon the Goddess seated on the lap of Śiva,
and having worshipped her according to the prescribed rite, one should drink after first performing the chewing of the offering.
O Goddess, having gratified the wife of another with the five "ma" syllables, one should repeatedly utter "Drink! Drink! seven times, O Śivā. (34)
By that means, the Goddess shall appear seated upon the lap of Śiva.
Such is this secret manual (paddhati) associated with the worship in the cremation ground. 35.
This divine work, composed of both prose and verse and containing the essence of all reality, has become renowned through affection for you; it must never be disclosed.
Thus, O Goddess, this most secret mystery, difficult even for the gods to attain, must not be disclosed; it should not be given away, but kept hidden like one's own womb. (37)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for Worshiping the Cremation Ground," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrī Devī Rahasya*.
(p. 78) Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
The Śrī Devī said:
O Blessed One, knower of all tantras, saluted by all the worlds,
[please explain] the Yantrarāja of the Śrī Devī, as well as her rosary and bracelet.
I wish to hear about purification, as previously mentioned by you yourself,
O Lord, by which there may indeed be the purification of both the ritual substances and the practitioner.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, O Goddess, I shall describe the purification that grants all desires,
a supreme and secret chapter common to the entire world.
On an auspicious day, O Goddess, having first gone to the cremation ground, the best of practitioners [should take] a skull,
a necklace of human teeth, and a bracelet, O Īśvarī.
Having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, one should place it within the yantra;
having again recited it one hundred and eight times, one should perform the libation with that very same [mantra]. || 5 ||
O Goddess, O Māyā, worshiped by the gods, [worship] the gods, ancestors, and sages with the seed-syllables of desire,
using pure ashes from the cremation ground smeared [upon you], O goddess honored by the gods.
Then, O Goddess, the best of practitioners should draw the yantra upon a skull;
he should fashion a rosary from human teeth for the attainment of all desired goals.
O Maheśvarī, O Śivā, for that illustrious one who is devoted to the left-hand path (vāmācāra),
if he does not employ the yantra and the rosary, the loss of his mantra is certain.
Having quickly taken a skull of one who has recently died, which has the luster of crystal,
and having purified it with cremation-ground ashes, the most excellent of practitioners [should proceed]. (9)
The wise one should accomplish his own mantra; otherwise, it brings about the loss of accomplishment.
O Goddess of Gods, the skull-yantra is the supreme crest-jewel (keśakaṅkaṇa).
O Maheśvarī, the practitioner should strictly conceal the garland of human teeth, the ritual substance, and the skull-bowl; he should contemplate himself as having the form of the Goddess.
For the practitioner who acts in this way, success is not far off;
otherwise, O Supreme Goddess, there would be a loss of success even for me.
Thus, this divine chapter is secret, the supreme essence of all;
it must not be disclosed, must not be given away, and must especially be kept hidden.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Purification of Substances and Other Matters," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrī Devī Rahasya*.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, I desire to hear in detail about the supreme worship of the garland and the yantra, which is purifying and bestows the ultimate truth.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, O Goddess, I shall declare the ritual manual (paddhati) in prose form.
For, O Maheśvarī, regarding the substances for purification, such as garlands and the like, || 2 ||
Therein, at the beginning, the practitioner, having risen while a portion of the night remains, and having assumed the bound lotus posture (*baddhapadmāsana*),

should meditate upon his own guru seated within the pericarp of a thousand-petaled lotus facing downward located at his own head, and meditate upon the Goddess in the region of the heart; having worshipped them with mental offerings, he should perform the recitation of the *ajapā* mantra for the sake of the guru and the Goddess.

Having offered [the vessel], one should prostrate. Then, having gone outside and proceeded to a river or similar body of water, one should perform the ritual bathing, the *saṃdhyā* prayers, and so forth.

Returning to the sacrificial hall and completing the daily rites (*nityakarman*), one should begin the purification of the *yantra* and other procedures. Therein, in the northeastern direction, one should properly construct a square altar (*vedi*) measuring one cubit in width, adorned with the *viśvaka* design, and smear it with [sacred substances].
Having visualized the Yantra of one’s own deity with vermilion and having worshipped it thoroughly with the prescribed worship,
one should bring forth the ritual substances and other items and purify the Yantra and the rest.
O Goddess, the best of practitioners should wear a bracelet made of women’s hair;
O Śivā, he should also carry a bracelet, a necklace of teeth, and the skull-bowl implement (kāpālika-yantra).
One should worship the Mistress of Bhairava with the five things beginning with the letter *ma*: liquor (*madhu*), fish (*matsya*), meat (*māṃsa*), mudrā, and sexual union (*maithuna*). || 4 ||
Having brought [the materials] to that very place and performed the purification of the seat and so forth, one should perform the Nyāsa of the Ṛṣi and others for one's own root-mantra (mūla),
preceded by the formal resolve (saṅkalpa). Then, having sipped water (ācamana) with the root-mantra and performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma),

and having established the vital breaths following the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and other rites, [one should prepare] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the seven medicinal herbs.
One should perform purification.
The best of practitioners should prepare the abundant five products of the cow (pañcagavya), consisting of milk, semen, curd-whey, buttermilk, and blood produced from its own source.
Kashmiri gorocana, pūga, and so forth, as well as musk, mūrvā, pūtāsa,
and sandalwood from Malaya— these are the great medicinal substances for the purification of the yantra.

Having properly smeared the yantra, the rosary, and the bracelet with these [substances], one should perform their purification individually with the root mantra: *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ devi yantreśvari klīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ oṃ, purify the yantra, purify it! Hraḥ śraḥ klaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā*.
The best of practitioners should recite this knowledge-mantra consisting of mantras one hundred and eight times; having invoked the Goddess into the yantra, he should worship her.

Therein, first, having purified the yantra with the root-mantra and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and medicinal herbs, and having placed it upon the *bindu* within the vermilion yantra (p. 81), one should worship it as before according to the sequence prescribed by oneself. Then, [one should purify] the rosary with medicinal herbs and so forth.
One should purify [the rosary] with the root mantra: *Oṃ oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ śrāṃ klīṃ klāṃ mālārūpiṇi sarvalokabhakṣiṇi hūṃ nṛdantamālāṃ śodhaya 2 phaṭ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā*.
Having recited this one hundred and eight times, one should purify it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) using the root mantra. Then—
Having fashioned a bracelet from *śatabālā* fibers using a woman’s hair, one should purify it with the root-mantra:
*oṃ hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ śrīṃ krīṃ keśini nirākeśini kaṅkaṇaṃ śodhaya 2 hūṃ krāṃ phaṭ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā*. Having thus recited this root-mantra one hundred and eight times, [one should proceed].

Having purified [the rosary] with water containing the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and medicinal herbs, and having tied it to the left and right hands, one should recite one's own root mantra as many times as possible using a rosary made of human teeth. Then, having performed the recitation of the *Kavaca*, the hymns, the *Sahasranāma*, and so forth, and having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) with the root mantra, one should perform the worship of the *Cakra* before it.

The practitioners, having sat in the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*) in an eleven-fold circular arrangement, should draw in the center a triangle with a dot, a hexagon, a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, three circles, and a square enclosure (*bhūgṛha*), and worship it with red flowers— externally [starting from] "Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśa; Dhaṃ..."

Having worshipped with "Obeisance to Dharmarāja, vaṃ; obeisance to Varuṇa, krīṃ; obeisance to Kubera," [one should worship] on the eight petals: "hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Karāla; hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Vikarāla;
hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Saṃhāra; hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Rurubhairava; hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Mahākāla."
