Speak, O Lord, how a Kaulika should act for the sake of attaining all perfections.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
"Kālī, Kāma, Kṛpā, Kuntī, Karamāle, Haraṃ Vanam"—
this is the mantra of Karamālā, which bestows purity and grants all accomplishments.
Within six months, the practitioner should perform the purification of the garlands;
thereafter, by reciting the Great Vidyā, he shall become a master of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
This indeed is the reality among all realities, the very essence, and the supreme deity;
it has been declared by me through devotion to you, for it is not to be told even by those who discourse upon Brahman. (69)
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Purification of the Rosary and its Mantras," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrī Devī Rahasya*.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Now, O Goddess of the gods, out of devotion to you and for the benefit of the Kaulikas, I shall describe the supreme purification of the yantra.
[The Śrīcakra may be made] of gold, silver, copper, crystal, or likewise of brass;
it may be fashioned from a skull-bowl, from a cord, or from Vaiṣṇava stone.
O Pārvatī, within these eight divine seats of yoga (yogapīṭhas),
one should contemplate the great yantra, which is celestial, terrestrial, and future. (3)

O Īśānī, the threefold yantra— consisting of an upper line, a lower line, and a third adorned with perfumes— is well-established as that which accomplishes the accomplished and the to-be-accomplished.
O Goddess, one should purify the noose of the thousand-rayed [sun] during the northern course;
then, every fifth [day], it shall become a bestower of accomplishment.
One should purify the arrow-hook and the Vaiṣṇava stone during the southern solstice;
then, at every fourth [period], one shall attain success.
At the end of the year, the wise person should purify the golden and crystal instruments;
and at the end of six months, one should purify the silver and copper instruments.
O Goddess, O Mistress, at the times thus described by me, the Kaulika should purify the yantra for the sake of success; this is now being correctly expounded by me. (8)
Śiva has been declared by me to be the seer (ṛṣi) of the mantra for purifying the yantra;
its meter (chandas) is known as Triṣṭubh, and the deity is Parāśakti.
O Goddess, the seed-syllable *ramā* is the supreme power (*parā śakti*), and *kāma* is the pin (*kīlaka*);
this application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed for the purpose of accomplishing the purification of the Śrīcakra. || 10 ||
One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the body and limbs starting with the *muni* [mantra], as well as the placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) and the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*).
Then, one should perform the purification of the seat (*viṣṭaraśuddhi*) and the ritual of offering the vital breath (*prāṇārpaṇavidhi*).
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of one's chosen ṛṣis and deities, as well as the placement of the hands and limbs;
having performed the Mātṛkā-nyāsa together with the dissolution-limb placement (layāṅga-nyāsa).
O Śivā, having performed the Ardhanārīśvara-nyāsa, followed by the Ṣoḍhā-nyāsa,
and then the Mūla-trikhaṇḍaka-nyāsa, one should perform the Prāṇacaya-nyāsa.
Having performed the worship of the seats (pīṭhapūjā) within one's own heart and illuminated the six chakras, one should place the Śrīcakra— the deity most desired by oneself— upon a golden throne.
O Goddess, one should purify it with honey, or with that which arises from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*,
or with the eight fragrances (*aṣṭagandha*), O Goddess, or with the fluid of a man (*pauruṣa-rasa*). (15)
O Great Goddess, having established [the deity] with the rich clarified butter in the Kula-worship, the Kaulika should worship the Śrīcakra there with the root mantra. || 16 ||
O beloved Mistress of the Cakra, having extracted the golden yantra consisting of the Vāgbhava and Śakti seeds— the Speech and the Power— one should purify it and extract the couple.
The mantra for the golden yantra consists of two *ṭha* syllables; it is the purifier.
One should extract the silver yantra by means of *tāra*, *sindhu*, and *tāra*. (18)
"Śodhaya dvayam āpaśca" is the mantra for purifying the yantra;
[it consists of] Tāra, Tārā, Tāra, Vadhū, Tāra, and Tārakā. (19)
"O Kulāmbikā, purify this Yantra of Tāmreśvarī for me;
[the mantra is] the beginning of the Veda (Om), Kamalā (Śrīm), Māyā (Hrīm), and Tāra (Oṃ). 20.
Purify the forest twice with the mantra that cleanses crystal stone:
the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of Kūvarī, Mā, and Māyā, which is honored by Vāyu. (21)
"O Rudreśvarī, purify the supreme yantra"—this is remembered as the mantra. [The sequence is:
Tāra (Om), Vāk (Aiṃ), Kāmarāja (Klīṃ), Śakti (Hrīṃ), and Kapālamālini. || 22 ||
"Śodhaya" (purify), followed by the pair of "ṭha" syllables (ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ), is the mantra for purifying the skull.
Then there is the syllable "Oṃ" (Tāra), "Gaurī," the third vowel "Ī," "Vāk" (Speech), and "Kāma" (Desire) upon the seat of the funeral pyre (Citāsana). || 23 ||
"Śodhaya yantram ṭha ṭha"—this mantra is for the purification of the noose (pāśa).
It begins with the first of the Vedas (OM), followed by Hari, Vāṇī, Śakti, Kāma, Ramā, and Ramā. (24)
O Īśānī, when the Viṣṇu-stone is fixed in the yantra, water is traditionally remembered as the purifier;
thus, O Īśānī, the yantra is situated upon a throne of jewels.
Having bathed [the image] with the root mantra using the water of the previously mentioned medicinal herbs,
one should worship it with perfumes and garlands while reciting these mantras.
Having worshipped and purified it, O Goddess, one should then perform the worship as declared by Śiva.
The practitioner should perform what has been described, preceded by the purification of the ritual substances. || 27 ||
Having performed the eightfold worship (*aṣṭāṅgapūjā*), one should perform the recitation (*japa*) at midnight. Śrī Bhairavī said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of Kulakaula, you who abide in the midst of the eight Bhairavas!"
Tell me the time of midnight; this is a great doubt of mine.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Midnight is threefold, consisting of four muhūrtas;
[the first is] niśītha, [the second] ardharātra, and the third is indeed mahāniśā.
In the second and third watches of the night, O Yāmalabhairavī,
taking up two muhūrtas [of each], likewise, O Maheśvarī.
Two muhūrtas constitute the midnight period (niśītha), and two muhūrtas beyond that;
for two muhūrtas, it is the hour of midnight (ardharātra), which is worthy of worship, O Supreme Goddess. (31)
O Goddess, taking one muhūrta from after [sunrise] and another from before [sunset],
midnight is described as the time for the attainment of Kaula success during the two watches of the night.
O Śivā, the junction of the two middle watches [or the junction of the two feet] is the "Great Night.
He who recites the *parā* [mantra] during that time shall become like Śiva himself. || 33 ||
At midnight one should worship the yantra, and at the hour of half-night one should recite the mantra;
during the deep of night, the best of Kaulikas should perform the supreme recitation.
What in this world would it not accomplish, even that which is difficult for me to obtain:
dust, semen, liquor, O Goddess, meat, fish, and sexual union? (35)
In every way, O Goddess, the practitioner of mantras should purify [himself] with the root mantra;
he may drink liquor, enjoy women, and meditate upon Bhairava and Bhairavī. 36.
One should mutter the name of the Guru and the Vidyā; this is the supreme Kaula doctrine.
Having performed the morning rites, O Śivā, one should then worship the Śrīcakra.
The practitioner of mantras should recite the great vidyā and then perform the recitation of the hymn;
he should always recite the supreme truth, and thereby he goes to the highest state. (38)
In great calamity, in great portent, in great sorrow, in great disease; in great delusion, in great unhappiness, and in the crisis of great poverty. || 39 ||
In a great forest, in a great void, on a great mountain, in great ignorance, in a great battle;
in misfortune, in false hope, in famine, and in ill omens; || 40 ||
O Goddess, one should remember the Primordial Mother (Prāmbikā) within the entire aggregate of afflictions;
Sarasvatī is in his mouth, and Lakṣmī is always in his house.
Blessed is his mother by whom the Goddess has been duly worshipped.
For this is the essence of all tantras, the supreme reality of all mantras;
it has been declared by me out of affection for you, though it is not to be disclosed even by those who discourse on Brahman. (42)

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Time for Recitation and Worship and the Procedure for the Purification of Yantras," in the *Paramārthapradīpikā*, a dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī within the *Śrīdevīrahasya* of the *Śrīrudrayāmala Tantra*.
This first half is completed.
Now, p. 128) atha...
The Twenty-sixth Chapter. Śrī Bhairavī said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, illuminator of the Kula-dharma!
O Lord of the Family, I wish to hear the latter half of this tantra. || 1 ||
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, O Goddess, Mistress of the Kula, out of a desire for the welfare of the followers of Kula,
I shall proclaim the latter half of the Tantra, known as the Secret Vijayā.
She is Durgā-devī, Parā-devī, Parā-śakti, and Parāmbikā;
she who is celebrated as Devadevī is remembered in the Śruti as Gāyatrī.
She is composed of splendor, the great dark one, the Great Tripurasundarī;
she is fivefold in nature, the Mistress of the Fifth, and the illuminator of the five voids.
Ugradurgā is the supreme Śrī; that light is the highest state. She who is Durgā as the Supreme Goddess (Parādevī) is remembered as Śiva and she is Hari. || 5 ||
She is Sūrya, she is Savitṛ, and she is remembered as Mahāgaṇapati;
she is the goddess Pañcamī, the Pañcikā, who abides in the fivefold conduct.
The five-syllabled Gāyatrī is celebrated as the Supreme Self;
she is the Goddess consisting of the fivefold activity, the auspicious one who embodies all goddesses. (7)
Sarasvatī, who takes the forms of Gaṇeśa, Arka, Harīśāna, and Durgā— the Great Śyāmā, the Great Vidyā— is to be worshipped in due order.
One who knows the supreme truth—whether a follower of the Kaula path or a Vaiṣṇava—should never create division among these: Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Hari, Īśāna, and Durgā.
The devotee, possessing devotion, should worship with a sense of oneness and through devotion to the Goddess alone;
he should worship all [the deities] within the circle of the Goddess, or else within the Śiva-liṅga, or in Śivā herself. (10)
O beloved, a wise person should not cause a division between the Śāligrāma stone and the solar seat (sūryapīṭha) by means of the wheel of the illustrious Lord of Gaṇas (Śrīgaṇeśvara). || 11 ||
He who indeed creates a division becomes a destroyer of Śiva;
the best of Kaulas should perform worship to Śiva individually.
O Goddess, he was a master of the mantras of Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, as well as of the Śrīdevī and Ugrā Durgā, and he was a knower of the secret of the Goddess.
Today, O Goddess of gods, out of love for you, I shall proclaim the Kula-natured Tantra named Rahasyavijaya, which constitutes the latter half of the Tantra.
The fivefold constituent of all these consists of the worship of all mantras;
likewise, there is the fivefold constituent of Gaṇeśa and the fivefold constituent of the Sun.
The five-limbed [Purāṇa] of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, that of Śrī Śiva, the five-limbed [Purāṇa] of Goddess Durgā, and the *Durgādevīrahasyaka*. (16)
O Maheśvarī, this latter half has been proclaimed as the essence of this Tantra;
O Queen of the Gods, this Tantra is the secret of the Goddess. (17)
The leader of the family should keep this secret from those who are unworthy;
O Goddess, first hear the five-limbed [mantra] of Mahāgaṇapati. 18.
By the mere hearing of which, the destruction of obstacles occurs in an instant—[to that] three-eyed Mahādeva, seated comfortably upon the summit of Mount Meru. (19)
It was joined by hosts of gods and asuras, and honored by Brahmā and Acyuta;
it was frequented by Siddhas, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas. || 20 ||
Śiva, accompanied by Pārvatī, was pleased by prostrations and hymns;
he was smiling as he conversed with Brahmā and Hari.
(130) Pārvatī, having bowed down, spoke these words.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
O Blessed One, knower of all reality, illuminator of all phenomena, [you who know] the purpose of the deities as well as that of human beings. (22)
"O God, by whom might an obstacle arise? O Śaṅkara, cut through my doubt.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"O Goddess, I shall tell you this great secret, the answer to your question."
It is unspeakable to those who are not devotees; to the devotees, it is the means for liberation.
The Lord who is Vināyaka, Gaṇādhyakṣa, and Gaṇeśa, is renowned as the creator of obstacles, the protector of the world, and the remover of obstacles. || 24 ||
O Maheśvarī, neither for that devotee of the god nor for a mortal who always worships him does any obstacle ever cause affliction. (25)
O Goddess, whoever should mutter that mantra, for him one should wear this armor;
one should recite the Thousand Names, a hymn whose sole means of accomplishment is the root mantra. (26)
"Neither obstacles hinder him, nor shall there be any failure in his undertakings.
The Goddess said:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Gaṇeśa, Lord of the universe!"
The mantra, the yantra, the hymn, the armor, and the supreme thousand names. || 27 ||
"O Supreme Lord, I desire to hear from you about the ritual worship [of him].
Śrī Bhairava said:
He who is the God of gods, the bestower of boons, Gaṇeśa, the leader of the obstacles..."
He is known as Gajānana, Gaṇādhyakṣa, and Vināyaka. || 28 ||
I shall describe its five limbs in their entirety for your pleasure;
therein, O Goddess of the Gods, I will first explain to you the extraction of the mantra.
p.
131) O Śivā, [I have taught] the extraction of the yantra and the limb of dissolution for Mahāgaṇapati.
Now, the extraction of the mantra:
*Tāram*, *sakalā*, *smaraḥ*, *maṭhaśivau*, *nāmno vareti*—this pair;
*sarpaḥ*, *sarvamatojanam*, *ḍulilate*, *jīmūtaśarmākṣaram*; *bhekī*, *kham*, *lavaṇam* together with *samīraḥ*, and the two *ṭha*s at the end of the mantra.
Thus, this mantra of Vaināyaka, consisting of twenty-eight syllables, has been declared. || 30 ||
Thus ends the extraction of the mantra. [To be recited] aloud: *oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye varavarada sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā*.
(28) The preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) is proclaimed to consist of one hundred and twenty-eight thousand recitations of the essential reality (*tattva*).
One should practice at a banyan tree, at a crossroads, in an empty house, or in a cemetery for the departed.
For him (or for that person), there is no obstacle anywhere, nor impurity, nor failure of the mantra; there is no affliction, nor wickedness of mind, nor delusion, nor sorrow. (32)
O Śivā, this Mahāgaṇapati mantra is effective in every way;
I shall now describe the extraction of its yantra, which fulfills all desires.
The wheel of Gaṇeśa, the Lord of the World, which deludes all; now follows the extraction of the yantra:
O Great Goddess, a triangle joined with the letter *kha*, a ten-spoked [wheel], a perfect circle, and likewise an eight-petaled lotus with six spokes.
This well-formed Śrīcakra, endowed with four gates and constructed for the Elephant-faced One (Gaṇeśa), is thus renowned. || 34 ||
Now I shall proclaim the meditation that bestows all accomplishments, by the mere remembrance of which every obstacle flees away. (35)
Holding with his arms a vessel resembling the rays of ten million rising suns, three eyes, a crown blazing with light, a bowl filled with sweetmeats, a praiseworthy jar, and a lotus-seed rosary;
possessing a body resplendent with pure serpents and shining with snakes.
One should meditate upon Gaṇapati, the wish-fulfilling gem of the three worlds, seated upon a pair of lions.

Then one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs, beginning with the hands as "gām" and so forth, followed by the six-limbed placement on the heart and other locations, and subsequently the auspicious placement (*kalyanyāsa*) using the portions of the seed-syllables of the six groups of consonants.
O Supreme Goddess, I shall now describe the limb of dissolution (layāṅga) of the yantra,
which has been concealed in all the tantras by the one born in the reed-thicket (Kārttikeya). 38.
Indra, Dharmeśa, Varuṇa, and likewise Kubera,
should be worshipped in the east and west, as well as in the south and north.
Thus are the gatekeepers:
Nandi, Vīreśa, Saubhāgya, Bhṛṅgirīṭi, Virāṭaka, Puṣpadanta, Vikartānta, Cittalohita, and Sundara. (40)
O beautiful one, the sixteen Gaṇas— whose forms are fierce with the movement of their rich anklets and who appear like dancers in sleep— are to be worshipped in the sixteen spokes.
Karāla, Vikarāla, Saṃhāra, and Ruru;
Mahākāla, Kālāgni, Sitāsya, and Asitātmaka. || 42 ||
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship the eight Bhairavas upon the eight petals:
Vināyaka, Vighnarāja, Gaṇādhyakṣa, and Gajānana.
One should worship Heramba— the consumer of modakas, the son of two mothers, the subduer of enemies,
the one with a single tusk, and the one with a curved trunk— within the ten spokes.
O beautiful goddess, one should worship Kumāra, Jayanta, and Pradyumna in the triangle, and the Lord Mahāgaṇapati in the bindu.
Gaṇeśa, Gāṅgeya, and after that the lion-throne;
O Īśvarī, Vighnāntaka, the mouse-vehicled one (Gaṇeśa), and Tripurāntaka.
Having worshipped [the previous items] one after another, he should then worship the weapons:
the hundred-petaled lotus, the thousand-spoked wheel, and the row of teeth, O Maheśvarī. (47)

Then one should worship the vessel marked with a *modaka*, the water-pot (*kalaśa*), and the axe; thereafter, the two conchs (*śaṅkha*). This is called the limb of dissolution (*layāṅga*) within the *bindu*. (48)
For this mantra of Gaṇeśa, Brahmā is proclaimed as the seer (ṛṣi);
Gāyatrī is stated to be the meter (chandas), and the deity is remembered as Gaṇapati. (49)
The seed-syllable of Śiva is the seed-mantra (bīja), and Māyā-śakti is declared to be the power;
the pair of 'ku' syllables is the pin (kīlaka), which is the sole means for accomplishing all mantras. (50)
O Goddess, the application (viniyoga) for Trailokyavijaya has been proclaimed;
one should recite the root mantra ten thousand times, having offered oblations of ghee and barley sprouts.
O Supreme Goddess, one shall delude [the enemy] and destroy the host of foes;
one should recite the root mantra ten thousand times after offering oblations into a funeral pyre fire beneath a banyan tree.
The practitioner himself shall quickly paralyze all the worlds, as well as the forces of disputants and thieves, by reciting the mantra ten thousand times at a river. (53)
One should offer the flesh of a goat as an oblation; this will certainly cause the enemy to be eradicated.
O Daughter of the Mountain, it will even create enmity with Brahmā; of this there is no doubt. (54)
Having offered the juice of the *nimba* tree in the forest and recited the root mantra ten thousand times,
one can bring even a king under control and attract women.
Thus, O Śivā, this chapter concerning Mahāgaṇapati is secret; it is the singular essence of all tantras and must be kept especially hidden.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Extraction of the Mantra of Mahāgaṇapati," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrī Devīrahasya*.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Today I shall proclaim the supreme manual (paddhati) of Mahāgaṇapati,
which is the singular essence of all prose compositions and a unique river of bliss.

At the end of the night, the practitioner should rise, assume the lotus posture (padmāsana), and perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) three times with the root mantra. Having meditated upon his own guru— adorned in white ornaments— seated within the radiant pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus at the crown of his head,
and having bowed and received his command, he should go outside to perform the purification of excrement.

Having performed the purification of impurities and having carried out the cleansing prescribed by the *varṇas* (or the *varṇa* of the branch), one should go to a river or similar place, cleanse the teeth with the *bīja* of Vāhlīka, perform mouth-rinses with the *bīja* of Śiva,
and carry out the bath for removing impurities with the mantra *śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*.

Having drawn a triangle there with the root mantra and the goad mudrā (*aṅkuśamudrā*), one should invoke the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) there with the verse: "O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in these waters! Then, having invoked the Deity together with Śiva (and Śakti) there by means of the root mantra, and having sprinkled the mouth three times with the root mantra, one should proceed.

Having immersed oneself three times in water with the mantra *hṛīṃ haṃsaḥ śrīsūryāya eṣa te 'rgho namaḥ*, one should offer three *arghya* oblations to the Sun. Then, having emerged from the water and performed the Vedic *sandhyā*, one should perform the Tantric *sandhyā*.
Thereafter, holding water in the left hand, one should veil it with the *varman* (kavaca) mantra and [sprinkle it] with the *mūla* mantra.

Having consecrated it seven times with the mantra, one should sprinkle one’s own head seven times with the drops of water dripping from it; then, having drawn that water inside through the *iḍā* [left nostril] and expelled it through the left nostril, one should discharge it into the right hand via the path of the *suṣumnā* and strike it against a stone situated on the left side while reciting the mantra: *astrāya phaṭ*.

Having thus performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* and sipped water (*ācamana*), one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*): inhalation (*pūraka*) for sixteen [counts], retention (*kumbhaka*) for thirty-two, and exhalation (*recaka*) for sixty-four. Having performed this, one should mutter the Gāyatrī three times: "Oṃ hrīṃ, we know the one with the curved trunk; śrīṃ klīṃ, we meditate upon the one with the single tusk; glauṃ gaṃ, may Gaṇapati impel us. (3) Thus.

Having recited the Gāyatrī mantra as much as possible and having offered three *arghya* oblations to the Goddess and the God, one should worship the Root Mantra— the remover of all obstacles within the worlds, the son of Hara, adored by Gaṇas, Gandharvas, and Siddhas,
the manifest and formidable form of both the higher and lower traditions, the Lord of the Gaṇas, the Elephant-faced One, Mahāgaṇapati.
Having offered libations twice with "I satisfy Varadagaṇeśa, obeisance," [one recites] the root mantra.
"I offer libations and pay homage to the gurus situated in the lineages of the Divine, Siddha, and Human Oghas.

Having satiated the retinue with one handful [of water] for each using the root mantra, and having mentally dismissed the Goddess and the God by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, one should return to the sacrificial pavilion. This is the ritual procedure for the twilight worship (*sandhyā-vidhi*). Having arrived at the sacrificial pavilion...
*Hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ gaṃ*, salutation to Gaṅgā in the east; *3 yaṃ*, salutation to Yamunā in the north;
*3 saṃ*, salutation to Sarasvatī in the south; *3 yāṃ*, salutation to the Yoginīs in the west;
*3 kṣāṃ*, salutation to Kṣetrapāla in the center. Having thus worshipped the deities of the doorway, one enters within the house. *3*.

Āṃ: For the mantra of purifying the seat, Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi), Sutala is the meter (chandaḥ), Kūrma is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the consecration of the seat. Aiṃ, obeisance to the Earth (pṛthivī). Aṃ, obeisance to Ananta. Vaṃ, obeisance to Vasundharā. Mūla-mantra: O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you were supported by Viṣṇu.
"Held [by you]; and you, O Goddess, hold me and make this seat pure. Thus is the meditation (*dhyāna*).
*Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ*, salutations to the Lotus Seat (*padmāsana*). (4 times) / Salutations to the Lion Seat (*siṃhāsana*).
(4 times) / Salutations to the Auspicious Seat (*bhadrāsana*). (4 times) / May those beings depart who are situated upon the earth. Those...

"May those elemental beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva. Having said this, one should perform the three *tāla* strikes, display the *nārāca-mudrā*, and meditate upon the Guru with these words: "Salutation to that venerable Guru, by whom the eye of me, who was blinded by the darkness of ignorance, has been opened with the collyrium-stick of knowledge. Thus [one should meditate on] the Guru.

Having meditated, one should sip water (ācamana) with the following: *glauṃ ātmatattvaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā* | 1 | *vidyātattvaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā* | 1 | *śivatattvaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā* | 1 | Having thus sipped water and performed the three previously mentioned breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*), one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). Having meditated upon Kuṇḍalinī with *hrīṃ*.

Having sprinkled the vital air through the path of the *suṣumṇā* with *śrīṃ*, having brought the presiding presence there with *klīṃ*, and having contemplated one’s own body as reduced to ashes, one should contemplate the individual soul (*jīvātman*) within the path of Brahman using *yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ*. Then, having brought nectar there with *haṃ kṣaṃ*, one should bathe one’s own self in that water, [resulting in] a body free from all impurity.
Having meditated upon one's own station and having brought forth the living soul (jīva), one should establish the vital breaths; this is the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ so 'haṃ saḥ haṃsaḥ. My vital breaths (prāṇas) are here;
my life-force (jīva) is established here. May all my senses—speech, mind, sight, hearing, taste, smell, and breath—having come right here, remain happily for a long time.

" Svāhā"—thus is the procedure for the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*). Then, having sipped water again and performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should perform the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) preceded by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
Of this mantra of the venerable Varada Gaṇeśa, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is the venerable Brahmā and the meter (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī.

The deity is Śrī Mahāgaṇapati; *gaṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *kuru kuru* is the pin (*kīlaka*). This is for the purpose of pleasing Śrī Mahāgaṇapati. [In the Trailokyavijaya recitation, this is the] application (*viniyoga*). Salutation to the Brahman-seer (*brahmarṣi*) upon the head.
Salutation to the Gāyatrī metre at the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Mahāgaṇapati at the heart;
salutation to the seed-syllable *gaṃ* at the navel; salutation to the power (*śakti*) *hrīṃ* at the private parts; salutation to the *kīlaka* "kuru kuru" at the feet.

"Salutation to Trailokyavijaya for the purpose of application; [this is] the nyāsa of the seers and so forth upon all the limbs. *Gāṃ* to the two thumbs, salutation to the heart; *gīṃ* to the two index fingers, svāhā to the head; *gūṃ* to the two middle fingers, vaṣaṭ to the tuft; *gaiṃ* to the two ring fingers...

*Namaḥ kavacāya huṃ*. *Gauṃ* to the two little fingers, *namaḥ* to the eyes, *vauṣaṭ*. *Gaḥ* to the palms and backs of the hands, *namaḥ* to the weapon, *phaṭ*. Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs upon the hands.
Oṃ, the principle of the Self (ātmatattva), salutation to the heart; Oṃ, the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), svāhā to the head;

Oṃ, the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock; Oṃ, the principle of the Guru (gurutattva), huṃ to the armor; Oṃ, the principle of yoga (yogatattva), vauṣaṭ to the eyes; Oṃ, the principle of all (sarvatattva), phaṭ to the weapon. Thus is the ritual placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa).

Oṃ aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ, *namaḥ* to the heart. Iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ, *svāhā* to the head. Uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ ūṃ, *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock. Eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ, *huṃ* to the armor.
Oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ; vauṣaṭ to the eyes.
Aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aḥ; phaṭ to the weapon. Thus is the *karanyāsa*.
This concludes the *kalpanyāsa*. Oṃ gaṃ; obeisance to Kāśīpīṭha at the heart. Oṃ gaṃ; [obeisance] to Kāñcīpīṭha...
*Oṃ gaṃ*, obeisance to the Madhupurī-pīṭha on the head; *oṃ gaṃ*, obeisance to the Uḍḍīyāna-pīṭha on the crest-lock (*śikhā*);
*oṃ gaṃ*, obeisance to the Ayodhyā-pīṭha on the armor (*kavaca*); *oṃ gaṃ*, obeisance to the Jālandhara-pīṭha on the two eyes;
*oṃ gaṃ*, obeisance to the [Kāmarūpa-]pīṭha on the weapon (*astra*). This is the *pīṭha-nyāsa*. *Oṃ*, obeisance to the heart.

*Hrīṃ* to Gaṇapati, for the head, *svāhā*. *Śrīṃ* O Giver of Excellent Boons, for the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*. *Klīṃ* [make] all people mine, for the armor, *huṃ*. *Glauṃ* bring [them] under control, for the eyes, *vauṣaṭ*. *Gaṃ* *svāhā*, for the weapon, *phaṭ*. Thus is the ritual placement on the hands; this is the ritual placement of the mantras. Having thus performed the ritual placement and meditated upon the Śrīcakra...

Having visualized a square, a sixteen-petaled lotus, an eight-petaled lotus, a ten-spoked wheel, a triangle, and a bindu, and having established [the seat] upon the auspicious pedestal (bhadrapīṭha) with the root mantra, one should perform the worship of the yoga-pīṭha: *hrīṃ maṇḍūkāya namaḥ*;
*hrīṃ kālāgnirudrāya namaḥ*; likewise to Mūlaprakṛti; to Ādhāraśakti.
To Kūrma, to Ananta, to Varāha, to Pṛthivī—having thus worshipped them one above the other, in their center [one should say]:

*hrīṃ*, obeisance to the Ocean of Nectar (*sudhārṇava*). In its center, obeisance to Śvetadvīpa, consisting of nine sections adorned with the nine gems. Therein, in the eight directions beginning with Īśāna...

Homage to the nine sections of jewels in clockwise order! In their center, homage to the section of rubies! In the center, homage to the Golden Mountain! Above, homage to the Nandana grove! In the center, homage to the Kalpa forest! Homage to the lake! Homage to the lotus forest!
Homage to the ground inlaid with various jewels! In its center is a hall fifty-four *yojanas* in extent, provided with a thousand pillars, yet devoid of a central pillar. (p.

In the center, salutation to the jeweled pedestal (*vedikā*) inlaid with nine gems. Above, salutation to the jeweled lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*). Above that, salutation to the lofty white umbrella. In the [four] corners of the throne, starting from the southeast (Agni), [one should offer salutations] such as: "Salutation to Dharma," and so forth. In the [four] directions, starting from the east, [one should offer salutations] such as: "Salutation to Adharma," and so forth. In the middle of the lion-throne...

Salutation to the bulb of bliss (*ānandakanda*). Salutation to the stalk of consciousness (*saṃvinnāla*). Salutation to the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasradalakamala*). Salutation to the petals consisting of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Salutation to the filaments consisting of transformation (*vikṛti*). Salutation to the pericarp (*karṇikā*), which is enriched with the fifty seed-syllables of the letters and is the form of all principles (*sarvatattva*). Above, *aṃ*.
Salutation to the Solar Orb (arkamaṇḍala). Soṃ, salutation to the Lunar Orb (somamaṇḍala). Raṃ, salutation to the Fiery Orb (vahnimaṇḍala).
Taṃ, to Tamas. Raṃ, to Rajas. Saṃ, to Sattva. Hrīṃ Gaṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the Seat of All Mantras (sarvamantrāsana).
Having uttered "Oṃ Aṃ Āṃ" and so forth up to Kṣaṃ, [one worships] Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, and Īśvara.

Having performed the worship of the Yoga-pīṭha with the mantra: *ityādisakalatattvātmane hrīṃ yogapīṭhāya namaḥ*, one should arrange the vessels. On one’s left side, having drawn a yantra consisting of a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square, and having displayed the conch-gesture (*śaṅkhamudrā*), [one should recite]: *gāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *gīṃ śirase* [namaḥ]; *gūṃ* [śikhāyai namaḥ].

*Śikhāyai* (to the tuft of hair), *Gaiṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *Gauṃ* to the eyes (*netra*), *Gaḥ* to the weapon (*astra*) *phaṭ*. Having thus washed the three-legged stand and established it with the root mantra (*mūla*), one should worship it with sandalwood paste and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) using the mantra: *Raṃ* obeisance to the seat of the vessel of Śrī Mahāgaṇapati, belonging to the fire-mandala (*vahnimaṇḍala*) consisting of ten digits (*kalā*). Upon that, [place] the vessel.

Having established it with: *Oṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya dvādaśakalātmane namaḥ śrīmahāgaṇapatyarghyapātrāya namaḥ*, and then having filled it with the root mantra, worship it with perfumes and unbroken rice grains (akṣata), saying: *Oṃ candramaṇḍalāya ṣoḍaśakalātmane namaḥ gaṇapatipātrāya namaḥ*.

Then, having invoked the sacred waters with the mantra: "O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Tāpī, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in this water," one should consecrate it eight times with the root mantra,
worship it with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), cover it with the fish-mudrā (*matsyamudrā*), and protect it by snapping the fingers while reciting *phaṭ*.
Having veiled [the objects] with *hum* and rendered them nectarine with *vam*, and having displayed the *śaṅkha*, *cakra*, *musala*, and *yoni* mudrās,
one should sprinkle the sacrificial materials with that very water while reciting the root mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ paramāmṛtarūpeṇa mahāgaṇapaticandramaṇḍalanivāsāya candrāmṛtena*.

Fill, fill! Purify the substance, purify it twice! Oṃ hrauṃ juṃ saḥ svāhā! With this, one should sprinkle everything. To the north of that, having placed and worshipped the vessels for the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamanīya), and the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and having meditated upon oneself as being of the same nature as Him, [one recites]: Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One.

Having worshipped with the mantra, "Salutation to the Infinite One, whose essence is all qualities and powers, who is the soul of the Yoga-pīṭha," one should invoke the Lord together with His Śakti using the root mantra (mūla-mantra). Having displayed the nine mudrās with the root mantra, performed the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) upon the root mantra, and established the vital breaths (prāṇas),
one should say "Welcome" and offer water for the feet (pādya) and the respectful offering (arghya) with the root mantra.

Having thus performed the rites of water for the feet (*pādya*), the guest-offering (*arghya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and the bath (*snāna*), and having worshipped with the letters of the *mātṛkā*, one should present to them incense (*dhūpa*), lamps (*dīpa*), food offerings (*naivedya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and so forth.

Having offered three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should worship the deities of the Lord’s enclosure (*āvaraṇadevatā*). Having offered a handful of flowers with "Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to the wheel that fulfills all desires (*sarvāśāpūrakacakra*)," [one worships]: "Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Indra" in the east; "3. obeisance to Varuṇa" in the west; "3. obeisance to Dharmarāja" in the south.
"Salutation to Kubera in the north. Having thus worshipped the square [mandala] with scents and unbroken grains (akṣata), this is the first enclosure (āvaraṇa).

Having offered a handful of flowers with the root mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ nandine namaḥ* | 3 | *vīreśāya namaḥ* | 3 | *saubhāgyāya namaḥ* | 3 | *bhṛṅgirīṭine namaḥ* | 3 | *virāṭakāya namaḥ* | 3 | *puṣpadantāya namaḥ* | 3 | *vikartāya namaḥ* | 3 | *antyagaṇāya namaḥ* | 3 | *cittagaṇāya* | 3 |
*Namaḥ*. 3. *Lohitāya namaḥ*. 3. *Sundarāya namaḥ*. 3. *Nūpurāḍhyāya namaḥ*. 3. *Vicārāya namaḥ*. 3. *Ugrarūpāya namaḥ*. 3. *Suptāya namaḥ*. 3. *Vinartakāya namaḥ*.
Thus, having worshipped the sixteen-spoked [cakra] with perfumes and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) in a clockwise direction, the second enclosure is completed. [With] the root mantra.
Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), [recite]: *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ karālāya namaḥ* (3 times); *vikarālāya namaḥ* (3 times);
*saṃhārāya* (3 times); *rurave* (3 times); *mahākālāya* (3 times); *kālāgnaye* (3 times); *sitāsyāya* (3 times); *asitātmane namaḥ*. Thus for the eight petals (*vasudala*).

One should worship with perfumes, unbroken rice, and *dūrvā* grass in a clockwise direction; this is the third enclosure (*tṛtīyāvaraṇa*). Having offered a handful of flowers with the root mantra, [one recites]: *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ vināyakāya namaḥ* (3 times); *vighnarājāya namaḥ* (3 times); *gaṇādhyakṣāya* (3 times); *gajānanāya* (3 times); *herambāya* (3 times); *modakāhārāya* (3 times).
To Dvaimātura, svāhā | 3 | To Arindama, svāhā | 3 | To Ekadanta, svāhā | 3 | Salutation to Vakratuṇḍa.
Thus, one should worship the ten-spoked [wheel] in a clockwise direction with scents, unbroken rice, and dūrvā grass; this is the fourth enclosure (caturthāvaraṇa).

Having offered a handful of flowers with the root mantra (three times), one should worship the triangle with scents, unbroken rice grains, and *dūrvā* grass as follows: "Salutation to Kumāra" in front; "to Jayanta" on the right; "to Pradyumna" on the left.
This is the fifth enclosure (*pañcamāvaraṇa*). Having offered a handful of flowers with the root mantra and having recited the root-vidyā, [one should utter] *hrīṃ*.
One should worship the Bindu seven times with the mantra: "Obeisance to Mahāgaṇapati, together with his own power.

This is the sixth enclosure (ṣaṣṭhāvaraṇa). Mūla-mantra: Hrīṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśa; Hrīṃ, obeisance to Gāṅgeya; Hrīṃ, obeisance to Siṃhāsana; Hrīṃ, obeisance to Vighnāntaka; Hrīṃ, obeisance to Ākhuvāha.
*Namaḥ*. *Hrīṃ*, obeisance to Tripurāntaka. Thus one should worship above with sandalwood paste (*gandha*), unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and *dūrvā* grass;

this is the seventh enclosure (*āvaraṇa*). Above, the root mantra: *Hrīṃ*, obeisance to the hundred-petaled lotus; *Hrīṃ*, obeisance to the thousand-spoked wheel; *Hrīṃ*, obeisance to the row of teeth; *Hrīṃ*, obeisance to the vessel of sweetmeats (*modaka*); *Hrīṃ*, obeisance to the jar of nectar (*sudhā-kalaśa*).
"Oṃ namaḥ hrīṃ to the axe, Oṃ namaḥ hrīṃ to the conch,
Oṃ namaḥ hrīṃ to Pāñcajanya"— what [is gained] by even the mere sight of the conch?
"Furthermore, by touch, sins go to dissolution like snow at the rising of the sun. Thus one should worship in seven ways;

this is the eighth enclosure (*āvaraṇa*). Having recited the root mantra, having performed the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) preceded by the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) with perfumes, unbroken rice, *dūrvā* grass, and flowers, and having meditated upon the deity with the root mantra—

Having worshipped the rosary according to one’s ability, one should recite the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Then, having uttered the root mantra and offered the recitation to the Deity, one should perform the recitation of the *Kavaca*, the *Sahasranāma*, and the *Stavarāja* before the Deity. Regarding the root mantra: from morning until evening, or from evening until morning, whatever I do, O Lord of the Gaṇas, may that be [for Your sake].
"This is your worship. Having thus bowed, one should dismiss the God, together with His Śakti, by means of the Saṃhāra-mudrā.
Thus, O Goddess, one should by all means guard this divine manual of the daily worship of Mahāgaṇapati, which is composed in prose. 1.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual Manual for the Worship of Varada Gaṇeśa," within the *Śrī Devī Rahasya* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
O Great Queen, I shall proclaim to you the armor (kavaca) of the high-souled Gaṇeśa, the bestower of boons, known by the name Vajrapañjara.

Of this *Śrīmahāgaṇapativajrapañjarakavaca*, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Śrī Bhairava, the meter (*chandaḥ*) is Gāyatrī, the deity (*devatā*) is Śrī Mahāgaṇapati, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is Gaṃ, the power (*śakti*) is Hrīṃ, and the pin (*kīlaka*) is Kurukuru.
Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of attaining the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of the Vajra-vidyā and others, in the recitation of the *Mahāgaṇapativajrapañjarakavaca*.
Having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with the mantra beginning with "gām" and so forth, one should meditate. The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
[one should contemplate] Vighneśa, who is worshipped by the universe, possessed of vast fame, and expert in the protection of the world.

I bow to Vighnarāja, the son of Pārvatī’s life-breath, who possesses a noble mind that directly pacifies all calamities; he who is generally worshipped by the lords of all Asuras, along with hosts of gods, sages, and practitioners; and who, through his compassion, pacifies obstacles and immeasurable fears. (2)
Oṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Gaṃ: May the Lord Mahāgaṇapati protect my head;
may Vināyaka protect my forehead, and Vighnarāja my eyebrows.
May the Lord of the Gaṇas protect my eyes; may the Elephant-faced one protect my nose; may Heramba protect my ears; and may the Eater of Sweetmeats protect my cheeks. (4)
May Dvaimātura protect my face, and may Arindama protect my lips;
may Ekadanta protect my teeth, and may Vakratuṇḍa protect my tongue. || 5 ||
May Gāṅgeya protect my throat; may Siṃhāsana protect my shoulders;
may Vighnāntaka protect my arms; and may Mūṣakavāhana protect my hands.
May the divine destroyer of Tripura protect my thighs forever;
may Kumāra Jayanta protect my heart and both my sides.
May Pradyumna protect my back; may the son of Śaṅkara protect my navel; may the host of Nandin protect my hips; and may Vīreśvara protect my penis.
May Saubhāgya protect my penis, and Bhṛṅgirīṭī my private parts;
may Virāṭaka protect my thighs, and Puṣpadantaka my knees.
May Vikarta protect my calves; may Antyagaṇa protect my two ankles;
may Cittagaṇa protect my feet; and may Lohita protect the area below my feet.
May Sundara, adorned with anklets, protect my feet and back;
may Vicāra protect my belly, and may Ugrarūpaka protect my vital organs.
May the Lord of the sleeping hosts protect the body from the head down to the feet;
may the Dancing One protect the body from the feet up to the head.
May Gaṇeśa always protect that place which has been forgotten.
May Karāla protect me in the east, and Vikarālaka in the southeast. (13) p. 141)
May Saṃhāra protect me in the south; may Rurubhairava protect me in the southwest;
may Mahākāla protect me in the west; and may Kālāgnibhairava protect me in the northwest. || 14 ||
May he with the white face protect me in the north; may he whose nature is dark protect me in the northeast.
May the hundred-petaled one protect me at dawn, and may the thousand-spoked one protect me at midday.
May the row of teeth protect me at the end of the day; may the alms-bowl always protect me by night;
may the water-pot protect me at midnight, and likewise the axe at the end of the night.
May the pair of conchs protect my body everywhere and at all times!

Oṃ oṃ, may they protect me in the royal court; ha hauṃ, in the fear of battle; hrīṃ hrīṃ, in gambling with dice; avatāt, may they protect me; śrīṃ śrīṃ, in the house of enemies; śa śauṃ, in the fear of water; klīṃ klīṃ, may they protect me in the depths of the forest.

Glauṃ glūṃ glaiṃ glaṃ guṃ! May Gaṇeśa protect me constantly from fear of beings, from the afflictions of great diseases, and from yakṣas, piśācas, bhūtas, and serpents—glauṃ ga gauṃ glauṃ gaṃ! || 17 ||
Thus, this secret armor of the great-souled Gaṇeśa, named Vajrapañjara, is hidden within all tantras. (18)
The mental [form] is a constituent part, consisting of mind and being the sole means for all conduct;
without this, there can be no success in worship or recitation. (19)
Therefore, O Great Goddess, one should always recite or wear this meritorious armor; for him, success in the world beyond is held in the palm of his hand.
Whatever desire one may long for, one attains it by reciting this;
if one recites it constantly at midnight, one shall obtain the fruit of all one's wishes.
Thus, O Supreme Goddess, one should protect this secret and excellent armor, which is dear to Mahāgaṇapati, divine, and consisting of all accomplishments. 22.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Mahāgaṇapati Kavaca," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrī Devī Rahasya*.
142) Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to my secret which was previously indicated by me;
out of devotion for you and Gaṇeśa, I shall declare the Thousand Names.
Śrī Devī said:
O Blessed One, my heart yearns with great eagerness to hear the thousand names of the high-souled Gaṇanātha, the bestower of boons.
Śrī Bhairava said: O Śivā, at the time of my destruction of Tripura, families of obstacles arose before me;
all of them, arrogant in their strength, were deluded by infatuation, and their minds were bewildered.
Then, having praised the Lord, the Chief of the Gaṇas, with thousands of names, the obstacles fled far away, like living beings before Kālarudra. || 4 ||
O Goddess, by his grace I was born as the destroyer of Tripura;
even today, I praise that Lord of the Gaṇas with a thousand names.
Today, out of devotion to you and for the benefit of practitioners,
I shall proclaim the divine thousand names of Mahāgaṇapati.
This Thousand Names of the Mantra bestows happiness and prosperity upon readers and donors, and removes suffering for those who hear it. (7)
For this mantra of the *Śrīvaradagaṇeśasahasranāmastotra*, Śrī Bhairava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandaḥ*),
Śrī Mahāgaṇapati is the deity (*devatā*), *gaṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *kuru 2* is the pin (*kīlaka*).
Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa during the recitation of the Thousand-Name Hymn, as before.
Meditation (p. 143):
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ, Gaṇādhyakṣa, glauṃ gaṃ, Gaṇapati Guṇin.
He who is beyond qualities yet possesses them, the protector, the elephant-faced one, and the source of light.
The Lord of All, the radiant one, the illuminator, the wise one, the wealthy one;
eternally peaceful, the protector of the world, Viṣvaksena, the maker of light. || 9 ||
He is trustworthy, victorious, a physician, and the unsurpassed ocean;
he is subtler than the subtle, all-pervading, most excellent, the eldest, fond of hymns, and the preceptor.
The creator of the world, the sustainer of the world, the nourisher of the universe, and the treasure-house of the world;
the Lord whose limbs are adorned with yellow [garments], who has red eyes and wears crimson robes. || 11 ||
Virūpākṣa, dwelling in his celestial chariot, is disciplined, possessed of policy, and happy;
he is handsome, virtuous, truthful, pure, and the delighter of Śaṅkara.
Nandīśvara is eternally blissful, worthy of praise and hymns, and discerning;
he is the crusher of the Daityas, intoxicated with pride, and his eyes are reddened by wine.
He whose essence is the core, the essence of the universe, who moves through the universe, the ointment;
the supreme Brahman, the supreme light, the witness, the three-eyed one, the boastful. || 14 ||
Vīreśvara, the destroyer of heroes, the possessor of good fortune, the increaser of fortune; Bhṛṅgirīṭī, adorned with a garland of bees, resounding with the humming of bees. || 15 ||
The destroyer of the seasons, the leader, the delighter of Vinatā, the honored one;
the son of Vinatā, he whose body is bowed, the leader of the universe, the remover of obstacles. || 16 ||
Virāṭaka and Virāṭa, Vidagdha, and Vidhi who is self-born;
Puṣpadanta, Puṣpahārī, and he who is adorned with a garland of flowers. || 17 ||
The one whose arrow is the flower, the crusher, the nourished, the cutter, the wielder of the knife;
the final one, the end-maker, the host of the mind, and the remover of mental anxiety. || 18 ||
He is inconceivable and of inconceivable form; he is the one with matted hair like sandalwood;
he is marked, red, and erased; he has blood-red eyes and is the one who causes detachment. || 19 ||
One whose disposition is greedy, who delights in greed, who bestows gain, whose body is inviolable,
who is beautiful, the son of Sundarī, and the slayer of all asuras. (20)
Nūpurāḍhya bestows prosperity; Naro is Nārāyaṇa and Ravi;
Vicārī bestows what has been vomited; Vāgmī is Vitarkī and Vijayeśvara. || 21 ||
He is the sleeping one, the awakened one, whose form is eternal; he is the bestower of happiness, who is served by bliss;
he is the transformer, the mover through the sky, the destroyer, the dancer, and the actor.
He is the drama, the lover of drama, the infinite sound, and the one whose nature consists of infinite qualities;
he is the universal form, the destroyer of the universe, the one whose mouth is Vinatā, and the dancer. || 23 ||
Karāla, Kāmada, Kānta, Kamanīya, Kalādhara,
Karuṇyarūpa, Kuṭila, Kulācārī, and Kuleśvara. || 24 ||
The formidable one, the best of the hosts, the destroyer, adorned with necklaces;
he whose face is beautiful like a ruru deer, the red one, the beloved of Revatī, the aesthetic essence (rasa). || 25 ||
Mahākāla, with great fangs, the dispeller of fear from the great serpents;
possessing a mad appearance, he is the fire of time (Kālāgni), with the fire, sun, and moon as his eyes. || 26 ||
White-faced, wearing white garlands, with a white staff and white rays;
he is the dark-souled Lord of the Terrible, the fortunate, the Blessed One, and the possessor of fortune.
The son of Bhṛgu, the abode of fortune, the giver of fortune, the increaser of fortune;
the maker of auspiciousness, the pure, the peaceful, the most excellent, the one worthy of being heard, the lord of Śacī. || 28 ||

He is the source of the Vedas, the author of the Vedas, and that which is to be known through the Vedas; he is the eternal one, the bestower of knowledge, the essence of the Vedas, the follower of the Vedas, and one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.

Delighting in the sound of the Vedas, the Hero, the Supreme, the knower of the meaning of the Vedas and Agamas—[these are his three names]. He is the knower of reality, all-pervading, the Holy One, the Compassionate, [the analysis of the names ends with "consisting of Being"]. He is both Being and Non-being. || 30 ||
Free from disease, formless, fearless, and bearing an eternal form;
free from enmity yet the destroyer of enemies, he resembles a rutting elephant. (31)
The bringer of auspiciousness, the son of Śiva, Śiva himself, the increaser of happiness;
the pure one, the white one, the hundred-faced, the charming one, and he whose food is sweetmeats. || 32 ||
The god of gods, the maker of day, the steadfast, the radiant, the sustainer; the pure-souled one, possessed of pure intellect, of pure luster, and of holy vows.
He is the refuge, the descendant of Śunaka, the hero, the bearer of the autumnal lotus;
he is the child, beloved by the one whose vehicle is the peacock, the cool one, and the favorite of Śaṅkara. || 34 ||
Śaṅkara is free from worldly existence, eternal, the cause of dissolution, and intent on the dance;
he is the one who has transcended, who revels in the joy of play, the playful one, the wandering one, and the delusion itself.
The wanderer, the moon-bearer, the sun, Saturn, the son of the Earth, the Awakened One, the one served by the gods, the king of the wise, and the sustainer of strength. || 36 ||
He is the living soul, the giver of life, the victorious, the one worthy of praise, the one worthy of hymns, and the lover of prostrations;
he is the progenitor, the knower of the path of the Jinas, and the establisher of the path of the Jinas. || 37 ||
The son of Gaurī, the teacher, the one without sound, the fair-limbed one, the one worshipped by elephants;
the supreme state, the supreme abode, the Supreme Self, the poet, the son of the Earth. (38)
Rāhu, the severer of the head of the Daitya; Ketu, adorned with golden earrings;
the lord of planets, who is to be grasped and who has grasped others; the leader, resounding with a deep, rumbling roar. (39)
Parjanya, Pīvara, Potrī, Pīnavakṣas, Parārjita, Vanecara, Vanapati, Vanavāsa, and Smaropama. || 40 ||

He is merit, the pure, and the purifier; he is the Supreme Self, whose form is complete. He has the appearance of a crescent full moon; he is wrath, and he whose desires are fulfilled. He is the soul of the ages, the sustainer of the ages, and the sacrificer. (300)
He is the performer of sacrifice, the lover of sacrifice;
he is glorious, beloved by those who offer sacrifices, the wielder of the thunderbolt, and the one whose very armor is the thunderbolt.
Maṇibhadra, made of jewels, venerable, and resting upon the Fish-bannered One (Kāmadeva).
He whose banner is the fish, the captivator of the mind, who increases the yoga of yogins. || 43 ||
The Seer, the Creator, the Ascetic, the Embodied One, the Lover of Ascetics; consisting of austerity, the Embodiment of Austerity, the Sun, and He whose Wealth is Austerity. || 44 ||
Rucaka, Mocaka, Ruṣṭa, Tuṣṭa, Tomaradhāraka, Daṇḍin, Caṇḍāṃśu, Avyakta, Kamaṇḍaludhara, and Anagha. || 45 ||
He is the lover, the one intent on action, Time, the boar, and he whose roar resounds through the quarters of the horizon;
he is the one who causes wandering, the one honored by all classes, the destroyer of dullness, and the slayer of the ignorant.
Jālandhara, the dweller of the world, the causer of laughter, the one who is to be invoked, the oblation;
the possessor of the oblation, the axle of the fire that carries the oblation, the golden one, and the one with golden armlets. || 47 ||
Sumeru, Himavat, Hotṛ, Haraputra, Halaṅkaṣa, Hālāpriya, Hṛdāśānta, and Kāntāhṛdayapoṣaṇa. || 48 ||
The dryer, the destroyer of afflictions, the fierce, the harsh, the one of hard form;
the leader, the embodiment of wisdom, the meditator, the object of meditation, the wise, the treasure-house of compassion. || 49 ||
The most distant, the subduer, the dweller in heaven, the giver, the protector, the white one, the even one;
the one who has gone forth, the leader of the community, the accessible, the unconquerable, the matted-haired one, and the ageless. || 50 ||
The life-force of all beings, the conqueror of enemies, pervading the universe and consisting of the universe;
resembling gold, beginningless, with eyes as broad as lotuses. (51)
He is the illuminator, the liberator, the counselor, and the one who rests upon ten million mantras;
he consists of the five elements, possesses five arrows, and has five faces. || 52 ||
The fifth is the last, the first; he is full, with disheveled hair, and has a crooked arm. He possesses a hard heart, is adorned by his neck, and has a graceful disposition.
Lolacitta (Fickle-minded), Bṛhannāsa (Large-nosed), Māsa-pakṣa-ṛtu-rūpavān (Possessing the forms of months, fortnights, and seasons)—these are his three names.
Dhruva (Stable), Drutagati (Swift-moving), Dharmya (Righteous), Dharmī (Virtuous), Nākipriya (Beloved by gods), and Anala (Fire). || 54 ||

Agastya, who has swallowed the world; the sole remover of the world’s impurity; the ocean; one whose path is heaven; the one with beautiful eyes; the blissful; and the one honored by the virtuous. (55)

The husband of Satī, he who is of equal flavor (samarasa), Sanaka, the straightforward one, the divine being, the beloved of the gods, the lord of wealth, Vāsava, and he who is worshipped by the Vasus. || 56 ||
The giver of wealth and the lord of wealth, the bestower of riches upon the wealthy;
the king with eyes like lotus petals, the giver of memory, and he who has the Kṛttikās as his garment.
He is the son of the Aśvins, horse-faced, radiant, the sustainer, and fond of the Bharaṇī asterism;
he sits upon Kṛttikā, is a boar, and wears sandals made of Rohiṇī. || 58 ||
He who is beloved by the R̥bhus, the crusher of enemies, the one who fascinates Rohiṇī, the nectar, the king of beasts, Mṛgaśiras, Mādhava, and the one with the sweet voice. || 59 ||
With a moist face, great intelligence, and adorned with great serpents;
he who bestows power with a mere contraction of his eyebrows, yet is formidable with his brows, is Maya once again.
Again he is Deva, again the Conqueror, again the Living One, and Punarvasu;
he is Tittiri, Timiketu, and the slayer of Timicāraka. || 61 ||
Tiṣya, Tulādhara, Jambhya, Viśleṣa, Aśleṣa, Eṇarāj, Mānada, Mādhava, Māgha, Vācāla, and Maghavopama. || 62 ||
Medhya, Maghāpriya, Megha, Mahāmuṇḍa, Mahābhuja, Pūrvaphālgunika, Sphīta, Phalgu, and Uttaraphālguna. || 63 ||
Phenila, Brahmada, Brahmā, the refuge of the sevenfold sacrifice (saptatantu), Ghoṇāhasta, Caturhasta, Hastivaktra, and Halāyudha. || 64 ||
Citrāmbara, whose feet are worshipped; he who has tasted the body of Svāti;
Viśākha, who is served by the peacock; and the uterine brother of Śikhidhvaja. || 65 ||
Aṇu, Reṇu, Kalāsphāra, Anūrū, Reṇusuta, Nara, Anūrādhāpriya, Rādhya, Śrīmān, Śukla, and Śucismita. (66)
Jyeṣṭha, whose feet are honored by the most excellent, is the root and the teacher of the three worlds;
Śuci, Pūrva, as well as Āṣāḍha and Uttarāṣāḍha are the Lord (Īśvara). (67)
He is worthy of being heard, the infinite self of the Abhijit constellation, the sacred revelation that causes the Dānavas to tremble;
he is the month of Śrāvaṇa, the act of hearing, the hearer, the wealthy one, the possessor of merit, and the lord of the Dhaniṣṭhā constellation.
Śātātapa, Śātakumbha, Śatañjyotis, and Śatabhiṣaj;
Bhadra is Pūrvābhādrapada, and [the one] from Uttarābhādrapadā [is] Uttara. || 69 ||
Rāma, the son of Reṇukā; Revatīramaṇa, the delightful one;
Aśviyuk; the beloved of Kārttikeya; Mārgaśīrṣa; and the best of deer (Mṛgottama). || 70 ||
Puṣyaśaurya, Phālgunātman, Vasanta, Citraka, Madhu, Rājyada, Abhijidātmīya, Tāreśa, and Tārakadyuti. (71)
He is the well-known, the abandoned, the delighted, the supreme, the highest, the beneficial;
he is the destroyer of the enemy, the one consisting of the five elements, the five winds, the worshipful, and the supreme light.
He is the knower of the Purāṇas and Āgamas, the one worthy of this pair of names, the buffalo, the donkey, the leader;
the crocodile, the ram, the bull, the dull-witted, the god of love, and he who is worshipped by the twins.

The one who bears lime (or is full of impurity) is the Kaṭaka; the wretched one is the Markaṭa; the crab is the Karkaṭa; the one full of loathing is the Kukkuṭa; the forest-born one is the Haṃsa; the supreme swan is the Parahaṃsa; and the jackal is the Śṛgālaka. || 74 ||

The lion, the one seated on a lion-throne, the rat, the deluder, the one whose vehicle is a mouse; (600) the giver of sons, the savior from hell, the one pleased by virgins, the upholder of the lineage. || 75 ||
Of incomparable form, the giver of strength, the bearer of the scales, the witness of equality;
the wielder of the bow with its string of bees, the tortoise, the sea-monster, and the jewel. (76)
He is steadfast, the Lord, the performer of great deeds, the possessor of great enjoyments, and of great fame;
he assumes the form of the Vasus, is ever-active, the destroyer of the Asuras, and the end-maker of Yama.
The leader of the gods, the presiding lord of the hosts, the lotus-eyed one of great intelligence;
adorned with armlets and earrings, he is fond of devotion and the increaser of his devotees.
The bestower of lordship over the Gaṇas, a master of illusion, one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāntas;
the son of Kātyāyanī, worshipped by Brahmā, the destroyer of obstacles. (79)
The destroyer of the fear of saṃsāra, broad-chested, the upholder of the earth; the ender of obstacles, large-necked, and exceedingly delighted by sweetmeats. || 80 ||

He who loves Vārāṇasī, the proud one, the dense one, the one whose vehicle is a rat; he who dwells in caves, the son of the daughter of Viṣṇu (Gaṅgā), the bestower of stations, and the eternal. || 81 ||
Content with the prosperity of others, stainless, wearing a crown, beloved by his dear ones, fond of the fourteenth lunar day, venerable, industrious, and full of self-confidence. 82.
Inconceivable, seated upon a pair of lions, assuming the form of a child;
steadfast, the best among the powerful, and endowed with great strength. || 83 ||
The physician who is the soul of all, the benefactor, the one of vast belly and great intelligence;
he is the instrument that takes away death and turns back the multitude of sins. (84)

The breaker-through, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the slayer of the great Daityas, the protector of the distressed; he who moves among spirits, he who moves among ghosts, whose form is intelligence, and who is composed of mind. || 85 ||
The Sāṃkhya Puruṣa has the form of ego (ahaṅkāra) and consists of the three guṇas;
he is the self of the elements in the form of the subtle elements (tanmātras), the self of the senses, and the subduer. 86.
For he stands outside the three impurities and is devoid of the three states;
he is formless and yet possesses many forms, being a Kinnara with the prowess of a Naga.
He who has a single tusk, possesses great speed, is the commander of the army, and the lord of the thirty gods;
he is the creator of the universe, the seed of the universe, prosperity, wealth, splendor, fortitude, and intelligence. (88)
The wind, which causes all things to wither, is subtle in form and perfectly still;
it is the destroyer, the creator, and the sustainer, resting in dissolution. || 89 ||
He whose form is universal is designated as the Atharva-śiras;
he who consumes the Yajus is the seer of the Ṛks; he is the author of poetry, the maker of phonetics, and the knower of etymology.
The foremost one assumes the form of Śeṣa and partakes of the nature of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman);
he is possessed of discernment, bears the conch, and is devoted to the vow of truth. (91)
He is of great austerity and terrible asceticism, the giver of all, possessed of fearsome prowess;
he bestows all prosperity, is all-pervading, and bears a voice as deep as a thundercloud.

Prosperous, the bestower of fortune, an enjoyer of pleasures, a lord, and affectionate toward Śaṅkara; devoted to devotion for Śambhu, he is the giver of liberation and the forest fire that consumes worldly existence. || 93 ||

He whose austerity is truth, whose form is the object of meditation, who is the great embodiment of action, who is both the collective and the individual, and who turns away from the five sheaths— [these are his two names].
He is the treasury of splendor, the embodiment of the universe, the bearer of the bodies of all moving and unmoving beings;
he is the giver of life, the embodiment of knowledge, the imperishable one endowed with the form of sound.
The state of the Taijasa [being] arises from Bhūtādi; it is partless, stainless, immutable, conscious, Rudra, the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), the Puruṣa, and the wise one. || 96 ||
Though without support and without form, he is the sustainer and faces in every direction;
his body is beyond the reach of logic, he is the younger brother of Skanda, the sun of great radiance.

The destroyer of sacrifice, the performer of sacrifice, the bestower of the fruits of sacrifices, the protector of sacrifice, the embodiment of sacrifice, and the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice. || 98 ||
He has a curved trunk and a massive body, with a radiance equal to ten million suns;
he has a single tusk, is dark-brown in hue, formidable, and smoke-colored.
Ṭaṅkadhārī, Jambuka, Nāyaka, Śūrpakarṇaka, Suvarṇagarbha, Sumukha, Śrīkara, and Sarvasiddhida. || 100 ||

Golden-hued, with limbs of gold, the Great-Souled One has the complexion of sandalwood; he is well-limbed, with beautiful eyes, the joy of Śatānanda, and his form is the delight of the world. || 101 ||
Indra, Viṣṇu, the smoke-bannered Vahni, the worshipful Destroyer of Demons, the Bliss of Fulfillment, the Supreme Bliss, and the Ancient Puruṣottama. || 102 ||
(151) Holding a water-pot, possessing a jar, being humpbacked, and well-satiated with fish and meat;
consisting of the zodiac signs, lunar mansions, and planets, and having the form of the lunar days—[these are his three names]—the All-pervading Lord of the World. 103.
He is majestic, beloved of the path of truth, and the second [fire] established in non-duality;
he is the third fire possessing three forms, whose form is the triple Veda and whose body is the triple Veda.
The Lord is the beloved of the fourth [tithi], the one who has gone to the further shore, the one whose roar is the fifth [tithi];
he is the taster of the six flavors, the unborn, the sixth [tithi], and the sixty-year cycle. (105)
He whose course is the seven oceans, the essence, the lord of the seventh, who is sought after; the delighter of the eighth, free from affliction, and permeated by devotion to the ninth. (106)
He is worshipped by the lords of the ten directions; he is the tenth, the swiftest Brahmā;
he is the eleven-fold self, the lord of the Gaṇas, and he is honored by the pair of the twelfth.
He who is praised by the thirteen Manus, who is dear to the fourteen gods, who is extolled by the fourteen Indras, and whose form is the bliss of the full moon. 108.
He is the new moon and the full moon, as well as the vision [of truth]; he is the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and the lord of sages;
he is silent and sweet-spoken; he is the root and the embodied one whose vehicle is the cloud.
The great elephant, the conqueror of anger, the vanquisher of enemies, the refuge of victory; the fierce one, the beloved of Rudra, the golden-hued, the son of Rudra, the scorcher of sin. || 110 ||

He who loves existence, who is beloved by Bhavānī, the bearer of the burden, the creator of beings, skilled in the art of music, the unimpeded, the one beyond the three guṇas (Vaikuṇṭha), and he who is served by Viṣṇu. || 111 ||
The slayer of Vṛtra, the destroyer of obstacles, the ploughman, the remover of all misfortunes; the charming one, the cleanser, the intoxicated, the son of Durgā, and the slow-moving. || 112 ||
The Hero, who is an infinite stream of the nectar of consciousness, whose sole accomplishment is valor, whose crown-jewel is radiant, and who possesses a network of tinkling bells; || 113 ||
Trunk-holder, moving-snout, earring-wearer, garlanded-with-shaven-heads;
lotus-eyed, lotus-handed, and worshipped by Padmanābha. (114)
Udgītha was adorned with ornaments consisting of garlands rich with human teeth;
Nārada was an elephant with flickering ears and ears like winnowing baskets. || 115 ||
He whose nose is filled with a great radiance pervades the entire circle of the three worlds;
he sustains life by bestowing grace upon those wandering within the circle of the earth.
The wind arising from the edges of his broad ears fanned the horizons,
while the roar from his vast mouth overwhelmed the entire formidable vessel of the universe.
He caused the seven netherworlds to tremble by the treading of his massive feet;
he was languid with the aesthetic flavor of joy arising from the exceedingly fierce roar produced by his great tusks.
With all his weapons held in his massive hands, he had conquered the dānavas;
his face was glowing with vermilion, and his eyes were blazing fires of radiant splendor. || 119 ||
Resounding with the tinkling of anklets set with glittering gems,
it was filled with droplets from the waters of rivers rich with flowing currents.
The lotuses of whose feet are worshipped by throngs of wandering elephants, and who is adored by the gods led by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahārudra. || 121 ||
He was attended by a multitude of serpents beginning with Aśeṣa and Śeṣa;
the surface of the earth and the sky were filled with the roars of the five-faced lions he had summoned.
His mind was utterly bewildered by the extremely fierce cries of "Hā! Hā!
and "Hūhū!", and his body was consecrated with mantras enriched by the seed-syllables of fifty letters.

The surface of the earth was flooded by the streams of nectar from the Vedānta scriptures, while the regions from the netherworld (Pātāla) up to the heavens were pervaded by the sound of conch shells. || 124 ||
He was a wish-fulfilling gem, a great wrestler, Bali with a spear in hand, and the Kali age;
he caused the three worlds to shine with the splendor of the Kṛta and Tretā Yugas.
The Dvāpara age is the moon for the darkness of actions pertaining solely to the next world;
its body is sprinkled with nectar, pervading the very shell of the cosmic egg and beyond.
(153) Blazing with rows of letters from the initial *a* to the final *kṣa*, it resounds with the loud, resonant chanting of the vowels *a* and *ā*. || 127 ||
He is intent on the circling of the rosary enriched by the mantras *ikāra* and *ekāra*;
he wears as a sacred thread a formidable serpent vomiting forth the syllables *ukāra* and *okāra*.
Marked by the vowel ṛ, it blazes with two lotuses of the letter ṛ;
joined with the letter ḷ, it fills the quarters of space with the conch of the letter ḷ.
He is expert in drinking from the breasts of the Mountain-Daughter (Girijā), which are the letters *e* and *ai*;
he is weary of the sequence of creation performed by Viśva and others, which are the letters *o* and *au*.
The circle of his head and the rest of his body was pervaded by the series of vowels and consonants;
he drove away the gods with the exceedingly loud sound of the wind produced by the flapping of his ears.
His feet were reddened by the crest-jewels of the crowns of the lords of birds;
his ears were intent upon the songs of all the proud gandharvas.
Worshipped by the gods led by Ghanavāhana and Vāgīśa,
he possesses a single tusk that shines, enriched by streams of the nectar of the letter *ṅa*.
His beautiful body is smeared with a paste of moon-like saffron;
his face is adorned with a crown enriched by jewels, a parasol, and chowries. || 134 ||
It was resplendent with rows of highly precious jewels bound within his matted locks,
and it resounded with the humming songs of swarms of bees.
His mallet was filled with the blood of the Daityas brought down by the letter *ña*;
his entire mass of hair trembled from tasting the fruit of the axe.
He is delighted by the joy of the letters ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, and dha;
he is a bearer of the nectar-stream of the syllable ṇa, like a cloud bearing ambrosia. || 137 ||
His forehead possesses the luster of a mass of vermilion as rich as molten copper;
he has gratified the assembly of twice-born brahmins with rows of wealth [represented by] the letter *tha*.
He who holds within the lotus of his heart, which consists of compassion, the entire mandala of the three worlds;
he whose lotus feet are served by the great yakṣas, such as Dhanada and others. (139)
He is adorned by the jewels in the crowns of the entire multitude of gods who have bowed before him;
he is skilled in severing the path to the higher realms, liberation, and other such goals for those belonging to the opposing side.
Adorned with a circle of necks encircled by hoods and wheels, he terrifies the gods and asuras with his pair of knitted brows, fierce and formidable. || 141 ||
The sole moon that increases the joy of Bhavānī’s heart, whose single lotus-hand is formidable with a full jar of wine; 142.
He had prepared his weapons for the destruction of the host that obstructed the sacrifice;
he increased the splendor and fame of the beloved of the daughter of the ocean.
With a large belly and a most formidable body that struck terror into the asuras, he was honored by the worship performed by the guardians of the directions, such as Varuṇa and the others. || 144 ||
He increases the joy of the eyes through his singular love for the beloved Śaṅkara,
and he is skilled in the singing and chanting of songs composed in the sixteen musical scales (svaritas).
He is the pilot’s boat for crossing over the ocean of all miserable states of existence;
he is the reciter of the hymns of Śiva and others, as well as the *Brahma-gītā* and other sacred texts. || 146 ||
He whose lotus-heart is filled with forbearance protects all things moving and unmoving;
his radiant form is the singular embodiment of the syllables of the mantra marked by the Tārā.
His body is adorned with the Vidyā-mantra beginning with the letter 'A' and ending with the letter 'Kṣa'.
Oṃ Śrīṃ Vināyaka, Oṃ Hrīṃ Vighnādhyakṣa, Lord of the Gaṇas. || 148 ||
Airāvata is the eater of sweetmeats; Vakratuṇḍa is remembered as the Creator (Brahmā).
He is celebrated in the Vedānta as the seeker of knowledge, and his pure mantra is the six-syllabled one.
The god Gaṇeśa, the giver of boons, is consecrated with the twelve-syllable mantra;
his entire body is consecrated with the seven crores of great mantras. || 150 ||
The son of Gaṅgā, served by the hosts, Oṃ Śrīṃ Dvaimātura Śiva;
Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ Glauṃ Gaṃ, the Lord Mahāgaṇapati. (1000) || 151 ||
(155) This thousand names of Mahāgaṇapati is remembered as secret, most secret, hidden, and concealed within all the tantras. (152)
This divine treasury of all mantras, which destroys all obstacles, consists of the planets and stars, and is endowed with rows of colors representing the zodiac signs. || 153 ||
It consists of all branches of knowledge, is the means for attaining Brahman, is dear to practitioners, is the very essence of Gaṇeśa, and is the secret of the gods.
It bestows desired fruits in this world, fulfills all heart's desires, consists of the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi), is the goal to be attained, and grants victory to practitioners. 155.

Without worship, without fire-offerings, without ritual placement, and without recitation, the means for attaining the eight supernatural powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā) is through mere remembrance. || 156 ||
On the fourth lunar day, at midnight, the mantra-practitioner should recite [this] at a crossroads;
O Goddess, he should write this meritorious *Nāmasahasra* on birch bark under the sun.
One should wear it on the fourteenth day at midday, either on the head or on the arm;
a woman, having bound it on her left hand, and a man on his right arm. (158)
One may even paralyze Brahmā, delude Śaṅkara, bring the three worlds under one's control, and slay all enemies. || 159 ||
One may cause the arrows of speech to be eradicated and pacify Dhanañjaya;
a barren woman shall quickly obtain sons, and one who is destitute shall attain wealth. 160.
O Śivā, O Goddess, he who recites this three times at night before Gaṇeśa—
whether naked or accompanied by his consort (Śakti)— shall enjoy all desired pleasures.
The best of practitioners shall behold Gaṇeśa, the granter of boons, directly, he who recites this thousand names with devotion. (162)
One who desires wealth and other riches, a wife, long life, and prosperity should always recite the Thousand Names in battle, in times of fear of kings, or at gambling. (163)
One attains victory everywhere through the grace of Gaṇeśa. (p.
156) Thus, this thousand names of the mantra is the entirety of merit. 164.
The secret of Mahāgaṇapati is to be guarded like one's own womb.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Thousand Names of Mahāgaṇapati," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrī Devī Rahasya*.
Now begins the thirtieth chapter.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Supreme Lord, please tell us truly the most excellent hymn of praise for the root mantra of the all-pervading Mahāgaṇapati.
The illustrious Bhairava said:

I shall proclaim the hymn of Mahāgaṇapati, which reveals the ultimate reality; when recited before the Lord at the body of a living being, it bestows liberation while living (jīvanmukti) swiftly in the Kali age.
Of this hymn to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati, Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ),
the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati is the deity (devatā), Gaṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Hrīṃ is the power (śakti), Kuru kuru is the pin (kīlaka),
and the application (viniyoga) is for the recitation of the King of Hymns to Mahāgaṇapati with the desire for liberation while living (jīvanmukti). Meditation (dhyāna):
Meditate upon Gaṇeśa, whose limbs are adorned with two, four, and fourteen colors, who has the moon, sun, and fire as his three eyes, the lord of the gods,
whose neck is decorated with serpents, and who is rotating a rosary at his heart.
O Lord, that supreme practitioner who constantly recites at night, by day, and at the break of dawn the *tāra* chanted by Nārada— the primordial mantra— in a charnel house or an empty temple;

His celestial courtesans, whose lotus-faces are ever smiling and radiant with the pride of their beauty, become submissive to him every day; likewise, all the kings on earth in the three worlds come under his sway. || 4 ||
When one recites the beloved mantra of Gaṇanātha a full hundred thousand times,
he shines upon this earth with his lotus feet gleaming upon the heads of all sovereigns.
And for one who, free from desire for wealth, meditates in his heart upon Kamalā as she stands in the midst of the gods,
by the power of your mantra, Kamalā shall then become firmly established in his home.
O Gaṇeśa, he who, afflicted by love, incessantly recites Your mantra in his heart,
becomes like a bee at the lotus-face of Urvaśī, drinking the nectar of the pollen of her lower lip.
He who, with devotion, recites the mantra of Gaṇanātha at night in a deserted house with his hair disheveled,
shall conquer enemies equal to Indra in battle and attain the sovereignty of a universal monarch.
O All-pervading Lord, if a practitioner recites the mantra beginning with the syllable *Śiva* within the forest grounds in the presence of Śiva,
he shall indeed wander through the world of moving and non-moving beings in a celestial chariot as a sovereign over the entire circle of immortals.

He who mutters, worships, hears, or recites the root mantra beginning with "Gaṇapataye" is saluted by the Gaṇas, Kinnaras, Siddhas, Suras, and Asuras, and he attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas (Gāṇapatya). || 10 ||
Whoever constantly recites this mantra, "O Bestower of Boons, grant me boons," whether by night or by day,
in their mouth dwells Sarasvatī, in their home dwells Lakṣmī, and in their heart dwells devotion to you.
Those who recite the king of mantras, "sarva janaṃ me," at the conclusion of their meal,
enjoy pastimes with celestial beauties among the trees of Nandana, such as sandalwood and others.

"O Blessed One, if one recites [this mantra] while burning with the heat of passion, thinking 'bring her under my control,' even Urvaśī, the daughter of the Kinnaras and ever-skilled in amorous arts, will come under one's power. (13)
One should mutter this pair of mantra-syllables, "svāhā," at the end of the day and even at times such as meals;
all diseases will quickly go to their dissolution, just as darkness vanishes when the sun has risen. (14)

Those who meditate upon him with three eyes, resembling fire, holding a lotus in his hand, resembling the moon, and bearing another pair of conchs— they depart for heaven, traveling in celestial chariots. (15)

O All-pervading Lord, those who meditate upon you of praiseworthy form— intent on the protection of the three worlds— in the center of the Bindu, Triangle, Ten-spoked Wheel, Eight-spoked Wheel, Sixteenth Part, Four Vedas, and Hermitages;
