having conquered the earth and enjoyed it along with their vast hosts of attendants, they eventually go to you, O Lord of the Gaṇas.
Your state, O Lord, is difficult to attain even for the gods and asuras.
Thus, one should daily recite, read, or listen with devotion to this supreme hymn of Gaṇapati, which consists of mantras and contains all secrets;
such a person quickly attains wealth, fortune, long life, and sons in this world, and becomes liberated while living and goes to heaven in the hereafter.
He is the practitioner. || 17 ||
Thus, O Goddess, this supreme hymn of the Great Gaṇapati is the highest;
it is always to be kept secret, O beautiful goddess, and this five-limbed [stotra] is ever to be guarded.
O Pārvatī, this five-limbed secret of Gaṇeśa must not be given to one who is not a disciple, nor likewise to one who is not a practitioner (sādhaka).
Without giving, one should not bestow; without giving, one should not cause [another] to receive.
Otherwise, there would be a loss of accomplishment; therefore, one should practice giving in every way. (20)
The chapter, the manual, the armor, the thousand names of the mantra,
and the hymn— these five limbs should be kept secret with great effort at all times.
Thus ends [the section on] the Great Gaṇapati in the Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra, within the Śrī Devīrahasya.
The thirtieth chapter: The Description of Praise (Stotra).
Thus ends the Pañcāṅga of Gaṇapati.
(p. 159) Now begins the thirty-first chapter.
Now, the Sūryapañcāṅga. The venerable Bhairava said: To the Lord, the Master of Bhairavī, seated upon the peak of Kailāsa (or Śrīśaila), [he spoke].
Bhairava, crowned with the moon and served by the Gaṇas and Gandharvas. || 1 ||
Adorned with ornaments of serpents and graced by a crown of matted locks,
he was white with ashes as body-unguent and wore bracelets made of snakes and *gonasa* vipers.
Clad in a lion’s skin with an elephant hide as an upper garment,
he carries a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and holds a bell and a ḍamaru drum.
Śiva, whose hands hold a trident and an arrow, who displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
and who wears a garland of severed heads.
It is terrifying to Kāma, Kāla, and Andhaka.
Saluted by Brahmā, Upendra, and Indra; as cool as ten million moons;
accompanied by the lords of the Yakṣas and Kinnaras; and worshipped by gods and asuras.
[He saw] the Lord, who is crowded with Rākṣasas, Mārīs, great Pretas, Bhūtas, and Vetālas, and who is bowed to by hosts of Sādhyas, Siddhas, and Piśācas, as well as by Bhairavas.
The omnipresent Lord, served by the Brahman-sages, accompanied by Pārvatī,
the bearer of the Gaṅgā, with a gracious countenance and a smiling lotus-face.
Having seen Śambhu worshipped by Nandirudra, Bhairavī spoke.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, bestower of fearlessness upon devotees;
you are Śiva, the Supreme Sovereign; you are Viṣṇu; you are Prajāpati.
Residing in *sattva*, having the nature of *rajas*, and characterized by *tamas*, he is the destroyer of the world;
he is beyond the *guṇas*, the presiding lord of Bhairava, and the cause of all causes.
Rooted in the Vedas, knowable through the Vedas, the protector of the world, and the Lord of the universe—you, O God, are dearer to me than my own life-breaths; I am yours, purchased as your servant.
"O Blessed One, formerly you were questioned by me with devotion;
if I am dear to you, tell that truth to me today. (11)
Śrī Bhairava said: O Śivā, what reality (tattva) shall I tell you, which is so very difficult for you to obtain?
Tell me quickly what you have forgotten; I shall speak it, for you are dearer to me than my own life.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, worshipped by the leaders of the Daityas, you who know the essence of all the Āgamas, out of a desire for the welfare of the Kaulikas! (13)
O ocean of compassion, speak quickly of the five-limbed [mantra] previously indicated,
which pertains to Sūrya, the God of gods, and is the most excellent among all supreme principles.
Śrī Bhairava said:
O Goddess Pārvatī, out of affection for you, I shall declare this most secret [teaching]—the five-limbed [system] of the twelve-fold Self—which contains the secret of all the Agamas. 15.
The chapter on daily worship, the ritual manual, the supreme armor, the thousand names of the mantra, and the hymn consisting of the root-mantra, O beloved. (16)
O Īśānī, this five-limbed [tantra] of the radiant God of gods is composed of the essence of all things; it is divine, secret, and difficult for me to obtain.
(161) "It must not be given to those who are not devotees; to the devotees, it bestows enjoyment.
Now, O Dear One, I shall proclaim this chapter consisting of the root mantra. (18)
Merely by hearing whose name one is liberated from all diseases—he is the God of gods, the Blessed One, the Sun, the treasury of splendors. (19)
The manifest deity, the author of the Vedas and the witness of all actions, is Savitṛ;
thus is the Supreme Self, the Lord of the universe, described in the Vedas. (20)
Sūrya, the beloved of Gāyatrī, the Lord of creation, preservation, and dissolution,
the soul of time, and the supreme abode, is celebrated as the Supreme Brahman.
O Śivā, I shall now declare the supreme extraction of the mantra of that primordial God of gods, the Sun, the progenitor, which bestows all accomplishments in the Kali age.

*Tāraṃ* (Oṃ), *ḍimba*, *bhūtiśaktī*, *sūrya* ending in *ṅi*, *viśva* in the middle, and *bhavāni* at the end—this extraction of the mantra of Savitṛ has been described to you; it consists of seven syllables and is the sole cause for both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 23 ||
O Auspicious One, for him there is no obstacle, nor any defect, nor fear of enemies to be overcome;
nor is there any requirement of ritual purity, nor indeed any fear of the contrary.
This supreme mantra bestows the eight siddhis, removes all diseases, and accomplishes all goals, O Goddess; it must not be given to just anyone.

O Īśvarī, the practitioner who recites the mantra along with its ancillaries one hundred thousand times according to the color [of the deity] obtains whatever he desires through the sealing by the Sun. (26)

The practitioner should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that, offer libations (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part of that, and perform the purification (mārjana) with a tenth part of that. || 27 ||
One should feed [the deity] with a tenth part of that; thus the mantra becomes like a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma).
[This should be done] at a banyan tree, in a forest, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, or at a crossroads.
One should perform the *paraścaraṇa* at midnight or at midday;
during a solar eclipse, it should be performed from the first contact (*grāsa*) until the final release (*vimukti*). (29)
Whatever one should recite becomes perfected, being the sole cause of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Great Goddess, Brahmā is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra. (30)
Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chandas), Savitṛ is remembered as the deity (devatā), Vyom is the seed-syllable (bīja), Parā Śakti is the pin (kīlaka), and Tāra is the nail (kīlaka), O Īśvarī.
The application for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa is thus remembered;
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the seed-syllable of Māyā, endowed with the six long vowels.

O Goddess, at the beginning of the recitation, the best of practitioners should duly and in proper sequence perform the placement on the hands (kara-nyāsa) and the six limbs (ṣaḍ-aṅga), and recite the three syllables of Kola.
O Goddess Pārvatī, the "unbolting" (utkīlana) of the king of mantras occurs when the practitioner recites the three arrows in the middle of the root mantra. (34)
O Maheśvarī, this is declared to be the Sañjīvana-mantra of this [deity].
O Pārvatī, having purified the mantra with the Mātṛkās, the practitioner [should proceed]. (35)
The mantra should be free from harshness (ṭuṭila) and bestows all accomplishments;
O Śivā, one should recite the syllable "Śakti" in the middle, which is as clear as the luster of the moon at the beginning of the Vedas.
"Release the curse of Śiva twice; you shall become the wife of Vibhāvasu again.
This knowledge which removes the curse should be recited by the best of practitioners. (37)
O Goddess, by means of these ten [methods] of Savitṛ, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) may attain Śiva;
O Goddess, he should recite the perfected mantra with a rosary according to his capacity.
For one who is liberated from all diseases shall obtain the fruit of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
O Goddess, at the end of the world-cycle, the Kaulika should recite the Śaradvāra.
This mantra, known as Saṃpuṭa, is the supreme jewel for protecting mantras;
it is the excellent Sūryāstra-mantra, to be understood through the instruction of the Guru. (40)
Having recited this, the mantra of Savitṛ quickly becomes like a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma).
First is the Tāra (Om), then the Vyoṣa (Hrīm), and immediately after that, "vidmahe sūryāya" (we know [the one] for Sūrya). || 41 ||
Having uttered the power of *māyā*, [we meditate] upon the one whose form is light;
may that Śiva and Śakti, the Supreme Self, impel us. (42)
The Sūryagāyatrī, which is concealed in all the Tantras, has been described;
it should be recited ten times by practitioners during the twilight rituals, in worship, and in libations.
O Goddess, I shall now proclaim his meditation, which is the secret of all the gods;
it removes all diseases and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (44)

I bow to the Sun, whose face is as radiant as ten million fires at the end of an aeon, who has the hue of vermilion powder and the *japā* flower, who wears a jeweled crown, possesses two eyes, and sits upon the center of a white lotus; adorned with various ornaments, with a smiling face, clad in red garments, and consisting of pure consciousness.
I worship Him who holds a golden lotus and a jewel-filled pitcher in His two arms. || 45 ||
O Śivā, I shall now describe the extraction of the yantra, which fulfills all desires,
which is divine, which deludes all, and which consists of all spiritual accomplishments.

O Goddess, this Śrīcakra, the most excellent of the Sun, is said to consist of the Bindu, the triangle, the eight-cornered figure, and the perfect circle; it is enriched with the shining eight petals and the fire-pitchers, and is graced by the three lines that form the abode of the Earth. 47.
O Pārvatī, I shall describe the method of dissolution for this Yantra along with its secret essence;
by merely hearing it, one obtains the fruit of ten million offerings. (48)
Śakra, Agni, Yama, Māṃsāda, Varuṇa, Anila, and Vittada,
together with Īśa, are to be worshipped at the outer gate of the King of Yantras by the practitioners.
Gaṇeśa, Caṇḍavetāla, Lolākṣa, and Vikarālaka—
the door-keepers within— should be worshipped by practitioners of Śiva in a counter-clockwise direction.

O Śivā, the practitioner of mantra should worship the three lineages of gurus— known as the divine, the perfected, and the human— within the three circles with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and other offerings.
O Goddess, the wise one should worship Candra, Bhauma, Budha, Jīva, Śukra, Saura, Tama, and Ketu on the eight petals, proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction. (52)
Then one should worship Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vimalā, Nirmalā, Vidyutā,
and Sarvatovaktrā upon the eight petals with the [nine] planets.
O Īśvarī, one should worship Sūrya, Divākara, Bhānu, Bhāskara, Ravi, Tvaṣṭṛ, Tapana, and Dharma in the eight directions.
O Goddess, one should worship Haṃsa Gṛhapati, whose body is the triple Veda, within the triangle;
O Goddess, one should worship Savitṛ within the circle of the Śrī-bindu.
O Goddess, one should worship the Kalās within the eight-cornered and the three-cornered [mandalas]:
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Bodhinī, and Rodhinī. (56)
Having worshipped Kelinī, Śoṣiṇī, and Vareṇyākarṣiṇī, the Kaulika [should do so] in the eight directions for the sake of attaining the Kula-siddhi. (57)
One should worship Māyā, who possesses all things, has the luster of gold, and is triangular;
and one should worship Visphurā and Savitṛ within the orb of the Bindu.
One should worship the Lord with lotuses alone, as well as his weapons; O Śivā, having worshipped a golden lotus, one should worship the jar enriched with jewels.
One should bow to the deity according to the rule with the root mantra for the sake of attaining absolute liberation;
this is declared to be the limb of dissolution (layāṅga), hidden in all the Tantras.
O Goddess, one should display the mudrā called Padma during the ritual of worship, by joining the two middle fingers together with the two thumbs turned away from them. 61.
Having joined the two little fingers and kept the middle and ring fingers separate, this is declared to be the Padma-mudrā; O beloved, now hear about the Bimba-mudrā.
Having brought the two thumbs face-to-face, one should extend the fingers toward each other;
having raised both hands upward, this is declared to be the Bimba-mudrā.
Below the navel, one should place the middle finger of the left hand; above that, the middle finger of the right.
In the same manner, the Kaulika should position the fingers from the left toward the right. (64)
This, however, is the Bhāskarī mudrā, which brings the three worlds under control; it is renowned as the remover of all diseases and should be displayed during the rite of worship. 65.
On the two thumbs are the Moon and Mars; likewise, Mercury and Jupiter are on the two ring fingers; Venus and Saturn are on the two index fingers; and Rāhu and Ketu are on the two little fingers.
But having meditated upon the god Bhāskara in the center, one should display the mudrā during the invocation, the offering of scents and other items, the food offering, and the dismissal. (67)
Incense, lamps, food offerings, and all else should be presented with the *khaśolkā*;
the great mudrā called *khaśolkā* removes all diseases. (68)
O Goddess, this [mudrā], which accomplishes all aims and destroys suffering and poverty, is formed by joining the two hands in fists and connecting each joint to its corresponding joint. (69)
Having bound the *aṅguṣṭhayoni* upward, it is the most excellent among all *yoni*s;
this great mudrā, called *khaśolkā*, is the crusher of the host of enemies. (70)
O Maheśvarī, having first seen and bowed to Ravi,
one should then behold the Mahāmudrā, which is to be kept strictly secret and is beloved by the Great Sun.
The wise person who displays this Bhānavī mudrā during worship shall obtain the fruit of worship performed for a hundred thousand years. || 72 ||
O Pārvatī, listen with respect as I shall describe the eight applications (prayoga), by the mere performance of which a mantra becomes a bestower of success (siddhi). (73)

Stambhana (paralysis), mohana (delusion), as well as māraṇa (killing) and ākarṣaṇa (attracting), then vaśīkaraṇa (subjugation) and vidveṣa (enmity), along with the rites of śāntika (pacification) and pauṣṭika (nourishment). 74.

Out of a desire for the welfare of practitioners, O Śivā, I shall describe their means of accomplishment—a method that removes diseases in the Kali age, which is not to be disclosed and must not be given away. (75)
O Great Goddess, at dawn, having risen from bed, the practitioner should perform his necessary duties;
then, having bathed, he should recite ten thousand [mantras] before the Sun.
O Goddess, one should offer lotus flowers, lotus seeds, and sugar in the tenth part [of the oblation];
with clarified butter, there is immediate immobilization of those who steal musical instruments and water. (77)
O Īśānī, at the time of midday, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times;
one should offer oblations consisting of ghee, lotus seeds, and ginger in a quantity equal to one-tenth of that number.
One should immediately satisfy [the deity] with milk; this will bewilder even the dwellers of heaven.
At sunset, standing on the bank of a river in a secluded place, one should recite the root mantra. (79)
One should offer ten thousand oblations of lotus seeds and parched grain with a tenth part of that amount;
having satiated [the deity] with ghee and curd, the slaying of enemies will come to pass.
O Śivā, having recited the root mantra ten thousand times at midnight on a Sunday,
one should offer a tenth part as a fire-oblation consisting of lotuses, *śaṭī*, ghee, and horse gram.
O Goddess, attraction occurs instantly, even for a celestial woman;
having bathed there at the hour of Brahmā during the sun's course, one should recite [the mantra] in that water.
The wise practitioner should offer one-tenth of ten thousand oblations of the root mantra,
using ghee, sugar, camphor, lotus, lotus seeds, and lotus filaments.
Even Indra comes under one's control, let alone a petty king;
at sunrise, the practitioner should recite the vidyā ten thousand times.
One should offer oblations of ghee, lotus, mustā, parpaṭa, and sugar;
by gratifying the deity with poison, one shall effect the sowing of dissension among enemies.
O Goddess, when the sun has half-risen, one should recite the mantra at the site of the well ten thousand times;
one should then perform an oblation with ghee, barley, and sesame seeds consisting of a tenth part of that number.
O Maheśvarī, by using lotus filaments and ginger, there is peace from excessive rain, drought, and fear of kings at that very moment.
O Great Goddess, even when half the sun has set, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times at the root of a *vānīra* tree, and one should offer oblations of ghee and cow’s milk.
The wise one should offer libations with curd, milk, and sugar— each consisting of a tenth part of lotus, lotus-seed, filaments, molasses, and arka-leaves. (89)
Great nourishment shall arise in the world, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain;
such is this secret chapter, most beloved of the Sun.
It consists of all mantras, divine, and must be guarded by those seeking liberation.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, the description of the Sūrya-paṭala, in the Śrī Devī-rahasya of the Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra. 31.
Now begins the thirty-second chapter.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Today, I shall declare the secret of the daily worship of Savitṛ;
O Pārvatī, listen with respect to this supreme and divine manual (paddhati). 1.
O Śivā, he who recites the Gāyatrī without first performing the fivefold duties becomes a sinner and a diseased person; such is the command of Śiva.
O beloved of my life, I shall now describe the prose manual for the daily worship of Savitṛ, which is rich with the secrets of all the principles (tattvas).

Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, assuming the bound lotus posture (*baddha-padma-āsana*), and having meditated upon and praised the venerable Guru—who is the very nature of consciousness and bliss—residing within the pericarp of the thousand-petaled, downward-facing lotus situated at the crown of one's own head; and having become flooded with the bliss of beholding Him, [one recites]: *Haṃsaḥ So'ham*.
Having recited "svāhā," having offered the recitation to the *haṃsa*, and having meditated upon and recited "so 'haṃ haṃsaḥ svāhā," he should offer it to the Guru. (p. 168)

Having received that command, he should go outside, discard impurities such as excrement, perform purification according to his caste, meditate upon the deity, perform three *prāṇāyāmas*, rinse with the three *tattvas*, and then perform the cleansing of the teeth. It is as follows: *klīṃ sarvajanamanoharāya kāmadevāya vauṣaṭ*.
Having cleansed the teeth and performed three mouthfuls of water with the syllable *hrāṃ*, and having sipped water three times with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*),

one should place the letters of the root-mantra (*mūlabīja*) individually upon the head, face, heart, belly, navel, back, genitals, knees, and feet. Then, having touched [the lips] with the *māyābīja* preceded by the *tāra* (*oṃ*).

One should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*): inhalation (*pūraka*) for sixteen [counts], retention (*kumbhaka*) for sixty-four, and exhalation (*recaka*) for thirty-two. Having thus restrained the *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *samāna*, *udāna*, *vyāna*, and other vital airs, one should go to a river or similar place, consecrate three lumps of earth (*mṛttikā*) three times with the root mantra, and perform a bath that removes impurities. Then, [one should recite]: *oṃ gāṃ gīṃ gūṃ gaṅge ca*.
O Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in these waters!

Having thus invoked the sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*) from the solar disc by means of the goad mudrā (*aṅkuśamudrā*), [he recites]: "O Blessed One, Lord of Bhava, Leader of the Planets, Bhāskara! O you whose form is consciousness, Lord of the two eyes of the Veda, Sovereign of non-dual ultimate reality! O Sun, as long as I shall offer libations to you, so long, come here! Having thus invoked him and smeared the third portion of clay upon his body,

Having recited the root mantra seven times and displayed the *kumbha-mudrā*, one should emerge from the water three times. Having thus bathed and meditated upon the Deity, one should offer three *arghya* oblations to the Deity with the root mantra. Having recited the root-vidyā ten times, one should offer three *arghya* oblations to the Great Sun (*Mahāmārtaṇḍa*) with the Sūrya-Gāyatrī: *Oṃ hrīṃ sūryarūpāya*.

We know the *haṃsa*; we meditate upon the one whose form is light; may that *haṃsa* inspire us. (3) *Oṃ haṃsaḥ*, to the Great Mārtaṇḍa, accompanied by the power of illumination (*prakāśa-śakti*), this is your *arghya*; obeisance. Having offered these three *arghya*s, and having performed the ritual rinsing (*mārjana*) and sipping of water (*ācamana*) three times with the root mantra, and having put on another garment, one should perform the twilight devotion (*saṃdhyā*).

Having formed a triangle in the water, touched one's own body, held water in the left hand, and covered it with the right hand, one should consecrate it three times with the mantra "laṃ vaṃ raṃ yaṃ haṃ. Then, holding it in the right hand,
one should sprinkle twelve times on one's own head with the dripping drops of water through the *iḍā* [nāḍī].

Having drawn that water inside, washed away the impurities of the body, and expelled it through the left nostril, one should strike that black water—which is the form of sin—against the diamond-stone (vajraśilā) situated on one's own left side;
thus having performed the removal of impurities, [one should recite]: *oṃ hrīṃ ātmatattvaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā oṃ hrīṃ*.

"Vidyātattvaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā, oṃ hrīṃ Śivatattvaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā"—having thus sipped water three times as before, and having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) three times with the counts of 16, 64, and 32, one should recite the Gāyatrī ten times. O Goddess, the Kaulika should recite the Gāyatrī of Savitṛ ten times; even one burdened with great sins [is purified] from all diseases.
One is liberated. Having thus recited the root mantra as many times as possible, and having offered the recitation to the Deity, one should utter the root mantra:
"The transcendent, unmanifest, supreme sky consisting of consciousness, the imperishable space of Being-Consciousness—today [I take refuge in it]..."

Having performed the ritual salutation with the mantra "jyotiruttamaṃ svāhā" and offered a handful of water, one should again draw the Śrīcakra or the Yonicakra adorned with a *bindu* in the water; at the end of the root mantra, [one recites]: "The Lord Sūrya, the Great Mārtaṇḍa."

Having offered libations twelve times, saying "May Savitṛ, together with Viṣṇu, be satisfied," and having individually offered libations to the attendant deities, performed the libation for the ancestors and others, sipped water three times (ācamana),
and bowed to the Lord together with his consort, saying "Oṃ hrūṃ śrūṃ vāṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa, vauṣaṭ," [one should proceed].

Having cast it off and meditated upon [the deity] dissolved within the calyx of the heart-lotus, and having wrung out the bathing-cloth, one should enter the sacrificial pavilion; such is the ritual of the twilight worship (sandhyā-vidhi).

There, having washed one's feet and entered the interior of the house, and having sprinkled it with water from the general *arghya* vessel, [one should offer salutations as follows]: "Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to the threshold (dehalī); Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati; Oṃ saṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī; Oṃ duṃ, obeisance to Durgā; Oṃ kṣāṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla; and in the center, obeisance to the Vāstu deities."

Having worshipped from the eastern door up to the northern door, one should worship as follows: "Salutation to Gaṅgā" above the door; "Salutation to Yamunā" on the right; "Salutation to Sarasvatī" below the door; "Salutation to Cakrā" on the left;
and "Salutation to Sudhārṇava" in the center. Having thus completed the worship, one should gaze at it with the root mantra while snapping the fingers.
Having struck [the ground] as is appropriate and sat upon the seat, one should perform the purification:

*Oṃ āṃ*. For this mantra for purifying the seat, Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Sutala is the meter (*chanda*), Kūrma is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the purification of the seat. *Oṃ prīṃ*, salutation to the Earth; *Oṃ mahi*, by you...

O Goddess, you uphold the worlds; you are upheld by Viṣṇu. O Goddess, do you likewise support me, and make this seat pure. *Oṃ krāṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ*, obeisance to the lotus-seat of the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*). *Aṃ*, obeisance to Ananta; obeisance to the lotus stalk;
obeisance to the lotus; obeisance to the filaments.
"Salutation to the eight-petaled lotus seat; salutation to the thousand-petaled lotus seat; Oṃ Haṃsaḥ, salutation to the venerable pericarp;

salutation to the seven horses. Having thus worshipped, one should [ward off] the celestial beings with a divine gaze and the triple clapping of hands, and the terrestrial beings with three strikes of the left heel.

"Having dispelled the obstacles: 'May those beings depart who dwell upon the earth; may those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva! Having thus expelled the beings by scattering unbroken rice-grains (*akṣata*), and having performed the binding of the directions with 'Oṃ hraḥ astrāya phaṭ', [one recites]: 'Oṃ haṃsaḥ, protect me, protect me, hūṃ phaṭ!'"

Having performed self-protection with "svāhā," one should fill the breath through the left nostril with "hūṃ phaṭ," retain it with "hrīṃ phaṭ," and exhale with "saḥ phaṭ. Then, having meditated upon one's own self in the form of a *haṃsa*, one should raise the *Kulakuṇḍalinī*— which has three and a half coils and a long form— by means of contraction with the mantra "oṃ hūṃ haṃsaḥ."

Having the form of a lamp-flame, thinner than a lotus fiber, possessing the brilliance of the tip of lightning, cooler than ten million moons, more difficult to behold than ten million suns, and as formidable as ten million fires— [one should lead it] through the path of the *suṣumṇā*, piercing the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) and leading it into the path of Brahman (*brahmapatha*).

Having united [the soul] with Paramaśiva and having gratified it with the nectar of bliss arising from their state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*), one should bring it back to the *mūlādhāra* by that same path; then, on the left, [one visualizes] the personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*), bearded and red-eyed.

Having visualized [the deity] as smoke-colored, holding a sword and a shield, and shaped like one's own thumb, one should perform the acts of drying, burning, flooding, and so forth, using the seed-syllables of the elements: *yaṃ raṃ vaṃ laṃ haṃ*. Thus, first, by means of the yoga of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should dry [the body] with the wind-seed syllable *yaṃ*, recited sixteen times. Then, with *raṃ*...

One should burn [the body] with the seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*), *ra*, recited sixty-four times. One should flood it with the seed-syllable of Varuṇa (*varuṇabīja*), *vaṃ*, recited thirty-two times. Having visualized the body as firm by reciting *laṃ*, the seed-syllable of earth, ten times, one should contemplate it as being of the nature of emptiness by reciting *haṃ*, the seed-syllable of space, ten times.
Having meditated upon one’s own self, one should meditate on the Lord, the Sun, within the pericarp of the heart-lotus.

One should remember the god with a brilliantly shining crown, adorned with jeweled earrings, possessing a thousand rays, and embraced by a shimmering [halo]. Having thus meditated and recalled one’s own self in the form of the deity—
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ. May my vital breaths (prāṇas) come here; may my life-soul (jīva) remain here.
May all my senses—speech, mind, sight, touch, hearing, taste, smell, and breath—having arrived right here, abide happily for a long time. Svāhā!

The sequence of elemental purification (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and the installation of vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*). Then, having performed the root-assignment (*mūlanyāsa*), one should worship the Sun three times on the head at the conclusion of the root-mantra and perform the ritual resolve (*mantrasaṅkalpa*):
"Oṃ, of this mantra for the worship of the auspicious Sun, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is the venerable Brahmā, the meter (*chandaḥ*) is the Gāyatrī, and the deity is the venerable Savitṛ."

The deity is *hrāṃ*, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *hrīṃ*, the power (*śakti*) is *hrīṃ*, and the pinning-syllable (*kīlaka*) is *oṃ*. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, in the worship of the Sun. *Oṃ*: Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the meter (*chandas*), on the face; salutation to Śrī Savitṛ, the deity (*devatā*), on the heart; salutation to *hrāṃ*, the seed-syllable, on the navel; salutation to *hrīṃ*, the power (*śakti*).
Homage to the Secret One; *oṃ kīlakāya*, homage to the two feet; homage to the application in recitation (*japa*), [homage] to all limbs.
*Hrāṃ* to the two thumbs, *hrīṃ* to the two index fingers, *hrūṃ* to the two middle fingers, *hraiṃ* to the two ring fingers, *hrauṃ* to the two little fingers.
*Namaḥ* *hraḥ* to both palms and backs of the hands; *namaḥ*. *Hrāṃ* to the heart; *hrīṃ* to the head;

*hrūṃ* to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*); *hraim* to the armor (*kavaca*); *hrauṃ* to the eyes; *hraḥ* to the weapon (*astra*). Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs upon the hands. *Oṃ namaḥ* on the head; *hrāṃ* on the two eyes; *hrīṃ* on the mouth; *saḥ* on the heart.

With *sūṃ* on the belly, *ryāṃ* on the navel, *yaṃ* on the knees, *naṃ* on the feet, and *maḥ* from the head down to the feet—one should thus perform the sevenfold pervasion; this is the placement (*nyāsa*) of the root-vidyā.

Oṃ hrāṃ, salutation to Sūrya, the soul of the Ṛgveda; [place this] on the head. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Sūrya, the soul of the Yajurveda; [place this] on the belly. Oṃ saḥ, salutation to Sūrya, the soul of the Sāmaveda; [place this] on the private parts. Oṃ, salutation to Sūrya, the soul of the Atharvaveda; [place this] on the feet. Thus one should perform the pervasion three times; this is the Vedanyāsa.

Oṃ hrāṃ, salutation to the Heart, to Sūrya, whose form is the Self. Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the Head, to Sūrya, the Supreme Self. Oṃ hrūṃ, [salutation] to the Crest-lock, to Sūrya, the Self of all beings. Oṃ hraiṃ...
To the Sun, whose nature is knowledge, for the armor: *oṃ hrauṃ* to the inner self, the Sun, for the three eyes.
*Oṃ hraḥ haṃsātmane sūryāya astrāya phaṭ*. Thus is the placement on the fingers. This is the self-placement (*ātman-nyāsa*).

Oṃ hrāṃ, to Sūrya, the essence of the Moon, with the two thumbs; oṃ hrīṃ, to Sūrya, the essence of Mars, with the two index fingers; oṃ hrūṃ, to Sūrya, the essence of Mercury, with the two middle fingers; oṃ hraiṃ, to Sūrya, the essence of Jupiter, with the two ring fingers; oṃ hrauṃ, to Sūrya, the essence of Venus...

With the two little fingers: Oṃ hraḥ, salutation to Sūrya, the self of the planet Saturn, with both palms and backs of the hands. Thus is the placement of the heart and other limbs. This is the *grahanyāsa* (placement of the planets).

Oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ, salutation to Sūrya at the *mūlādhāra*. Hrāṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ, salutation to Sūrya at the *maṇipūra*. Hrīṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ, salutation to Sūrya at the *svādhiṣṭhāna*. Saḥ.
Ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ, obeisance to Sūrya in the Anāhata [cakra]. Taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ, obeisance to Sūrya in the Viśuddhi [cakra]. Naṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ, obeisance to Sūrya in the Ājñā [cakra].
Maḥ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ, obeisance to Sūrya.
At the aperture of the head (*karandhra*). Thus, one should pervade [the body] in seven ways; this is the *mūlaśuddhi-mātṛkā-nyāsa*.
Aṃ Āṃ, salutation to Sūrya of the Gāyatrī metre at the Brahmarandhra; Iṃ Īṃ, salutation to Sūrya of the Triṣṭubh metre at the Ājñā; Uṃ Ūṃ, salutation to Sūrya of the Anuṣṭubh metre at the Viśuddha;
Ṛṃ Ṝṃ Ḷṃ Ḹṃ, salutation to Sūrya of the Uṣṇik metre at the Anāhata; Eṃ Aiṃ...

"Oṃ! Homage to the Sun of the Virāṭ meter, in the Svādhiṣṭhāna. Oṃ! Homage to the Sun of the Samrāṭ meter, in the Maṇipūra. Aṃ Aḥ! Homage to the Sun of the Bṛhatī meter, in the Mūlādhāra. Thus one should pervade [the body] sevenfold; this is the Nyāsa of the Seven Meters.

Oṃ, obeisance to Gaurāśva Sūrya at the *brahmarandhra*; hrāṃ, obeisance to Pāṇḍurāśva Sūrya at the *ājñā* [cakra]; hrīṃ, obeisance to Sitāśva Sūrya at the *viśuddha* [cakra]; saḥ, obeisance to Śvetāśva Sūrya at the *anāhata* [cakra]; obeisance to Himāśva Sūrya at the *svādhiṣṭhāna* [cakra].

*Naṃ* to the Sun with the white horse, salutation in Maṇipūra; *maḥ* to the Sun with the jasmine-white horse, salutation in Mūlādhāra. Thus one should extend [the mantra] three times. This is the Saptaturaganyāsa (the ritual placement of the seven horses).

Oṃ, salutation to the Sun, the deity Ajapā, in the aperture of the crown (*karandhra*). Hrāṃ, salutation to the Sun, the deity Gāyatrī, in the *ājñā* [cakra]. Hrīṃ, salutation to the Sun, the deity Sāvitrī, in the *viśuddha* [cakra].
Saḥ, salutation to the Sun, the deity Sarasvatī, in the *anāhata* [cakra]. Salutation to the Sun, the three-syllabled deity. Salutation to the Sun.
*Namaḥ* to Svādhiṣṭhāna; *naṃ* to the deity Brahmavādinī and to Sūrya; *namaḥ* to Maṇipūra; *maḥ* to the deity Pañcamukhī. (p. 172)
"Salutation to Sūrya at the Mūlādhāra. Thus one should pervade [the body] three times; this is the Gāyatrī-nyāsa.

Oṃ, salutation to the Sun of the Śiva-tattva at the Brahma-randhra; Hrāṃ, salutation to the Sun of the Śakti-tattva at the Ājñā; Hrīṃ, salutation to the Sun of the Māyā-tattva at the Viśuddha; Saḥ, salutation to the Sun of the Vidyā-tattva at the Anāhata; salutation to the Sun of the Kalā-tattva.

At the Svādhiṣṭhāna: *naṃ* to the Sun, whose self is the principle of necessity (*niyatitattva*). At the Maṇipūra: *maḥ* to the Sun, whose self is the principle of the soul (*ātmatattva*). At the Mūlādhāra: *namaḥ*. Thus one should pervade [the body] three times; this is the Nyāsa of the Principles (*tattvanyāsa*).

Oṃ, obeisance to the Sun, Lord of the Kāmarūpa seat, at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). Hrāṃ, obeisance to the Sun, Lord of the Uḍḍīyāna seat, at the Ājñā [cakra]. Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Sun, Lord of the Jālandhara seat, at the Viśuddha [cakra]. Saḥ, obeisance to the Sun, Lord of the Pūrṇagiri seat, at the Anāhata [cakra].

Obeisance to Sūrya, the Lord of Madhupurī-pīṭha; obeisance to Sūrya in Svādhiṣṭhāna. Naṃ, obeisance to Sūrya, the Lord of Avantī-pīṭha, in Maṇipūra. Maḥ, obeisance to Sūrya, the Lord of Vārāṇasī-pīṭha, in Mūlādhāra. Mūlaṃ, obeisance to Sūrya, the Lord of Kurukṣetra-pīṭha, in all the limbs. Thus.
"One should pervade [the body] three times" refers to the *pīṭhanyāsa*. Thus end the twelve *nyāsas*. As it has been said:

"The Sage, *māyā*, the root-vidyā, the Vedas, the self, the planets, the purifications, the meters, the horses, the *gāyatrī*, and furthermore the principles (*tattva*), the seats (*pīṭha*), and so forth."
For these twelve nyāsas are hidden in all the tantras;
they have been described for you, O Goddess of Gods, as the removers of all diseases.
For one who performs these placements (nyāsa) for the sake of all success,
there shall be the attainment of fortune, wealth, health, knowledge, fame, and happiness.
At the conclusion of the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should meditate upon the Sun; thus, one obtains the fruit of ten million acts of worship. So it is said.

Now, the Mātṛkā-nyāsa: Aṃ Kaṃ 5 Āṃ—to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*. Iṃ Caṃ 5 Īṃ—to the two index fingers, [svāhā]. Uṃ Ṭaṃ 5 Ūṃ—to the two middle fingers, [vaṣaṭ]. Eṃ Taṃ 5 Aiṃ—to the two ring fingers, [huṃ].
Oṃ Paṃ 5 Auṃ—to the two little fingers, [vauṣaṭ]. Aṃ Yaṃ Raṃ Laṃ Vaṃ Śaṃ Ṣaṃ Saṃ Haṃ Laṃ Kṣaḥ.

"Aḥ, salutation to both palms and backs of the hands. Thus is the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*). In this manner is the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). Thus concludes the ritual placement of the Mātṛkā beginning and ending with the vowels.

Now, the placement of the pure Mātṛkās (śuddhamātṛkānyāsa): Aṃ, salutation to the head; Āṃ, salutation to the perimeter of the mouth. Likewise: Iṃ to the right eye; Īṃ to the left eye; Uṃ to the right ear; Ūṃ to the left ear; Ṛṃ to the right nostril; Ṝṃ to the left; Ḷṃ to the right cheek; Ḹṃ to the left; Eṃ to the upper lip; Aiṃ to the lower lip.

Oṃ, on the upper row of teeth; auṃ, on the lower row of teeth; aṃ, on the head; aḥ, on the mouth; kaṃ, at the root of the right arm; khaṃ, at the elbow; gaṃ, at the wrist; ghaṃ, at the base of the fingers; ṅaṃ, (p. 173).
*Caṃ* at the tip of the finger; *chaṃ* at the base of the left arm; *jaṃ* at the elbow; *jhaṃ* at the wrist;
*ñaṃ* at the base of the fingers; *ṇaṃ* at the tip of the fingers; *ṭaṃ* at the base of the right foot; *ṭhaṃ* at the knee; *ḍaṃ* at the ankle;
*ḍhaṃ* at the base of the toes; *ṇaṃ* at the tip of the toes; *taṃ* at the base of the left foot; *thaṃ* at the knee; *daṃ*.

*Dhaṃ* at the ankle; *naṃ* at the base of the fingers; *paṃ* at the tips of the fingers; *phaṃ* on the right side; *baṃ* on the left; *bhaṃ* on the back; *maṃ* at the navel; *yaṃ* in the belly; *raṃ* at the heart; *laṃ* at the right shoulder;
*vaṃ* at the crown of the head; *śaṃ* from the heart to the tip of the right hand; *ṣaṃ*.

One should perform the pervasion three times: *saṃ* from the heart to the tips of the left hand; *haṃ* from the heart to the tips of the right foot; *laṃ* from the feet to the top of the head; and *kṣaḥ* from the head to the feet with the mantra *namaḥ*. This is the Mātṛkā-nyāsa. [Then: *hrīṃ namaḥ* on the head, *haṃ namaḥ*...
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by reciting "Oṃ namaḥ" three times over the heart, the feet, and from the root of the head down to the feet,
one should meditate upon the Lord situated within the pericarp of the heart-lotus—
[described as] having the luster of a ripe pomegranate fruit, two-armed, and clad in beautiful red garments.
It was yoked to a chariot drawn by seven horses and adorned with jeweled earrings.
I worship Savitṛ, the Lord of the World, adorned with armlets, necklaces, and ornaments, holding a water-pot and a lotus, and embraced by Visphurā.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should draw a triangular circle within a mandala on one's left.

Having worshipped it with "Oṃ, obeisance to the fire-mandala consisting of ten kalās," and having placed a washed tripod thereon, one should place a conch upon it. Within the conch, [one worships] "Oṃ, to the sun-mandala..."

Having worshipped with "Obeisance to the one whose self consists of twelve digits," and having filled [the vessel] with water from a sacred site (tīrtha), one should worship with "Obeisance to the lunar maṇḍala, whose self consists of sixteen digits" while reciting "sauḥ. Then, having worshipped three times with sandalwood paste, unbroken rice, and flowers, using "haṃsaḥ sūryāya hrīṃ namaḥ," one recites: "Oṃ gāṃ gīṃ gūṃ, O Gaṅgā and Yamunā..."
With these and other verses, having invoked the sacred sites from the solar disc by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*, one should worship with "Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ,
haṃsaḥ śuciṣade sūryāya namaḥ svāhā," and after displaying the *dhenu*, *yoni*, *matsya*, and *khaśolka* mudrās, one should prostrate.
Even by the mere sight of Śaṅkha, sins go to dissolution— how much more so by touching him— just as they do at the rising of the sun upon the Himavat mountains.

Having thus performed the general *arghya* (offering of water), one should perform the nectar *arghya*. Just as for the general *arghya*, having drawn a triangle, a circle, and a square on the right side, and having sprinkled it with the water from the general *arghya*, [one recites]:
"Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to the heart" in the east; "Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the head" in the south; "Oṃ hrūṃ, [obeisance] to the crest-lock" in the southwest.
*Vaṣaṭ* to the west;
*Oṃ hraiṃ kavacāya huṃ* to the north; *Oṃ hrauṃ netrebhyo vauṣaṭ* below; *Oṃ hraḥ astrāya* [to the weapon].

Having worshipped with "phaṭ" above, and having worshipped the triangle with "oṃ" in the northeast (īśāna), "haṃ" in the southeast (āgneya), and "saḥ" in front, one should place the washed support and worship there with: "Oṃ, obeisance to the fire-mandala consisting of ten kalās."
One should place a pot made of gold, silver, or even clay that is red in color,
adorned with divine garlands and smeared with saffron.

Having thus established [the vessel], he worships it with "Oṃ, salutation to the solar orb consisting of twelve kalās," fills it with pure honey, and then fills it there by pouring a stream of nectar with the ring finger and thumb,
saying: "Sauḥ, salutation to the lunar orb consisting of sixteen kalās."

Having meditated on nectar by means of the *amṛtīkaraṇa-mudrā* from the moon-maṇḍala, having brought it there and poured it into the jar, one should utter the syllables from *aṃ āṃ* up to *kṣaṃ*, then utter the root mantra, and finally:
*mrāṃ mrīṃ mrūṃ mraiṃ mrauṃ mraḥ aḥ amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛtākarṣiṇi*.
"O showerer of nectar! O Sovereign of the great orb of the sun! O Goddess of ambrosia! O Sovereign of supreme bliss! Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Saḥ! Haṃsaḥ So'ham Svāhā!"—thus one should recite ten times.
Having thus recited: "O you who are born from the solar orb! O you who are born from the abode of Varuṇa!"
O Goddess, consisting of the seed-syllable *amā*, may [this] be liberated from the curse of Śukra.
If the *praṇava* is the seed-syllable of the Vedas and consists of the bliss of Brahman,
by that truth, O Goddess of gods, may it be liberated from the curse of Śukra.
The Supreme Brahman alone is eternal, consisting of both the gross and the subtle;
by means of that, I destroy for you the sin of killing a Brahmin born from a mere flash of thought.
Released from the curse of Kṛṣṇa, liberated from the curse of Brahmā,
and freed from the curse of Rudra, become pure now.
Pavamāna is supreme bliss; Pavamāna is the supreme essence;
Pavamāna is the supreme Brahman—with that, I purify you.

Having thus worshipped three times and invoked the holy fords such as the Gaṅgā, having displayed the cow, yoni, and fish mudrās, and having consecrated [the water] with nectar by reciting "Haṃsaḥ So'haṃ Svāhā," one should mutter the root mantra ten times, worship with sandalwood paste, unbroken rice, and flowers, and meditate upon the holy ford as consisting of great nectar.
The placement of the jar.
Having drawn a triangle within the interior of the jar, placed a vessel upon its stand, and filled the jar with nectar,
one should recite the Mātṛkā from "aṃ namaḥ" up to "kṣaṃ namaḥ," and then recite the root mantra over it.

Having recited the *divyakhaṇḍa*, one should meditate; thus [is described] the supreme vessel (*parama-pātra*). At the conclusion of the supreme vessel, having placed the vessels for the Guru, Śakti, and Vīra—namely the *pādya*, *ācamanīya*, and *madhuparka*—and having filled the vessels for the Guru, Śakti, and Vīra with the nectar of the sacred waters (*tīrthāmṛta*), one places water in the *pādya* and *ācamanīya* vessels.

[Having filled the vessels for the water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and the water for sipping (ācamanīya) with water,] one should place clarified butter, honey, sugar, and so forth into the vessel for the honey-mixture (madhuparka). Then, having sprinkled the articles of worship with the nectar from the supreme vessel (paramapātra), and having displayed the mudrās of the Cow (dhenu), the Yoni, and the Nectarification (amṛtīkaraṇa), [one should place] the Śrīcakra upon the support of the jewel-throne (ratnapīṭha).

Having meditated upon and either drawn or established the Śrīcakra— the abode of the earth, shining with a central point (*bindu*), adorned with a triangle, graced by an eight-cornered figure, beautified by a circle, inlaid with eight petals, and resplendent with three circles— recite: *oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ*.
Having uttered "Haṃsaḥ so 'haṃ saḥ svāhā" and the [phonemes] from *aṃ* to *kṣaṃ*,

one should [worship] Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Śuddhavidyā, Māyā, Kāla, Niyati, Rāga, Vidhi, Puruṣa, Prakṛti, Buddhi, Ahaṃkāra, Manas, Śrotra, Tvak, Cakṣus, Jihvā, Ghrāṇa, Vāk, Pāṇi, Pāda, Pāyu, Upastha, Śabda, Sparśa, Rūpa, Rasa, Gandha, Ākāśa, Vāyu, Tejas, Ap, and Pṛthivī.
Namaḥ! Oṃ hrāṃ, salutation to the eight-petaled lotus. Salutation to the twelve-petaled lotus.
Salutation to the thousand-petaled lotus. Salutation to the seven meters (chandas). Salutation to the seven horses.
Having worshipped with "Salutation to the root, the glorious jewel lion-throne," [one offers] a handful of lotus filaments.

Having formed the *arghya* mudrā and meditated upon the previously mentioned Śrīdeva, at the end of the root mantra, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*), water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamanīya*), honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamanīya*), the *arghya*, and flowers to the illustrious Sun together with *visphurā*. Then,
one should visualize the mere flowers as being in the form of wind and fire, having emerged from the solar channel (*sūryanāḍī*).
O Blessed One, Lord of all worlds, O Lord of a thousand rays,
as long as I worship you, so long, O Sun, remain here.

Thus, having offered a flower into the *bindu-bimba*, one should deposit the life-force (*jīva*) by means of the *bimba-mudrā*: *Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ haṃsaḥ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ. The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of the illustrious Sun, together with Visphurā, are here the vital breaths. The life-force (*jīva*) of the illustrious Sun, together with Visphurā, is established here.* (16)

"May all the sense organs—speech, mind, skin, eyes, ears, tongue, nose, and breath—of the glorious Sun together with his radiance, having come here, remain happily for a long time; svāhā. Thus [he offers] the vital breaths (prāṇas).

Having offered [the oblation], one should perform the sequence beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*), stabilization (*saṃsthāpana*), confinement (*saṃnirodhana*), veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*), facing [the deity] (*saṃmukhīkaraṇa*), making [the deity] well-pleased (*suprasanna*), nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), and supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*).

Having displayed the mudrās of the cow, the fish, the lotus, the discus, the sun, the sword, and the arrow, at the end of the root mantra, one says: "O Lord Sun, please be seated upon this jeweled lion-throne. At the end of the root mantra, having meditated that the deities of the supreme enclosure have emerged from the circle of rays, one offers the root mantra for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the respectful reception (*arghya*).

Having offered everything from the vessels for the *madhuparka* and the water for rinsing the mouth, [recite]: "O Blessed One, accept this *arghya*, vauṣaṭ" at the end of the *mūla-mantra*. "O Blessed One, accept the fragrance, namaḥ.
"O Blessed One, accept the flowers, vaṣaṭ. "O Blessed One, may the water of the Gaṅgā be applied to all limbs, namaḥ. [Recite] the *mūla-mantra*.
O Blessed One, accept the jewels, garments, ornaments, and so forth; *namaḥ* [Mūlamantra]. O Blessed One, accept the jeweled sandals;

*namaḥ* [Mūlamantra]. O Blessed One, accept the jeweled lion-throne; *namaḥ* [Mūlamantra]. Accept the flowers preceded by perfumes and unbroken rice grains; *namo vauṣaṭ* [Mūlamantra]. O Blessed One, accept the incense; *namaḥ* [Mūlamantra]. O Blessed One...

Saying "Take the lamp, *namaḥ*," and having offered everything with the *khaśolka* [mantra], one should draw a triangle with a circle inside upon the ground in front of oneself; having placed a vessel with its support there and presented the food offering (*naivedya*),
one should consecrate it as nectar (*amṛta*) with the root mantra, gaze at it with the *khaśolka*, and recite the root mantra ten times.

Having displayed the *dhenu-yoni-mudrā* and offered water with the mantra: *oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ bhagavan sūrya apośānaṃ namaḥ amṛtopastaraṇam asi svāhā*, and having displayed the *puṇḍraka-mudrā* and smelled [the offering] with the *grāsa-mudrā*, one should meditate on the Lord as fully satiated at the end of the root mantra, [offering] this *ācamanīya*.

Svadhā (Amṛtāpidhānamasi svāhā). [Recite] Mūla [mantra]. "Tāmbūlaṃ namaḥ. At the end of the Mūla mantra, satisfy [the deity] seven times with the nectar from the supreme vessel (paramapātra), and also satisfy Visphurā three times, then prostrate.
Thereafter, one should meditate upon the attendant deities as follows:
One should meditate upon the limbs of the Sun as being gentle, red in color, two-armed, adorned with ornaments, and holding a boon-granting gesture and a lotus in their hands.
One should thus contemplate this weapon, which is terrifying with its fangs, exceedingly fierce, possessing the brilliance of a blazing fire, and threatening the entire host of obstructors.
Soma is like the white lily and the jasmine; Bhauma has the luster of refined gold;
Saumya resembles a blue gem; and Guru is like yellow orpiment.
Śukra is like cow’s milk, and Śani has the luster of blue collyrium;
all of them can assume any form at will and are adorned with divine garments and ornaments.
With her beautiful left hand resting on her thigh and her right hand bestowing fearlessness,
the Kaulika should worship the planets with great devotion, preceded by meditation, in this manner.

Having thus offered the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), one should worship with the nectar from the hero’s vessel (vīrapātra) by means of the process of withdrawal (saṃhṛtikrama) and moving counter-clockwise (vāmāvṛtti). The sequence of worship ends with the meditation on and the adoration of the deities stationed at the gates and so forth, along with their weapons; such is the teaching of Śiva.
For example: *Laṃ*, I worship and satiate the sandals of the venerable Indra; *namaḥ* with the nectar from the hero’s vessel.
One should satisfy them: *Raṃ*, worship the venerable sandals of Agni; *Ṭaṃ*, the venerable sandals of Yama; *Kṣaṃ*, the venerable sandals of Nirṛti;

*Vaṃ*, the venerable sandals of Varuṇa; *Yaṃ*, the venerable sandals of Vāyu; *Saṃ*, the venerable sandals of Soma; [Kh: *Kuṃ*, the venerable sandals of Kubera]; *Haṃ*, the venerable sandals of Īśāna; *Oṃ*, the venerable sandals of Brahmā; *Hrīṃ*, the venerable sandals of Ananta. Thus one should worship with lotus petals.
(Abhīṣṭasiddhiṃ0)—thus ends the first enclosure.

Oṃ Gaṃ, worship the sandals of Gaṇeśa Śrī. Oṃ Caṃ, worship the sandals of Caṇḍavetāla Śrī. Oṃ, worship the sandals of Lolākṣa Śrī. Oṃ, worship the sandals of Vikarāla Śrī. Having thus worshipped with perfumes, unbroken rice, and flowers—
One should worship the inner door-keepers by turning counter-clockwise in the east, south, west, and north; thus [ends] the second enclosure according to the *Abhīṣṭasiddhi*.

Having worshipped and satiated the Guru-vessel with nectar using the mantra "Guṃ, I worship the sandals of my own guru; obeisance! I satiate them; obeisance!", one should worship the three lineages—Pañca-paramaguru-śrī and Pañca-parameṣṭhi-guru-śrī—in the three circles from the northwest to the northeast.
The third enclosure.

*Sauḥ* Jyotsnādevī together with Dīpta, [to] Soma Śrīpāda. Thus, one should satisfy [them] with the nectar from the planetary vessel (*grahapātra*). *Saṃ* Sūkṣmā together with Maṅgala Śrīpāda. *Baṃ* Jayā together with Budha Śrīpāda. *Juṃ* Bhadrā together with Jīva Śrīpāda. *Śrīṃ* Vimalā together with Śukra Śrīpāda. *Śaṃ* Nirmalā together with Śani Śrīpāda. *Rāṃ*...

"Vidyutāsahita-Rāhu-Śrī... and "Kaṃ Sarvatovaktrāsahita-Ketu-Śrī..."—thus, with perfumes, unbroken rice, and lotus pollen, one should worship in the eight petals from the east to the northeast in counter-clockwise order;
this is the fourth enclosure.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ, to the venerable feet of Sūrya accompanied by Tāpinī; 3. To the venerable Divākara accompanied by Tāpinī;
3. To the venerable Bhānu accompanied by Bodhinī; 3. To the venerable Bhāskara accompanied by Rodhinī; 3. To the venerable Ravi accompanied by Kālinī;
3. To the venerable Tvaṣṭṛ accompanied by Śoṣiṇī; 3. To the venerable Tapana accompanied by Vareṇyā; 3.

[The worship of] Dharmaśrī together with Ākarṣiṇī. Thus, one should worship with the nectar of the supreme vessel (paramapātrāmṛta) by moving counter-clockwise on the eight petals of the lotus in the eight-cornered [mandala]; this is the fifth enclosure (pañcamāvaraṇa).
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ, [to] the venerable Haṃsa accompanied by Māyā, in the northeast. Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ, [to] the venerable Lord of Planets (Grahapati) accompanied by Viśvāvatī, in the southeast.
"O you whose body is the glory of the Trinity, accompanied by the golden radiance [of Lakṣmī]," and so forth. Thus, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata);
this is the sixth enclosure (āvaraṇa).

3. Having worshipped with "Obeisance to the Mother Ghaṇṭā, who consists of the sound of the universe," while ringing the bell slowly and reciting the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), one should worship exclusively with hundred-petaled lotuses twelve times with "Obeisance to the Śrī [Devi] together with the Radiant Savitṛ. This is the seventh enclosure (*āvaraṇa*).

3. Ratnakalaśaśrīpāda. 3. Suvarṇakamalaśrīpāda. Thus, one should worship with the nectar of the supreme vessel the lotus-like hands on the left and right; this is the eighth enclosure (*āvaraṇa*). Having worshipped in this manner, one should satisfy the root deity three times with the root mantra and prostrate. Then, [one should offer] to the one accompanied by the root deity...
Having offered supreme rice (*paramānna*) as a food offering (*naivedya*) to the illustrious Sūrya together with his retinue, saying "I offer [this], obeisance," while reciting the root mantra;

and having performed seven circumambulations at the conclusion of the root mantra; and having displayed the *merupuṇḍraka* mudrā at the conclusion of the root mantra; one should prostrate again and again.
O Goddess, one should join the fingers such that the right ones are within the left and the left ones are within the right; the two thumbs should be brought together facing each other.
Having rotated the two hands like the sky with the thumbs facing downward toward the goddess,
this is the divine Meru-puṇḍraka mudrā, beloved of the Sun.
One should display the mark known as *puṇḍraka* during the offering of food (*naivedya*) and during prostration (*praṇāma*).

Having thus bowed down, performed the ritual resolve (*saṃkalpa*), executed the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should recite the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) as many times as possible using a rosary of *arka* wood. At the conclusion of the recitation:
You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us.
O God, O Maker of Light, beloved of the world, may success be mine through your grace.

Having thus offered the recitation (*japa*) to the deity, one should prostrate with the *yonimudrā*. Then, one should perform the recitation of the *kavaca*, the *sahasranāma*, and the *stavarāja* (and perform the daily rites such as the *vaiśvadeva*).
Having also offered that to the deity with the *bimbamudrā*, one should prostrate like a staff (*daṇḍavat*).

Oṃ hrīṃ vīṃ, obeisance to Vīravaṭuka. Oṃ yāṃ yūṃ yoṃ, obeisance to the Yoginīs. Oṃ kṣāṃ, obeisance to the Kṣetrapālas. Oṃ trāṃ troṃ, obeisance to Teja and Caṇḍa—having thus offered the *bali*, [one offers] Oṃ hrāṃ hrūṃ to all the *bhūtas*.
Having offered the bali with the mantra "To all those who create obstacles, bali vauṣaṭ," one should then ask the Sun for forgiveness.

Having performed the salutation to the heroes (vīra-vandana) together with the illustrious members of the assembly (śrīsāmayika), at its conclusion, one should place the vessel of bliss (ānanda-pātra) upon the head while reciting "Oṃ so'haṃ haṃsaḥ svāhā. Then, becoming filled with supreme bliss (paramānanda-maya),
one should contemplate one's own self as consisting of light in the form of the sun, and meditate on the solar weapon (sūryāstra) while reciting "Oṃ hraḥ astrāya phaṭ."

Having prostrated and offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), and having displayed the solar gesture (*bhānavī-mudrā*), one takes from the point of the *bindu* within the *śrīcakra* a flower consisting of solar splendor by means of the withdrawal gesture (*saṃhāra-mudrā*). Having smelled it with the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī], one unites that solar radiance with Paramaśiva, and then brings it back to one’s own self at the *mūlādhāra*.
Manifesting his divine form consisting of light, he should sport at ease together with his own power (Śakti).
Thus, this manual for the daily worship, composed in prose, has been determined out of affection for you; it must not be disclosed by the Kaulikas, O beloved.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual Procedure for the Worship of the Sun," within the *Śrīdevīrahasya* of the *Śrīrudrayāmala Tantra*.
Now begins the thirty-third chapter.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
He who is the God of gods, the Blessed One, the Sun, the treasury of splendors,
the leader of the Gāyatrī, the Radiant One, is celebrated as Savitṛ.
I shall bestow upon him his divine armor, known as the Vajrapañjara,
which consists entirely of mantras, is secret, and contains the mystery of the root vidyā.
O Goddess, it removes all sins, destroys suffering and poverty,
cures great leprosy, is meritorious, and eradicates all diseases.
[The Refutation] || 3 ||
It is the destroyer of all hosts of enemies, the bestower of victory in battle,
consisting of all splendor, and worshipped by all gods and dānavas.
This armor, which destroys all calamities in battle and in the face of terrible danger from kings,
emerged from the mouth of Bhairava and is encircled by the Mātṛkās.
O Goddess, it removes the afflictions caused by planets and destroys all calamities;
O Mistress of the Gods, by wearing this, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [attained his status]. || 6 ||
O Goddess, Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa shall conquer the Daityas in battle,
as will Śaṅkara, the lord of all worlds, and Vāsava, the lord of heaven.
O Goddess, the Moon is the Lord of Herbs; I am Śiva, the Lord Bhairava.
This supreme armor consists of mantra; it is the most excellent essence of the Sun.
O Maheśvarī, he who wears [this] on his arm or head on Sunday shall be beloved by kings in the world, radiant, and a crusher of enemies.
O Goddess, what is the use of saying much? By wearing this armor (kavaca), prosperity, wealth, and health increase in this world; it is not otherwise.
O Goddess of the Gods, the supreme liberation in the hereafter is difficult even for the gods to attain,
yet it is [attained] through this armor which consists of the root-vidyā.
The Sage for that which is called the Vajrapañjara is declared to be Brahmā;
Gāyatrī is said to be the metre, and Savitṛ is remembered as the deity. (12)
O Goddess, *māyā* is the seed-syllable, *śarat* is the power (*śakti*), and *namaḥ* is the pin (*kīlaka*);
O Sovereign Lady, this is proclaimed as the application (*viniyoga*) for the accomplishment of all aims. || 13 ||
Of this *Śrīvajrapañjara-kavaca*, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Gāyatrī is the meter (*chanda*), the illustrious Savitṛ is the deity (*devatā*),

*hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *saḥ* is the power (*śakti*), and *namaḥ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the recitation of the *Vajrapañjara-kavaca* for the accomplishment of all aims.
Oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ: may the Sun, whose form is mantra, protect my head. Uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ: may Hrāṃ Ravi, who consists of pure consciousness, protect my forehead. (14)
May Ḷṃ Ḹṃ Eṃ Aiṃ protect my eyes; Hrīṃ, may my red charioteer protect [me];
Oṃ Auṃ Aṃ Aḥ, may he, the Lord of the entire universe, protect my ears. || 15 ||
May Sūrya, worshipped by the gods, protect my two cheeks with *kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ*; and may the Lord Aryamā protect my nose with *caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ*. || 16 ||
May he who is worshipped by the lords of yogins protect the face with *ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ*; may he who is beloved by Nārāyaṇa protect the throat with *taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ*. (17)
May the treasure of splendors, *paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ*, protect my two shoulders;
may the root, the leader of all, *yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ*, protect my two arms. (18)

May the eternal Lord, whose essence is the root mantra, protect the chest with the syllables *śaṃ-ṣaṃ-saṃ-haṃ*. May the Sun, the lord of the planets, always protect the belly with the syllables *laṃ-kṣaḥ*. || 19 ||
May the Lord of the Day protect my back with the syllables ṅaṃ ñaṃ ṇaṃ naṃ maṃ;
may the Dispeller of Darkness protect my navel with aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ. || 20 ||
May the Lord of Planets protect my genitals with the syllables *ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ*; may the Sun protect my waist with the syllables *kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ*. || 21 ||
May the radiant Bhāsvat protect my knees; may the Maker of Light (Vibhākara) protect my shanks with the syllables ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ, paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ. || 22 ||
May Śaṃ, Saṃ, Haṃ, Laṃ, and Kṣa protect my root; may the one whose body is the triple Veda protect my feet; and may Savitṛ protect my entire form with the syllables Ṅaṃ, Ñaṃ, Ṇaṃ, Naṃ, and Maṃ.
May Soma protect me in the east, and may Bhauma always protect me in the southeast;
may Budha protect me in the south, and Guru himself protect me in the southwest.
May the White One protect me in the west; may Śanaiścara protect me in the northwest;
may Tamas protect me in the north; and likewise may Śikhin protect me in the northeast. (25)
May Mihira protect me from above, and may the Lord of the World protect me from below.
May Bhāskara protect me at dawn, and may Dineśvara protect me at midday. (26)
May he who is fond of the Vedas protect me in the evening; at midnight, may the Lord of Lightnings protect me;
and everywhere and at all times, may Sūrya, the leader of the [solar] disc, protect me. (27)
May the Lord Savitṛ protect me in battle, in the royal court, at dice, in dispute, in the peril of enemies, in combat, in fever, and in disease. 28.
Oṃ oṃ oṃ, and Oṃ-u-ū-ha-samaya, may the Sun protect me from fear: Hrāṃ hrīṃ hruṃ hahaha hrasauḥ hasahasauḥ.
May Haṃsa protect me from all sides!

May he—Saḥ Saḥ Saḥ Sasasa—the leader of the clan and the Sun himself, protect me always from the king, from forest-dwellers, from thieves, from battle, and from distress; Oṃ Hrīṃ Hasauḥ, [protect me] at all times. 29.

May the Sun protect me from the fear of fever, leprosy, and the disease of colic— *drāṃ drīṃ drūṃ dahana*, likewise *taraṇi*, *bhāṃ bhaiḥ bhāskara*, *rāṃ rīṃ rūṃ rururūṃ ravi*; and may Mārtaṇḍaka protect me from the fear of great illness— *aṃ aṃ āṃ vi vi vīṃ*.
May that supreme Haṃsa, whose body is pervaded by the root-mantra and who possesses a thousand rays, protect [us] forever. || 30 ||
Thus ends the divine Śrī-kavaca, known as the Vajrapañjara,
the secret of all the gods, encircled by the Mātṛkā-mantras.
O Śivā, this [mantra] which destroys the fear of great diseases and destroys sin, spoken from my own mouth, is secret, brings fame, is meritorious, and bestows all that is auspicious.
Having written it on a Sunday, or under the asterism Tiṣya or one's own birth-star, O beloved Pārvatī, with divine eight-fragrance and the milk of the Sudhā plant; || 33 ||
O Maheśvarī, at the rising of the sun, one should write the armor (kavaca) on birch bark with holy milk of the Arka plant, using a stylus made of Kanakī wood.
One should wrap the pill with white, red, or black thread;
then, having wrapped it with gold, one should wear it on the head or on the arm.
O Goddess, he shall conquer his enemies in battle, and he shall be victorious in debate within the assembly.
He shall always be honored by kings and become endowed with all splendor. (36)
O Goddess, when situated in the throat, it bestows sons; when situated in the belly, it destroys diseases;
and when this divine pill is situated on the head, it brings the world of kings under one's control. (37)
Held in the hand, she is the constant giver of wealth and the increaser of splendor and intellect;
she [bestows this] upon a woman who is barren, or one who bears only a single child, or one whose children have died.
O Maheśvarī, she who always wears this pill on her neck shall give birth to many sons; he in whose body this pill remains constantly [shall likewise attain such results]. 139.
O Pārvatī, the great missiles discharged by Indra, such as the Brahmāstra and others, will become useless upon reaching his body; of this there is no doubt.
O Great Goddess, for him who constantly recites this Vajrapañjara armor at the three times of day, the Sun-god shall immediately become a granter of boons.
O Goddess, if one worships the embodiment of the Three Vedas without knowing the armor-mantra (kavaca), the merit earned from that worship shall be fruitless for ten million births. 42.
O Goddess, one who recites the armor-mantra (varma) one hundred times on the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday is liberated from even great leprosy; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, he who is free from disease and recites this armor-mantra, the Vajrapañjara,
becomes wealthy immediately through the grace of the Sun.
O Goddess, O Beloved, he who recites this armor-protective hymn daily with devotion shall enjoy prosperity in this world and attain liberation at the end of the body. || 45 ||
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Sun-Armor Known as Vajrapañjara," within the *Śrīdevīrahasya* of the *Śrīrudrayāmala Tantra*.
(p. 184) Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess of gods, O Great Goddess, bestower of all fearlessness and boons!
You are dearer to me than life; being pleased with me, I stand here as your granter of boons.
"Ask me anything out of love; I shall tell you that.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Mahārudra, Maheśvara! (2)
If a boon is to be granted to me, and if I am worthy of a boon,
then tell me the thousand names of Savitṛ, the God of gods.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess Pārvatī, this is the most secret of secrets, my very essence;
it is the mystery of all the gods, difficult to attain, and the fulfiller of desires.
Who is able to praise that divine Lord Sūrya, the author of the Vedas, the Lord of Creatures, the witness of all actions, and the eye of the world? (5)
Of that primordial God of gods, the Sun, the Lord of the universe, whose beginning, middle, and end cannot be reached even by the gods; (6)
O Goddess, I shall declare to you the Thousand Names of Mantra, which bestows the attainment of universal sovereignty,
removes all sins,
and has been extracted from the Tantras, Mantras, Vedas, and Āgamas. (7)
It is auspicious, nourishing, a destroyer of demons, and a great purifier;
it is the most auspicious of all auspicious things and the eradicator of all sins.
I shall declare the supreme reality, which is the nature of the root-vidyā, the highest, the bestower of wealth, the bestower of merit, meritorious itself, and the bringer of prosperity and fame. (9)
That which is the supreme Brahman of Brahman, that which is the highest even of the highest; that which is the reality of all mantras, and that which is the splendor even of all splendors. || 10 ||
He who is the peace of the peaceful, the Manu of Manus,
the Yogi of yogis, and the Praṇava of the Vedas.
He who is the radiant sun among the planets, Indra among the gods, the king of the stars, and the shatterer (Vāyu) among the winds; || 12 ||
He who is the supreme among the senses, as well as among the goddesses;
he who is Meru among mountains, and Vāsuki among serpents. (13)
He who is the fire among all luminous bodies, who is Śiva among all causes,
and who is the Sun of the Gāyatrī— He is celebrated as the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
I shall proclaim the thousand names of that Paramahaṃsa, which pacify all poverty and destroy all suffering. (15)
It pacifies all sins and bestows the fruits of all sacred fords;
it destroys fevers, diseases, and untimely death, and always grants freedom from all fear. || 16 ||
It is the reality and the supreme reality, the most excellent essence of all essences;
it is the cause of victory through royal favor and the manifestation of prosperity and power. || 17 ||
It bestows long life, brings about nourishment, and grants the fruit of all sacrifices;
it is the cause of infatuation, paralyzing, attracting, and subjugation.
This thousand names of the Sun, which fulfills all desires, must not be given to one who is unworthy; listen with full attention. 19.

Of this *Śrīsūryanāmasahasra*, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is the venerable Brahmā, the meter (*chandaḥ*) is *gāyatrī*, the deity (*devatā*) is the venerable Lord Savitṛ, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *hrāṃ*, the power (*śakti*) is *saḥ*, the pin (*kīlaka*) is *hrīṃ*; its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation in the recitation of the Thousand Names of the Sun. The meditation (*dhyāna*):

His face is as radiant as ten million fires at the end of an aeon; he has the color of vermilion powder and the *japā* flower, wears a jeweled crown, possesses two eyes, and sits upon the center of a white lotus.

I worship Him who is adorned with various ornaments, whose face is smiling, who wears red garments, who is composed of pure consciousness, and who is like the sun; He holds in His two arms a golden lotus and a jeweled pitcher. || 1 ||

I worship the primordial god Mihira within the lotus of my heart— he who is directly perceptible, thus manifest, who beautifies the region of the earth with a thousand rays, who is borne by seven horses, and whose hand holds a noble banner.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ haṃsaḥ so 'ham. Savitṛ, Bhāskara, Bhaga;
the Blessed One, Lord of all worlds, Lord of beings, the creator of beings. || 3 ||
The self of all beings, the creator of creation, the progenitor, the doer, the destroyer, the Lord of the universe;
the sun, the giver of boons, the hero, the one who delights heroes, the illuminator of the universe. || 4 ||

The creator of the universe, the sustainer of the universe, the devotee, the enjoyer, the formidable one who removes fear, the soul of the universe, the Supreme Person, the witness, the Supreme Brahman, higher than the highest. || 5 ||
He is the powerful one, the source of the universe, the Lord of the universe, whose face is turned in every direction;
he is the lover, the practitioner of yoga, the one of great intelligence, the wise one, and the imperishable Manu.
Prajāpati, worthy of universal homage, the Lord of the World who has been saluted;
the soul of the past, present, and future, the essence of reality, possessed of knowledge and the [three] qualities.
He is of the nature of sattva, rajas, and tamas; he is the storehouse of compassion;
he is the thousand-rayed, radiant sun; he is the descendant of Bhṛgu, Bhṛgu, and the Lord.
Devoid of qualities, free from possessiveness, eternal, eternally blissful, and without support;
an ascetic, the maker of time, time itself, possessing a lovely body yet emaciated. || 9 ||
Difficult to behold, yet easy to see; a giver, a kinsman of the distressed, and a source of compassion;
two-armed, eight-armed, steadfast, ten-armed, and transcending the ten directions.
Viṣṇu bestows the fruit of ten-fold portions; Jigīṣu is victorious and triumphant;
Jaṭila is fearless; Bhānu has a lotus in his hand; and Kuśīraka is [so named].
He whose course is composed, the Sustainer, the Ordainer, he for whom auspicious rites have been performed;
the Sun, the Supporter of the world, the Protector, Rudra, the Lord who bestows welfare. (12)
The pacifier of enemies, the peaceful one, the benefactor, the lotus-seated;
he of inconceivable form, the most excellent, the Lord of the Great Cīna-krama. (13)

The subduer of great suffering, the self-controlled, the remover of great delusion, Hari; the one of restrained soul, the lord of time, the lord of the day, and the one who is affectionate toward his devotees. || 14 ||
The doer of good, as hard as a tortoise shell, the beloved of desire, the traveler of the sky, the great one, the truthful, Śambhu, and the beloved of the lotus. 15.
Sāmaga, Pañcama, Dravya, Dhruva, Dīnajanapriya, Trijaṭa, Raktavāha, Raktavastra, and Ratipriya. || 16 ||
The yogi of time, the great sound (or great bliss), immovable, assuming a visible form; deep-voiced, resonant, with a jar in hand, consisting of great light (or consisting of illusion). || 17 ||
Clad in red garments, red in hue, adorned with red garlands and unguents;
thousand-armed, victorious, moving like a deer, the Lord of the Deer. || 18 ||
The shaven-headed one, the bearer of the water-pot, the lord of serpents, the charioteer honored by Suratha;
the dweller in the banyan tree, the banyan tree itself, the ear of the tree, and the upholder of the lineage.
He has a crest-lock, is fierce, wears matted hair, and possesses flaming locks; he is the all-pervading lord consisting of the splendor of fire.
He is golden, the maker of gold, the taker-away, and is seated upon a throne of emerald gems.
He whose horses are green (the sun), who dwells in the world, the lord of the worlds, the moving one (iṅgila);
he who shines brightly, the playful one, the three-eyed one, and the divider (of the day). || 21 ||
The leader, the radiant one, the light, the lord of lights, the protector;
the wise one, the one possessed of delight, the one with beautiful eyes, the large-eyed one, the lord of the people. || 22 ||
He who has the form of a child, who wanders the mountains, the Lord of Speech, the Lord of the Gomati;
the bearer of the Ganges, the presiding lord of the Gaṇas, served by the Gaṇas, and the Sovereign of the Gaṇas. || 23 ||
He dwells in the eye of the Lord of the Mountains, he is the dweller in all things, the beloved of Satī,
whose nature is truth, who upholds truth, who is true to his promise, and who possesses a thousand rays.

Of boundless majesty, he is liberated, the giver of liberation, and the bestower of the desires for liberation; he is embodied, yet difficult to sustain, formless, the very nature of contentment, and composed of infinitesimal particles.
He is the lord of the vital breaths, possessing the forms of vyāna, apāna, samāna, and udāna;
he is the caṣaka measure, the form of the ghaṭikā, the muhūrta, and the day. || 26 ||

He is the fortnight, the month, the season, the rainy season, and the Lord of the Lords of Time; he is the solstice, the form of the Yugas, and the Kṛta age consisting of three quarters, as well as the Tretā Yuga.
He is Dvāpara and Kali, Time itself and the destroyer of Kali;
the God who is the soul of the Manvantaras, Śakra, the Lord of the three worlds.
Vāsava, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, the Lord of aquatic creatures,
Vāyu, Vaiśravaṇa, Śaivya, Girija, and Jalajāsana. || 29 ||
Ananta, of infinite majesty, the supreme lord, free from all feverish affliction; the reckoner of the end of the eon, the fierce one, the fire of time, and the slayer of Time.

The performer of the great dissolution, the one whose duty is accomplished, the one who destroys evil spells, the one who turns the ages; the whirlpool of time, the sustainer of the ages, the beginning of the ages, the Lord of Śākha.
He is the form of the treasury of space, the impeller of all time;
he is inconceivable, possessed of great strength, the child, the beloved of the crane, and the supreme boon-granter.

The bestower of boons, the giver of vigor, the eloquent one, the lord of speech, the giver of the play of words; the Lord of Sāṃkhya, accessible through the Vedas, the Lord of Mantras, and the leader of the Tantras.
Devoted to family traditions, worthy of praise, satisfied by praise, and fond of praise;
189) he is diligent in serving the *tulasī*, contented, and the destroyer of diseases.
Praskandana, Vibhāga, Nīrāga (or Nīroga), and Daśadikpati;
Vairāgyada, seated in a celestial chariot, holding a jewel-pitcher as his weapon. || 35 ||
He has great feet, great hands, a great body, and a great abode;
he is the embodiment of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and he is Tvaṣṭṛ, the master of the Atharvaṇa branch.
He is the man who is a virtuous tree with a thousand branches, dear to the great aeon;
he is the wish-fulfilling tree, the Mandāra, and as beautiful as Mount Mandāra. (300) 37.
Meru, Himālaya [G, Gh: Himācala], Mālin, Malaya, and the Malaya tree;
covered with *santāna* flowers, bestowing *santāna* fruits, he is the sovereign (*virāj*). 38.
The ocean of milk, the ocean of ghee, the ocean that destroys the afflictions;
the mine of jewels, the highly venerable one, the one born of the *veṇu* (reed), the bearer of the *veṇu*, the merchant. 39.
Spring is the vassal of Māra; summer is the destroyer of impurity;
the rainy season is the lord of rain; and autumn is the beloved of the lotus. || 40 ||
Hemanta, Hemakeyūra, Śiśira, Śiśuvīryada, Sumati, Sugati, Sādhu, Viṣṇu, Sāmba, and Ambikāsuta. || 41 ||
The great king Sāragrīva was served by Sunanda and Nandin;
he dwelt upon the peak of Mount Sumeru and roamed through the seven netherworlds.
Moving through space, eternal in nature, he bestows sovereignty and victory;
the beloved of the Kula, the lord of the Kula mountains, the disciplined one, the victorious, he who dwells in the sky.
The sustainer of the universe, moving through the sky, whose form is the sky, and whose chariot is the sky;
he who possesses a beautiful chariot, who is praised by the Sugatas, and who is intent upon playing the flute.

The cowherd, the protector of cows, the guardian, the one who is firmly established, Prajāpati; he who is to be known through the Vedas, whose eyes are the Vedas, possessing a great divine form, the sovereign lord of the gods. (45)
Lifeless yet living, the practitioner of mantra, bearing the resonance of the great ocean;
eternally the one who causes the eightfold world to revolve, the Lord of all traditions, the wise one.

He who extinguishes logic, the trident-bearer, the skull-bearer, he who dwells in the center of the lotus, whose abode is the triangle, and who resides in the center of the circle of the point (bindu). || 47 ||
