Possessing many garlands, possessing great garlands, wearing divine garlands, he is the reciter (Japa);
resembling the Japā flower, he bestows the fruit of recitation and worship. || 48 ||
The thousand-headed lord of gods, the thousand-eyed sun,
the refuge of all principles, the radiant one, the one praised by heroes, the source of light.
Viśvāvasu, Lord of Wealth, Master of Riches, possessed of emission;
the Primordial One, Lord of the Solar World, the All-pervading, and the Refuge of the Arts. (400) 50.
He is the lord of enjoyments, the god of gods, the lord of men, and the bearer of oblations;
he is the lord of the Vidyādharas, the lord of knowledge, the lord of Yakṣas, the protector, and the teacher.
The sole bestower of boons upon the race of Rākṣasas, honored by the race of Gandharvas, saluted by Apsarases, unconquerable, the conqueror, and the destroyer of the Daityas. || 52 ||

Lord of the Guhyakas, Lord of the Piśācas, honored by the Kinnarīs, the son of the Earth (Mars), served by the Siddhas, the traditional transmission, served by the virtuous, and the lord of rivers. || 53 ||
He whose eye is on his forehead, whose body is the universe, who is self-restrained and has controlled senses;
he who is the sun, the lord of the sun-stone (sūryakānta), who possesses infinite arms, and who is non-destructive.
He who holds the vessel of wine, who is bodiless yet the lord of the sky, whose refuge is the garment;
he who is the master of the alphabet beginning with 'A', and who is the primordial form of the gods. || 55 ||
The bringer of health, the embodiment of bliss, the subduer, the grasper;
the maker of light, likewise the Sun, the Heroic Sun, and the lord of creatures. || 56 ||
His own form is the nature of space, worshipped by the gods such as Indra;
he is honored by Indirā, the moon, and the sages who take refuge in the world of Indra. (57)
Īśāna, Īśvara, Candra, Īśa, and the beloved of the letter Ī;
he whose face is uplifted, whose body is vast, who wanders upon the lofty mountain, and who is the Guru. (58)
Utpala is one whose banner is raised high and who possesses the gait of a horse;
he is happy and finds joy in the form of the letter U. Likewise, Ūṣman is a treasury and a purifier. || 59 ||
He whose charioteer is Anūru, the sun, and who is dear to Ukāra;
he who removes debt, whose hand bears the mark of the Ṛ-sign, and who is adorned with the ornaments of Ṛ and Ṝ.
With well-formed limbs, abiding in the supreme state, radiant with a pair of cheeks like the syllables *ḷ* and *ḹ*,
bestowing the nectar of the moon, wearing a fine Chinese silk garment, he has many spheres of perception. (61)
He is the bearer of the single wheel, the one with many eyes, and the bestower of unity;
he delights in the seed-syllable *Eka* (E), and is the source of the nectar of the vowels *E*, *Ai*, and *O*.
Brahman is the cause of the syllable *oṃ*; he is adorned with the propriety of the syllable *au*;
he is devoid of the sequence ending in *au*; he is honored as the Lord of the great.
He whose ornament is ignorance, yet who is worthy of adornment; the Lord of Lakṣmī, possessing the form of the syllable *ambī*;
whose nature is the sound *aḥ*, consisting of all sounds, and whose supreme self is the essence of every sound. (500) || 64 ||
His limbs are the mantras whose nature is the syllables *aṃ* and *aḥ*; he is the one who turns back the Kali age;
he is the sole bestower of boons for ritual action, the witness of all actions, and the destroyer of impurities. || 65 ||
He who destroys the knot of worldly existence, the tawny-hued one, the wanderer upon the golden mountain,
the beloved, desire itself, the monkey, the fierce one, the parrot, and the destroyer of Keśin (or the enemy of hair).
Kṛṣṇa, the Kāpālika, the hunchbacked one, the refuge of Kamalā, the noble-born,
the remover of skulls, the reed-grass, and the bearer of saffron and camphor.
The King of the Kurus, who delights in the songs of the warbling Kinnaras, is Kulandhara;
he dwells in the sacred site (kuvāsa), is the Lord of the Kulakaula, and is adorned with the letter 'Ka'. || 68 ||
Khavāsī, Kheṭakeśāna, the sky-goer holding a sword and a severed head,
Khageśvara, the sky-wanderer, who is served by hosts of sky-faring goddesses. (69)
The one with harsh rays, the wielder of the discus, the destroyer of the wicked, the one whose color is like the sky;
the traveler, the lover of song, the one who is sung of, the dweller at Gayā, and the refuge of the Gaṇas. || 70 ||
Transcending all qualities, moving through the spheres, free from attachment, and served by the virtuous;
the bearer of the mace, the remover of disease, the bestower of boons upon Bhīṣma, and the wise one who is ever praised.
Gingila, Gaṭila, Gānta, the sun of the syllable *ga*;
possessing radiance, making a *ghurghura* sound, with a bell in hand, and having the form of a water-pot. || 72 ||
He is covered by clouds, moves through the clouds, and is satisfied by his cloud-vehicle;
he is the end of the letter *ṅa*, the lord of *ṅa*, has the letter *ṅa* as his limb, and is perfumed with moonlight and saffron.

He who has the moon as his refuge, who wears the moon, who is infallible, who resembles the campaka flower, who has the luster of refined gold, who is the fierce sun, and who is the beloved of Caṇḍeśa. || 74 ||
He is the beloved of the restless cakora birds and the kokila, he is agile and takes refuge in the fickle;
he possesses fluttering banners, he is the fierce mountain, he wears the single saffron robe, and though he is the Unmoving One, he moves.

He is augmented by the digit of consciousness (*citkalā*), he is the object of contemplation, the destroyer of thought, and he possesses the syllable *ca*. He bears the parasol, his heart is free from deceit, he is the meter (*chandas*),
and his body is severed by the dagger (*churikā*).
Jāmbūnadāṅgada, Ajāta, Jinendra, Jambuvallabha, Jambāri, Jaṅgiṭa, Jaṅgī, and Janalokatamopaha. || 77 ||

The bringer of victory (600), the sustainer of the world, the destroyer of old age and death; the protector of the world, the creator of the world, the object of meditation for the world, and the treasure-house of the world. || 78 ||
The witness of the world, the eye of the world, beloved by the Lord of the world, the unconquered;
he whose crown has the form of the letter Ja, whose form is veiled by a gale, and who is swift (Jhaṭa).
Lord of the cricket, master of the letter *jha*, with a lotus-hand adorned by the *jhañjā* gesture, he is established upon the ṭaṅka, the ṭiṭṭibha bird, and the *āsana*. (80)
He who makes the sound "ṭīṭ," who holds the edge of a chisel, whose nature is the syllable "ṭhaḥ," and who is the sovereign of the letter "ṭha";
he who is full of pride, the performer of the Ḍāmara dance, the letter "ḍiṇḍī," the lord of the Ḍāmarī, and whose form is the letter "ḍa."
Served by ḍākinīs, possessing fangs, with the brilliance of firm ankles and toes;
beloved by the Lord of the letter ṇa, the sovereign of the nine vowels, whose lotus-feet are marked by the syllable ṇa. || 82 ||
Tārādhipeśvara is the truth; Tripureśa is devoted to playing the lute; Trinetreśa is the body of the triple Vedas; and Adhokṣaja is the one who is beyond the senses.

He who is beloved by the lotuses of the night, the dispeller of darkness, the enemy of the quality of ignorance (tamas), the remover of lethargy, he whose form is darkness itself, and the bestower of the fruits of austerities. || 84 ||
Adorned with the letter *ta* and embraced by the divisions of time beginning with the *tuṭi*,

he is eternally situated in the place of Sthāṇu; he is the ancient one (*sthavira*), the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), the gross (*sthūla*), whose knees are born from the letter *tha*, the inner self (*adhyātman*), and the leader of the leaders of the gods.
Invincible, the destroyer of suffering, the giver, the cutter of poverty, the self-controlled. || 86 ||

The Lord of Devas, who removes misfortune, who dwells in the center of the twelve-spoked lotus, whose sole abode is the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta), the twelve-fold self, and the lord of the day. || 87 ||

Difficult to traverse, the subduer of demons, far-reaching, and insurmountable; difficult to contemplate, the destroyer of wicked lineages, the lord of compassion, and the one whose nature is mercy. 88.
Dāmodara, the radiant one, whose first syllable is the letter *da*, the kinsman of Dharma, the treasure-house of Dharma, the King of Dharma, and the bestower of wealth. || 89 ||
The bestower of wealth, the presiding lord of wealth, the mirror of the earth, the bearer of the burden;
the dweller in the eye of Dhūrjaṭi, the field of righteousness, and the sovereign of the earth. || 90 ||
The bearer of rain-clouds, the foremost leader, the soul of righteousness, the lover of dharma, the beloved of the mountains, the virtuous one, adorned with the letter 'Dha'. || 91 ||
He who delights in play, the joyous Rudra, the leader, he who loves policy, and the one possessed of right conduct.
The beloved of the lotus, the impeller, the creator of the dance, and the increaser of the dance. || 92 ||
The lord of men, praised by kings, moving through the sky, beloved of those who bow;
ending in the syllable *namaḥ*, having humbled his enemies, he is the refuge of Nara and Nārāyaṇa. || 93 ||
Nārāyaṇa, of blue luster, with a bowed body, blue and red;
whose form is sound, consisting of sound, and whose essential nature is the sound-bindu.
The Lord, the lord of serpents, the serpent, the mountain-dwelling serpent;
he who dwells in heaven, whose body is manifold, and who is the source of the alphabet beginning with the letter 'Na'.
The supreme light resting upon a lotus, the broad-shouldered Lord of Puṭa;
he who is dear to affection, the bestower of love, and the remover of the fear and suffering of those who bow before him. || 96 ||
The protector of others, the destroyer of others, the enemy of the cities, he who dwells within the city;
consisting of perfect bliss, possessing full splendor, the Lord of the Full Sovereign Goddess. || 97 ||
The color of a patola leaf, possessing excellence, the lord of the pale-red, the possessor of the supreme self;
having the body of the Supreme Lord, tall, intoxicated with bliss, and the bestower of desires upon those who bow before him. 98.

The one who brings across to the further shore, the full-bodied, the lover of yellow garments, the thunderbolt, the ripener, the picula tree, the scorched, and the bestower of happiness upon women. || 99 ||
He is the one who rejoices, the destroyer of adversaries, whose matrix is the letter *pa*;
he is the fruit of enjoyment and liberation, the Lord of the *phalinī* plant, and whose very nature is the fruit. || 101 ||
He who dwells in the midst of a full-blown lotus, who holds a full-blown lotus;
who is brilliantly radiant, whose form is manifest, and who wanders upon the mountain of crystal.
He is garlanded with flashing rays, has the syllable *pha* at his side;
he is a child, fond of strength, the letter *ba*, the remover of darkness from the hole, and the powerful one.
He is the destroyer of the barbarians beginning with Bāla; he is the drinker of the nectar of the *babūla* tree; he is the wise one, the planet Jupiter, the tree, Bṛhadaśva, and Bṛhadgati. || 104 ||
He who is unasked, of terrifying form, the one who causes the world to revolve, the beloved of the Lord of Beings;
he who is fortune, Bhr̥gu, the dweller in Bhr̥gu, the descendant of Bhr̥gu, and the crest-jewel of sages. || 105 ||
The bestower of fortune, he whose limbs are radiant as the sun, the one with a wheel-navel, and the one whose mother is the earth;
Mahākāla, the great overseer, the great sound, and the one of great intellect. (106)
Exceedingly radiant, captivating the mind, moving at the speed of thought, born of the mind; bestowing honor, the slayer of Malla, the wrestler, whose abode is Mount Meru and Mandara. || 107 ||
Adorned with garlands of mandāra flowers, worthy of honor, consisting of mind, delighted, feeding on wine, like the sun, and shaven-headed. || 108 ||
Mahāvarāha, the lord of Pisces, who goes to Aries and bestows what is desired upon Gemini;
Madālasa, praised by the immortals, the enemy of Mura, the granter of boons, and the Manu. 109.
Mādhava, Medinīśa, the destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, Mālyavat, Medhana, Māra, Medhāvī, and Musalāyudha. || 110 ||
Mukunda, the Lord of Murari, the bestower of the fruit of the swan, intoxication, the god of love,
the eater of sweetmeats, and the source of the alphabet beginning with the letter 'Ma'.
The sacrificer, the Lord of Sacrifice, the one who goes, the one residing in the hearts of yogins;
the traveler, the bestower of the fruit of sacrifice, the goer, and the leader of the Yamalas. || 112 ||
He who is fond of yogic sleep, the cause of yoga, and compassionate toward yogins; the bearer of the staff, the lord of the machine, and he who dwells in the center of the circle of the womb.
Desirous of victory in battle, a warrior who follows the dharma of the age (yuga), he stands in the midst of the circle of Yoginīs and is worshipped by the Lord of the Age (Yugaleśvara). || 114 ||
He who goes, the preeminent among Yakṣas, adorned with the letter *ya*;
Rāma, whose nature is to delight, the sun of jewels, and he who is fond of the ruru deer. 115.
Wearing a jeweled crown, with a lofty jewel, seated upon a jeweled throne;
garlanded with the rays of jewels, rich in gems, and adorned with jeweled bracelets and anklets. || 116 ||
With arms adorned with beautiful jewel bracelets, decorated with jeweled sandals,
taking refuge in Rohiṇī, he is the protector and the destroyer of night-stalkers. || 117 ||
He whose form is the syllable *ra*, who rests upon the seed-syllable of modesty (*lajjā*), who is the letter *la*;
he who is the sun of Lakṣmī, who dwells in the creeper, who possesses shimmering luster, and who sustains the world. 118.
The ender of the world, the beloved of Lāmā, the hairy one, the one without limbs;
the lord of the long, the sound of the *liṅga*, the performer of divine play, and the one with hanging lips. || 119 ||
Possessing fortune, the destroyer of the world, adorned with the syllable *la*, the dwarf, the lord of heroes and great warriors, eloquent, and beloved by the Lord of Speech. (900) 120.
Beyond the range of words, he has cast them off; he holds the lute and the flute in the forest.
He is born of speech, the destroyer of the ignorant, and the leader of the leaders of knowledge. 121.

He whose crest is the mother-vowel *va*, who bestows the desired fruits of Śambhu, the parrot, the moon, the maker of beauty, the peaceful one, the performer of peace, and the lover of pacification. || 122 ||
He is the maker of auspiciousness, clad in white garments, the Lord of Śrī, endowed with glory, and renowned;
he is accessible through the Vedas, adorned with the seed-syllable of the autumn season, and served by the learned. || 123 ||
He is the conduct of the disciplined, the auspicious conduct, the Residue, and the one who strikes the moss;
he is pervaded by the rays, the Auspicious One, the one served by Śukra, and the source of the syllables of the alphabet.
Six-faced, possessing six hands, adorned with the sixteen vowels, delighted by the sound of the six-footed bee, and the promoter of the six traditions (āmnāyas). || 125 ||
Satisfied by the tasting of the six flavors, whose mother is the syllable *ṣa*, the sun of the sun, the light of the wise, the source of happiness. (126)
The destroyer of the entire race of Daityas, served by all the gods, the lord of all practitioners of spiritual discipline, and the crest-jewel of all lineages.
The sun of the gods, the sun of nectar, the sun of heaven, the Lord of the Imperishable;
the sun of the quarters, the sun with green rays, the consumer of oblations, and the carrier of sacrificial offerings. || 128 ||
The Sun of Hālā, the Sun of the oblation, the Sun of what is offered, the Lord of Tawny Steeds;
the Sun of the seed-syllable *hrāṃ*, the Sun of *hrīṃ*, and the one whose alphabet consists of the syllable *ha*. || 129 ||
The Sun adorned with the seed-syllable *laṃ*, the Sun of the Earth, the Lord of the Earth, the Sun of Hunger, the Sun of Forbearance, the Sun of the syllables *laṃ-kṣaḥ*, and Sadāśiva. || 130 ||
The sun of the letter A, the sun of Kṣa, the sun of all, the treasure-house of compassion;
the sun of Bhūḥ, the sun of Bhuvaḥ, the sun of Svaḥ, and the leader of the suns. || 131 ||
He is the Sun of the planets, the Sun of the constellations, the Sun of the ascendant, and the Great Lord;
he is the Sun of the zodiacal signs, the Sun of the astrological configurations, the Sun of the mantras, and the most excellent of Manus. || 132 ||
The sun of reality, the supreme sun, the powerful Viṣṇu-sun;
the Rudra-sun, the Brahma-sun, the hero-sun, the most excellent of the best. || 133 ||
The Sun of Dharma, the Sun of Karma, the Sun of the Universe, the Leader—(1000) thus, O Goddess of the God of Gods, is this thousand names of the mantra. 134.
It belongs to the God of gods, Savitṛ, the Sun of immeasurable splendor;
it is divine, consisting of the essence of all things, and increases the luster of Brahman.
Consisting of the knowledge of Brahman, it is meritorious and bestows the fruit of sacred pilgrimage sites;
it is equal to the fruits of all sacrifices and grants the essence of all eloquence.
It is the supreme bringer of all prosperity in the world, bestowing fame and wealth;
it excels the fruits of all vows and grants the fruit of all righteous duties.
O Goddess, it removes all diseases and increases physical health;
such, O Queen of the Gods, is the power of this thousand names. (138)
Even in hundreds of millions of years, I am not able to describe that which one may contemplate as a desire, even if it be difficult for the gods to obtain. (139)
O Pārvatī, he who recites this, or causes it to be heard, or listens to it with his senses restrained, shall suddenly attain each and every [goal]. (140)
That hero becomes a king among the righteous, endowed with prosperity;
he is born wealthy in this world, possessed of sons, and a favorite of the king. (141)
O Great Goddess, that Kaulika who recites this while worshipping the Sun shall always possess long life and health, and become the abode of all prosperity. (142)

Having meditated upon the Sun at sunrise, one obtains all desires as wished; O Goddess, he who recites this three times a day with devotion during the solar transits (saṃkrānti) [attains the same]. || 143 ||
Having enjoyed prosperity in this world, one is liberated from all diseases who recites [this] on the seventh day of the bright fortnight when the sun has set. (144)
The best of Kaulas should maintain a body consisting entirely of health;
O Goddess, at midday during a Vyatīpāta, he should recite this with his senses restrained.
O Goddess, by worshipping the discus and reciting the root mantra while meditating upon the Sun, one shall obtain wealth, sons, fame, and honor through the grace of the Sun. 146.
Having become like the sun, skilled in the practice of the Great Cīna tradition, the majestic one quickly conquers all enemies and attains prosperity. 147.
He who, residing in a foreign land, is devoted to the worship of Vaṭuka, shall become like Śiva himself—free from fear and supported by his beloved. || 148 ||
He who recites the Śatāvarta at the interval between sunrise and the end of the Yuga,
Savitṛ, the lord of all worlds, will suddenly become a granter of boons.
O Pārvatī, what is the use of saying much more here?
By reciting this, one shall always enjoy prosperity in this world and attain that supreme state in the next.
O Goddess, on a Sunday, one should write the thousand names of the mantra upon birch bark with divine eight-fold fragrance, blue flowers, and turmeric.

Having drawn the yantra according to the rules, surrounded by the eight syllables, in the center of which the practitioner has written the five nectars, the medicinal herbs, and drops of human semen and nectar; 152.
Having prepared the pill and wrapped it while recollecting the root mantra,
one should wrap it with a thread spun by a virgin and dyed with red lac. (153)
Having wrapped it in gold, one should purify it with the five products of the cow [or, according to kh and g, consecrate it with the root mantra].
One should accomplish it with the King of Mantras and wear it on the head or on the arm. 154.
O Goddess, what indeed would she not accomplish, even that which is very difficult for me to attain?
[She cures] one afflicted by leprosy, one with colic, one with urinary disorders, and one with abdominal disease. (155)
Even one afflicted by fistula, hemorrhoids, urinary stones, or dysuria is suddenly liberated by taking this most rare pill. (156)
A barren woman, one whose children die at birth, or a woman who desires offspring—such a woman, satisfied with pride, should wear this pill upon her breast. (157)
O Pārvatī, a barren woman shall obtain a beloved son, and even a woman whose children have died shall obtain many handsome sons who are long-lived. (158)
Having gone to battle, having worn the pill, and having conquered his enemies, he shall obtain prosperity;
with his limbs uninjured, the great king shall enter his own city in happiness. (159)
Whoever would constantly wear on his arm this pill, which brings the world of kings under one's power and is capable of enchanting, attracting, paralyzing, and driving away [enemies], [150]
He shall become like the sun, a treasury of splendors through his own majesty;
O Goddess, he shall be a giver of wealth through his riches, and a Śaṅkara through his power.
O Goddess, he was Indra in splendor, Rāma in fame, Bhārgava in manliness, Bṛhaspati in speech, and the joy of the Bhṛgus in statesmanship.
In strength he is like the wind, in compassion he is the Supreme Person;
in health he is the Pot-born (Agastya), and in luster he resembles the full moon. || 163 ||
He is a King of Dharma through his righteousness, a mine of jewels comparable to the ocean of gems, a deep sea in his profundity, and Bali himself in his generosity. 164.
Through this accomplishment, Śrī Bhairava himself, the Lord of Consciousness (cidīśvara), is attained through bliss.
O Śivā, what is the use of much talk? One should either recite [this] or retain it in memory. (165)
Whoever should hear this supreme, divine Thousand Names of the Sun shall become the Sun himself, the embodiment of supreme bliss. (166)
At the end, he proceeds independently to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
This is the divine and great reality, the Thousand Names of the Sun. (167)
O Pārvatī, it must not be revealed, nor given, nor spoken to a wicked soul, one who lacks devotion, one who wears dirty clothes, or the disciple of another.
To one who is harsh, of low birth, wicked, and of sinful intellect;
to one devoid of devotion to the Guru; and to a reviler of the Śiva-āgama. (169)
It should be given to a disciple who is tranquil, devoted to the guru, of noble birth, deeply devoted, and dedicated to the worship of the Sun. (170)
This is indeed the reality among all realities, the secret of the Vedas and the Agamas; it consists of all mantras, and must be kept hidden, to be guarded like one's own private parts. 171.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Thousand Names of the Sun," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrī Devī Rahasya*.
Now begins the thirty-fifth chapter.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, O Goddess, I shall declare the hymn that defines the mantra—
the reality consisting of the fifth limb, which is certainly a deliverer from all calamities.
Consisting of the eight supernatural powers, it is the object to be accomplished, the bestower of success, and the increaser of intelligence;
it pacifies all diseases and increases splendor and strength. (2)
O Śivā, O Pārvatī, this secret of mine bestows great wealth, grants sons and grandsons, and provides both worldly enjoyment and liberation in this world. (3)
O Great Goddess, for this hymn, Brahmā is declared to be the seer;
Gāyatrī is said to be the meter, and Savitṛ is remembered as the deity. || 4 ||
The seed-syllable is declared to be Vyoman, and Māyā is said to be the Śakti;
O Goddess, Praṇava is the Kīlaka, and from that follows the binding of the directions with the universe.
The application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed for the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Of this mantra of the Śrī Sūrya-stotra, the Seer (*ṛṣi*) is the venerable Brahmā, the metre (*chandaḥ*) is Gāyatrī, the Deity (*devatā*) is Savitṛ, *hrāṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), *oṃ* is the peg (*kīlaka*), and *namaḥ* is the binding of the directions; [all this is] for the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The application is in the recitation. The meditation:
Having meditated upon Him whose crown is brilliantly shining, who is adorned with jeweled earrings, and who is embraced by the radiant [Śakti], one should utter this hymn. (6)

I bow to the Sun, whose faces shine with the brilliance of ten million fires at the end of an aeon, who is the color of vermilion powder and hibiscus flowers, who wears a jeweled crown, has two eyes, and sits upon the center of a white lotus; adorned with various ornaments, with a smiling face, clad in red garments, and consisting of pure consciousness.
I worship Him who holds a golden lotus and a jewel-filled pitcher in His two arms. || 7 ||
He who meditates upon the root mantra— the beginning of the Vedas, adorned with the *nāda*, the *bindu*, and the digit of the moon— though devoid of Vedic study and filled with dullness and poverty,
shall instantly have his feet honored by the shimmering gems on the crowns of radiant kings, and he shall conquer even Bṛhaspati.
[He] was instantly overcome in the assembly of gods by words filled with nectar. || 8 ||
O Lord, he who recites the mantra should meditate in his heart upon the fire in the form of Śiva, adorned with the digit of the moon and the bindu, which is the crest-jewel of all mantras.
Having swiftly conquered the entire host of enemies in battle, he shall become an emperor upon the earth; indeed, when his life departs, he goes to your abode.

He who meditates upon Him as mounted on the fire of the sky (the letter *ra*), beautiful with the dot (*bindu*) of the left eye and the digit of the moon (*indu-kalā*),—in his mouth, O All-pervading Lord, resides speech that rains down the nectar of prose and verse, and prosperity rests in his hand. 10.
If one endowed with devotion recites the mantra while remembering the Sun-god in its midst— whether he be afflicted by disease, or desirous of his own power,
or addicted to wine, or a hero full of valor— he shall become free from ailment in this world, enjoy prosperity, and, fanned by celestial women, dwell in heaven.
O Blessed One, he shall go to the imperishable abode. || 11 ||
O God, he who mutters the syllables of the name "Sūryāya" at sunrise— even if he is mute, filled with grief, beset by great disease, or distressed by poverty—
his speech immediately issues forth from his mouth as prose and excellent verse, flowing and lucid; and his body becomes endowed with health.
O Blessed One, may all prosperities always be under my control. || 12 ||

O All-pervading Lord, for one who, at night, with his body absorbed in the art of love and filled with longing and curiosity, recites within his mind this entire universe— which is contained within the hem of Viśvamanas—
she who is most excellent even among the best of women, Tilottamā, delightful in her beauty and peerless, will immediately come under his control.
They were full of majesty, splendor, and pride. || 13 ||

I bow to the Lord Sūrya, the beloved of Sarasvatī, who is accessible through all the Vedas; whose forehead is radiant and expansive with the rays of his jeweled crown; whose lotus-hands hold a divine lotus and a golden pitcher; and whose limbs are embraced by shimmering [halos]. 14.

[The mandala] is adorned with the earth-abode (the square), beautified by the city-forest (the lotus), decorated with eight petals, endowed with a self of nine corners, possessing divine angles, and [marked] with a drop at the center.
I worship the Lord, the infinite and primordial deity, whose body shines with thousands of joyful rays.
Thus, one who has bathed at dawn should recite this hymn in the form of mantras, extracted from all the tantras, dedicated to you, Mihira-Bhuvaneśvara.
Such a person shall become an enjoyer of pleasures on earth, endowed with prosperity and fame; and at the end, in the hereafter, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
The abode of Savitṛ. || 16 ||
Thus, O Goddess, these five limbs of the radiant God of gods have been declared by me out of affection for you; they must not be told to just anyone.
Whatever merit exists in the house of the Supreme Self, the Sun—the entirety of all things, the secret, the most excellent mystery—is contained therein. (18)
In his house, the goddess Lakṣmī shall dwell as steady as a maidservant;
there shall be no fear of fire, no poverty, no disease, nor any calamity.
There is no fear of kings, nor is there grief; there is always the fulfillment of all goals in the home.
This indeed is the reality of realities, a secret difficult even for gods to attain. (20)
This supreme Sūryapañcāṅga, the secret of secrets, is not to be given to one who is unworthy, but must be given to a high-souled person. 21.
It must always and in every way be guarded and concealed, like one's own private parts.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sūrya Stotra," in the *Śrī Devī Rahasya* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*.
The Sūryapañcāṅga is completed.
(p. 204) Now begins the thirty-sixth chapter.
The Five-fold Ritual Manual (Pañcāṅga) of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Upon the lofty peak of Kailāsa, resplendent with rows of jewels...
It was filled with forests of wish-fulfilling trees and adorned with golden stones. || 1 ||
Adorned with rubies, pearls, gems, and rubies (māṇikya),
it was carried solely by the wind, which bore the fragrance of spring flowers.
The Supreme Lord, the God of gods, the Master of the world, the all-pervading one, together with Pārvatī, seated upon a beautiful throne made of nine-jewel stones. || 3 ||
He was dwelling [and sporting], reciting prayers, and meditating upon the eternal Brahman;
adorned with serpent ornaments and graced by a crown of matted locks.
Hara holds a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff in his hands and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
he is served by gods, dānavas, lords of yakṣas, piśācas, and uragas. || 5 ||
Having beheld the Lord Maheśvara, whose countenance was gracious, who is worshipped by hosts of Gaṇas, Gandharvas, and Siddhas, and by Nārada, and who is imperishable; the Goddess [beheld him].
Having prostrated and suddenly risen with palms joined in reverence before him,
the goddess Pārvatī spoke to Śiva, the leader of the three worlds.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, you who are saluted by gods and asuras!
You are Śiva, the Lord of all worlds, the Truth, whose nature is existence and consciousness.
Ananta is the Supreme Self, the Lord who is the cause of the three worlds;
he is the eternal creator of origin and sustenance, and the destroyer, the Sovereign of the universe.
The god who is without beginning or end, though consisting of the three qualities, is yet devoid of qualities;
what is that supreme Great Principle (mahattattva) which you now chant continuously? 10.
"I desire to hear that very reality from you; I am your devotee, your servant.
Śrī Bhairava said: "Though you have been refused a hundred thousand times, again and again,"
O Great Goddess, it is due to the nature of women that you ask me again.
O Pārvatī, I am truly pleased with this devotion of yours;
I shall now declare this supreme secret, which is hidden even from the dwellers of heaven.
O Maheśvarī, this reality is inexpressible and should not be given away;
yet out of affection for you, I shall speak of it, though it must not be disclosed even to great-souled ones.

He who is the God of gods, the granter of boons, the all-pervading Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, who effects creation and maintenance in the world, and brings about dissolution at the end of the cosmic destruction.
He alone is the supreme lord of gods, serpents, and rākṣasas;
of daityas, kinnaras, and lords of yakṣas; and of humans, fire, and water.
The Supreme Lord is the cause of the three worlds from Brahmā down to a mere insect; He is the presiding witness, the essence of goodness, and the Self of all beings.
O Śivā, for that deity there is the five-limbed [rite], the Paṭala, the Paddhati,
the Kavaca consisting of the principles (tattvas), and the Thousand Names of the Mantra.
O Goddess of gods, I mutter this hymn and always remember it with my mind;
being tranquil, I recite day and night this cause of supreme bliss.
The illustrious Goddess said:
"Indeed, [I shall describe] the five-limbed [mantra] of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the God of gods."
O Lord, I desire to hear this; you should speak of it now.
Śrī Bhairava said:
O Goddess, I shall declare to you the five-limbed [mantra] of the Supreme Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, which bestows the ultimate truth and grants all perfections.
Therein, I shall first declare the chapter on the secret of the root-mantra;
I shall explain to you the extraction of the mantra of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. (21)
It bestows the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi) immediately upon practitioners, though it is very difficult to attain;
it consists of the syllable *tāra*, the goddess *parā*, the word *harita*, again *parā*, and then the name [of the deity] followed by *lakṣmī*. (22)
The mantra ending with "Viśva" for Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is thus remembered;
for one who possesses it, there is no obstacle, no defect, no fear, and no adversity. (23)
This mantra directly bestows liberation and grants the fruit of all goals; yet, without performing the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) of one hundred thousand recitations, it incurs a defect.
Just as a body devoid of life is incapable of any action, so too a mantra devoid of *puraścaraṇa* does not yield fruit. || 25 ||
One should perform the *puraścaraṇa* rite at a banyan tree, in a forest, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, at a crossroads, at midnight, or at midday. (26)
O Maheśvarī, one should perform the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) for one hundred thousand recitations, or half of that;
it may extend up to one hundred thousand, but never less than that. (27)
First, [the mantra should be received] by the hand of the guru or by the hand of the practitioner;
thereafter, one should personally perform many preliminary rites (puraścaryā) according to the prescribed injunctions.
From the recitation, the fire-oblation (homa) should be one-tenth; the libation (tarpaṇa) one-tenth of that;
the sprinkling (mārjana) one-tenth of that; and the feeding (bhojana) one-tenth of that. || 29 ||
Without performing the *daśāṃśa* oblation, one shall not obtain that fruit— namely,
the *vidyā* of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa known as Pañcaratneśvarī. (30)
One should recite that [mantra] five times along with [the other five]; thus one obtains the fruit of the preliminary rite (puraścaryā).
Then, O Goddess of the Gods, one should perform the ritual of consecration (saṃskāra) for the mantra. 31.
O Goddess, by that rite through which the practitioner may immediately become a possessor of siddhi,
one should then "uproot" the mantra and subsequently restore it to life.
O Goddess, one should recite the vidyā that removes curses from the mouth of a true guru;
at the end, one should recite the perfected mantra and perform it again as a *saṃpuṭita* (enclosed) recitation.
This supreme mantra of yoga is difficult for yogins to obtain in the Kali age.
Now, O Maheśvarī, I shall explain the "unbolting" (utkīlana) of this mantra.
One should recite "parārṇam," "haritam," "bhūtim," "mām," and the entire name;
at the end of each word, O Goddess, the wise one should utter the Praṇava once.
O Śivā, this shall be the extraction of the mantra (mantrotkīlana), consisting of all reality;
I shall now speak of the reviving of the mantra—listen with respect, O Pārvatī. (36)
O Maheśvarī, this supreme manifestation is the syllable *mā*, with *tāra* (*om*) uttered at the end; it is proclaimed as "Viśva" and declared to be the King of Mantras named Sañjīvana.
One should mutter this lore, which was described by Śiva and which removes curses upon Śivā;
out of devotion to you, I shall declare this secret [mantra] that bestows all desired objects. (38)
One should recite *tāram*, *parā*, *virdeveśi*, and then *brahmaśāpam*;
having extracted the two [mantras] "mocaya" and "dvayam", one should mutter *parā* and the two *ṭha*s. (39)
This knowledge, beloved of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, is difficult to obtain in the world;
the practitioner of mantras should recite the perfected mantra and then perform the *saṃpuṭita* (encasement) again.
I shall declare the mantra of the *saṃpuṭa*, extracted from all the Āgamas:
O Dear One, one should first recite the *viśva* mantra, then the name [of the deity], and finally [the *viśva* mantra] at the end. (141)
O Goddess, this mantra known as Saṃpuṭa has been described for the attainment of its fruits.
O Great Goddess, Śiva is described here as the seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra. (42)
The Triṣṭubh meter has been declared by me, and the deity has also been proclaimed;
O Goddess, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is the deity, and Lakṣmī is declared to be the seed-syllable (bīja). || 43 ||

The supreme power (śakti) is likewise declared to be the seed-syllable (tāra), and it is proclaimed as the pin (kīlaka). The ritual application (viniyoga) is celebrated for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment (bhoga) and liberation (apavarga). || 44 ||
I shall describe to you the meditation upon this Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, by the mere practice of which meditation Lakṣmī will come into one's presence. (45)
I worship Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, whose face is like the full moon, who wears yellow garments, who is seated upon a lotus, who is attended by Lakṣmī, and who possesses four arms.

O Maheśvarī, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the six limbs and so forth, preceded by the purification of the hands and other preliminaries, using the seed-syllables of Tāra and Mābhūti with the six long vowels at their ends.
I shall now proclaim the extraction of the yantra, which is supreme and bestows the fulfillment of all desires;
it is the yantra that fascinates all and grants whatever is wished for. (48)

[The mandala] consists of a bindu, a triangle, an eight-sided figure, adorned with circles and an eight-petaled lotus, a sixteen-spoked wheel, a circle, and beautified by an enclosure of earth. || 49 ||

This Śrīcakra of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa bestows the supreme goal; O Goddess, I shall now describe its constituent parts of dissolution (layāṅga), which grant the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Rich with the secrets of the Vedas and Agamas, it bestows the fruit of ten million acts of worship.
Then follow the vajra, śakti, staff, sword, noose, rod, and banner. (51)
These [deities] along with Śūla and Śiva are always to be worshipped at the outer gates:
Indra, Agni, Yama, Māṃsāda, Varuṇa, Anila, and Vittada. (52)
Therefore, Brahmā, Ananta, and the others, who possess a Lord, are to be worshipped by practitioners;
likewise Keśava, Mādhava, Kṛṣṇa, Govinda, and Madhusūdana.
[He saw] Janārdana, the bearer of the Gaṅgā, the bearer of the conch, the wielder of the discus, four-armed,
having the lotus as his weapon, the enemy of Kaiṭabha, and possessing terrible fangs.
O Goddess of the gods, the practitioner should worship Vaikuṇṭha and Vāmana, who has Garuḍa as his banner,
in the sixteen spokes in a counter-clockwise direction. (55)
There, O Great Goddess, the practitioner of mantra should worship the fourfold lineage of gurus;
he should honor Asitāṅga, Haṃsaketu, and Vaṃśīpāṇi.
O Goddess of the gods, within the three circles, the practitioner [should worship] with perfumes and flowers:
Saṃhāra, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Bhūteśa, and Kālabhairava. (57)
O Maheśvarī, for the sake of attaining siddhi, the practitioner should worship Kapāla, Bhīṣaṇa (the correct reading is *Kapālibhīṣaṇau*), and likewise Śmaśānabhairava on the eight-petaled lotus.
And Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva, and the god Dāmodara, as well as Nṛsiṃha, O Great Goddess, and the god Saṅkarṣaṇa. || 59 ||
O Goddess, the practitioner should worship Trivikrama, Aniruddha, and Viṣvaksena,
marked with the word "Lakṣmī," in the eight corners.
O Pārvatī, one should worship Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and likewise Sarasvatī within a triangle, according to the sequence starting from the front, followed by Agni, Īśa, and Krama.
One should worship the deity Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa within the Bindu-maṇḍala;
one should also worship Mahālakṣmī, Rājyalakṣmī, and Siddhalakṣmī.

One should worship the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus within the circle of the bindu with perfumes, unbroken grains of rice, flowers, and so forth, as well as with garlands and ornaments for the Guru. (63)
Having performed worship with drops from the jar of nectar consecrated by mantras,
the practitioner should satisfy the supreme deity with the five "makāras."
O Pārvatī, these eight preliminary applications (prayoga) have been declared as the limbs of absorption (layāṅga);
I shall now describe that by which the accomplishment (siddhi) of this mantra occurs specifically.

Stambhana (paralysis), mohana (delusion), then māraṇa (killing) and ākarṣaṇa (attraction); likewise vaśīkāra (subjugation), uccāṭa (expulsion), then śāntika (pacification) and pauṣṭika (nourishment). || 66 ||
O Maheśvarī, I shall now describe the means for accomplishing these applications;
by the mere accomplishment of these, the perfection of the mantra is produced. (67)
O Great Goddess, having bathed at Ravau and gone beneath the shade of an Aśvattha tree,
one should mutter [the mantra] ten thousand times, O Īśānī, and perform oblations there by a tenth part of that amount.
By means of flowers produced from ghee, sugar-candy, or molasses, mixed with *ānanda*, there occurs an immediate immobilization (*stambhana*) of speech, wind, the sun, and water. (69)
At the time of midnight under the moon, the wise man should go to a crossroads,
bind the directions, purify his seat, and perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).

O Goddess, having meditated upon Hari, one should mutter the root mantra and perform oblations with clarified butter, nagara, punnāga, and karanja flowers in quantities amounting to one-tenth [of the recitation].
O Maheśvarī, having offered libations with a tenth part [of the mantra] and performed the ritual purification,
the best of practitioners should apply a tilaka mark on his forehead with that ash.
Having suddenly beheld the three worlds, his face will fall into delusion;
having gone to a cremation ground on earth, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times.
O Goddess, by performing the tenth-part oblation (daśāṃśa-homa) with ghee, wheat-pudding,
and dūrvā grass along with liquor, even Death himself perishes in an instant.
Having gone to a distant forest on a Wednesday, one should recite the root mantra ten thousand times on an auspicious shore of a stormy sea, and offer oblations of ghee, barley, and grains.
Dūrvā grass, pūtāsa, lotus petals, flowers, and even plantains shall immediately appear before him. (76)
Having gone to the riverbank in the presence of the Guru, one should perform the recitation (japa) there for ten parts;
one should offer oblations of ghee, honey, *śaṭī*, *candana*, and *karīra*.
By means of the ashes thus consecrated, the three worlds shall come under one's control.
Having gone to an Aśoka tree during the month of Śukra, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times.
Having offered *hunet* oblations with ghee, *nāgapaṭa*, rice powder, and husks,
one should satisfy [the deity] with *āsava*, wine, clarified butter, and sugarcane juice, having consumed [the offerings] in a tenth part of the quantity. (79)
The eradication of an enemy who is equal to Śambhu will certainly occur;
having gone to a riverbank on a Saturday, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times.

A human figure should be fashioned from ten parts [of the ingredients] using ghee, milk-rice, saffron, sarala resin, and rose-apple fruits; through this, pacification (śāntika) occurs instantaneously.
O Īśānī, having gone to a grove on an auspicious lunar mansion or an auspicious day,
one should recite the mantra ten thousand times and perform oblations with ghee and lotuses.
Accompanied by blue lotuses, grains of rice, and sour substances, great nourishment is produced;
this supreme secret has been declared to you by me out of devotion. (83)
O lady honored by heroes, this entire essence of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, which bestows the supreme goal, must not be given to those who are not devotees or to the wicked. 84.
O Śivā, this reality (tattva), which bestows enjoyment and liberation in the Kali age upon those established in the great land of China,
is to be kept secret; it is the most secret of secrets, more secret than the secret, the cause of bliss, to be guarded and concealed like one's own womb.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, the description of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Paṭala, within the Śrī Devī Rahasya of the venerable Rudrayāmala Tantra. || 36 ||
Now begins the thirty-seventh chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Now, O Goddess, I shall describe to you the manual for the daily worship of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, which consists of both prose and verse.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and assumed the *padmāsana* posture,
[one should meditate upon] one's own guru seated within the pericarp of a thousand-petaled lotus facing downwards located at the crown of one's head.

Having meditated upon [the deity] adorned with white ornaments and worshipped with mental offerings, one should recite the root mantra before him according to one's capacity. Having offered that recitation to the Guru and received his permission, one should go outside, discard impurities and the like at a distance, perform the purification prescribed for one's caste, and go to a river or similar place, [reciting] *oṃ klīṃ*.

Having purified the teeth with the mantra, "Obeisance to Kāmadeva, beloved of all people," and having performed self-purification, one should cleanse three portions of earth with the root mantra, perform the bath for the removal of impurities, and then perform the mantra-bath. Therein, with earth, [one recites]: *oṃ gāṃ gūṃ gaṅge ca yamune caiva godāvari sarasvati*.
"O Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, take up your residence in this water! Having thus invoked [the deities] with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*, one should say:

"O Lord of Devas, who are easily accessible through devotion, together with Your retinue; O God, as long as I shall offer libations to You, so long remain here. Having thus displayed the *āvāhana* and other mudrās, as well as the *dhenu*, *yoni*, and *matsya* mudrās, [one proceeds].

Having shown [the mudrā] and smeared clay upon his body, he should visualize a triangle in the water, draw the root mantra within that triangle, and emerge from the water three times while reciting the root mantra. Then, he should offer three *arghya* oblations to the Sun:
having offered the three *arghya*s with "Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, this is your *arghya*, obeisance to Śrī Sūrya," he should emerge from the water.
Having caused [the person] to put on garments, having performed the purification of the body,
having performed the placement of the root-sages (*mūlarṣinyāsa*) and so forth, and having recited the root mantra according to one's ability, one should perform the *aghamarṣaṇa*.
Holding water in the left hand and covering it with the right hand, [one should recite] *yaṃ raṃ vaṃ laṃ haṃ*.

Having consecrated it seven times with mantras, one should sprinkle the head fourteen times with droplets of water dripping from it while reciting the root mantra; then, holding the remaining water in the right hand, drawing it inward through the *iḍā* [left nostril], washing away all evil, and exhaling that turbid water out through the left nostril (*vāmanāsāpuṭa*).
One should strike against the stone situated on the left side; this is the *aghamarṣaṇa*.

Then, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as before, one should mutter the *Gāyatrī*: *oṃ hrīṃ lakṣmīnārāyaṇāya vidmahe hsauḥ parabrahmaṇe dhīmahi hrīṃ śrīṃ tannaḥ paramātmā pracodayāt* (three times).
Having thus recited [the mantra] according to one's ability,

and having offered three *arghya* libations with the words, "To Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, together with his limbs, vehicles, retinue, and powers— this is your *arghya*, obeisance," and having performed three rounds of *prāṇāyāma*, inhale air through the *iḍā* [left nostril] sixteen times.

Abandon the sixty-four internal [breaths] gradually, by tens, by tens, by tens, and with two more, along with the *piṅgalā* [channel]. Having thus performed the three types of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), [recite] *oṃ hrīṃ*.

"Oṃ hrīṃ, I purify the *ātmatattva*, svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ, I purify the *vidyātattva*, svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ, I purify the *śivatattva*, svāhā! Having rinsed the mouth (*ācamana*) with these mantras, one should offer three *arghya* oblations to the Sun as before, meditate upon the *yantra* in the water, and perform libations (*tarpaṇa*) therein according to one's capacity while reciting the root mantra (*mūla*).

Having offered libations three times, saying: "May the illustrious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, together with his limbs, his vehicle, his retinue, and his goddess, be satisfied," and having uttered the syllables of the root-mantra, one should satisfy the members of the retinue with individual handfuls of water.
Having gratified the gods, sages, and ancestors as before, and having offered three *arghya* oblations to the Sun,
one should enter the sacrificial pavilion after bowing to the deity with the *saṃhāramudrā*; such is the procedure for the twilight worship (*sandhyā-vidhi*).
Having entered the house there, having washed one's feet, and having sprinkled the doorway,
one should draw a square and circular maṇḍala in front of the threshold. Having placed a washed vessel upon it,
and having established the vessel together with its support while reciting "Astrāya Phaṭ," one should then recite "Oṃ Hṛdayāya Namaḥ."

Having filled [the vessel] with the heart-mantra and worshipped it with "Oṃ, salutation to the general arghya of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa," one should invoke the sacred ford (tīrtha) with "Gaṅge," display the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā), and sprinkle the door;
this is the procedure for the general arghya. To the east, "Gaṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati"; to the south, "Vāṃ, to Vaṭuka."
Having worshipped the deities of the door with "Homage to Kṣāṃ Kṣetrapāla in the west; homage to Yāṃ Yoginīs in the north;
homage to Gāṃ Gaṅgā on the right; homage to Yaṃ Yamunā on the left; homage to Saṃ Sarasvatī above;
and to the Weapon (astra) phaṭ at the threshold below," one enters within the door.
Having sat upon the prepared seat, one should gaze at it with the *mūla-mantra*, sprinkle it with water while reciting the *kavaca-mantra*, and strike it with the *astra-mantra* saying "phaṭ.
Then, having incensed the worship pavilion with smoke, one should perform the purification of the seat (*viṣṭara-śuddhi*). "Oṃ Āṃ:
For this mantra for purifying the seat, Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Sutala is the meter (*chanda*), and Kūrma is the deity (*devatā*)."
The application is for the purification of the seat. *Prīṃ*, salutation to the Earth. *Oṃ*: O Great One, by you the worlds are supported;
O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu. Support me in this world, and make the seat pure. *Oṃ krāṃ*, salutation to the Lotus Seat of the Support-Power (*Ādhāraśakti*), to Ananta.
"Salutation to the Lotus, salutation to the Lotus-stalk; having sat there and performed the triple clapping of the palms, [one should recite]:
'May those beings depart who dwell upon the earth; may those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva. Thus, one should dispel the obstacles with three strikes of the left heel."

One should display the *nārāca-mudrā*. Having thus purified the seat, one should prostrate to the Guru: "Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom that state was revealed—the state which is of the nature of an unbroken circle and by which the moving and the unmoving are pervaded. Salutation to the Gurus; salutation to the Supreme Gurus; salutation to the Gurus who are both supreme and non-supreme."
Having worshipped at the head with "Oṃ, salutations to the supreme teachers; salutations," and having prostrated before the Deity,

one should draw [the consciousness], shaped like the flame of a lamp, through the path of the *suṣumnā* by means of contraction with the syllable "Oṃ hrīṃ," lead it into the interior of the path of Brahman, unite it with Paramaśiva, and contemplate the oneness of the two.
Having satiated the lineage gurus (*kulaguru*) with the stream of nectar arising from that [lotus],
and having caused Kuṇḍalinī— who is gratifying the powers such as the Ḍākinīs by that same path— to reach her own station,
one should meditate on the Person of Sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) in the left nostril, the size of a thumb and smoke-colored, while reciting *yaṃ raṃ vaṃ laṃ*.
One should perform drying, burning, flooding, and so forth.
One should dry [the body] with the seed-syllable of wind (*vāyubīja*) recited sixteen times; one should burn it with the seed-syllable of fire (*vahni-bīja*) recited sixty-four times.

One should burn [the body]. One should flood it with the seed-syllable *vaṃ* of Varuṇa, recited thirty-two times. With the seed-syllable of the earth, *laṃ*, recited ten times, one should form the body into a solid mass and perform the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*). This is the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). *oṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ so 'haṃ saḥ*

"Haṃsaḥ! My vital breaths (prāṇas) are here; my life-force (jīva) is stationed here. All the senses—speech, mind, sight, hearing, taste, smell, and breath—having come right here, may they remain happily for a long time, Svāhā! This is the procedure for the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā). Having offered the vital breaths and performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), [one should proceed].
Having sipped water as before, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) preceded by a formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*).
Of this mantra for the worship of Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Śiva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*),
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is the deity (*devatā*), *śrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *oṃ* is the peg (*kīlaka*).

The application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of worldly enjoyment and liberation through the worship of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. Salutation to Śiva the Seer (ṛṣi) on the head; salutation to the Triṣṭubh metre on the face; salutation to the deity Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa on the heart;
salutation to the seed-syllable *śrīṃ* on the private parts; salutation to the power (*śakti*) *hrīṃ* on the feet; salutation to the *kīlaka* *oṃ*.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) on all the limbs, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and so forth: *oṃ hrāṃ śrāṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*;

*oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ* to the two index fingers, *namaḥ*; *oṃ hrūṃ śrūṃ* to the two middle fingers, *namaḥ*; *oṃ hraiṃ śraiṃ* to the two ring fingers, *namaḥ*; *oṃ hrauṃ śrauṃ*... [to the two little fingers, *namaḥ*].
To the two little fingers, *namaḥ*. *Oṃ hraḥ śraḥ*, to the palms and backs of the hands, *namaḥ*.

Thus is the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). Now, again, the purification of the hands: *Oṃ kāmarūpapīṭhāya namaḥ*, to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*. *Hrīṃ jālandharapīṭhāya namaḥ*, to the two index fingers.

Namaḥ | Hsauḥ, salutation to Pūrṇagiri-pīṭha; salutation to the two middle fingers. Hrīṃ, salutation to Avanti-pīṭha; salutation to the two ring fingers. Śrīṃ, salutation to Saptapurī-pīṭha; salutation to the two little fingers. Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ hrīṃ śrīṃ, salutation to Vārāṇasī-pīṭha.

"Salutation to the palms and backs of the hands"—thus is the purification of the hands (*kara-śuddhi*). Likewise is the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍ-aṅga-nyāsa*). *Aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ* from the left foot up to the ankle. *Ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ* from the right foot up to the ankle. *Kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ*.

From the ankle to the base of the left foot: *caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ*. From the ankle to the base of the right foot: *ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ*. From the navel to the base of the left arm: *taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ*.

One should perform the threefold pervasion as follows: *paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ* from the navel to the base of the right arm; *yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ* from the waist to the left ear; *śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ* from the right shoulder to the right ear; and *lakṣaḥ* from the head to the feet. One should thus pervade [the body] three times.
Aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ, salutation to the two thumbs (aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ).
Iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ, salutation to the two index fingers (tarjanībhyāṃ namaḥ).
Uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ ūṃ, salutation to the two middle fingers (madhyamābhyāṃ namaḥ).
Eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ; salutation to the two ring fingers (anāmikā).
Oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ; salutation to the two little fingers (kaniṣṭhikā).
Aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaḥ aḥ.
"Salutation to the palms and backs of the hands"— thus is the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*). In this same manner,
the ritual placement of the six limbs beginning with the heart (*hṛdayādi-ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed.

Now, the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa): *aṃ* namaḥ on the head; *āṃ* on the perimeter of the mouth; *iṃ* on the right eye; *īṃ* on the left eye; *uṃ* on the right ear; *ūṃ* on the left ear; *ṛṃ* on the right nostril; *ṝṃ* on the left nostril;
*ḷṃ* on the right cheek; *ḹṃ* on the left cheek; *eṃ* on the upper lip; *aiṃ*...

Oṃ on the lower lip; auṃ on the upper row of teeth; aṃ on the lower row of teeth; aḥ on the head; kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ on the joints of the right arm; caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ on the joints of the left arm;
ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ on the joints of the right leg.
There, one should place *taṃ* on the joints of the left foot; *paṃ* on the right side; *baṃ* on the left side;
*bhaṃ* on the back; *maṃ* at the navel; *yaṃ* in the stomach; *raṃ* in the heart; *laṃ* on the right shoulder;
*vaṃ* on the crown of the head; *śaṃ* on the left shoulder; and *ṣaṃ* from the heart up to the tips of the fingers of the right hand.

One should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) three times: *saṃ* from the heart to the tips of the left hand; *haṃ* from the heart to the tips of the right foot; *laṃ* from the feet to the top of the head; and *kṣaḥ* from the head down to the feet. Then, one should place [the syllables] from *aṃ* up to *kṣaṃ*, reciting *aṃ oṃ aṃ*. [Then] *aṃ hrīṃ am*.

One should place the *kṣānta* [syllable] in the locations of the *mātṛkā*. One should place the *kṣānta* as *aṃ hsrauḥ am*. One should place the *kṣānta* as *aṃ hrīṃ am*. One should place the *kṣānta* as *aṃ śrīṃ am*. Having thus performed the sixfold placement (*ṣoḍhā-nyāsa*) by placing the root mantra alone in the locations of the *mātṛkā*, one should effect the purification of the body while reciting the root mantra.

One should perform the worship of the jar (*ghaṭapūjā*). Therein, having drawn a circle, a hexagon, and a square to the left of the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*), one should worship them with "Oṃ, salutation to the seats" (*pīṭhebhyo namaḥ*).
Having placed the washed base (*ādhāra*) there, [one worships it] with "Raṃ, salutation to the fire-mandala consisting of ten digits" (*vahnimaṇḍalāya daśakalātmane namaḥ*).

Having worshipped with unbroken grains (*akṣata*) and having established the auspicious jar (*śrīghaṭa*) there, [he says]: "O Goddess, just as formerly by Brahmā, just as of old by Viṣṇu, and just as by Śambhu, so do I establish you.
Having thus established [it], [he recites]: "Aṃ, obeisance to the solar disc (*arkamaṇḍala*), whose self consists of twelve digits (*kalā*)."

Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, one should fill [the vessel] with supreme nectar using the root mantra in reverse order along with the Mātṛkā. Then, having worshipped it with "sauḥ, obeisance to the lunar maṇḍala consisting of sixteen digits," and having struck the substance in the jar with "astrāya phaṭ" while reciting the root mantra, one should inhale the fragrance three times through the nose. Therein is a triangle.

Having written the root mantra and worshipped it three times with the root mantra, one should recite ten times over the substance: *oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ sudhe śukraśāpaṃ mocaya mocaya amṛtaṃ srāvaya srāvaya svāhā*. Then [one should recite]: *oṃ sūryamaṇḍalasaṃbhūte varuṇālayasaṃbhave*.

O Goddess, who consists of the seed-syllable *Amā*, may [this one] be liberated from the curse of Śukra. If the *praṇava* is the seed-syllable of the Vedas and consists of the bliss of Brahman, by that truth, O Goddess, may the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) be removed from you. The purifier is supreme bliss; the purifier is the supreme essence.
Pavamāna is supreme knowledge; by means of that, I purify you.
Having recited this three times, and having recited ten times over the substance: *oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaṃ srāvaya srāvaya aṃ hrīṃ amṛteśvaryai namaḥ*.

Having meditated upon Ānanda Bhairava and Bhairavī, one should recite *hsakṣamalavaraya-ūṃ ānandabhairavāya vaṣaṭ* (or *vauṣaṭ*) ten times. Then, having recited *sudhodayai vauṣaṭ* ten times over the substance, one should draw a triangle there with the mantra beginning *gaṅge ca yamune caiva*.

Having invoked the Tīrtha, one should place the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*, the sixteen consonants beginning with *ka*, and the sixteen consonants beginning with *tha* within the three triangles starting from the east. Having written *haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ* in the center and recited the root mantra ten times, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*). Then, one should purify the Matsya-mudrā and other gestures; this is the purification of the substances (*dravya-śuddhi*).

Having displayed the *dhenu-yoni-matsya* mudrās over the fish, one should purify the fish by reciting the root mantra three times: "Oṃ, we worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of nourishment; may He deliver me from death, as the cucumber from its stem, yet not from immortality. This is the purification of the fish (*mīna-śuddhi*).

Having displayed three mudrās over the meat and recited the root mantra three times— *oṃ pra tadviṣṇuḥ stavate vīryeṇa mṛgo na bhīmaḥ kucaro giriṣṭhāḥ | yasyoruṣu triṣu vikramaṇeṣvadhikṣiyanti bhuvanāni viśvā*— one should purify the meat; this is the purification of the meat (*māṃsaśuddhi*).

Having displayed three mudrās over the [first] mudrā, one should recite the root mantra three times: "Oṃ, the wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye stretched across the sky; the inspired poets, eloquent and vigilant, kindle that which is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Having thus recited it, one should purify the mudrā. Then...

Having placed pieces of *mudrā*, pieces of fish, pieces of meat, and so forth into a jar, and having drawn a square, one should place a vessel with its support (*sādhāra*) for the Guru on one's left; filling it with the *kulāmṛta*, one should worship it with the root mantra (*mūla*).
Then, [one prepares] the vessel for one's own enjoyment, the vessel for the *śakti*, the vessels for the *yoginīs* and the heroes (*vīras*), and the vessels for the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*).

Having set it down and filled it with the nectar of the jar, and having filled the vessel for the madhuparka offering with ghee, honey, and sugar, one should perform the worship of the yoga-pīṭha [as follows]: "O you who are adorned by the point, shining with the triangle,
decorated with the eight-cornered [figure], encircled by the circle, resplendent with the eight petals, and inlaid with sixteen petals."

Having drawn the King of Śrī-yantras, which is square and adorned with three circles, and having placed it upon a sacred golden pedestal or similar surface, one should worship the Lord together with the Goddess within one’s heart using mental offerings (mānasopacāra), and then perform the external worship.
In that regard: *Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Maṇḍūka* (twice); *obeisance to Kālāgnirudra* (twice); *obeisance to Mūlaprakṛti*.
Salutations twice. Salutations to the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti) twice. Salutations to Kūrma twice. Salutations to Ananta twice.
Salutations to Varāha twice. Salutations to Pṛthivī. (p. 217)
2. Homage to the Ocean of Nectar. 2. Homage to the Gateway of Jewels. In the eight directions: 2.
Homage to the Fragments of the Nine Jewels. 2. Homage to the Golden Mountain. 2. Homage to the Nandana Garden. 2. Homage to the Kalpa Forest. 2. Homage to the Lotus Forest.
Salutation to the ground inlaid with various jewels. Salutation to the pavilion of wish-fulfilling gems.

Salutation to the altar of the nine jewels. Salutation to the lion throne. Salutation to the lofty white parasol in the directions beginning with the east. Salutation to Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in the intermediate directions.

To Adharma, Ajñāna, Avairāgya, and Anaiśvarya, svāhā. To Sattva, svāhā. To Rajas, svāhā. To Tamas, svāhā. Salutations to the Tattvas, svāhā. Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ, salutations to the pericarp adorned with the syllables of the mantra;
salutations to the petals consisting of Prakṛti; salutations to the filaments consisting of Vikṛti; salutations to Garuḍa.

"Obeisance to the Lotus Throne adorned with fifty letters; obeisance to the Śrī Yogapīṭha, the essence of all principles"—having thus worshipped and meditated upon the God, and having tied the three-sectioned rosary filled with flowers, [one should pray]:
"O Lord of Gods, easily accessible through devotion, together with Your retinue, for as long as I shall worship You..."

"O God, come here! Having thus offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and displayed the mudrās for invocation (*āvāhana*) and the others, [one recites] the root mantra together with its limbs (*sāṅga*) and the Goddess: "O Lord Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, come here, come here! Stay here, stay here! Be present here, be present here! [Then follows] the root mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ haṃsaḥ*.

"O Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, may your vital breaths (prāṇas) come here; O Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, may your life-force (jīva) remain here. O Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, may all your senses—speech, mind, sight, hearing, smell, and breath—come here and dwell happily for a long time, Svāhā! Having thus offered the vital breaths with the *lelihāna-mudrā* (the tongue-licking gesture).
O Mūla, together with the Goddess Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, please be seated upon this seat. At the end of the Mūla-vidyā, [offer] water for the feet,
water for sipping, honey-mixture, water for sipping, the arghya offering, perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains,
the bath, ornaments, the jeweled throne, perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains.

Having offered incense, lamps, food offerings, water for sipping, betel, an umbrella, chowries, the *ārātrika* lamp, and so forth, and having prostrated, one should worship with the root mantra and the *kalaśāmṛta* (nectar from the vessel) using the *tattvamudrā*: "I worship Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, together with His limbs (*sāṅga*), vehicles (*savāhana*), weapons (*sāyudha*), goddesses (*sadevīka*), and retinue (*saparicchada*); obeisance! I satisfy Him; obeisance!"—thus three times.

Having satisfied [the deities] and received the command of the gods, one should worship the attendant deities. Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one recites the root mantra: "I worship and satisfy the *śrīpādukā* of Mahālakṣmī; obeisance. [Recite] the root mantra for Rājyalakṣmī-śrīpādukā, and the root mantra for Siddhalakṣmī-śrīpādukā. Thus, at the *bindu*, is the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*). Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ gaṃ...
Gaṅgā-Śrīpādukāṃ: Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ yaṃ Yamunā-Śrī; Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ saṃ Sarasvatī-Śrī. Thus is the second enclosure in the triangle. Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ Śaṅkha-Śrī;
Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ Cakra-Śrī; Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ Gadā-Śrī; Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ Padma-Śrī. Thus.
The third enclosure is in the *bindu*. The root mantra is: *oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ lakṣmīviṣṇuśrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi* (p.
*oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ lakṣmīvāsudevaśrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. *oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ lakṣmīdāmodaraśrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.
Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha-śrī; Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ Lakṣmīsaṅkarṣaṇa-śrī;
Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ Lakṣmītrivikrama-śrīpādukā; Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ Lakṣmīaniruddha-śrī;
Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ Lakṣmīviśvaksena-śrī. Thus ends the fourth enclosure in the eight corners. Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ.
Mahābhairava-Śrīpāda 3; Rurubhairava-Śrī 3; Caṇḍabhairava-Śrī 3;
Bhūteśabhairava-Śrī 3; Kālabhairava-Śrī 3; Kapālibhairava-Śrī 3; Bhīṣaṇabhairava-Śrī 3; Śmaśānabhairava-Śrī 3—thus is the fifth enclosure on the eight petals.
Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ, Śrī Asitāṅgabhairava 3; Śrī Haṃsaketubhairava 3; Śrī Vaṃśīpāṇi 3; Śrī Svaguru 3; Śrī Paramaguru 3; Śrī Parāparaguru 3;
Śrī Parameṣṭhiguru 3. Thus, from the northwest to the northeast, within the three inner circles, is the sixth enclosure.

Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ. Keśava-śrī 3. Mādhava-śrī 3. Kṛṣṇa-śrī 3. Govinda-śrī 3. Madhusūdana-śrī 3. Gadādhara-śrī 3. Śaṅkhapāṇi-śrī 3. Cakrapāṇi-śrī 3. Caturbhuja-śrī 3. Padmāyudha-śrī 3. Kaiṭabhāri-śrī 3. Ghoradaṃṣṭra-śrī 3.

Janārdanaśrī 3, Vaikuṇṭhaśrī 3, Vāmanaśrī 3, Garuḍadhvajaśrī 3— thus, on the sixteen petals is the seventh enclosure. Oṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ laṃ Indraśrī 3, raṃ Vahniśrī 3, ṭaṃ Yamaśrī 3, kṣaṃ Nirṛtiśrī 3, vaṃ Varuṇaśrī 3, yaṃ Vāyuśrī 3.

*Saṃ* Somaśrī 3; *Haṃ* Īśānaśrī 3; *Hrīṃ* Anantaśrī 3; *Hrīṃ* Brahmaśrī—thus is the eighth enclosure in the square (*caturaśra*). *Oṃ Hrīṃ Hsauḥ* Vajraśrī 3; Śaktiśrī 3; Daṇḍaśrī 3; Khaḍgaśrī 3; Pāśaśrī 3; Dhvajaśrī 3; Yaṣṭiśrī 3; Śūlaśrī—thus [is the ninth enclosure].

The ninth enclosure is in the outer gate-circles. Having recited the root mantra three times, one should worship with the words: "I worship Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, together with his limbs, vehicles, weapons, retinue, and Lakṣmī; obeisance! I satisfy him; obeisance! Having thus worshipped and satisfied him three times, one should prostrate with the *yonimudrā*.

The Tenth Enclosure: Then, having again offered the food offering (*naivedya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), betel leaf (*tāmbūla*), the parasol (*chatra*), and so forth, one should worship the rosary before the deity with the root mantra (*mūla*).

Having recited the root mantra as many times as possible, one should offer the recitation (*japa*) to the deity with the verse beginning, "You are the protector of the most secret of secrets," and then perform the recitations of the armor (*kavaca*), the thousand names (*sahasranāma*), and the hymns (*stava*) before him.
Having performed that as well and offered it to the Goddess and the God, the practitioner, together with the other practitioners, should perform the veneration of the vessel (*pātravandana*).
As long as the gaze does not waver, and as long as the mind does not waver...
"Drink should be offered until [the deity] drinks like a beast"; having thus offered the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*),

recited the *Śāntistotra*, and presented a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should smell the flower with the nose, lead the Lord together with the Goddess through the aperture of the hand (*karandhra*), and then bring them back to the heart-lotus (*hṛtkamala*) oneself as well.
Having assumed an external form fashioned after Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and being devoted to Vaiṣṇava conduct, one should live happily; and with the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should prostrate.
Thus [ends the section] concerning the God of gods, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
The manual for the daily worship has been described; keep it secret.
O Maheśvarī, this secret reality, the essence of worship, must be concealed;
a Vaiṣṇava should indeed keep it hidden—this is the true command of the Supreme Lord.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual Manual for the Worship of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa," within the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, in the *Śrī Devīrahasya*.
Now begins the thirty-eighth chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Now, O Goddess, I shall describe to you the armor (kavaca) of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, which contains mantras within it and is known by the name Vajrapañjara.
The armor named Śrīvajrapañjara is most wonderful;
it is the secret of all the gods, and especially of practitioners.
Holding which the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Person, becomes pleased;
by the mere wearing of which Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, [attains his status]. (3)
"I am Īśvara, Śiva, Bhīma, and even Vāsava, the lord of heaven; O Goddess, I am Sūrya, the treasury of splendor, and Candramas, the lord of the stars. (4)
Vāyu is powerful in the world, Varuṇa is the lord of aquatic creatures, Kubera is the presiding deity of wealth, and Yama is remembered as the King of Dharma. || 5 ||
Holding which Viṣṇu will suddenly annihilate the Dānavas and slew Rāvaṇa and the others—what more can I say beyond this? (6)
O fortunate one, for this armor-mantra (kavaca), Śiva is declared to be the sage;
the Triṣṭubh is the meter, and Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is considered the deity. || 7 ||
O Goddess, the seed-syllable is *ramā*, the supreme power (*parā-śakti*) is the *kīlaka*,
and the *tāra* (om) is known as the application (*viniyoga*) for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
I worship Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, whose face is like the full moon, who wears yellow garments, who is seated upon a lotus, who is attended by Lakṣmī, and who possesses four arms.
Oṃ, may Vāsudeva protect my head along with its hair;
Hrīṃ, may Lakṣmī-Viṣṇu always protect my forehead from all sides.
Hasauḥ: May Lakṣmī-Govinda, the Lord of the worlds, descend upon the eyes. Hrīṃ: May the Lord Dāmodara, the giver of prosperity, protect the nose at all times. (11)
May the Lord Lakṣmī-Trivikrama protect my face constantly;
may the Goddess Lakṣmī and Janārdana protect my throat forever.
May Nārāyaṇa protect my arms; may Lakṣmī’s elder brother, the wielder of the mace, protect them. May he who is the sole delight of Lakṣmī’s joy always protect my sides. 13.
May AṂ ĀṂ IṂ ĪṂ protect the chest; OṂ, may Lakṣmī-Tripureśvara protect it.
UṂ ŪṂ ṚṂ ṜṂ may protect the belly; HRĪṂ, may Lakṣmī-Garuḍadhvaja protect it. (14)
May *ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ* protect the back; may *hasauḥ*, Lakṣmīnṛsiṃhaka, [protect it].
May *oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ* protect the navel; may *hrīṃ*, Lakṣmīviṣṭaraśravaḥ, [protect it]. (15)
May the destroyer of Kaiṭabha, Lakṣmī, protect the anus, the genitals, and the anus;
may the Lord, the Sovereign of Lakṣmī, protect the penis with the syllables *caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ*. (16)
May the Leader, Nārāyaṇa, protect the hips with the syllables ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ;
may the Lord of the World, Lakṣmī, protect the thighs with taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ. May there be salutation to him.
May Paṃ Phaṃ Baṃ Bhaṃ protect the knees; Oṃ Hrīṃ, may the four-armed Lakṣmī protect [them].
May Yaṃ Raṃ Laṃ Vaṃ protect the shanks; Hasauḥ, may Lakṣmī, the wielder of the mace, protect [them]. || 18 ||
May Śaṃ-Śaṃ-Haṃ protect the ankles; may Lakṣmī, who bears the discus, protect [them] with Hrīṃ Śrīṃ;
may Laṃ Kṣaḥ always protect the feet; and may the Mūla-mantra, Lakṣmīsahasrapāt, protect [the whole body].
May Lakṣmīśa protect my entire body from every side;
may Indra protect me from the east, and may Agni always protect me in the southeast.
May Yama protect me in the south, and Nirṛti protect me in the southwest;
may Varuṇa protect me in the west, and may Marut protect me in the northwest.
May Dhanada protect in the north, and may Īśvara guard in the northeast;
they are marked by the thunderbolt, spear, staff, sword, noose, rod, and banner.
May the lords of the directions, who bestow the supreme goal, protect me always from pain;
may Ananta protect me eternally below, and may Brahmā protect me above.
May the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa protect me always in the ten directions;
may Viṣṇu protect me at dawn, and Vāsudeva at midday.
May Dāmodara protect [us] at evening; may Narasiṃha protect [us] at the beginning of night;
may Saṅkarṣaṇa protect [us] at midnight; and may Trivikrama protect [us] at dawn. (25)
May Aniruddha protect [me] at all times, and Viṣvaksena everywhere;
in battle, in the royal court, in gambling, in dispute, and in danger from enemies—Oṃ Hrīṃ Hasauḥ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Mūla—may Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa protect [me]. 26.
Oṃ oṃ oṃ raṇa-rāja-caura-ripu-taḥ, may Keśava protect me; hīṃ hīṃ hīṃ ha ha ha hā ha sauḥ ha sa ha sau, may Mādhava protect me from the fire.
May the all-pervading Ananta protect me from the fear of water, mountains, and fire—*hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ*;
may the Lord of Lakṣmī, *śrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ*, protect me every day—*śaśaśālalaṃ*. (27)
Thus, this divine armor, known as the Vajrapañjara, is beloved by Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life. (28)
It is the abode of all good fortune, the bestower of all eloquence,
the enchantment of Lakṣmī, the ultimate reality, and the elixir of the supreme truth.
The best of Vaiṣṇavas should recite ten times at night, after sexual union, this secret mantra-essence, the core of the world, which belongs to the dwellers of heaven.
The wise person who daily recites at the three junctions of the day this armor-mantra spoken from my own mouth shall see Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the granter of boons, in a dream.
That best of Vaiṣṇavas goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu,
even if he dwells in Mahācīna, provided he recites this while contemplating the Self. || 32 ||
Filled with bliss, that practitioner shall quickly attain liberation;
he should write [the mantra] on birch bark with the eight fragrances at sunrise while reciting the mantra.
Having wound it with a yellow thread, one should then encircle it with gold;
remembering Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, one should wear the pill upon the head.

Having swiftly conquered her enemies in battle, the auspicious woman shall enter her home; so too shall the woman who is barren, or one whose children are like crows, or one whose children have died. (35)
She should tie it around her neck; she will obtain long-lived sons.
Having received it through the instruction of a guru, meditating upon the guru while reciting the mantra... (36)
The practitioner obtains the fruit of performing one hundred thousand recitations of the *varṇa-lakṣa* mantra;
O Goddess Pārvatī, what is the use of saying more regarding this armor (*kavaca*)? (37)
O Maheśvarī, without this [knowledge], there can be no accomplishment of this mantra;
it is rich with the secrets of all the Āgamas, the reality beyond realities, and higher than the highest. (38)

It should not be given to one who lacks devotion, nor to one with poor clothing, nor to one of evil nature; it should be given to one who has been initiated, to one of noble lineage, and to one's own high-souled disciple. (39)
This supreme armor should be given to one who stands upon the great Chinese seat.
O Great Goddess, this secret must be guarded; it is dear to Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
This armor, the Vajrapañjara, must be concealed like one's own private parts.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Dialogue," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrī Devī Rahasya*.
Now begins the thirty-ninth chapter.
