Purify the sacrificial substances twice with the nectar from the vessel—the great *amṛta* of Śrī Amṛteśvarīśvara Mahāmṛtyuñjaya, consisting of lunar nectar, [invoked] by means of the ten-syllable root mantra; fill them with the nectar of immortality (*sudhā*) and so forth. Having thus purified the sacrificial materials with "Oṃ Hauṃ Svāhā," visualize a downward-pointing triangle together with the syllable *saḥ* beneath the general *arghya*.
Having worshipped the triangle with the three root-seeds (mūlabīja), and having worshipped the point (bindu) with the root-mantra (mūlavidyā),

one should worship the mandalas of fire, sun, and moon therein; then, having placed the divine vessel and filled it with the nectar from the jar, one should worship it with the root-mantra, as well as the thirty-six principles beginning with earth (pṛthivī).

Having worshipped [the deity], having displayed the Mahāmudrā, having displayed the Agni, Padma, and Amṛta mudrās, having worshipped the goddess Mātṛkā, having worshipped the root-syllables within that [space],
and having invoked the holy fords such as the Gaṅgā and worshipped the Īśāna-kalās;
Having worshipped the portions of Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta, and Vāmadeva, and having meditated upon [the self] as consisting of Śiva,

one should kindle the lamp of consciousness by drinking the *bindu* with the thought that it is the supreme nectar; thus, one should contemplate the entire world as consisting of Śiva— this is the procedure for the supreme *arghya* vessel.
To the left of the general *arghya* vessel, one should place the vessels for the Guru, Śakti, Yoginī, Vīra, Vaṭuka, and Kṣetrapāla;
likewise, to the north, one should place the vessels for the *pādya*, *ācamanīya*, *madhuparka*, *ācamanīya*, and *arghya*.
This is the arrangement of the vessels (*pātra-saṃsthāpana*).

In the vessels for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, one should regard the water as divine nectar (*divyāmṛta*) within the guru’s vessels and other containers; having worshipped the Self therein with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), one should raise Kuṇḍalinī from her own support (*svādhāra*) and unite her with Paramaśiva.

Having become composed of consciousness and bliss (*cidānandamaya*), having meditated upon the universe as if it were white, and having meditated upon Śiva together with the Goddess within the lotus of the heart,
one should remember [the mantra] as prescribed, worship Him with mental offerings, and [realize] oneself as being of that same nature.

Having meditated upon the Śrīcakra as previously described— resplendent with three enclosures illuminated by four squares, adorned with an eight-petaled lotus, decorated with a hexagon, and shining with a triangle and a circle of dots— or having drawn this King of Yantras, washed it, and placed it upon the venerable jewel-throne (ratnapīṭha), one should perform the worship of the Yoga-throne (yogapīṭha).

Oṃ juṃ saḥ haṃsaḥ so 'haṃ saḥ juṃ oṃ | aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ | kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ | caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ | ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ | taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ | paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ ||

Having worshipped in the Śrīcakra with the mantra: *yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaḥ oṃ śiva-śakti-sadāśiva-īśvara-śuddhavidyā-māyā-kalā-vidyā-rāga-kāla-niyati-puruṣa-prakṛti-śrīyogapīṭhāya namaḥ*, one should worship on the eight petals with: *vāmāyai namaḥ*.

To Jyeṣṭhā, to Raudrī, to Kālī, to Kalavikaraṇī, to Balavikaraṇī, to Balapramathanī, and to Sarvabhūtadamanī, salutation! Having worshipped thus, [one should recite]: *Oṃ juṃ saḥ, salutation to the Blessed One, who is endowed with the power of the essence of all qualities, the supreme and infinite one, the self of the seat of yoga; salutation!*

Having worshipped the *yogapīṭha* and formed the *amṛtīkaraṇa-mudrā*, one should perform the ritual resolve (*saṅkalpa*) with the root mantra and invoke [the deity]. Having drawn forth the light residing in the heart-lotus through the *suṣumnā* by means of the root mantra and having visualized it as abiding within the flowers held in the hands, one should invoke the God.
O Supreme Lord, I invoke you— who abide within your own self, unborn and pure— into this drop, just as one brings the fire-eater from the forest.
O Lord of Gods, easily accessible through devotion, accompanied by your retinue:
until I have gratified you [or: until I have worshipped you], O Śiva, remain here.

Thus: having recited the root mantra, having offered flowers upon the yantras, having invoked [the deity], established [him], and restrained [him], one should display the ten mudrās with the root mantra: *oṃ juṃsaḥ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ oṃ juṃsaḥ*.

Hamsa! The vital breaths of the Lord Mṛtyuñjaya, together with Amṛteśvarī, are here; the vital breaths are here. The individual soul (jīva) is established here. All the sense organs—speech, mind, sight, hearing, taste, smell, and the vital breath—are here.

"Having come right here, may they remain happily for a long time, svāhā! Having thus bestowed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the Goddess and the God, having displayed the five mudrās, having rendered them nectar-like with the *dhenumudrā*, having perfected them with the *mahāmudrā*,
and having integrated them with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), [he displays] the mudrās of the conch, the discus, the triple-segmented [staff], the noose, the jar, and the garland.

Having displayed [the deity], saying: "O Blessed One, O Mṛtyuñjaya, accompanied by Amṛteśvarī, please accept this seat! Phaṭ!"—and having uttered "Welcome, O Blessed One," and having prostrated with the mudrā; [he offers]: Mūla-mantra: O Blessed One, together with the Goddess, this water for the feet (pādya); obeisance. Mūla-mantra: O Blessed One, together with the Goddess, this water for sipping (ācamanīya); svadhā. Mūla-mantra: ...

O Blessed One, together with your consort, this honey-mixture (madhuparka), svadhā. Root mantra: O Blessed One, together with your consort, this water for sipping (ācamanīya), namaḥ. Root mantra: O Blessed One, together with your consort, this respectful offering (arghya), svāhā. Root mantra: O Blessed One, together with your consort, this fragrance (gandha), namaḥ. Root mantra: O Blessed One, together with your consort, preceded by unbroken grains (akṣata), these flowers, vauṣaṭ.

Having taken water from the Gaṅgā mixed with *śyāmāka* grain, *dūrvā* grass, *kāsa* grass, and *śivā* fruit, one should consecrate it with the root mantra: Root mantra: O Blessed One, together with the Goddess, for the purpose of bathing all limbs with Gaṅgā water, *namaḥ*. Root mantra: O Blessed One, together with the Goddess, for the pair of great white and highly precious garments, *namaḥ*.

O Lord, together with the Goddess, I offer pearl ornaments; obeisance! O Lord, together with the Goddess, please be seated upon the jeweled lion-throne. O Lord, together with the Goddess, accept the perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and flowers; *vauṣaṭ*! O Lord, together with the Goddess, accept the incense!

Homage! O Blessed One, together with the Goddess, I offer this lamp; homage! Having offered the incense and the lamp, having displayed the Paramīkaraṇa mudrā, having visualized a triangular and circular maṇḍala, and having placed a vessel upon its stand, [one offers] divine rice endowed with the six flavors and accompanied by various side dishes.

Having consecrated [the offering] with the *dhenumudrā* as nectar, having offered it while reciting "Oṃ, you are the under-layer of nectar, svāhā," and having recited the root mantra ten times, one should display the five *mudrās* of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth; then, having given water to the Blessed Lord Śiva while reciting "Oṃ, you are the covering of nectar, svāhā," one should offer betel-leaf with the root mantra.

Having satisfied the retinue deities ten times with the nectar from the divine vessel and having prostrated, one should visualize them as emerging from the limbs of the deity, establish them in their respective positions as previously accumulated, and after meditating upon them and performing three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) preceded by prostration, one should worship the retinue deities within the Śrīcakra.

"Oṃ juṃ saḥ, I worship the śrī-pādukā of Kāmeśvara; obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance"—with these words, one should worship with the nectar from the hero's vessel (vīrapātra) at the corners of Īśāna, Agni, and the front. "Oṃ juṃ saḥ, I worship the śrī-pādukā of Mahākāla; obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance. "Oṃ juṃ saḥ, [I worship] the śrī-pādukā of Svacchanda. Having thus worshipped, [one should proceed].

Having worshipped Mūladeva with the root mantra (mūla) and having offered libations, thus ends the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa) hereafter: Oṃ juṃsaḥ Kālāgnirudra-śrī° | 3 | Netreśa-śrī° | 3 | Viśvanātha-śrī° | 3 | Maheśvara-śrī° | 3 | Sadyojāta-śrī° | 3 |
p.

260) 3/ Having thus worshipped Vāmadevaśrī, and having gratified the Root Deity (Mūladeva) with the root mantra (mūla), [one worships] the second enclosure (dvitīyāvaraṇa) in the six corners: 3/ Oṃ juṃsaḥ, to the venerable Asitāṅgabhairava; 3/ to the venerable Rurubhairava; 3/ [and so on].

Having worshipped Caṇḍabhairava-Śrī, Krodharājabhairava-Śrī, Unmattabhairava-Śrī, Kapālīśabhairava-Śrī, Bhīṣaṇabhairava-Śrī, and Saṃhārabhairava-Śrī— each with three [offerings]— and having gratified the Root Deity with the Root Mantra, one performs the third enclosure on the eight petals by circling to the left.

Oṃ juṃ saḥ. Brahmāṇī Śrī [Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā] (3 times). Māheśvarī Śrī [Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā] (3 times). Vaiṣṇavī Śrī [Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā] (3 times). Vārāhī Śrī [Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā] (3 times). Nārasiṃhī Śrī [Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā] (3 times). Indrāṇī Śrī [Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā] (3 times). Cāmuṇḍā Śrī [Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā] (3 times).
Mahālakṣmī Śrī [Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā] (3 times). Having thus gratified the Yoginīs with the nectar from their vessels, [one should satisfy] the Root Deity with divine nectar.

Having gratified [the deities] together with the Goddess by circling counter-clockwise around one’s own left, this is the fourth enclosure on the eight petals: *oṃ juṃ saḥ svaguruśrī0* (three times), *paramaguruśrī0* (three times), *parāparaguruśrī0* (three times), *parameṣṭhiguruśrī0* (three times).
Having thus gratified them with the nectar from the Guru-vessel, one should gratify the Lord together with the Goddess in the *bindu* with divine nectar.
The fifth enclosure in the three circles: Oṃ Laṃ Indraśrī; Oṃ Raṃ Agniśrī; Oṃ Ṭaṃ Yamaśrī;
Oṃ Kṣaṃ Nirṛtiśrī; Oṃ Vaṃ Varuṇaśrī; Oṃ Yaṃ Vāyuśrī; Oṃ Saṃ Somaśrī; Oṃ Haṃ Īśānaśrī; Oṃ Hrīṃ Anantaśrī; Oṃ Brahmaśrī. Thus.
Having satisfied [the deities] with the nectar from the hero’s vessel, and having satisfied the deity in the *bindu*, one performs the sixth enclosure within the square.

Oṃ Vajraśrī, Śaktiśrī, Daṇḍaśrī, Khaḍgaśrī, Pāśaśrī, Dhvajaśrī, Gadāśrī, Triśūlaśrī, Cakraśrī, Padmaśrī. Having thus worshipped and satiated [these deities] with the nectar from the hero-vessel (vīrapātra), and having satiated the deity in the drop (bindu) with divine nectar, [this concludes] the seventh enclosure. Root [mantra].
I worship and offer oblation to the venerable sandals of Śrī Mṛtyuñjaya, accompanied by the power (śakti) of Śrī Amṛteśvarī.

[Recite] the root mantra; [worship] the venerable sandals of Śrī Amṛteśvara. [Recite] the root mantra; [worship] the venerable sandals of Īśāna. [Recite] the root mantra; [worship] the venerable sandals of Bhuvaneśvara. [Recite] the root mantra; [worship] the Leader of Initiation (dīkṣānāyaka), accompanied by the illustrious Śrī Amṛteśvarī.
Having thus worshipped ten times with "Śrīmahāmṛtyuñjayaśrīpādukāṃ" and having offered libations, [this concludes] the eighth enclosure.
*Mūlaṃ* Trikhaṇḍā-Śrī. *Mūlaṃ* Pāśa-Śrī. *Mūlaṃ* Sudhākalaśa-Śrī.

*Mūlaṃ* Muktākṣasūtra-Śrī. Having thus satiated the Bindu with the supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*) and worshipped the Lord together with His Śakti in the Bindu, [this is] the ninth enclosure (*navamāvaraṇa*). *Mūlaṃ* Muṣṭimudrā-Śrī. *Mūlaṃ*.
Sāraṅgamudrā-śrī0. Root mantra. Liṅgamudrā-śrī0. Root mantra. Yonimudrā-śrī0.

Root mantra. Pañcamukhamudrā-śrī0. Having thus satiated [the deity] with the supreme nectar (paramāmṛta) in the *bindu*, and having uttered the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*), one should worship the *śrīpādukā* of Śrī Mahāmṛtyuñjaya together with the power (śakti) of Śrī Amṛteśvarī. Thus.
Having worshipped three times in the Bindu, this is the tenth enclosure.

Having prostrated thus, one should again offer the food offering (*naivedya*), reciting: "Oṃ! This divine food, situated in a jewel-vessel, enriched with various condiments, and flooded with supreme nectar—having quickly offered this divine rice, [one should present it] with the deer-mudrā. Thus, having offered it with the deer-mudrā.

Having prostrated at the end of the root mantra, and having offered divine articles such as water for sipping (ācamanīya), betel (tāmbūla), the waving of lights (ārātrika), an umbrella (chatra), a fly-whisk (cāmara), a mirror (ādarśa), and so forth, to the God together with His Goddess, one should prostrate with the eight limbs (sāṣṭāṅga). Then, taking the rosary before the God and reciting the root mantra as many times as possible, one should offer the recitation by saying "guhyāti" before the God.

Having performed the recitation of the *Kavaca*, the *Sahasranāma*, and the *Stavarāja*, and having offered that as well to the Goddess and the God, one should present the sacrificial offering (*bali*) with the mantra: *Oṃ kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣaiṃ kṣauṃ kṣaḥ kṣetrapālebhyaḥ vauṣaṭ*.
Then: *Oṃ yāṃ yīṃ yūṃ yaiṃ yauṃ yaḥ hsauḥ saḥ juṃ oṃ sarvayoginībhyaḥ balir namaḥ*.
Having offered the *bali* with the mantra: "Oṃ hrīṃ! To all spirits who create obstacles, this *bali* is offered; vaṣaṭ svāhā!

and having displayed the *praṇāma-mudrā*, one should prostrate like a staff. Then, having performed the *vīrapāna* together with the lords of heroes (*vīrendra*), having offered the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*), and having brought about one's own power (*śakti*) to be overflowing with bliss, one should satisfy it through union (*rata*).

Contemplating myself as Śiva, the Lord together with the Goddess, in the form of light, one should raise [the deity] from the Śrīcakra by means of the *saṃhṛti-mudrā* and lead it inward through the left nostril. Having meditated upon that radiance as merged within Brahman, the supreme light of consciousness, one should reflect: "I alone am the supreme Haṃsa, Śiva, the ultimate cause; He indeed resides within my vital breath."

Having meditated thus—"The animal-self is dissolved and has entered the state of *samarasī* (equilibrium with the Divine)"—and having become Paramaśiva, one should sport happily together with one's own Śakti. Externally, one should spend time devoted to the conduct (*ācāra*) of a Vaiṣṇava. Then, having raised the Śrīcakra and washed it with the root mantra, [one should remove] the *nirmālya* (remains of the offering) with: *oṃ juṃsaḥ hūṃ oṃ svāhā*.
Thus one should cast the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) in the northeastern direction.
Thus, O Kulasaundari, this sequence for the daily worship of the God of gods, Mahāmṛtyuñjaya, has been correctly determined for you.
You are the protector of the most secret of secrets, the manual for daily rites described by the Lord of the Eye; it must not be disclosed even by those who discourse on Brahman.
I have declared this secret concerning the reality of worship, which is the singular essence of all tantras, pertaining to the world beyond, and to be kept hidden from those seeking liberation.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual Manual for the Worship of Śrī Mahāmṛtyuñjaya," within the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, in the *Śrī Devīrahasya*.
262) Now begins the forty-third chapter.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Supreme Goddess, to this armor (kavaca) spoken from my own mouth;
it is most wonderful and must not be given away by you, O Great Conqueror of Death.
O Maheśvarī, by wearing, reciting, and hearing this supreme armor, I have become the sovereign of the three worlds and am now happy.
I shall describe that very thing to you out of affection, O fair-faced one;
nevertheless, this supreme reality must not be given to one who is evil-minded.

Of this *Śrīmahāmṛtyuñjaya-kavaca*, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Śrī Bhairava, the meter (*chandaḥ*) is Gāyatrī, the deity (*devatā*) is the Great Rudra Śrī Mahāmṛtyuñjaya, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is Oṃ, the power (*śakti*) is Juṃ, the pin (*kīlaka*) is Saḥ, the principle (*tattva*) is Haṃ; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the recitation of the *Mṛtyuñjaya-kavaca* for the accomplishment of the four aims of life.
(Regarding meditation:

Having visualized Rudra situated on the forehead in the center of a lunar disc, one should contemplate the person to be accomplished (sādhya) as being located there; even if they have encountered death, they live. || 1 ||
Oṃ juṃ saḥ hauṃ: may the Lord Mṛtyuñjaya protect my head.
Oṃ śrīṃ: may Śiva protect my forehead; oṃ hauṃ: may Sadāśiva protect my eyebrows. || 2 ||
May the blue-throated one protect my eyes; may the one with matted hair protect my ears. May the three-eyed one protect my cheeks; may the destroyer of Tripura protect my nose.
May he who bears a jar of nectar protect my face; may he whose garment is the Kṛttikās protect my lips; may Hāṭakeśāna protect my jaw; and may Vaṭukabhairava protect my mouth. || 4 ||
May the Destroyer of Kāla protect my neck; may the Beloved of Gaṇa protect my throat. May the Father of Skanda protect my shoulders, and may Giriśa protect my hands. (5)
May the Lord of Girijā protect my nails along with my fingers;
may the Lord of the Stars protect my breasts, and Paśupati protect my chest.
May Kubera, the bestower of boons, protect my belly; may Māraśāsana protect my two sides;
may Śarva likewise protect my navel, and may the wielder of the trident protect my back. (7)
May Śaṅkara protect my penis; may the beloved of the Guhyakas protect my private parts; may Kālāntaka protect my waist; and may the slayer of Andhaka protect my thighs. || 8 ||
May Jānū protect my knees; may Kālabhairava protect my shanks;
may Jaṭādhārī protect my ankles; and may Mṛtyuñjaya protect my feet. || 9 ||
May Aghora protect me always from the feet up to the head;
may Sadyojāta protect me from the head down to the feet. (10)
May the Lord of Immortality protect the body that is devoid of protection yet not devoid of name.
May Balavikaraṇa [protect it] in the east, and Kālaśāsana in the south. || 11 ||
May Pārvatīnātha protect me in the west, Mānomanas in the north,
Īśvara in the northeast, and Agnilocana in the southeast.
May Śambhu protect me in the southwest; may he whose vehicle is the wind protect me in the northwest;
may Balapramathana protect me above; and may Parameśvara protect me in the netherworld.
May Mahāmṛtyuñjaya protect me always in the ten directions—
in battle, in the royal court, at gambling, in adversity, and when my life is in danger.
May Oṃ Juṃ Mahārudra, the ten-syllabled God of gods, protect me;
may Brahmā protect me at dawn, and may Bhairava protect me at midday. (15)
In the evening, he is Balapramathana; at night, he is Nityacetana;
at midnight, he is Mahādeva; and at the end of the night, he is Mahomaya (or Manonmana).
"Oṃ juṃ saḥ hauṃ, may Mṛtyuñjaya protect [me] at all times and from all sides!
(p. 264) Thus is this meritorious armor (*kavaca*), difficult to find in the three worlds. (17)
It consists of all mantras, is secret, and is hidden within all tantras;
it is meritorious, the bestower of merit, divine, and the supreme deity of the gods of gods. || 18 ||
O Great Goddess, the eight siddhis of Tryambaka reside in the hand of that mantra-practitioner who recites this or wears it as a protective armor (kavaca). || 19 ||
Having taken up arms in battle, he shall engage in combat; having slain his enemies, he shall obtain victory.
Having achieved victory, O Goddess, he will return home and once again attain happiness. (20)
In times of great fear, great disease, and likewise the terror of pestilence,
during famine, or in the destruction wrought by enemies, one should recite this armor with reverence.
All that comes to rest through the grace of Mṛtyuñjaya:
wealth, sons, happiness, fortune, health, and all prosperity. (22)
The practitioner attains [the goal] immediately, O Goddess; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
This is the meritorious armor (kavaca) of the Great Mṛtyuñjaya;
it is secret, bestowing success, hidden, and must be guarded like one's own private parts.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Mṛtyuñjaya Kavaca," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrī Devī Rahasya*.
(p. 265) Now begins the forty-fourth chapter.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now listen, O Goddess of gods, to this supreme hymn known as the *Sahasra*,
which is the most excellent essence among the essences of this *Mahāmṛtyuñjaya*.

Of this *Śrī Mahāmṛtyuñjaya Sahasranāmastotra Mantra*, Bhairava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Uṣṇik is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Śrī Mahāmṛtyuñjaya is the deity (*devatā*), Oṃ is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), Juṃ is the power (*śaktiḥ*), and Saḥ is the pin (*kīlaka*).
It is employed (*viniyoga*) for the recitation of the thousand names for the sake of attaining the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*). The Meditation (*dhyāna*):
I bow to the supreme Śiva, whose splendor is equal to the rising moon, the sole cause of the bliss of nectar;
who is the one protector of the creation, dissolution, and emergence of the worlds through the syllables *oṃ juṃ saḥ*;
whose body is adorned with the glorious ten-syllable Tāra mantra; who possesses three eyes and two arms.
I worship Śrī Mṛtyuñjaya, who is filled with praiseworthy valor and virtues, within the lotus of my heart.
Oṃ juṃ saḥ hauṃ! Mahādeva is the knower of mantras, the bestower of honor, the honorable one, possessed of beautiful limbs, the wise, and the increaser of dignity. || 1 ||

The creator of illusion, the wrestler in the form of a combatant, the sage who is the slayer of Māra, the Great Lord, the highly honored one, the counselor, and the beloved of those who follow counsel. || 2 ||

Māruta, the best of the Maruts; the monthly, the fortnightly, the immortal; Mātaṅgaka, the one with a maddened mind, the one with maddened consciousness, and the one whose meditation is maddened. || 3 ||
The bestower of human desires, the beloved of Menakā’s husband,
whose body is pride, who steals honor, joined with Māra, and one who has conquered the senses. || 4 ||
Victory, the giver of victory, the conqueror, the lord of victory, the beloved of victory;
the lord of the *ḍāmara*, the three-eyed one, the enjoyer of the universe, and the fire. (5)
The Lord of the Universe, the Master of the Universe, the Progenitor of the Universe, the Leader of the Universe;
the Discipliner, the Self-disciplined, the Debater, the One who has vomited out [impurities], the Source of Speech, the Youthful Student.
He is the gross and the subtle, the immovable and the restless, the one with a flickering tongue and the formidable one;
he is the one to be overcome, the passionless, the playful, and the one longing for the dance.
He has tremulous eyes and a restless intellect; he is the possessor of dharma, the giver of wealth, and is worshipped by Kubera.
He is wealthy, the object of meditation, and the one who should be studied; he is righteous, composed of dharma, and compassionate.
Compassionate, the progenitor of the gods, served by the gods, the lord of mercy;
with eyes like a whirlpool, dwelling in caves, humble, and whose nature consists of the divine. || 9 ||

He is ill-formed yet bestower of fame; he is lovely yet of a non-impotent nature, though appearing as one who is impotent; he is wise and composed of knowledge; he is full of desire and the destroyer of Kāma, Kāla, and Andhaka—[these are three names]. || 10 ||
Jīva, Jīvaprada, Śukra, Śuddha, Śarmaprada, Anagha, Śanaiścara, Vegagati, Vācāla, Rāhu, and Avyaya. (100) 11.
He is the banner, the lord of the prison, Time, the Sun of immeasurable prowess;
He is the Moon who bestows auspiciousness, the radiant one who grants good fortune, and the bearer of the form of Bharga.

He is the fierce one, the rogue, the separated one, and the united one; he is the bearer of the Gaṅgā, the elephant, the beloved of Gajānana, the sung one, the singer, and the one who delights in bathing and worship. 13.
He is supreme, possessed of a robust body, the great beloved of Pārvatī;
he is the Supreme Self, the Virāṭ, the dwelling place [of all], the monkey who performs immeasurable deeds.
He is the bliss of consciousness, of beautiful form, the one belonging to Garuḍa, and the beloved of Garuḍa;
he is Nandīśvara, the guide, the serpent, and adorned with ornaments of serpents. || 15 ||
The one who seizes the Nāgas, the Great Nāga, the one who sustains the earth, the Lord of Cattle, the Ascetic,
the Three-eyed One, the Lord of the Three Worlds, the Triple-formed One, and the Destroyer of Tripura. (16)

He consists of the three-fold path, he consists of the world, and he is the remover of the world’s sole affliction; though appearing afflicted, Śambhu is satisfied; he possesses three forms and bears three colors.
The Lord of the three cities, the master of the triple light, who is peaceful in a threefold way and possesses a threefold course;
he who possesses the three qualities, the creator of the universe, the sustainer of the universe, and the primordial Puruṣa.
Umeśa, Vāsuki, the heroic Vainateya, the investigator;
Vivekākṣa, Viśālākṣa, the non-creator, the supreme creator. || 19 ||
The treasure-house of knowledge, lotus-eyed, free from passion, the destroyer of passion;
possessed of memory, the giver of memory, the one known through tradition, Brahmā, the best among those who know Brahman. (20)
He who observes the vow of Brahmā, the celibate student, the four-faced one, the four-headed one;
he who is both moving and unmoving, whose gait is immovable, the impetuous, the sovereign of heroes, and the most excellent. || 21 ||
He who dwells in all, whose movement is everywhere, who is honored by all, the eternal;
he who pervades all, who is all forms, the ocean, and the Lord of the Sama-veda. (200) || 22 ||
He has even eyes, even luster, and an even body; he is a great lake, possessed of a lake, truthful in speech, truth itself, the embodiment of truth, wise, and happy.
Surāṭ, Satya, Satyamati, Rudra, Raudravapuḥ, Vasu, Vasumān, Vasudhānātha, Vasurūpa, and Vasuprada. || 24 ||
The Lord of all gods, the Lord of all who possess awakening;
the Sovereign, the Remainder, the whole composed of parts, the one who reclines upon Śeṣa, the husband of Śrī. || 25 ||
Indra, adorned with the moon as his crest-jewel, he who is the sustainer of the moving and unmoving world;
the steadfast one, the immovable pillar, the subtle, the full, the broad-chested, and the one beyond the highest.
He is multiformed, wearing matted hair, and filled with a mass of matted locks;
he is the form of the sacrificial animal, the Lord of Animals, the knower of the nature of animals, and the ocean of milk. || 27 ||
He who is to be known, the Knower, consisting of the Vedas, the knower of ritual, the one possessing ritual, the compassionate one;
the wielder of the trident, the maker of auspiciousness, the one to be purified, the performer of good deeds, and the Lord of Śacī. || 28 ||
The Lord is white as the moon, wielder of the thunderbolt, conch, and mace;
he has four arms, eight arms, and is adorned with a thousand arms. || 29 ||
Holding a sacrificial ladle in his hand, with long hair and a tall stature, he was free from deceit;
he was a divine god, a great ocean, possessed of celestial fame, and a maker of light.
Of fierce form, lord of the fierce, with a formidable chest, consisting of austerity;
an ascetic, with matted hair, performing penance, the remover of heat, and free from all suffering. || 31 ||
The carrier of the oblation, the lord of horses, the giver of horses, adorned by Hari;
he who has Hari as his vehicle, possessed of great majesty, eternal, the eternal self, and fire. || 32 ||
He is the honored one, the captivating cycle of worldly existence, the creator, the proximate presence, and the lineage.
He is the holder of knowledge, the possessor of celestial chariots, and the bestower of the boon of those who travel in celestial chariots.
Vācaspati, Vāsāsāra, Vāmācārī, Baladhara;
Vāgbhava, Vāsava, Vāyu, and adorned with the seed-syllable of Vāsanā. (34)

He whose fame is like that of a sharp axe, the skillful one, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the son of Dakṣa, the remover of misfortune, the crusher of the Daityas, and the increaser of enjoyments. || 35 ||
The enjoyer, the remover of disease, the one to be abandoned, the destroyer, the ornament of Hari;
the multiform, the highly intelligent, the possessor of great wealth, and the far-sighted. || 36 ||
He who brings satisfaction to the minds of dancers, who is skilled in dance and song,
who is richly adorned with the colors of autumn, who burns away the throat [of sin], and who is the destroyer of evil.

He is the female serpent, the essence of the serpent, Ananta, the one of infinite forms, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the dancer, the lord of Hāṭaka, the most excellent, and the bearer of the colorless. || 38 ||
He is the one who utters the sound "jhāṅkāra," who holds a hammer in his hand, who wields a noose, who bears the Śārṅga bow, and who possesses the luster of the moon;
he is of a thousand forms, equal in gait, and the bestower of fearlessness upon the virtuous.
He is served by the virtuous, he is the goal of the virtuous, the all-pervading Lord who bestows the fruit of service;
he is exceedingly great, a drinker of wine, intoxicated, possessing an intoxicated form, and the excellent bringer of an end.
The one who strikes the stake, the creator of play, the one who has transcended, the sole liberator from the bonds of existence;
the radiant one, Viṣṇu, the infallible, the one who has shaken off [impurity], the ever-new, the fresh. || 41 ||
He has the form of a banyan tree; he is the giver of fear and the destroyer of fear, the bestower of fearlessness;
he is served by the upholders of the earth and is the husband of the daughter of the mountain-king.
The upholder of the earth, the enemy of Andhaka, the possessor of discernment, free from delusion;
he whose hair is like a pillar, wearing matted locks, the rustic one, the delighter of the village, and the beloved of Ramā. || 43 ||

The doer of what is dear, the one of pleasing form, the one separated from union, the scorcher, the maker of light, the one radiant with splendor, the wrathful one, and the bestower of the desires of men. || 44 ||
Sharp-armed, sharp-handed, sharp-rayed, and sharp-eyed; sharp-minded, the embodiment of the Triple Veda, the source of the Triple Veda, and whose body is the Triple Veda.
The consumer of oblations, the light of offerings, Hālāhala, the lord of the plow-bearer, the eye of the sacrificial offering, consisting of wine, and the bearer of green form. || 46 ||
Mṛdima is the mango tree; Hutāśa is the fire-eater;
Guṇin is the one who knows qualities; Garuḍa is the one intent on song; Vikramī is the one who strides. || 47 ||
The Lord of the Krama, devoted to the Krama, the maker of the Krama, with a weary mind;
possessed of great splendor, the Great Māra, deluded, and the beloved of delusion. || 48 ||
The great one, the thirty-fold, the child, the lord of children, the remover of sin;
the child-like, the destroyer of enemies, the one who abandons the world, the one honored by cows, and the one devoid of qualities. 49.
Saguṇa, Vittarāj, Vīrya, Virocana, Vibhāvasu, Mālāmaya, Mādhava, Vikartana, and Vikatthana. || 50 ||

The bestower of honor, the giver of liberation, the incomparable, the foremost, the terrifier of enemies, the one whose wealth is fire, the fortunate one, the lord of virtuous women, and the master of the veins.
The lord of Meṇakā’s sister, the bearer of supreme form;
the Sun, the sovereign of the sons of Diti, the bringer of destruction to the sons of Diti.
Vasudeva, the highly fortunate Viśvāvasu, Vasupriya, Samudra, Amitatejas, Khagendra, Viśikhin, and Śikhin. (53)
Garutmān, Vajrahasta, the Lord of Paulomī, Īśvara, Yajñapeya, Vājapeya, Śatakratu, and Śatānana. || 54 ||
He is the firm foundation, possessed of intense confidence, profound, and the increaser of all states of being;
he is the most excellent singer, sweet-voiced, intoxicated by honey, and the Lord of Spring (Mādhava). || 55 ||
He whose nature is illusion, the protector of those who enjoy worldly pleasures, the bestower of desires upon the inhabitants of heaven,
the lord of the celestial beings, the progenitor, the one who is born, the paralyzer, and the destroyer of Rambhā.
Śaṅkara, Īśvara, Īśa, the one whose crest-jewel is the Lord of Night; the presiding lord of the Liṅga, the presiding lord of the gods, the presiding lord of the Vedas, the investigator. || 57 ||

He is the effulgence (Bharga), the priceless one, the lord of men, served by Nara-vāhana; he will be clever, the future one, the giver of existence, and the destroyer of the fear of worldly existence.
The lord of beings, honored together with Īśānī; Rāma, the cessation, the beloved of the night;
Maṅgala, the son of the Earth, the auspicious one who increases intelligence. || 59 ||
The victorious one, the lord of living beings, the lover, the digestive fire within the belly, the scorcher of Jahnu;
he who holds the daughter of Jahnu, the cosmic eon, the year, and the one assuming the form of the month.
Ṛtu, Ṛbhūsutādhyakṣa, Vihārī, Vihagādhipa, Śuklāmbara, Nīlakaṇṭha, Śukla, Bhṛgusuta, and Bhaga. || 61 ||
He is peaceful, the bestower of auspiciousness, indivisible, the maker of non-duality, and the performer of peace;
he is the Lord, the self-controlled one, appearing in the form of a mendicant, the most excellent giver, and the sovereign of the people.
The Youth, the wrathful one, the angry, the adversary, the combative, the essence, the tasteless, the flavorful, the perfected, the bull, and the slayer of the bull. || 63 ||
He has five faces and six mouths; he is turned away from the face, yet dear to those with beautiful countenances.
He is of ill countenance, difficult to conquer, sorrowful, joyful, and the bestower of the play of happiness.
The vessel, the grandson, the purifier, the self of beings, the destroyer of Pūtanā,
the imperishable, the supreme reality, the powerful one, and the slayer of Bala. (65)
Bhallī, Bhauli, Bhava, Abhava, the liberator from existence and non-existence;
Nārāyaṇa, Muktakeśa, Digdeva, and Dharmanāyaka. || 66 ||

He is the bestower of liberation from bondage, the unconquerable one, the great-limbed, the singer of the Sāman hymns; he is the one who effects union with that [Brahman], the one who moves through all states, and the destroyer of the god of love.

Kṛṣṇa, clad in black garments, worthy of praise, possessing the color of the stars, overcome with modesty; possessed of shame, the protector from misfortune, difficult to attain, and the destroyer of fortresses. (600) || 68 ||
He has great feet; he is free from misfortune and is the destroyer of calamities for men;
he has mighty arms and a broad chest, and is the bestower of great bliss. || 69 ||
He has great eyes, he is a great giver, and he is proficient in various scriptures;
he has a great head, great teeth, great ears, and is like a great serpent.
He has great eyes, a great nose, and a great neck; he dwells in the quarters and is clothed in the quarters.
He is the lord of the sons of Diti, shaven-headed, and a bearer of a shaven head and a rosary of beads.
Dwelling in the cremation ground, free from passion, possessing great hips, ever-new, the ancient person, boundless, the supreme self, and the great doer. (72)
Mahālasya, Mahākeśa, Mahoṣṭha, Mohana, Virāṭ, Mahāmukha, Mahājaṅgha, Maṇḍalī, Kuṇḍalī, and Naṭa. || 73 ||
Asapatna, Patrakara, Pātrahasta, Pāṭava, Lālasa, Sālasa, Sāla, Kalpavṛkṣa, and Kampita. (74)
Kampahā, Kalpanāhārī, Mahāketu, Kaṭhoraka, Anala, Pavana, Pāṭha, Pīṭhastha, and Pīṭharūpaka. || 75 ||
Pāṭhīna, Kuliśī, Pīna, Merudhāman, Mahāguṇin, endowed with a great quiver, and the destroyer of the pride of gods and demons. 76.
The Atharvaśīrṣa, whose mouth is the Soma, whose eyes are measured by a thousand Ṛks,
whose face is the Yajus and Sāman, the secret one who is proficient in the Yajurveda. (77)
He was a performer of sacrifices, the very embodiment of sacrifice, a knower of sacrifice, and a lord of the earth;
he was moving (jaṅgamī), the giver of destruction (bhaṅgada), skilled in speech, and one whose appearance was accessible to all.

Unapproachable yet easy of access, dwarfish, a rider of a donkey, with the face of a donkey, a leader, one whose purpose is unfailing, lord of the Sindhu river, born in Sindh, and dwelling in the midst of mountains. 79.

Majestic, victorious over his subjects, performing sacrifices at dawn, midday, and evening, a knower of the three periods of time, an excellent astrologer, residing at Puṣkara, he was devoted to the welfare of others. (80)
He is the benefactor and the destroyer, compassionate, and the bestower of victory in battle;
he is the righteous one, clad in skins, beautiful in form, and adorned with lovely ornaments.
Wandering by night, subject to time yet self-controlled, the lord of the Viśis who is himself uncontrolled;
he who brings others under his control, the master of subjugation, who sleeps upon ashes and is smeared with ashes.
With limbs smeared with ashes, his body soiled, and his hair adorned with garlands;
he should perform the duties of a Gaṇa, follow the family tradition, observe all modes of conduct, and remain an equal friend to all.
He possesses form; he is the breaker of the lineage, the protector, the one of terrifying appearance, and the fearsome;
he is the dawn-red, the uniquely contemplative, Triśaṅku, and the bearer of the spike. || 84 ||
The Brāhmaṇa is an ascetic, the Kṣatriya is a wielder of the thunderbolt for the sake of duty;
the Vaiśya and Śūdra abide as pigeons, while Tvaṣṭṛ is both pleased and agitated by anger. || 85 ||

The remover of disease, the sick, the hero, Kapila, the leader of the monkeys, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the one of eight forms, the possessor of the earth, and likewise the possessor of fortitude. || 86 ||
The form of water, the form of wind, fire, the one possessing the form of the moon, the divine sun, the sacrificer, space, and the Supreme Lord. || 87 ||
Bhavahā, Bhavamūrti, Bhūtātmā, Bhūtabhāvana, Bhava, Śarva, Rudra, Paśunātha, and Śaṅkara. || 88 ||
p.
273) Girija, Girijānātha, Girīndra, Maheśvara, Girīśa, Khaṇḍahasta, Mahānugra, and Gaṇeśvara. || 89 ||
Bhīma, Kapardin, Bhītijña, Khaṇḍa, Caṇḍavikrama,
Khaṇḍabhṛt (or Khaḍgabhṛt), Khaṇḍaparaśu, Kṛttivāsas, Viṣāpaha, Kaṅkāla, Kalanākāra, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Nīlalohita.
Gaṇeśvara, Guṇin, Nandin, Dharmarāja, and Durantaka. || 91 ||
Bhṛṅgirīṭī, Rasāsāra, Dayālu, Rūpamaṇḍita, Amṛta, Kālarudra, Kālāgni, and Śaśiśekhara. (800) || 92 ||

Sadyojāta, who wears a girdle of golden muñja grass, the remover of ill omens, the dispeller of bad dreams, the victorious, the possessor of qualities, and the one established in the sound of the Guṇas. || 93 ||
He is white, three-fold white, perfected, pure, and frequented by the elements;
he is the form of sacrifice, the mouth of sacrifice, the bestower of desires upon sacrificers, and the pure one.
He is steadfast, wise, and skillful; he is the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the snatcher of serpents, the wearer of ashes, and his body is adorned with sacred ash. || 95 ||
The bearer of the skull, the wearer of earrings, the radiant one, the destroyer of the afflictions of his devotees, the all-pervading Lord;
he whose banner is the bull, who is mounted upon the bull, and who causes the bull of Dharma to increase. || 96 ||
He is of great strength, the source of all holy places, and marked with all auspicious characteristics;
he has a thousand arms, possesses every limb, is the refuge of all, and the creator of all worlds.
The purifier, the mantra of the triple peak, the youngest, dark-brown in hue;
the fashioner of Brahmā’s staff, possessed of the *śataghnī*, the noose, and the spear. (98)
The one whose womb is the lotus, the one of great womb, the one whose womb is Brahman, the one born from the waters;
the creator of gods and asuras, and the ultimate refuge of gods and asuras. || 99 ||
The god who is the preceptor of the gods and asuras, honored by gods and asuras alike; beloved by Guha, served by the Gaṇas, pure, and the purifier of all. (100)
He whose eye is on his forehead, who is the god of the universe, the subduer, white and tawny;
he is liberation, the splendor of liberation, and the supreme goal for devotees. || 101 ||
The god beyond gods, the divine seer, the bestower of boons upon gods and asuras, he who dwells on Mount Kailāsa and takes refuge on the Himavat mountain. 102.
Worthy of worship by his lords, praised by the perfected ones (siddhas), and honored by the nine lords;
he has matted hair, is the creator of the cosmic cycles, is Rudra, is benevolent, and is affectionate toward righteousness. 103.
Vṛṣākapi, the creator of the cosmic cycles, self-restrained, undisturbed;
Nīlakaṇṭha, the lord of wealth, the protector, and the leader of the Pramathas. || 104 ||
He is without beginning and without end, the source of prosperity, whose very form is prosperity;
he is like an army, the great cosmic cycle, yoga, the creator of the ages, and Hari.
He is the form of the ages, the great form, the great song, and possessed of great qualities;
he is the emission, the form of the linga, the pure one, and the destroyer of sins. (106)
The worshipful Maheśvara, Śambhu, the lion among gods, the bull among men, the supreme among the wise, the subtle one, the essence of the austerity of all the gods. || 107 ||
Well-yoked, beautiful, wielder of the thunderbolt, the source of the gods, immutable, Guha, the beloved, self-created, pure, and the purifier of all. || 108 ||
The horned one, the lover of horns, the tawny-hued, the king of kings, the one free from disease;
the presiding lord of the hosts of gods and asuras, the one who increases self-restraint and the senses;
the destroyer of Tripura, the auspicious-throated, the three-eyed, the five-faced. (109)
He is the one who has taken away time, the solitary Self, and the possessor of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
The Lord of all beings, the Sovereign of all Rakshasas, the Overlord of Brahman, the Lord of Brahman, and likewise the Overlord of the Veda. 111.
He is Brahmā, Śiva, eternally blissful, eternally infinite, and the ever-auspicious;
he is the form of the sun, possessed of beautiful limbs, and the bearer of the form of Gāyatrī. || 112 ||
To those who are not terrible, and to those who are terrible, and to those more terrible than the most terrible—
to all you Rudra-forms, O Śarva, from every side, homage to you! (113)
Vāmadeva, as well as Jyeṣṭha, Śreṣṭha, Kāla, Karālaka, Mahākāla, Bhairaveśa, Veśī, and Kalavikaraṇa. || 114 ||
The transformer of strength, the child, and likewise the crusher of strength;
the subduer of all beings, the god of gods, the mover of the mind. 115.
I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta!
O Bhavodbhava, in every birth, do not transcend me; favor me! 116.
He is the meditator, the act of meditation, the object of meditation, the bestower of strength, and the supreme state;
he is the Supreme Śiva, the supreme object of meditation, supreme knowledge, and higher than the highest. || 117 ||
Pārāvāra, Palāśī, and Māṃsāśī are the best of Vaiṣṇavas;
Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hsauḥ is the God, and Oṃ Śrīṃ Hauṃ is the supreme Bhairava. || 118 ||
The mantra "Oṃ hrāṃ namaḥ śivāya" is for the student (vaṭu) and possesses excellent weapons;
"Oṃ hrīṃ sadāśivaḥ" and "Oṃ hrīṃ āpaduddhāraṇaḥ" are mantras [for Sadāśiva and the deliverer from calamity]. 119.
Oṃ hrīṃ, Mahākarālāsya; Oṃ hrīṃ, Vaṭukabhairava;
the Blessed Tryambaka, Oṃ hrīṃ; Oṃ hrīṃ, the one whose crest is the half-moon. || 120 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ, the one with matted locks and smoke-colored [hair]; oṃ hrīṃ, the destroyer of Tripura;
hrāṃ hrīṃ hruṃ, the left limb of Hari; oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ, the three-eyed one. || 121 ||
Oṃ! You are the embodiment of the Vedas, the knower of the Vedas, possessing the form of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
you are Rudra, the terrible roar yet not terrible—Oṃ Kṣmyūṃ, Aghora-Bhairava! || 122 ||
Oṃ juṃ saḥ! You who are attached to nectar, the presiding lord of immortality, and one who delights in ambrosia.
Oṃ! We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant one who increases nourishment. 123.
May I be released from death, as a cucumber from its stalk, yet not from immortality.
Oṃ hauṃ juṃ saḥ; Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ; Oṃ juṃ saḥ; Mṛtyuñjaya (1000).
(276) This thousand names, however, is a supreme and most wonderful secret;
it is the very essence of all the inhabitants of heaven, O Goddess—what need is there to mention living beings on earth? (125)
Out of devotion for you, I have declared this thousand names, which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds, secret, and the very embodiment of nectar. (126)
O Śivā, listen to the fruit obtained by one who recites, causes [others] to recite, causes [others] to hear, or likewise hears [this hymn] of the god Mṛtyuñjaya. || 127 ||
In fortune he is Kṛṣṇa, in intellect he is Jīva, in majesty he is Divākara;
in splendor he is the god Vahni, and in poetic skill he is Bhārgava.
In valor he is like Hari, in statesmanship he resembles Druhiṇa, and in sovereignty, O Queen of the Gods, he is equal to me; what could be greater than this? (129)
The practitioner who, endowed with fortitude, recites this Thousand Names at midnight—that practitioner attains perfection. (130)

At a crossroads, at a solitary linga, in the Maru desert, in a forest, in a desolate place, in a cremation ground, in a wilderness, or in a fortress—through recitation, success is attained without a doubt. (131)
On a boat, amidst a band of thieves, in times of distress, when life is at stake,
wherever danger has arisen— such as from poison, fire, and the like— (one should remember her).
If one recites the Thousand Names, one is swiftly liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
On the new moon day falling on a Tuesday, at midnight, the wise man should go to a cemetery.
Having recited it, O Goddess, he becomes like Indra himself, worshipped by the gods;
on a Saturday or the new moon day, O Goddess, at night on the bank of a river.
One should indeed recite the Thousand Names and mutter them one hundred and eight times;
by the grace of Mṛtyuñjaya, one shall swiftly become Sudarśana.
The practitioner, naked and with disheveled hair, should recite [the mantra] ten times;
he shall become a king in this world, and liberation will occur in the next. || 136 ||
This supreme secret has been declared by me to you out of devotion; it is the essence of mantras, consisting of mantra, and must not be told to one of evil nature. (137)
One should not give this secret, which is my very essence and must be guarded most strictly in the Kali age, even to one's own disciples, and especially not to one's sons. 138.
This should not be spoken even to the Six-faced One (Kārttikeya), but must be kept secret from oneself;
it should be protected from the wicked and recited day and night. 139.
"It should be heard from the mouth of a practitioner and guarded like one's own son.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Thousand Names of Mṛtyuñjaya," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrī Devīrahasya*.
Now begins the forty-fifth chapter.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess, I shall declare to you a hymn that bestows all accomplishments;
it is the sole essence of the root mantra and must be guarded with great effort. (1)

O Śivā, one should recite [this] at the time of initiation, during worship, at the end of the recitation (japa), as well as at the dismissal and the invocation; such a person shall obtain the fruit of initiation.
O Īśvarī, the seer of this king of hymns is Bhairava;
O Śivā, Gāyatrī is said to be its meter, and it is Mahāmṛtyuñjaya.
The deity is the *praṇava*, the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the power (*śakti*) is remembered as being Śivā;
the heart is said to be the pin (*kīlaka*), and likewise the sun is the binding of the directions.
The application is proclaimed for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 4 ||

With eyes like the moon, the sun, and fire; a smiling face; seated within two lotuses; with hands resplendent holding a mudrā, a noose, nectar, and a rosary; possessing the luster of the moon; his body bathed in the nectar flowing from ten million moons; and radiant with ornaments such as necklaces— Please perform the visualization of the Lord in this manner. Then, recite the mantra: oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ sauḥ oṃ namo bhagavate śrīmadgopālakumārāya divyamaṅgalavigrahāya mahābālāya kṛṣṇāya govindāya gopījanavallabhāya namaḥ svāhā | This is the mantra of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord. It consists of fifty-one syllables and is extremely powerful. By its mere recitation, one attains all desires. One should worship the Lord with flowers, incense, lamps, unbroken rice grains, parched grain flour, water for the feet, water for rinsing the mouth, food offerings, betel leaves, and other articles of worship. One should also offer prayers, circumambulations, prostrations, and obeisances. Furthermore, one should offer oblations into the fire with ghee and other substances according to the prescribed rites. One should also chant the mantra one hundred thousand times. By doing so, one will attain all supernatural powers (siddhis), including the power to become invisible at will. One will also achieve the eight great yogic powers (aṣṭaiśvaryas) and the fourfold perfection (caturvarga). One will be liberated from all sins and attain the supreme abode of Vaikuṇṭha. There is no doubt that by the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, one will obtain everything one desires. Thus ends the description of the mantra of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Now follows the description of the mantra of Śrī Rādhā. Listen attentively. It is as follows: oṃ śrīṃ rāṃ rāmāyai namaḥ | This is the mantra of Śrī Rādhā. It consists of seven syllables and is exceedingly auspicious. By its mere recitation, one attains all desires. Now follows the description of the mantra of Śrī Gopījanavallabha. Listen attentively. It is as follows: oṃ klīṃ gopījanavallabhāya svāhā | This is the mantra of Śrī Gopījanavallabha. It consists of twelve syllables and is extremely powerful. By its mere recitation, one attains all desires. One should worship him with flowers, incense, lamps, unbroken rice grains, parched grain flour, water for the feet, water for rinsing the mouth, food offerings, betel leaves, and other articles of worship. Now follows the description of the mantra of Śrī Govinda. Listen attentively. It is as follows: oṃ goviṃdāya namaḥ | This is the mantra of Śrī Govinda. It consists of six syllables and is most auspicious. By its mere recitation, one attains all desires. One should worship him with flowers, incense, lamps, unbroken rice grains, parched grain flour, water for the feet, water for rinsing the mouth, food offerings, betel leaves, and other articles of worship. I meditate upon Paśupati, the conqueror of death, who deludes the entire universe with his splendor. || 5 ||
The jewel of nectar-rayed moonlight, bearing a jar of nectar in his palm, situated within the embrace of nectar-like radiance, a bearer of streams of nectar—
may he whose beautiful body is lovely with nectar-rays, the companion of the Fortune of Nectar, [protect me].
May the Conqueror of Death, who rains down a flow of nectar, gladden us day after day. || 6 ||

I bow to the primordial god, the conqueror of death, who has the sun, fire, and moon as his eyes; who holds a vessel of nectar and a jar; whose two arms possess the luster of the moon; and who is adorned with the crescent moon upon his crest.

One should meditate at night upon Rudra, who stands in the center of the lunar disc and has the crescent moon as his crest; even one who has encountered death lives on by meditating thus upon the auspicious seat.
One should contemplate the practitioner situated there—Rudra, located in the center of a lunar disc upon the exceedingly broad forehead; even if he has encountered death, he lives.
O Īśvarī, he who recites this *mātrādyam*, the fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree rooted in the *Mātṛkā*, shall become the abode of universal sovereignty.
The seed-syllable *hṛt* (hrīṃ) belongs to Śiva, who is skilled in the discernment of the conduct of his lineage;
indeed, the goddess of speech dances within the lotus-face of him who recites it.
O Śiva, the practitioner who recites the seed-syllable of Śakti together with the visarga shall,
before long, become a vessel for universal sovereignty. (12)
He who contemplates in his mind the seed-syllable of the Lord of Gods (the letter *Ha*), adorned with the dot (*bindu*), the orb, and the moon, shall attain non-duality with Śiva. (13)
He who naturally worships Bhṛgu with the Visarga as Bharga— the cause of creation and dissolution— merges within the supreme state.
O Śambhu, for one who recites the syllables of the word "lakṣmī" adorned with the nasal bindu, Lakṣmī resides in his hand, Vāṇī in his mouth, and victory in battle. 15.
"O God, he who recites 'Protect the Yuga' in the presence of a hero shall enjoy universal sovereignty and, at the end, attain residence in the same world [as You]. (16)
He who recites the mantra "Śaradam varadām vīrasādhanīm savisargakām" shall have his fame wander about, white as an autumnal cloud.
He who recites the seed-syllable of space together with space while seated upon a bed of kuśa grass shall become one whose pair of feet is colored by the crest-jewel of the Kaulikas.
O Śambhu, one who recites the seed-syllable of doubt (ŚA) along with the letter RA while seated upon a lotus will become like Bhairava, adorned with ornaments of skeletons and garlands. 19.
O Śambhu, to him who recites the seed-syllable *hṛt*, the seed of the universe, which is of the nature of splendor, you shall grant your own eternal abode. (20)
O Giriśa, he who— rejoicing in incomparable supreme bliss within the lotus of his heart— recites the syllable *oṃ*, along with the letter *ā* and the concluding part of your mantra,
shall enjoy sovereignty upon the earth with the crescent moon as his shimmering crest-ornament, and in the end, he departs for the celestial realm.
The state of union with Śiva. || 21 ||

At dawn, I meditate upon you seated within the circle of the maṇḍala, which is enriched by the subterranean chamber (bhūgṛha), its circumference shimmering with the essence of the six flavors, adorned with dots and red corners. (22)

I bow to the Lord who removes death, who is seated upon the orb of the moon— the embodiment of all nectar— richly adorned with various kinds of offerings and ornaments, and whose body is the entirety of Śeṣa’s speech.
Whoever recites this divine hymn— the sole touchstone for all kings of mantras— at the conclusion of worship, or during the rite of adoration in a temple of Śiva or at home,
shall conquer his enemies in battle and enjoy royal fortune through his own splendor; in the end, he becomes a hero.
He is served by all the gods and is equal to Śiva. || 24 ||
Thus, one should daily recite or cause others to recite this supreme hymn, which is dear to Mahāmṛtyuñjaya; it is the very essence of all things, difficult even for the gods to obtain. (25)
This supreme reality is ungraspable, the destroyer of great sins;
it consists of the Great Mantra, is divine, and through its practices, it is the means for attaining wealth.

The practitioner of mantra should recite this, which is the essence of the three worlds and the bestower of fearlessness upon the three worlds, at midnight; then, in the Kali age, success shall be attained immediately. (27)
O Goddess, by reciting this at a crossroads at midnight, or even during the Brahma-muhūrta, the Kaulika becomes like Bhairava himself.
Thus, this is my entire essence, a most wonderful secret;
it must not be told to just anyone—such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, the Exposition of the Mṛtyuñjaya Stotra, in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, within the *Śrī Devī Rahasya*.
The *Mṛtyuñjaya-pañcāṅga* is completed.
p. 281) Now begins the forty-sixth chapter.
Now begins the *Śrīdurgā-pañcāṅga*.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all principles, who brings victory to practitioners!"
O Lord, that supreme five-limbed ritual manual of Durgā which was previously indicated— || 1 ||
It is the all-in-all of all the gods and the secret of all mantra-practitioners;
please tell me that today out of compassion, if you have any mercy for me.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess, this most secret [teaching], consisting of five limbs and characterized by the essential principles, is the very essence of Durgā; it has not been told by me to anyone.
Out of affection for you, O Īśvarī, I shall proclaim the five-limbed Durgā-pañcāṅga, which is secret, most to be guarded, and divine— a teaching not to be given by those who discourse upon Brahman.
The goddess who subdues the Daityas, Durgā, known by eight syllables, the auspicious one,
was formerly propitiated by the gods, led by Brahmā and Acyuta.
For the sake of Indra’s welfare and for the destruction of the enemies of the gods,
that Supreme Goddess, in her aspect of passion (rājasī), thus creates all beings.
The *sāttvikī* protects at the end [of creation], while the *tāmasī* shall withdraw [it];
thus, she consists of the three qualities (*guṇatrayī*) and has the nature of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
The eight-syllabled Great Vidyā is beyond number and is of the nature of the Supreme Self.
Now, its five limbs constitute the secret of the dwellers of heaven. (p. 282) 8.
I shall speak with supreme affection; this must not be told to a wicked person.
I shall declare to you the chapter concerning the most excellent reality of Durgā.

O Goddess, I shall now declare the extraction of the mantra of Durgā, which is based on the supreme [reality], which is not proclaimed in any other tantras, and which bestows the fruit of all desires— by the mere hearing of which one obtains the merit of ten million offerings. (10)

O Bhavānī, the extraction of the root mantra of Durgā has been described to you; this eight-syllabled, secret mantra consists of *tāra* (oṃ), *māyā* (hrīṃ), the wheel (*cakri*), the one with the wheel (*cakrin*), *dūrvā* (sa), the syllable of Vāyu (*ya*), and *viśva* (la) at the end. 11.
For him there is no abundance of obstacles, nor any corruption by enemies and the like;
nor is there union with toil, nor the ruin of conduct and the age. || 12 ||

This eight-syllabled mantra of Durgā, which bestows direct spiritual accomplishment and destroys the Kali age, is the lord of the eight supernatural powers; it must be kept secret by those who are naked (Digambara).
O Great Goddess, this king of mantras brings victory to practitioners established in the Mahācīna-krama; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation instantly. (14)
O Maheśvarī, the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) consists of one hundred thousand recitations, or half of that;
one may perform it up to the limit of one hundred thousand, but never less than that.

Having first accomplished the rite of uprooting the root (mūlotkīlana) and well-performed the rite of restoration to life (sañjīvana), one should subsequently perform the preliminary service (puraścaryā); thereafter, one should practice the mantra enriched with the "encasement" (saṃpuṭa).
Then one should daily recite the mantra of Durgā, which bestows the eight supernatural powers (siddhis);
by reciting which, the practitioner may roam upon the earth like Bhairava himself.
O Goddess, Maheśvara is remembered as the seer of this mantra;
its meter is Anuṣṭubh, and its deity is remembered as the eight-syllabled Śrī Durgā. (18)
The wheel is the seed-syllable mixed [with the others]; Māyā is known as Śakti.
O Īśvarī, Tāra is the Kīlaka of the directions, and the universe is the bond. (19)
The application for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa has been proclaimed;
O Goddess, the ritual placement (nyāsa) is performed with the syllables *tāra* and *māyā*, which possess the six long vowels.
O Goddess, having slain the six enemies, one should meditate upon Durgā, the Mistress of the Kula—
she who resembles the color of dūrvā grass, has three eyes, wears a radiant crown,
and holds a conch, a lotus, a sword, an arrow, a shield, a trident, and a bow.
I worship Durgā, who holds the threatening gesture, who is seated upon a buffalo throne, and who resides on the sacred seat of the nine-fold lineage. || 21 ||
I shall now describe the extraction of the yantra of Durgā, the abode of the Kula;
it is a wheel that bestows all accomplishments and fulfills all desires. (22)

O Moon-crested Lord, this yantra is declared as the refuge of Durgā; it consists of a central bindu, a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, an eight-petaled lotus adorned with a circle of fire, and illuminated by a square enclosure of the earth.
I shall explain the limb of dissolution of this machine, which is hidden in all tantras;
by the mere utterance of which one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices. (24)
O Goddess of gods, the lord of practitioners should worship Gaṇeśa, Kumāra, Puṣpadanta, and Vikartana at the four gates.
The goddess Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Aparājitā;
Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vārāhī, and Nārasiṃhikā. || 26 ||
O Goddess Pārvatī, one should worship the eight Bhairavas upon the eight petals of the lotus: Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmatta, Kapālin, [Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra]. || 27 ||
O Goddess Śivā, Bhīṣaṇa and Saṃhāra should be worshipped separately by practitioners with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, turning to the left. (28) p. 284)
Having offered a handful of flowers and recited the root mantra,
the practitioner should worship the six Mother Goddesses of the families within the hexagon with the filaments of lotuses.
O Īśvarī, one should worship Śailaputrī, the celibate Brahmacāriṇī, Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, Kūṣmāṇḍā, and Skandamātṛ from the tip of one's own left [hand].

Having fully worshipped Kātyāyanī with dūrvā grass, perfumes, and unbroken grains (akṣata), and having again offered a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) upon the Śrīcakra, which bestows the supreme goal; 31.
O Pārvatī, one should worship the three deities who abide in the Kula and are the mothers of Tripura:
Kālarātri, Mahāgaurī, and Devadūtī.
O Śivā, at the tip of the triangle, one should worship with vermilion, unbroken rice, and flowers;
having offered a handful of dūrvā grass blades, [one worships] upon the king of yantras that bestows the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi).
One should worship Ambikā Durgā, adorned with the eight-syllable mantra;
the eight-armed Goddess, the eight-syllabled Vidyā, within the Bindu, O Śiva.
The practitioner should worship Śiva, the blue-throated one, and the Mother of the Universe within the Bindu;
there, O Goddess of the Gods, the adept should worship the eight weapons.
O Īśvarī, one should worship with various flowers the conch, the lotus, the sword, the arrows, the bow, the shield, the trident, and the divine gesture of threat.
One should worship the God and Goddess upon the seat of the Bindu for the attainment of all perfections.
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall declare the ritual applications for the sake of the eight Siddhis.
By performing these rites in the Kali age, the practitioner becomes like a wish-fulfilling tree;
[he achieves] paralyzing, bewildering, killing, and attracting. (38)
O Maheśvarī, I shall now describe the accomplishment of these applications: subjugation, as well as eradication, pacification, and nourishment. (39)
And for the benefit of practitioners established in the Mahācīna-krama,
the practitioner should recite the root mantra ten thousand times at night in a cremation ground. (40)
By consuming ghee for ten days and avoiding barley, meat, and blood for a month, one quickly achieves the power of immobilization over speech, desire, people, and water. (41)
O Goddess, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads from a banyan tree;
the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with ghee, lotus seeds, and lotuses, consisting of one-tenth of that number.
By means of *āragvadha* roots and *sudhā* roots, enchantment occurs in an instant even for gods and demons; what need is there to mention men of small intellect? (43)
The best of practitioners should recite the root mantra ten thousand times in the forest;
or, staying at the root of a cane tree, he should perform oblations there by one-tenth that amount.
An enemy who consumes ghee, milk-rice, and snails shall enter the jaws of death;
one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times at night in an empty house, O Kuleśvarī. (45)
A human figure should be fashioned from ten parts of ghee, *vyoṣa*, *śaṭī*, and reeds, along with the seeds of monkeys; by using this in the morning, one will achieve the attraction of women.
One should recite the root mantra ten thousand times and quickly perform a fire sacrifice at a crossroads,
O Pārvatī, using clarified butter, lotuses, kṣura-grass, stones, and red flowers.
Even Śakra comes under one's control, let alone a petty king;
the practitioner, seated at the root of an Aśvattha tree, should recite the root mantra ten thousand times.
With a tenth part of human fat, ghee, hair, the skin of women, and long pepper, one shall swiftly drive away an enemy, even if he were equal to Indra himself. (49)
The practitioner should recite the root mantra ten thousand times and perform an oblation at the foot of a celestial tree (kalpavṛkṣa) with ghee,
akṣa seeds, cock's feet, and various flowers.
There will be immediate pacification of the time of disease and calamity;
one should recite the root mantra ten thousand times within the circle of the Līlā-grove.
O Īśānī, a *homa* should be performed with ten parts of ghee, fish, and goat-head;
when done with eight verses, nourishment is immediately produced. (52)
Thus, this divine chapter, which embodies the nature of all mantras,
though it constitutes the secret of Durgā, must be kept hidden by those seeking liberation.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, the Description of the Chapter on Durgā, within the Śrī Devī Rahasya of the venerable Rudrayāmala Tantra. || 46 ||
Now begins the forty-seventh chapter.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Pārvatī, I shall speak the manual in prose form,
by the mere hearing of which one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices.

Having risen during the *brāhmī* hour and assumed the *padmāsana* posture, one should visualize one's own Guru— white in color, adorned with white ornaments, and possessing two arms— seated within the pericarp of a thousand-petaled downward-facing lotus situated upon the crown of one's head, together with his Śakti, who is likewise adorned in white garments.
Having meditated upon [the Guru] as united with [the Goddess] on his left side and having worshipped him with mental offerings, one should prostrate like a staff.
Salutations to that venerable Guru by whom that state was revealed— the state which is of the form of an unbroken circle and by which the moving and the unmoving are pervaded.
Salutations to that illustrious Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance was opened with the ointment-stick of knowledge.
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, and the Guru is Maheśvara himself;
the Guru alone is the entire universe—salutations to that illustrious Guru.

Having thus prostrated and received his command, he went outside, discarded excrement, urine, and so forth, performed the purification prescribed for his caste, and having gone to a river or similar place, [prepared] a tooth-stick twelve finger-breadths long with a fine tuft of hair.

One should perform [the following]: having cleansed the teeth with the mantra *oṃ klīṃ kāmadevāya sarvajanapriyāya namaḥ*, and having performed six gargles with the *cākrika* seed-syllable (*gaṃ*), one should sprinkle the face three times with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*). Then, having tied the topknot with the mantra *oṃ hrīṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi śikhāparisare rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

Having performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) with the three principles (*tattva*), having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra (*mūla*), and having performed the bath for the removal of impurities (*malāpakarṣaṇa-snāna*), one should perform the mantra-bath (*mantra-snāna*). Then, having brought earth with the root mantra, one should sprinkle the water.
Having meditated upon the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*) with the "mantra-earth" and having invoked the sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*) such as the Gaṅgā and Yamunā into the water...

Having visualized the *yantra*, one should invoke Durgā together with Nīlakaṇṭha. Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) there and meditated upon the Goddess along with Śiva, one should recite the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) as many times as possible, then submerge and emerge from the water three times.
There, having formed the *kumbha-mudrā* and sprinkled water over one's own head, one should bathe the God and the Goddess.
"Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, to Mārtaṇḍabhairava together with the Śakti Prakāśā, this is your arghya; obeisance.

Having thus offered three arghyas to the Sun and having caused him to put on another garment, one should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) with the three principles, perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), perform the morning twilight worship (pūrvasaṃdhyā), perform the six-limbed rite (ṣaḍaṅga), and [offer] water from the joined palms (culuka).
Taking water and covering it with the *tattvamudrā*, one should consecrate it three times with the syllables *yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ haṃ*.

Reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one sprinkles the falling drops of water seven times upon one's own head. Holding the remaining water in the left hand, one draws it inside through the *iḍā* [nāḍī] and washes away all evil within the body; then, through the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī],...

Having first purged [the water], one should cast it to the left onto the previously prepared diamond-stone (*vajraśilā*) with the mantra "phaṭ. Having thus performed the *aghamarṣaṇa*, having sipped water as before, and having meditated upon the *yantra* in the water, one should mutter the root-mantra (*mūla*) as many times as possible;

then, at the end of the root-vidyā, [one should offer oblation] to the Lord together with His retinue, including His limbs (*sāṅga*), vehicles (*savāhana*), weapons (*sāyudha*), and attendants (*saparicchada*), accompanied by the illustrious Nīlakaṇṭha.
Having offered libations eight times with the mantra "O Mother Durgā, may you be satisfied," and having offered libations three times to Nīlakaṇṭha,

he should offer libations to the attendant deities with one handful [of water] each; then, meditating upon the God and Goddess in his heart and drawing a square in the water, he should offer libations to the lineage of Gurus there, starting from the northeast (Īśāna) in due order, and [then to] the Goddess Gāyatrī.

One should recite: *oṃ hrīṃ duṃ durgāyai vidmahe aṣṭākṣarāyai dhīmahi tannaścaṇḍī pracodayāt*. Having thus recited this according to one's capacity, and having offered three *arghya* oblations to the two gods of gods with this *gāyatrī*, and having surrendered the recitation (*japa*), one should proceed to the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*). This is the ritual for the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā-vidhi*).

Then, having returned home and washed one's feet, one should worship the deities of the door: Oṃ gāṃ gūṃ, salutations to Gaṇeśa in the east. Oṃ kṣāṃ hrīṃ, salutations to Vaṭuka in the south. Oṃ kṣāṃ kṣeṃ, salutations to Kṣetrapāla in the west. Oṃ yāṃ yūṃ, salutations to the Yoginīs in the north. Gaṃ...
"Salutation to Gaṅgā at the threshold; salutation to Yamunā below; sauḥ, salutation to Sarasvatī in the middle. (p.

Having performed worship and entered the interior of the house, one should purify the seat as appropriate [according to the preparations]. For the mantra of purifying the seat: Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Sutala is the meter (*chanda*), and Kūrma is the deity; its application (*viniyoga*) is for the consecration of the seat. Oṃ prīṃ, to the Earth.

Salutations! O Goddess, the worlds are supported by you, and you are supported by Viṣṇu. Therefore, O Goddess, support me and make this seat pure. (Om, firm is the sky, firm is the earth, firm are these mountains; firm is this entire world, and you, O Queen, are the firm one of all.)
Oṃ Āṃ, obeisance to the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti).

Maṃ, obeisance to the Root-Nature (Mūlaprakṛti). Aṃ, obeisance to Ananta. Paṃ, obeisance to the Lotus. Prīṃ, obeisance to the Lotus-Stalk. Having sat there, one should perform the triple-snap (tālatraya) and [recite]: "May those spirits depart who..."
"May those beings who are established on the earth, and those beings who create obstacles, perish by the command of Śiva.

Having thus performed the three *tāla* strikes and driven away the obstacles with three blows of the left heel, he should display the *nārāca-mudrā* and bow to the Guru with the mantra: "The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu... and "For one blinded by the darkness of ignorance..."

Having recited "akhaṇḍamaṇḍalākāram," one should worship with scents and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) while saying "Salutation to the venerable Guru" on one's left, followed by: "guṃ, salutation to the Gurus; salutation to the Supreme Gurus; salutation to the Higher-Lower Gurus; salutation to the Parameṣṭhi Gurus. Having thus worshipped, one should perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) preceded by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Of this...

For the mantra of Śrī Durgā Devī (Yogapīṭhapūjā): Maheśvara is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), Śrī Durgā is the deity (devatā), *duṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja), *hrīṃ* is the power (śakti), *oṃ* is the bolt (kīlaka), and *namaḥ* is the binding of the directions (digbandha). Its application (viniyoga) is for the sake of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation in the worship of Durgā. Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Salutation to the sage Maheśvara on the head; salutation to the Anuṣṭubh meter on the face;
salutation to the deity Śrī Durgā on the heart; salutation to the seed-syllable *duṃ* on the navel; salutation to the power (*śakti*) *hrīṃ* on the private parts;
salutation to the *kīlaka* *oṃ* on the feet; "salutation to the binding of the directions" on all limbs. *Oṃ hrāṃ*.

Oṃ, *namaḥ* to the two thumbs. Oṃ *hrīṃ*, *namaḥ* to the two index fingers. Oṃ *hrūṃ*, *namaḥ* to the two middle fingers. Oṃ *hraiṃ*, *namaḥ* to the two ring fingers. Oṃ *hrauṃ*, *namaḥ* to the two little fingers. Oṃ *hraḥ*, *namaḥ* to the palms and backs of the hands. Thus is the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*).
Thus is the ritual placement of the six limbs beginning with the heart.

Now, the root-placement (mūlanyāsa): *Oṃ namaḥ* on the head; *hrīṃ* on the face; *duṃ* on the chest; *duṃ* on the two arms; *rgāṃ* on the navel; *yaiṃ* on the back; *naṃ* on the two knees; *maḥ* on the two feet. Thus, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) three times. *Oṃ ātmatattvāya namaḥ* on the head; *hrīṃ vidyātattvāya namaḥ* on the face; *duṃ śivatattvāya*... [on the heart].

Namo hṛdaye (Salutation to the Heart). Oṃ gurutattvāya namo nābhau (Oṃ, salutation to the principle of the Guru at the navel). Oṃ hrīṃ śaktitattvāya namo jaṅghayoḥ (Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the principle of Śakti at the shanks). Oṃ duṃ śivaśaktitattvāya namaḥ pādayoḥ (Oṃ duṃ, salutation to the principle of Śiva-Śakti at the feet). (p. 289)

Oṃ aṃ āṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ iṃ īṃ, homage to the heart (hṛdayāya namaḥ). Hrīṃ uṃ ūṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ, svāhā to the head (śirase svāhā). Duṃ ḷṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ ḹṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhāyai vaṣaṭ). Oṃ.

*Eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ* for the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ*. *Hrīṃ oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ* for the eyes (*netra*), *vauṣaṭ*. *Duṃ aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaḥ aḥ* for the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*. This is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart and other limbs. The same applies to the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*). Thus ends the ritual placement of the pure alphabet (*śuddhamātṛkānyāsa*).

Now, the placement of the root syllables (*mūlamātṛkānyāsa*): Aṃ, salutation to the head; Āṃ, salutation to the circumference of the mouth; Iṃ, to the right eye; Īṃ, to the left eye; Uṃ, to the right ear; Ūṃ, to the left ear; Ṛṃ, to the right cheek; Ṝṃ, to the left cheek; Ḷṃ, to the right nostril; Ḹṃ, to the left nostril; Eṃ...

Aiṃ on the upper lip; Oṃ on the lower lip; Auṃ on the upper row of teeth; Aum on the lower row of teeth; Aṃ on the forehead; Aḥ on the tongue; Kaṃ, salutation, on the root of the right arm; Khaṃ on the elbow; Gaṃ on the wrist; Ghaṃ on the base of the fingers; Ṅaṃ...
*Caṃ* on the tip of the finger; *chaṃ* at the base of the left arm; *jaṃ* at the elbow; *jhaṃ* at the wrist;
*ñaṃ* at the base of the fingers; *ṇaṃ* on the tip of the finger. *Ṭaṃ*—homage—at the base of the right foot; *ṭhaṃ* at the knee; *ḍaṃ* at the ankle;
*ḍhaṃ* at the base of the toes; *ṇaṃ* on the tip of the toe. *Taṃ* at the base of the left foot; *thaṃ* at the knee.
Daṃ at the ankle; dhaṃ at the base of the fingers; naṃ at the tips of the fingers; paṃ on the right side; phaṃ on the left side;
baṃ on the back; bhaṃ at the navel; maṃ in the abdomen; yaṃ at the heart; raṃ on the right shoulder;
laṃ at the crown of the head; vaṃ on the left shoulder; śaṃ from the heart to the tip of the right hand; ṣaṃ.

One should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) three times: *saṃ* from the heart to the tips of the left hand; *haṃ* from the heart to the tips of the right foot; *laṃ* from the feet up to the head; and *kṣaḥ* from the head down to the feet. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in this manner, one should perform the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅga*) as before.

Having performed three breath controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *praṇava*—[specifically] inhalation for 12 [units], retention for 16, and exhalation for 32—and having sipped water (*ācamana*) three times with the mantras: "Oṃ hrīṃ, I purify the *ātmatattva*, svāhā; Oṃ hrīṃ, I purify the *vidyātattva*, svāhā; Oṃ hrīṃ, I purify the *śivatattva*, svāhā."
One should perform the purification of the elements through the yoga of breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Oṃ hūṃ! By means of contraction [or the hook], having led the light in the form of a lamp-flame through the path of the *suṣumṇā* into the interior of the *brahmapatha*, and having brought it to Paramaśiva, one should meditate there upon the lineage gurus amidst a shower of nectar and satisfy them with that very [light]; then, by that same path...

Having pierced the family of the six cakras and brought that radiance to its own place, one should meditate on the personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*)— black in color, with a red beard, and the size of a thumb— located in the left side of the abdomen, using the wind-seed syllable *yaṃ* recited sixteen times, and thus dry him up. [Then] using the fire-seed syllable *raṃ*.
