"Seated in purity, the Vasu; seated in the intermediate space, the Hotṛ; seated on the altar, the guest; seated in the house;
seated among men, seated in the best, seated in truth, seated in the sky; born of the waters, born of the earth, born of the mountains—the Truth.
Having recited this three times and meditated there upon Ānandabhairava and Surādevī, [one should utter]: *hasa rakṣa ma la va ya ūṃ*.

Having worshipped the God and Goddess three times with "Vauṣaṭ to Ānandabhairava" and "Vauṣaṭ to Surādevī," one should draw the *śakticakra* in the midst of the substance by circling clockwise three times in a row with "Aṃ 16 Kaṃ 16 Thaṃ 16," and then, through absorption into that, [place] "Haṃ Kṣaṃ" in its center.

Having visualized nectar within the substance and consecrated it as nectar with the *dhenumudrā*, one should hold the jar while reciting the nectar-seed syllable *vaṃ* and the root mantra eight times.

Then, having drawn a triangle, hexagon, circle, and square between oneself and the *Śrīcakra*, one should offer obeisance to the Pīṭha of Pūrṇagiri within the square: "Obeisance to the Pīṭha of Pūrṇagiri."

Having worshipped [the seats] with "To Uḍḍīyāna-pīṭha," "To Kāmarūpa-pīṭha," and "To Jālandhara-pīṭha," and having worshipped the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in the hexagon, one should worship the triangle from the tip toward the right and left using the *trikhaṇḍa* mantra, and having worshipped the supporting powers (*ādhāraśakti*) in the center, one should place the *yantrikā* within the triangle, saying "Namaḥ."
Having sprinkled [the area] with general *arghya* water, [one should worship]: *Yaṃ* to Dhūmrārcis, *Namaḥ*; *Raṃ* to Ūṣmā, *Namaḥ*; *Laṃ* to Jvalinī, *Namaḥ*;

*Vaṃ* to Jvālinī, *Namaḥ*; *Śaṃ* to Visphuliṅginī, *Namaḥ*; *Ṣaṃ* to Suśrī, *Namaḥ*; *Saṃ* to Svarūpā, *Namaḥ*; *Haṃ* to Kapilā, *Namaḥ*; *Laṃ* to Havyavāhā, *Namaḥ*; *Kṣaṃ* to Kavyavāhā, *Namaḥ*, in the center.

Having worshipped with "Raṃ, obeisance to the fire-maṇḍala consisting of ten kalās," and having worshipped the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in the hexagon, one should worship the Goddess in the center with the root mantra (mūla). Then, having washed the vessel with "Phaṭ," one should place it upon the yantra. Therein, [one worships]: "Kaṃ Bhaṃ, obeisance to Tapinī; Khaṃ Vaṃ, obeisance to Tāpinī; Gaṃ Phaṃ..."

To Dhūmrā, [Ghaṃ Paṃ]! To Marīci, [Ṅaṃ Naṃ]! To Jvalinī, [Caṃ Dhaṃ]! To Ruci, [Chaṃ Daṃ]! To Suṣumnā, [Jaṃ Thaṃ]! To Bhogadā, [Jhaṃ Taṃ]! To Viśvā, [Ñaṃ Ṇaṃ]! To Bodhinī, [Ṭaṃ Ḍhaṃ]! To Dhāriṇī, [Ṭhaṃ Ḍaṃ]! Salutation to Kṣamā. Aṃ.

Having worshipped with the mantra "Salutation to the solar orb consisting of twelve digits," one should draw a triangle, a circle, and a hexagon within the vessel; having worshipped them with the entire mantra and its individual parts, and reciting the Varuṇa seed-syllable, the root-mantra, and the Mātṛkā in reverse order, one should fill the triangle with nectar and one part with water.

Having filled it there and cast in fragrant substances and so forth, [one should worship with]: *aṃ* to Amṛtā, *namaḥ*; *āṃ* to Mānadā, *namaḥ*; *iṃ* to Pūṣā, *namaḥ*; *īṃ* to Tuṣṭi, *namaḥ*; *uṃ* to Puṣṭi, *namaḥ*; *ūṃ* to Rati, *namaḥ*. (p. 495)
Ṛṃ to Dhṛti; Ṝṃ to Śaśinī; Ḷṃ to Caṇḍikā; Ḹṃ to Kānti; Eṃ to Jyotsnā; Aiṃ to Śrī; Oṃ to Prīti; Auṃ to Aṅgadā; Aṃ to Pūrṇā;
Aḥ to Pūrṇāmṛtā, salutation. Oṃ, salutation to the lunar maṇḍala, whose essence consists of sixteen kalās.

Having worshipped as before, one should write the mantra upon the substance; then, having written the *mātṛkā* letters from *aṃ āṃ* up to *kṣaḥ* three times each within the three lines of the triangle, one should worship the triangle with the three sections of the root mantra.
Then, having worshipped the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in the hexagon, one should invoke the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) with the mantra beginning with "Gaṅge" and [invoke] Ānandabhairava and Bhairavī.

Having worshipped with one's own mantra starting from the east and so forth: *glūṃ* salutation to the jewels of the sky (*gaganaratna*); *slūṃ* [salutation] to the jewels of heaven (*svargaratna*); *mlūṃ* [salutation] to the jewels of the mortal world (*martyaratna*); *plūṃ* [salutation] to the jewels of the netherworld (*pātālaratna*); and in the center, *nlūṃ* [salutation] to the jewels of the Nagas (*nāgaratna*). Having thus worshipped, having purified the meat and other offerings, and having veiled them with the syllable *hūṃ*.

Having rendered [the vessel] nectar-like (*amṛtīkṛtya*), having bound the directions with three claps of the hands (*tālatraya*), having worshipped the root mantra seven times over that [vessel], having invoked the Goddess therein, having performed the binding of the directions with three claps of the hands, having veiled [her] and rendered [her] nectar-like, having displayed the *yonimudrā*, and having worshipped her with "Hsauṃ Namaḥ," one should display the *śaṅkhamudrā*.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), having brought the vessel forward with the fish-gesture (matsyamudrā), and having recited the root mantra ten times,
one should contemplate the vessel as being the form of the Goddess. Then, having obtained the permission of the Goddess, [one places] near the jar the Guru-vessel,
then the Śakti-vessel, the Bhoga-vessel, one’s own vessel, the Yoginī-vessel, and the Vīra-vessel.

Having arranged the vessels for the bali, pādya, arghya, and ācamanīya, and having drawn drops from the Śrīpātra using the Tattvamudrā by means of the *carvaṇa* [offering], one should satisfy Ānandabhairava three times with his mantra, saying: "I satisfy Ānandabhairava; obeisance. Thereafter, [one satisfies] the Śrīguru...
Having offered libations three times with "I worship and satisfy the venerable *śrīpādukā* of the illustrious *Śrī-Amukānandanātha*;

obeisance," one should offer libations with the nectar from the *śrīpātra* vessel, saying: "I satisfy the Root Goddess, together with her weapons, vehicles, and retinue; obeisance. This is the procedure for the worship of the *kalaśa*.

Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*) upon the *Śrīcakra* as before, and having meditated upon the venerable Bālā, one should bring the Goddess from one's own heart into the hollowed palms of flowers through the left nostril by means of the seed-syllable of air (*vāyubīja*), and establish her upon the *Śrīcakra*.
"O Queen of Gods, who are easily accessible through devotion, accompanied by your retinue; O Goddess, for as long as I shall worship you..."
Having recited "ihāvaha," one should recite the root mantra followed by: "O Bālā Tripurā, together with Śrī Kāmeśvara Śiva, come here, come here!

Stay here, stay here! Be present here, be present here! Be firmly established here, be firmly established here! Accept my worship accompanied by all the ritual offerings! Then, having displayed the mudrās for invocation and so forth, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) upon the *śrīcakra*.

Having performed the binding of the ten directions with the *lelihāna-mudrā*, having performed the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*), the ritual integration of the limbs (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and the supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*), and having displayed the *dhenu* and *yoni* mudrās, [one should visualize] the hand-gestures (*mudrās*) of the boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, the book, the rosary, the knowledge-hook (*jñānāṅkuśa*), the noose, the bow, the arrow, the skull-cup, the lotus, and so forth.

"Oṃ, with the nectar of the Śrīpātra, I satiate the venerable Bālā Tripurā, together with her weapons, vehicles, retinue, and enclosures, accompanied by the venerable Kāmeśvara Bhairava; obeisance!"— thus three times.

Having satisfied [the deity] once more with the root mantra, one should satisfy [her] three times with "I satisfy the venerable sandals of Śrī Bālā Tripurā, *namaḥ*. Then, having recited the root mantra, one offers water for the feet at her feet with "This water for the feet (*pādya*) is for the venerable Śrī Bālā Tripurā together with Kāmeśvara, *namaḥ*. Likewise, one offers the respectful offering (*arghya*) at the head with "Svāhā," and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*).
Having bathed [the deity] well with the mantra "Sudhā mukhe" for the face and "Snānīyaṃ namaḥ sarvāṅge" for the entire body, and having wiped the limbs with a clean silk cloth,
one should offer various ornaments such as a multicolored garment, saffron, musk, sandalwood paste, vermilion, a crown, earrings, necklaces, and so forth.
One should again offer water for sipping (*ācamanīya*). Then, with the middle, ring, and thumb fingers, one should worship with perfume, saying "Gandho Namaḥ";

with the thumb and forefinger, one should worship with flowers, saying "Puṣpāṇi Vauṣaṭ. Having worshipped the incense vessel with "Phaṭ" and placed it before [the deity], one should touch it with the left forefinger.

Having offered the incense with the words, "I offer incense with the nectar of the Śrīpātra," and having worshipped the bell with the mantra *jagaddhvani-mantramātaḥ svāhā*, while sounding it with the left hand and holding the incense with the middle finger, ring finger, and thumb, one should recite the Gāyatrī and the root mantra.

"This divine essence of the forest tree, rich in fragrance, the most excellent scent, the invocation of all the gods—may this incense be accepted. Having thus raised [the incense] three times, one should fumigate the Goddess. Then, having placed the lamp in front and performed the sprinkling and worship as before, one should [hold] the lamp-vessel with the middle finger of the left hand.
Touching the lamp, he offers it with the words, "I offer the lamp," and as before, ringing the bell,
he holds the lamp-vessel between his middle and ring fingers with his thumb, displaying it while reciting the Gāyatrī and the root mantra:
"The great lamp, well-illuminated, dispelling darkness everywhere, both outside and within."

"May this lamp of light be accepted. Thus one should offer the lamp. Then, having fashioned a *caru* in the form of the moon with eight petals using *kuṅkuma* in a vessel of gold or other material, and having placed one lamp in the center and eight lamps on the eight petals, [one recites]: *Śrīṃ sauṃḥ glūṃ slūṃ mlūṃ plūṃ nlūṃ sauṃḥ śrīṃ*.

Having worshipped with "Obeisance to Ratneśvarī" and having worshipped again with the root mantra (mūla), one should lift the vessel up to the head and recite the root mantra nine times: "O Goddess Navātmikā, who art united with all the wheels and their presiding deities, accept this ārātrika for my spiritual accomplishment. [This is done] with the *cakramudrā*.
One should perform the *nīrājana* rite.
Then, having placed various food offerings (*naivedya*) upon a leaf of gold or other precious metal, one should veil them with the syllable *HŪM*,
transform them into nectar (*amṛta*) by means of the *dhenu-mudrā*, and recite the root mantra seven times while touching [the offering] with the left thumb.

Touching the vessel of the food offering, at the end of the root mantra, [one should say]: "O Supreme Goddess, accept this divine, well-prepared supreme rice-milk (paramānna) contained in a golden vessel, consisting of five types and endowed with six flavors. Saying, "I offer the food offering," one should release it with the right ring finger and thumb. Then, once again, the water for sipping (ācamanīya).
Having offered [the gift], one should present the betel-leaf mixed with camphor and other ingredients at the end of the *mūla-mantra*, saying "I offer," as before.

497) The dismissal (*utsarga*) of all [deities] should be performed with the water from the *arghya* vessel. Then, having gratified the Goddess three times with the *tattva-mudrā*, [one should proceed].
Having displayed the previously mentioned mudrās— Kṣobhiṇī at the heart, Drāviṇī at the mouth, Ākarṣiṇī between the eyebrows, Vaśinī at the forehead, and Āhlādinī at the aperture of Brahmā—
one displays the five-fold mudrās and, with palms joined in reverence, [worships] the coverings of Śrī Bālā Tripurā.
Having received the command, "I worship," one should begin the worship of the enclosure (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
Therein, first, in the space between the eastern *yoni* and the central *yoni*, with the vessel of the Guru:
"I worship the *śrīpādukā* of [Name]ānandanātha; obeisance, I satiate you, obeisance. Thus.
Worship the sandals of the supreme guru (paramaguru-śrīpādukāṃ pū0); the supreme teacher (paramācārya-śrī0); the supreme-most teacher (parameṣṭhi-guru-śrī0);

the divine lineage teacher (divyaugha-guru-śrī0); the perfected lineage teacher (siddhaugha-guru-śrī0); the human lineage teacher (mānavaugha-guru-śrī0); and again, the [one's own] personal guru (svaguru-śrī0). Thus one should worship and offer libations.

One should worship and offer libations as follows: in the southeast, the venerable Heart (hṛdaya-śrīpāda); in the northeast, the venerable Head (śiras-śrīpāda); in the southwest, the venerable Crest (śikhā-śrīpāda); in the northwest, the venerable Armor (kavaca-śrīpāda); in the center, the venerable Eye (netra-śrīpāda); and in the four directions, the venerable Weapon (astra-śrīpāda).
Thus one should worship and offer libations.
Then, in the southeast triangle: *aiṃ raṃ* [to] Ratiśrīpādukā; in the northeast: *klīṃ prīṃ* [to] Prītiśrīpādukā; in the front triangle:
*sauḥ maṃ* [to] Manobhavāśrīpādukā. Thus one should worship and offer libations.

There, specifically to the north of the triangle: *drāṃ* Śrī Kṣobhaṇabāṇa; *drīṃ* Śrī Drāvaṇabāṇa; *klīṃ* Śrī Ākarṣaṇabāṇa; *blūṃ* Śrī Vaśīkaraṇabāṇa; and at its tip, *saḥ* Śrī Unmādanabāṇa—having thus worshipped and offered libations [to these], likewise to the north of that: *sauḥ* Śrī Kāma; *klīṃ* Śrī Manmatha.
To her right: Aiṃ Kandarpaśrī; Blūṃ Makaradhvajaśrī; in front: Strīṃ Mīnaketuśrī.
Thus one should worship and offer libations.

Then, in the eight wombs starting from the east: one should worship and offer libations to Anaṅgakusumāśrī, Anaṅgamekhalāśrī, Anaṅgamadanāśrī, Anaṅgamadanāturāśrī, Subhagāśrī, Bhagāśrī, Bhagasarpiṇīśrī, and Bhagamālāśrī. Thus one should worship and satisfy them.
Then, on the eight petals starting from the east: *aṃ* Śrī Asitāṅgabhairava; *āṃ* Śrī Brāhmī; *iṃ* Śrī Rurubhairava; *īṃ* Śrī Māheśvarī; *uṃ* Śrī Caṇḍabhairava; *ūṃ* Śrī Kaumārī;
*ṛṃ* Śrī Krodhabhairava; *ṝṃ* Śrī Vaiṣṇavī; *ḷṃ* Śrī Unmattabhairava; *ḹṃ*.

Vārāhī-Śrī... | Eṃ Kapālibhairava-Śrī... | Aiṃ Māhendrī-Śrī... | Oṃ Bhīṣaṇabhairava-Śrī... | Auṃ Cāmuṇḍā-Śrī... | Aṃ Saṃhārabhairava-Śrī... | Aḥ Nārasiṃhī-Śrīpāda... | Thus one should worship and offer libations.
Then, at the locations of the knots, starting from the west: *Śrī Kāmarūpa-pīṭha*, *Śrī Malayagiri-pīṭha*, *Śrī Kaulagiri-pīṭha*, *Śrī Kulāntaka-pīṭha*, *Śrī Cauhāra-pīṭha*.
One should worship and offer libations to the Śrī-Jālandhara-pīṭha, the Śrī-Uḍḍīyāna, and the Śrī-Devakūṭa.
Then, within the circular mandala, starting from the west and proceeding upwards and downwards: Herukabhairavaśrī, Vetālabhairavaśrī, Tripurāntakabhairavaśrī, Agnijihvabhairavaśrī,
Kālāntakabhairavaśrī, Kapālibhairavaśrī, and Ekapādabhairavaśrī.
"Bhīmarūpa-bhairava-śrī, Malayabhairava-śrī, Hākaṭeśvara-bhairava-śrī"—thus one should worship and offer libations.
Then, in the square, starting from the east: Indra-śrī, Agni-śrī, Yama-śrī, Nirṛti-śrī.

[One should worship and offer libations to] Varuṇaśrī, Vāyuśrī, Kuberaśrī, and Īśānaśrī. Between Indra and Īśāna, [one worships] Brahmaśrī; between Varuṇa and Rākṣasa, Viṣṇuśrī. Then, in their vicinity, [one worships] Vajraśrī, Śaktiśrī, Daṇḍaśrī, Khaḍgaśrī, and Pāśaśrī.

I worship the *pādukā* of Dhvajaśrī, Gadāśrī, and Triśūlaśrī; *tarpayāmi*. Then, in the western square: *Vāṃ*, obeisance to Vaṭuka, [I worship] Vaṭukaśrī. In the north: *Yāṃ*, obeisance to the Yoginīs, [I worship] Yoginīśrī. In the east: *Kṣāṃ*, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla, [I worship] Kṣetrapālaśrī. In the south: *Gāṃ*...

"Obeisance to Gaṇapati; [offering] to the glory of Gaṇapati. Thus one should worship and offer libations. Then, in the northwest (vāyavya), "obeisance to the eight Vasus"; in the northeast (īśāna), "obeisance to the twelve Ādityas"; in the southeast (āgneya), "obeisance to the eleven Rudras"; in the southwest (nairṛta), "obeisance to the nine Grahas"—thus one should worship and offer libations. To the left of that [Gaṇapati], [one should worship] "to the glory of the rosary," "to the glory of the boon-granting gesture," and to its left, "to the glory of the book" and "to the glory of the gesture of fearlessness. Thus one should worship and offer libations.

Again, having worshipped the Root Goddess within the *bindu* as before and having gratified her, one should worship her with three handfuls of flowers and perform the daily fire-sacrifice (*nityahoma*).
It is as follows: having visualized the *cakra* in the fire—or having drawn it in water—one offers: "Svāhā to Prāṇa; Svāhā to Apāna."
Having offered with "Svāhā to Vyāna! Svāhā to Udāna! Svāhā to Samāna!", one should perform the six-limbed oblations (*ṣaḍaṅgāhutīḥ*).

Then, having offered to one's own Goddess with the root mantra and dismissed her into one's own heart, one should prepare a mandala in the northeast and [offer] "Vāṃ, obeisance to Vaṭuka; come, come, O Lord Vaṭuka, son of the Goddess, radiant with a mass of tawny matted locks, three-eyed!"

O Jvālāmukha, destroy all obstacles, destroy them! Accept this *bali* offering together with all ritual services, svāhā! [In the southeast: Homage to the Yoginīs! Whether above the Brahmāṇḍa, or in heaven, in the expanse of the sky, on the surface of the earth, in the partless realm, or in the netherworld (pātāla), or in the depths of water or wind—wherever you may be situated, whether above...

May the goddesses, who have taken their seats upon the *prīṭhas*, *upaprīṭhas*, and other sacred sites, and who are ever pleased by incense, lamps, and the like, protect us through the rite of auspicious offerings, O best of heroes!
*Yāṃ yoginībhyo phaṭ svāhā*—this is the offering for the Yoginīs. In the southwest:
*Kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣaiṃ kṣauṃ kṣaḥ*, O Kṣetrapāla, accept this offering together with the offering for the [attendant] spirits! *Baliṃ gṛhṇa 2*.

" Svāhā"—this is the offering to the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla). In the northwest: "Gāṃ Gīṃ Gūṃ! O Gaṇapati, bestower of boons, bring all people under my control; accept this offering, accept it, svāhā!"—this is the offering to Gaṇapati. Having thus prepared the offering and having presented the offering of the goat and other items according to the procedure taught in the Āgamas, one should meditate upon the Guru and the Goddess.

Having performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, and having again performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the ritual placement of mantras on the limbs (*ṛṣyādikarāṅganyāsa*), and so forth, one should offer the fruit of the recitation— which is of the nature of radiant energy— into the left hand of the Goddess by means of the libation (*tarpaṇa*) known as "the secret" (*guhyātīti*).
Then, having recited the armor (*kavaca*), the thousand names (*sahasranāma*), and the hymn of praise (*stava*), one should prostrate with the eight limbs (*sāṣṭāṅga-praṇipāta*).

Having performed circumambulation together with the initiates (sāmayika), and having offered salutation to the vessels (pātra-vandana) in the manner previously described, one should recite the previously mentioned hymn of peace (śāntistotra), beginning with:
"May all practitioners rejoice; may detractors perish; may the state of Śambhu be mine;
may the Guru be forever gracious," and so forth, while facing the northeast (īśāna).

One should discard the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings) with the mantra: "Obeisance to Nirmālyavāsinī. Then, one should offer everything—whatever has been spoken, whatever has been done, by me, through mind, speech, action, feet, belly, and genitals, and by virtue of my life-force, body, and authority, during the previous states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—with the following: "All this [I offer]."
May this be an offering to Śrī Bālā Tripurā. Having placed the *arghya* (offering water) in a vessel made of copper or another material, one should offer it to the Sun with the mantra:

*oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ sūrya eṣa te 'rghaḥ svāhā*. Then, one should ensure that there are no defects in the ritual. After partaking of the *naivedya* (food offering) and other items together with one's kinsmen, one should enjoy oneself happily while contemplating one’s own self as the form of Kāmakalā.
This manual for the goddess Śrī Bālā Tripurā, composed by the Lord of the Three Worlds who is compassionate toward his own devotees, has now reached completion.
Thus ends the Śrī Bālā Tripurā Paddhati in the Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra, within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. || 2 ||
(p. 500) Now follows the armor (kavaca) of the illustrious Bālā Tripurasundarī.
Śrī Bhairavī said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who increase the devotion of your devotees!
Please tell me that armor (*kavaca*) of the Goddess which was indicated by me [to you].
Śrī Bhairava said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim this armor (kavaca), which is difficult even for the gods to obtain;
it is not to be disclosed, a supreme secret that grants the desired accomplishments of the practitioner.
O Goddess, the sage of the Kavaca is the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
Paṅkti is declared to be the metre, and the goddess Tripurasundarī is the deity.
Its application is for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa in the practice of spiritual accomplishment.

Of this *Śrī Bālā Tripurasundarī Kavaca*, the Seer (*ṛṣi*) is Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the Metre (*chandas*) is Paṅkti, the Deity (*devatā*) is Śrī Bālāsundarī, the Seed-syllable (*bīja*) is Aiṃ, the Power (*śakti*) is Sauḥ, the Bolt (*kīlaka*) is Klīṃ, and the Application (*viniyoga*) is for the accomplishment of the four aims of human life. Salutation to the Seer Dakṣiṇāmūrti upon the head.
Salutation to the Paṅkti meter at the mouth; salutation to the deity Bālāsundarī at the heart; salutation to the seed-syllable Aiṃ at the secret place;
salutation to the Śakti Sauḥ at the navel; salutation to the seed-syllable Klīṃ at the feet;
salutation to the application (viniyoga) in all limbs. Aiṃ, salutation to both thumbs; Klīṃ, salutation to both index fingers; Sauḥ...

*Madhyamābhyāṃ namaḥ*. *Aiṃ* to the two ring fingers (*anāmikābhyāṃ namaḥ*). *Klīṃ* to the two little fingers (*kaniṣṭhikābhyāṃ namaḥ*). *Sauḥ* to the palms and backs of the hands (*karatalapṛṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*). In this manner, perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the heart and other limbs. The visualization (*dhyāna*):
[She is] resplendent with a crest-jewel of pearls, earrings, armlets, jeweled necklaces, a heavy necklace, rings, bracelets, and so forth.
She bears the crescent moon, which has a pearl-stringed crest like a conch fastened to its ruby-like belly;
and she holds a noose, a goad, a book, and a rosary in her right arms, starting from the upper one.
Aiṃ, the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], shall protect the head; likewise, Klīṃ, the Kāma [seed-syllable], shall protect the heart;
and Sauḥ, the Śakti seed-syllable, shall protect the navel, the secret place, and the two feet. (5)
Aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ—may Bālā protect my face for the attainment of all siddhis;
hasakalahrīṃ sauḥ—may Bhairavī protect the region of the throat.
May Sundarī always protect the region of the navel; may Sakalā protect the head;
and may Mahātripurasundarī protect the space between the eyebrows and the nose.
May Subhagā protect my forehead; may Bhagā protect me from the region of the throat; may the goddess Bhagā protect my heart, and Bhagasarpiṇī my belly.
May Bhagamālā protect [me] at the region of the navel; may Manobhavā protect [me] at the linga; may the Great Goddess Śivā, the Queen of the Kings of Kings, protect [me] at the secret place. 9.
May the Mother of the Universe, whose form is consciousness, protect [me] at the feet;
may Nārāyaṇī, who brings auspiciousness in all undertakings, protect me throughout the entire night.
May Brahmāṇī protect me in the east, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī in the south;
may Vārāhī protect me in the west, and Maheśvarī in the north. (11)
May Kaumārī protect [me] in the southeast, and Mahālakṣmī in the southwest;
may Cāmuṇḍā protect [me] in the northwest, and Indrāṇī protect [me] in the northeast.
May Mahāmāyā protect me in the water; may Sarvamaṅgalā protect me on the earth;
may Varadā protect me in the sky; and may Bhuvaneśvarī protect me everywhere.
This, however, is called the Armor (Kavaca), which is difficult even for the gods to obtain;
one should recite it upon rising in the morning, being pure and with a restrained mind. (14)
For him there shall be no diseases nor any fear anywhere;
likewise, he shall have no fear of pestilence nor fear of sins.
One shall not fall under the power of poverty, nor shall one remain under the power of death;
one shall go to the city of Śiva, O Goddess—this I tell you as the truth, the absolute truth. (16)
O Śivā, he who recites the Śrīvidyā without knowing this armor (kavaca) does not obtain its fruit; instead, he shall incur the death of Indra. (17)
Thus ends the *Śrībālātripurasundarī-kavaca* from the *Śrīrudrayāmala-tantra*, in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava. 3.
Now follows the *Bālāsahasranāma*.
Once, at a certain time in a secluded place, Pārvatī joyfully spoke to him who was resting in samādhi, who was filled with a mass of supreme bliss, and who was exultant. || 1 ||
Śrī Devī said: O Śrīman Nātha, O Śaṅkara, tell me the cause of your bliss;
O Lord of Goddesses, O ocean of nectar, O you who are full of love, that which is attainable by the lords of yogins.
O Śambhu, if out of compassion for me, please tell it even though it is a most secret matter.
Śrī Bhairava said: A mass of intense bliss arises through the state of Śakti;
therein lies the maiden, an ocean of loveliness and a cavern of aesthetic essence (rasa).
I meditate every moment upon that very auspicious Goddess;
therefore, O beloved, I shall recite her thousands of names for you.
O goddess with thighs like plantain stalks, although [these things] are most secret, because of the play of my deep affection, I praise her alone and meditate upon her every moment.
The source of the mass of happiness is the cause of the bliss of knowledge. || 5 ||

Of this *Śrī-Bālā-Tripurasundarī-Sahasranāma-Stotra*, Bhārgava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandas*), Śrī-Bālā-Tripurā is the deity (*devatā*), and Aiṃ Bīja, Sauḥ Śakti, Klīṃ Kīlaka are the seed-syllables. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of all human goals through the power of their unification [Kh: for my non-dual attainment] during recitation. To Bhārgava, the seer...

*Namaḥ* to the head. *Namaḥ* to the *anuṣṭubh* meter at the mouth. *Namaḥ* to the deity Śrībālā at the heart. *Aiṃ*, *namaḥ* to the seed-syllable (*bīja*) at the private parts. *Sauḥ*, *namaḥ* to the power (*śakti*) at the feet. *Klīṃ*, *namaḥ* to the *kīlaka* at the navel.
*Namaḥ* to the application (*viniyoga*) in all limbs. *Aiṃ*, *namaḥ* to both thumbs. *Klīṃ*.
*sauḥ* with the two index fingers; *aiṃ* with the two middle fingers; *klīṃ* with the two ring fingers;
*sauḥ* with the two little fingers; *sauḥ* with the palms and backs of the hands. Thus is the placement (*nyāsa*) on the heart and other limbs.
Meditation (*dhyāna*).

I meditate upon the Youthful Goddess, clad in red garments, adorned with the crescent moon, resembling the rising sun, and possessing three eyes; she holds a book, a rosary, and displays the gesture of granting fearlessness in her hands, seated upon a reddish lotus.
The ocean of bliss, the embodiment of joy, the source of delight, the dispeller of sorrow—Tripurasundarī is the unsurpassed ocean of love. (1)
She who is the source of the profound meaning of the left (Vāmārtha), she who is existence (bhūti) and sovereign power (vibhūti), she who belongs to Śaṅkara and is auspicious (śivā);
she whose form is erotic love (śṛṅgāra), the giver of boons, the aesthetic flavor (rasa), and the sphere of the auspicious. || 2 ||
She is the wave of supreme bliss, delight, the path to the stage of existence,
the garland of passion, the art of love-play, and the digit that bestows absolute liberation.
She is like a medicinal elixir, a wish-fulfilling creeper, and a source of wonder; she is the very path of delight, most affectionate, charming in her innocent form, and captivating to the mind.
She possesses the radiance of ten million rising suns and the coolness of ten million moons;
her limbs are smeared with flowing nectar, and she is envisioned for the sake of attaining heaven.
The beloved one with eyes like those of a deer, the auspicious state, the succession of happiness;
the sovereign queen of the king of kings, the royal lady saluted by Mahendra. (6)
The Mistress is the course of phenomenal proliferation; she is the supreme course of phenomenal proliferation.
She is Durvāsā, the unbearable power, with her tinkling golden anklets. (p. 504) 7.
Her breasts are like Mount Meru and Mount Mandara; she holds the goad, the noose, and the excellent weapon (the trident);
she is resplendent with her two hands joined together, grasping an arrow and a bow.
Her face was like the orb of the moon, adorned with the moonlight of a beautiful crest-jewel;
she bore a tilaka of vermilion, possessed lovely braided hair, and wore a spotless garland.
Delighted by garlands of mandāra flowers, adorned with jeweled necklaces, pleased by golden ornaments, and charming with the luster of pearls. 10.
With her mouth filled with betel, her mind delighted by the joy of love,
easily propitiated, the essence of austerity, and an ocean of compassion, she is the Sovereign Goddess of Fate (or the Mistress of Treasures).
The splendor of the jewels shimmering on her breast is sweet and intoxicating;
she is devoid of the utterance consisting of *bindu* and *nāda*, and is of the nature of the Fourth State (*turya*).
She is of lovely form, the blessed one, the joy-cluster of Śaṅkara;
she is the manifestation of the universe, the fifth [note], the full, dwelling in the Pūrṇa-pīṭha. || 13 ||
She is the sovereign fortune, the glorious Lakṣmī, the Great Lakṣmī, and the one with excellent sovereignty;
she is the limit of contentment, prosperity, and likewise the golden radiance.
The Mother (Ambikā) is the perfect sustainer of the world, the creator, and the increaser of strength;
she is the sovereign glory of universal monarchs and the path to imperial dominion.
She has lotus-eyes and a long gaze, she is skilled in casting sidelong glances; she is a river of aesthetic delight, a connoisseur of beauty, the foremost one, whose very form is rasa.
She is the ocean of aesthetic flavors, possessed of beautiful limbs, grey-hued, and intent upon sexual union;
she is attached to uninterrupted virtues, the power whose very essence is amorous dalliance. || 17 ||
Kāmākṣā, Kamanīyā, Kāmeśī, Bhagamaṅgalā, Subhagā, Bhoginī, Bhogyā, Bhāgyadā, Subhagā, and Bhagā. (18)
She is the digit of bliss of the *bhaga* and *liṅga*, residing in the center of the *bhaga*;
she is the form of the *bhaga*, composed of the *bhaga*, the machine of the *bhaga*, and the most excellent *bhaga*. (19)
The Yonimudrā is the Kāmakalā, devoted to the supreme nectar of the Kula;
she dwells in the cavity of the Kula, is subtle, the individual soul (jīvātman), and has the form of the Liṅga.
She is the primordial action, the primordial form, whose essential nature is the original manifestation;
she is full of longing, the bliss of the lotus, the state of pure consciousness, the goal of the self, and auspicious.
White and reddish, in the form of a drop, the source of the Vedas, she is the momentary resonance;
her sound is like the ringing of a bell, a wondrous roar arising from the solar orb.
Merged within the end of the sound (nāda), she is complete, abiding in fullness, and possessing manifold forms;
she is the resonance of a water-pot, the movement of a flute, musical instruments, and the sound of a drum.

The garland of letters, the digit of accomplishment, she who dwells in the sequence of the six chakras; she who delights in the root-play, the self-consecrated one who resides in the fourth state. || 24 ||
Abiding in the Maṇipūra, she is smooth and devoted to the wheel of the tortoise;
her movement is in the Anāhata, and she has the form of a jewel, shining with the splendor of bliss.
Pure, purified of sound, the resonant ground of the awakening of the individual soul (jīva), she resides within the lotus of the wheel of command (ājñācakra); throbbing, skillful, and threefold.
She is moonlight possessing the splendor of ten million moons, composed of the radiance of ten million suns;
she has the crimson glow of a ruby, an eternal luster consisting of pure bliss.
And Pānaśrī, the beloved minister Niścalā, and Amṛtanandinī—delighted by the touch of their lover’s body and filled with the sweetness of nectar. (28)
Seated upon a great couch, unsmeared, satisfied, and proud, she possesses excellent provisions;
sprinkled with flowing nectar, she causes the ocean of blood to swell.
Deeply red, sprinkled by her beloved, eternally abiding in the sacrificial pit, and fearless;
she is the hearing of the auspicious scriptures and the garland of fruits from the nine solitary Aśoka trees. (200) 30.

She is the delighted one, the auspicious one, the beloved of Śiva, the consort of Śaṅkara, the power of Śambhu, the radiant one; she is the self-existent, her own dear one, belonging to herself, belonging to her own, and the mother of all beings.
Her own garden, her own refuge, virtuous, a stream of nectar ever-increasing, auspicious Ujjayinī, worthy of honor, she who clings to all that is auspicious. (32)
Bhadrā, Bhadrāvalī, Kanyā, Kalitārdhendubimbabhāk, Kalyāṇalatikā, Kāmyā, Kukarmā, Kumatimanu. (33)
With eyes like those of a doe and glances intoxicated with wine, she is pungent and maddened by the passion of rasa;
delighted by the drinking of *vāruṇī* liquor, her refuge is fashioned from intoxicating drink.
She has a taste for drinking *kādambarī* wine, she is free from the fear of snares,
she is joyful, her side-glances are full of delight, and her long eyes are slightly tremulous with a playful smile.
She is the crest-flame of the fire to the race of Daityas and the luster of the nectar of her desires;
she is a married woman with full limbs and full, swelling breasts.

Her hair is beautifully braided, her pearls are radiant with the luster of her teeth, her lips are like the bimba fruit, her face is effulgent, and she possesses the supreme brilliance of coral. || 37 ||
Her nose-tip is like a sesame flower, her forehead bears a golden kakkola mark,
her face is like the spotless moon, and she is radiant with a crescent moon as her crown-ornament.
Her beauty is like that of dancing wagtails; her ear-lobes quiver;
she has the crescent moon as her half-canopy; and she wears a crown with a jewel like the sun.
She wore earrings of gold and rubies, as well as pendants of gems and gold;
she possessed a most beautiful chin, a neck like a conch shell, and was enchanting with her jewels.
She possesses the sound of intoxicated cuckoos like the waves and garlands of the Gaṅgā’s ripples;
her arms shine with lotus stalks, and she holds a noose, a goad, and a bow. (41)
Adorned with armlets and bracelets, beautiful with various jewels,
she possesses the splendor of a copper-colored lotus in her hand and the radiance of gems upon her nails.
Her fingers were a continuous row shimmering with a series of excellent finger-rings;
her lovely breasts were like twin *mandāra* flowers, and the line of hair on her body was like a serpent.

She had a deep navel, was adorned with the three folds of skin encircling her waist, possessed a slender middle, was bound by the tinkling string of her girdle, and wore a beautiful upper garment of fine silk.
Her hips are enriched by mounds like Mount Meru; she possesses a pair of thighs like the trunks of elephants;
and she is endowed with a pair of shapely calves that hang gracefully down to her ankles.
With hidden ankles, adorned with beautiful jingling jeweled anklets, her pair of feet are meditated upon by yogis; she is the embodiment of nectar, flowing with the essence of immortality.
She is an ocean of loveliness, adorned with a vermilion tilaka, and possessing curling locks of hair;
she is perfected by the virtuous, possessed of excellent intellect, wise, and the source of prosperity for the gods.
Reddish like the rays of the rising sun, she is the bee of the lotus of love for Śrī;
she is a lotus in a lake deep with aesthetic flavor, and she is the essence of that flavor. (300) 48.
She is the gracious one who bestows boons, the autumnal goddess who grants good fortune;
she is the beloved of the King of Dancers, the universal dance, and the dancer among dancers. 49.
The beautiful course is the creeper of knowledge, the mind-machine that diversifies the machine;
it is the peakless peak, the immutable, and the fifth, consisting of five peaks.
She who possesses four peaks, three peaks, and so forth, who has six peaks and is worshipped by the Vedas;
she who is endowed with sixteen peaks is the Fourth (Turīyā), the supreme digit (Kalā).
The Sixteenth [Vowel] is the sovereign of mantras and yantras, the mandala of Mount Meru;
she consists of sixteen syllables and three letters, and her nature is that of the Bindu and Nāda. (52)
Beyond color, the mother of colors, the great bliss of the Word-Brahman;
the creeper of consciousness, the peak-soul, Kāmeśī, who dwells within the objects seen in dreams. 53.
Svapnāvatī awakens consciousness; Jāgṛti is the support of waking;
Suṣupti rests upon sleep; and Mādhavī is free from drowsiness.
Lopāmudrā, Kāmarājñī, Mānavī, Vittapārcitā, Śākambharī, Nandividyā, and Bhāsvadvidyotamālinī. || 55 ||
The prosperity of heaven belongs to Mahendra; the Veda is practiced by Durvāsas; the goal of the chief of practitioners is virtuous; and the cave of perfection is easily attained. 56.
She is the Mistress of the Three Cities, the Conqueror of the Cities, and the one worshipped by the City-gods;
she is Nourishment, the Remover of Obstacles, Prosperity, the One Beyond Qualities, and the Wish-fulfilling Cow who is worthy of worship.
Hiraṇyamātā, Gaṇapā, Guhamātā [K: Gurumātā], Nitambinī, Sarvasīmantinī, Mokṣā, Dīkṣā, and Dīkṣitamātṛkā. || 58 ||
She is the Mother of the practitioner, the Mother of the Siddhas, the delightful Sovereign of practitioners;
she is intoxicated with youth, exalted, possessed of beautiful hips, and slow-moving due to passion.
Possessing red lotuses and blue water-lilies, adorned with red garlands and ointments, delighting in red wreaths, with a crest of peacock feathers, she is exceedingly beautiful. (60)
She is pleased by the dance of Śikhaṇḍin; she is the daughter of Surabhi, the Earth, the fragrant one, the bestower of desires, the desirable one, and the giver of desirable objects and wealth.
Nandinī is possessed of auspicious marks and is the presiding deity of Vasiṣṭha’s abode;
she is the goddess of Goloka, the Fortune of the World, and the protectress of Goloka. (400)
The mother of the gods, the bearer of the oblation, followed by the most excellent of the Vṛndārakas.
She is the consort of Rudra, the mother of auspiciousness, the stream of nectar, and the one who drenches with water.
She is the sacrificial fee, the embodiment of sacrifice, the daughter of Subāla, and the delight of the wise;
she moves upon the ocean filled with milk, is the source of nectar, and possesses beautiful eyes.
She follows Rāma, is worthy of being served well, dwells in fragrant abodes, possesses excellent conduct,
is the destroyer of the three cities, has beautiful breasts, and is affectionate toward her breast-nursed children.
She is the one with menstrual flow, she who is joined with passion, the colorer, and the painter of colors;
she who loves the red, she who is deeply impassioned, and she whose very nature is the theater of love.

She is the culmination of passion, semen, and the Mother; she is the essence of sexual pleasure and the longing for it; she is the manifestation of amorous gestures and emotions; she is the very soul of erotic play and the livelihood of the gods.
She who finds bliss in the flowers of the Self-Existent, she who is dear to the flowers of the Self-Existent;
she who is satisfied by love for the Self-Existent, and she who brings an end to those who revile the Self-Existent.
The pair of powers residing in Svayambhū is the pedestal that is the very essence of delight;
she is the messenger who is exceedingly intimate, clever, and honored with affection. (69)
She is the churner, the abode of the machine, dwelling upon the seat of yoga;
she possesses auspicious marks, has the nature of mercury, and is characterized by all auspicious signs.
Adorned with various ornaments, worshipped by the five-arrowed god [Kāmadeva], residing in the upward-pointing triangle, she is likewise the youthful Kāmeśvarī. (71)
The leader of the Gaṇas, the leader of the Kulas, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī;
Prīti, who delights in the spring season and is bent by the weight of her breasts. 72.
Kalādharamukhā, Mūrdhā, Pādavṛddhi, Kalāvatī, Puṣpapriyā, Dhṛti, Ratikaṇṭhī, and Manoramā. || 73 ||
Madanonmādinī, Mohinī, Pārvaṇīkalā, Śoṣiṇī, Vaśinī, Rājinī, Atyant-subhagā, and Bhagā. (74)
Pūṣā, Vaśā, Sumanā, Rati, Prīti, and likewise Dhṛti.
Ṛddhi, Saumyā, Marīcyaṃśumālā, and likewise Pratyaṅgirā. || 75 ||
She is Śaśinī and Succhāyā, arising with a full orb;
she is contented, filled with nectar, and dwells within the mechanism of the Bhaga.
The abode of the liṅga-machines (500), she is the form of Śambhu, the yoginī of union;
she is the liquefier in the form of the seed-syllable, unshakable, and dear to the practitioner. || 77 ||
Consisting of the seed of royalty, she bestows the happiness of sovereignty and grants all desires; she is the power of passion and virility, and her form is the splendor of semen.
She is the essence of all essences, composed of the essence, the radiance consisting of the power of Śiva;
she is the abode of the bliss of union and the source-mother of the joy of union.
She is the bliss of the flower of union, she who increases yoga through union;
she is the state that bestows the happiness of union, served solely by the bliss of consciousness.
She is the perfection of the worshiper who offers the *arghya*, whose very self is the substance of the *arghya*;
she is the supreme state of aesthetic union (*sāmarasya*), delighted, and whose form is the union with the Beloved. || 81 ||
She is the messenger of knowledge, accessible through knowledge, the source of knowledge, and the abode of Śiva;
she is the digit of consciousness, complete with knowledge, belonging to a lineage, and whose very nature is the lineage.
The lotus-lake of the Supreme Self consists of four digits; it is exceedingly subtle and is the playground for the sport of the swans, casting its shadow as it unfolds for the two swans. (83)
Dispassion (virāgatā) possesses the digit of liberation (mokṣakalā) and the digit of the Supreme Self (paramātmakalā);
it abides within the digit of knowledge (vidyākalā) as the inner self, possessing these four digits. || 84 ||
The fourfold power consists of Vidyā, Santoṣaṇā, Tṛpti, and Parabrahmaprakāśikā; it is intent upon the Supreme Self and merged within the ultimate reality. 85.

Peace is the attainment of the power of awakening; it is the power consisting of supreme knowledge. Abiding in the Supreme Self as the Visionary (paśyantī), it is the power of the inner self, free from agitation (akula).
She is the Madhyamā and Vaikharī, the bliss of the self's power (kalā), and the possessor of all powers;
she is the Savior, the Deliverer, the Star, the abode of the Śiva-liṅga, and the knower of the Self.

Umā is indeed one whose conduct toward others is auspicious, who delights in the bliss of Brahman, who is languid with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), who brings an end to the dance of worldly existence, who possesses a multitude of meanings, and who is dear to the caravan-leader [Śiva]. (88)
Free from birth and other such conditions, she increases the bliss of yogis and yoginīs;
she bestows the state of a hero, is divine, is the mother of heroes, and grants the state of a hero. (89)
She is the path to the heroic state for those who were once bound as cattle, the source of great prosperity through union with heroes,
the consecrated royal fortune, and the mother of the highest among Kṣatriyas.
Skilled in weapons and missiles, she is the splendor residing in the aesthetic flavors; her livelihood is war.
She is Vijayā, the Yoginī, the expedition that crushes the enemy armies. || 91 ||

Pūrṇā (600), who seeks wealth, who possesses wealth, who is endowed with an accumulation of riches; she resides in the treasury, she is the jewels, and she dwells within the storehouse of gems. || 92 ||
The queen is for the king's enjoyment; the courtesan provides enjoyment for the multitude;
the female elephant, the mare, the wrestler, and the foot-soldier are each fit for their respective roles.
She is the army-rank devoted to valor, whose dwelling is upon banners and flags;
she possesses beautiful parasols, is the Mother Ambikā, and is the true refuge for the protection of subjects. 94.

Fragrant, following the conduct of a worshiper, and devoted to the duties of royalty, she is the embodiment of the Brahmanical and Kṣatriya orders, the inner ruler of both the Moon and the Sun. || 95 ||
She is fond of priesthood, virtuous, the consort of Brahmā, the continuity of sacrifice,
devoted to drinking the Soma juice, joyful, rich in people, the sun, and patient.
Devoted to receiving gifts, she is the giver, the created species, and the refuge of the virtuous;
she is the Gāyatrī obtainable through the Vedas, the initiation, and she who is intent upon the twilight prayers.

Ratna is the radiance of the [inner] jewel; Saddī is the latent impression of the universe; Dhitir is the livelihood of the universe; Viśva is agriculture and commerce; Bhūti is prosperity; Vṛddhi is intelligence; and Kusīdikā is usury. || 98 ||
She is the support of the lineage, the wide-expanding one, the state beyond mind, and the supreme goal;
she is the Śūdra who attains the state of a Brāhmaṇa, the servant, and the worshiper of wonders. 99.

Skilled in various deliberations, youthful yet mature, composed of all arts, she is a boat with an excellent helmsman; she reaches the further shore and releases one from the difficult path of all desires. (100)

Durgā, who dwells in the Vindhya forest; she who fulfills the principles of love; the remover of the earth’s burden; Kṛṣṇā; she who is to be worshipped for protection; and she who glows with aesthetic delight (rasa). 101.
She quiets the three kinds of portents, a treasure-trove of all happiness, the splendor of the five-membered syllogism, and the moonlight in the garden of conceptual proliferation. 102.
She who brings happiness to the assembly of Siddhas, she who is worshipped by the host of Yoginīs, she who possesses the eternal sixteen forms, Kāmeśī, and Bhagamālinī. 103.
Nityaklinnā, Bhīruṇḍā, Vahnimaṇḍalavāsinī, Mahāvidyeśvarīnityā, and the one renowned as Śivadūtī. (104)
Tvaritā, Prathitā, Khyātā, Vikhyātā, Kulasundarī, Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, and Sarvamaṅgalā. || 105 ||
Jvālāmāla (700), Vicitrā, Mahātripurasundarī, Guruvṛndā, Paraguru, and Prakāśānandanāthinī. || 106 ||
She is the form of Śivānandānātha, whose essential nature is Śaktyānanda;
she consists of Devyānandānātha and is the mistress of Kauleśānandānātha.
She is the form of Divyaughaguru, the seeker of the bliss of the Samaya;
she is Śukladevyanandanātha, the seeker of the bliss of Kuleśa. || 108 ||
She whose form is the bliss of moistened limbs, seeking the bliss of the pledge (samaya);
she who consists of the bliss of the Lord of the Vedas, seeking the innate bliss (sahajānanda). || 109 ||
She is the form of the lineage of Siddha-gurus and the form of the other gurus;
she is Gaganānandanātha and Viśvānandasvanāthinī. || 110 ||
Vimalānandanāthā and Madanānandanāthinī;
Bhuvanādyā and Līlādyā, as well as Nandanānandanāthinī. || 111 ||

She whose nature is the bliss of the joy of her own self, who seeks the joy of [her] beloved and others, who is the most excellent teacher for the multitude of human beings, and who possesses the splendor of the supreme teacher (parameṣṭhiguru). 112.
The secret power of the Guru is hidden from others; she delights in the praise of her own Guru.
Known as the Enchantress of the Three Worlds, she fulfills all hopes. (113)
She who agitates all, whose majesty is celebrated in the ancient tradition,
is the power of Śiva (Śivā-śakti), the energy of Śiva (Śiva-śakti), and the abode of the three wheels of Śiva.
She is known as the Bestower of All Good Fortune, she is called the Accomplisher of All Aims,
and she is named the Performer of All Protection— the deity of the Southern Tradition.
The deity of the Western Tradition resides in the solar wheel at midday;
the deity of the Northern Tradition has made her abode in the nine wheels.
Worshipped by Kubera, of noble birth, the promoter of the family tradition;
she whose dwelling is made in the Bindu-cakra, the sovereign of the central lion-throne. 117.
Śrīvidyā, Mahālakṣmī, Lakṣmī, who consists of the triad of powers, and Sarvasāmrājyalakṣmī—she is renowned as the five Lakṣmīs. (118)
Śrīvidyā, the supreme light, the supreme Niṣkala-Śāmbhavī, Mātṛkā, Pañcakośī, Śrīvidyā, and likewise Tvaritā. (119)
Pārijāteśvarī, Trikūṭā, Pañcabāṇagā, Pañcakalpalatā, Pañcavidyā, and Amṛtapīṭhikā. || 120 ||
Sudhāsū, Ramaṇeśā, Annapūrṇā, Kāmadhuk, Śrīvidyā, Siddhalakṣmī, Mātaṅgī, and Bhuvaneśvarī. (121)
Vārāhī is the sovereign of the five jewels, abiding in the color of the Mothers;
she is the supreme light, whose form is a treasury, and who is endowed with a digit of the moon.
Surrounded by the vision of power, O Mistress, she is joined with the solar point;
she is the embodiment of the vision of Brahman and the embodiment of the vision of Śiva.
She has the form of Viṣṇu’s vision and dwells in the wheel of emanation;
she has the form of the Sun’s vision and makes her abode in the wheel of maintenance.
Mahātripurasundarī is the embodiment of the Buddhist perspective;
she is the very nature of the *tattva-mudrā*, gracious, and the seal of wisdom (*jñāna-mudrā*). (125)

The deity of the heart consists of the essence of the mind and is satisfied by all ritual offerings; the deity of the head consists of Brahman and resides in the crest-lock; she who delights in the three eyes consists of Brahman and abides in the forehead.
Astrasthā is square-shaped and dwells at Dvārakā;
Aṇimā is situated in the west, and Laghimā is the deity of the north.
Having presided over greatness (mahimā) in the east, she is the deity of the southern gate;
having presided over sovereignty (vaśitva) in the northwest, she is the deity of Īśāna presiding over the power of will (prākāmya). || 128 ||
Bhukti resides in the southeast, Icchā dwells in the southwest, Prāptisiddhi is the state [of power], and Prākāmyā delights in the half [of the northwest]. || 129 ||
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, as well as Vārāhī, Aindrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī, who are the refuge of the quarters. || 130 ||
The Kṣobhiṇī, Drāviṇī, Ākarṣaṇī, Unmādanakāriṇī, Mahāṅkuśā, Khecarī, the one called Bījā, and the Yonimudrā. (131)
She resides in the Sarvāśāpūraka-cakra and likewise brings about the accomplishment of all tasks;
she is the power (Śakti) that attracts desires and has the form of attracting the intellect.
She who attracts the ego, she whose form is the attraction of sound, she whose form is the attraction of touch, and she whose form is the attraction of form. || 133 ||
She is the form of the attraction of taste and the form of the attraction of fragrance;
she is the form of the attraction of the mind and the form of the attraction of fortitude. || 134 ||
She is the form that draws forth mindfulness, she whose form is the drawing forth of seeds, she who draws forth the nectar of immortality, and she whose form is the drawing forth of names. || 135 ||
The goddess who draws forth the body, whose form is the drawing forth of the self, she who is the embodiment of the sixteen vowels, and whose abode is flowing nectar. 136.
Tripureśī is the perfected form, dwelling in the petals of the *kalā*s;
she is the Mistress of the Wheel of Universal Agitation (*sarvasaṃkṣobhacakra*), the Śakti whose name is most secret. 137.
She is the power of Anaṅgakusumā, the waist-belt of Anaṅga;
she is the intoxication of Anaṅga, whose form is afflicted by the passion of Anaṅga. (138)
Anaṅgarekhā, Anaṅgavegā, Anaṅgāṅkuśā, and Anaṅgamālinī—these are the Śaktis associated with the eight directions of the [syllabic] groups. 139.
The illustrious Tripurasundarī, who makes her abode upon the eight petals, is the sovereign bestower of all imperial sovereignty and all auspicious fortune. (140)
The Mistress of the Tradition (Saṃpradāyeśvarī), who likewise causes universal agitation, who causes universal subjugation, and who effects the drawing-in of all things. || 141 ||
She possesses the power to gladden all, she causes all to expand,
she possesses the power to paralyze all, and likewise she is the deluder of all.
She is the power that brings all under control, she who delights everyone in every way, she who possesses the power to intoxicate all, and she who effects the accomplishment of all goals. || 143 ||
She is the power that bestows all prosperity, likewise composed of all mantras;
she is the perfection that brings about the destruction of all dualities, the dweller in Tripura. (900) 144.
She is the mistress who accomplishes all aims and bestows the success of every purpose;
she is the mistress of the fourteen-spoked wheel, endowed with the sacrifice of the Kalās.
The Goddess who bestows all accomplishments, likewise the bestower of all prosperity;
the Power who makes all dear, and the performer of all auspiciousness. (146)
It fulfills all desires, liberates from all suffering, pacifies all death, and destroys all obstacles. || 147 ||
Goddess Sarvāṅgasundarī, the bestower of all good fortune, the Mistress of Tripura, and the giver of all perfections, resides in the ten-cornered [figure]. (148)
She is the Mistress who creates all protection, as well as the Yoginī of the Inner Essence;
she is the All-Knowing One, the All-Powerful One, and likewise the Bestower of all sovereignty. || 149 ||
The Goddess consists of all-knowledge, she is the destroyer of all diseases;
she is the very nature of the support of all, and likewise the remover of all sins. (150)
The Goddess Sarvānandamayī, whose very nature is universal protection,
is the Goddess Mahimāśakti, the bestower of all prosperity.
The goddess Tripuramālinī is the mistress of the inner ten-spoked wheel;
she is the mistress who removes all diseases, as well as the Yoginī of the secret [tradition]. (152)
Vāgdevī and Vaśinī, likewise the goddess Kāmeśvarī;
Modinī and Vimalā, as well as Aruṇā and Jayinī. || 153 ||

She is the Sovereign of All, Kaulinī, the bestower of all supernatural powers (*siddhi*) within the eight-spoked [mandala], the granter of all desires, and the knower of the supreme and the non-supreme secret. (154)
The triangular and the quadrangular [forms] consist of all sovereign powers and weapons;
Kāmeśvarī is in the form of arrows, and Kāmeśī is in the form of bows. 155.
Kāmeśī is of the form of the noose, and Kāmeśī is of the form of the goad;
she is Kāmeśvarī, the power of Indra, whose abode is established in the fire-wheel (agnicakra). 156.
And Kāmagiryadhidevī resides in the triangle, occupying the foremost corner;
she is the sovereign of the right-hand corner, the Śakti of Viṣṇu, whose abode is Jālandhara. (157)
The power of Rudra, residing in the solar wheel (sūryacakra), occupies the corner of the left side;
the power of Brahmā, residing in the lunar wheel (somacakra), is enamored with Pūrṇagiri. 158.
The glorious Great Goddess Tripura, whose nature is the three cities, dwells in the auspicious triangular realm;
she is the Mistress of all-bliss and the secret bearer of the movement of the Bindu.
And Mahātripurasundarī is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman;
she resides within all the cakras and is the sovereign of all the cakras.
She is the sovereign of all wheels, likewise the sovereign of all mantras;
she is the sovereign of all vidyās, and likewise the sovereign of all speech. || 161 ||

She is the sovereign of all yoginīs, the mistress of the sacred seats (pīṭha), and the sovereign of all; she is the sovereign of all desires and the sovereign of the scriptures of the sovereignty of all principles (tattva). || 162 ||

Power (śakti) is the radiance of the vision of power; she is free from duality, pregnant with non-duality, devoid of phenomenal expansion, the Great Illusion (mahāmāyā), and yet, as the dweller within herself, she possesses phenomenal expansion. 163.
The sustainer of the origin of the entire universe, beautiful with supreme bliss—this divine cause of supreme bliss has thus been described. (1000) 164.
O Pārvatī, having extracted the essence of the Tantras consisting of a thousand names, this is the temple of joy for the young girl who is a wave from the ocean of loveliness. 165.
By this, O Dear One, for one who constantly praises at midnight, at the beginning of night, at the time of dawn, and during worship—at all times—[the following occurs]. 166.
The young maiden, who bestows the happiness of universal sovereignty, is well-pleased;
she grants him various jewels and abundant wealth. (167)
The Supreme Goddess grants [boons] that lie within the path of one's desires;
sons and grandsons increase, and the lineage flourishes for all time. (168)
His enemies perish and his powers increase;
his diseases remain far away and all medicinal herbs become available to him. (169)
His various temples shine forever;
his agriculture is fruitful, and his land is an inexhaustible cow of plenty.
His kingdom was a flourishing land, free from calamities; there, elephants and tall birds were sprinkling themselves with the waters of rut.
At his gate, joyful elephants and horses shine resplendently;
his subjects flourish, and his ministers remain free from dispute. (172)
His kinsmen are pleased with him, his conduct is exceedingly beautiful, prosperity is eternally under his control, and his own seat is delightful. (173)
His speech, consisting of both prose and verse, was like the waves of the Gaṅgā,
enriched by the skillful expression of various words and their meanings. (174)
Possessing the perfection of all aesthetic flavors and garlanded with graceful dance, even those scriptures never seen before are continuously revealed. (175)
In the assembly, he achieves the refutation of the arguments of others;
indeed, kings praise him like bards and treat him as a servant. (176)
Weapons and missiles do not cause him pain in his limbs;
indeed, women come under his control in all circumstances. (177)
Poison becomes non-poisonous, and water turns into nectar; it causes the paralysis of the opposing faction and the yawning [defeat] of the adversary. (178)
By practicing for nine nights, he becomes a knower of the yoga of that practice;
he who, free from drowsiness and with a tranquil mind, recites it day and night. || 179 ||
All beings and all worlds certainly come under his control;
through the practice of yoga for six months, he certainly attains union (yoga). 180.
Whoever constantly meditates upon Kāmakalā and recites this supreme hymn will find that women, overcome by the intoxication of passion, become subject to his will.
For he indeed brings even Urvaśī— who is visibly full of loveliness, intoxication, cleverness, and joyful glances,
and who is overflowing with love— under his control.
On an auspicious day, [one should write] on birch bark with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron,
or even with liquid lac-dye, or especially with barley-juice (yāvaka).
Or, O Goddess, a yantra inscribed with mineral pigments, beautifully adorned, placed within a vessel of gold or silver, well-purified, and properly consecrated; 184.
Worshipped with a childlike mind and having established the vital breath (samīraṇa),
one should hold [the mantra] upon the head, the throat, the base of the arms, and likewise in the heart.
Worn upon the navel, it is auspicious, victorious, and the granter of all desires;
there exists nothing else in the three worlds that provides such protection. (186)
It removes the fear of planetary afflictions and diseases, increases happiness and virtuous activities, bestows strength and vigor, and destroys cruel spirits and enemies. (187)
That city on earth is blessed, where this best of practitioners resides—a place that increases sons and grandsons with their multitude of virtues and provides wealth and grain. (188)
O fair-faced Śivā, in whichever house this hymn remains written,
there I, as well as Hari and Kamalā, shall always dwell eternally.
We dwell there, for the origin of all sacred fords (tīrthas) arises therein;
or whoever, being the best of practitioners, should cause this to be read or should read it with devotion. (190)
Through the union with the digit of the bliss of knowledge, he attains the state of oneness;
O Goddess of gods, by means of this hymn, one obtains the fruit of your worship. (191)
Having assumed a body through the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa), one should recite [the mantra] with effort;
this is the method of worshipping Bālā, the most excellent among all tantras. (192)
Among those, the sixteen-syllable [mantra] is the most excellent; herein lies this supreme hymn.
It must not be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who is impure or deceitful.
O beautiful one, [this is not for] one who is indolent, lacking effort, or a non-devotee of Śiva;
nor for one devoid of devotion, impure, or intent on reviling the guru. (194)

This cause of liberation, which increases devotion, should be given to one who is the best among devotees, and not to one devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu whose intellect is shrouded by conceptual constructions. || 195 ||
O fair-faced one, for him who recites this hymn during the Latā-yoga,
that very [practice] becomes a wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpalatā) that grants the fruits of his desires.
O gazelle-faced one, the practitioner who, remaining undisturbed, recites this during the conjunction of the flowering creeper, shall partake in the merit of a hundred sacrifices. (197)
O Queen of the Gods, even Brahmā and the others pray for her two feet;
he alone should be known as Śiva himself who is devoted to the nature of the young girl (Bālā). 198.
The moonlight consisting of the bliss of Brahman, held within the heart of Sadāśiva—
under its control abide even that bliss which the Vedas proclaim. (199)
Delight arises from meditating upon the Child; the name of the Child is proclaimed;
and through the yoga of constant practice of bliss, eternal bliss is produced. (200)
Thus ends the *Śrībālātripurasundarīsahasranāma* from the *Śrīrudrayāmala Tantra*, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. (4)
Now, the Śrībālāstotra.
Śrī Bhairava:
Now, O Goddess Pārvatī, I shall proclaim the hymn of the young girl (Bālā), which is my fifth limb and a secret; having heard it, one must conceal it with great effort. (1)

Of this *Śrībālātripurasundarī-stotra-mantra*, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Paṅkti is the meter (*chandas*), Śrībālātripurasundarī is the deity (*devatā*), Aiṃ is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), Sauḥ is the power (*śakti*), and Klīṃ is the peg (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in recitation for the sake of pleasing Śrībālā. *Namaḥ* to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the seer, on the head; *namaḥ* to Paṅkti, the meter.

Salutation to the deity Śrībālā in the mouth; salutation to the seed-syllable Aiṃ in the heart; salutation to the power Sauḥ in the navel; salutation to the pin Klīṃ in the secret place; salutation to the application in the recitation in the feet; and salutation to all the limbs.
Aiṃ to the heart; Klīṃ to the head; Sauḥ to the crest-lock; Aiṃ to the armor; Klīṃ to the two eyes;
Sauḥ to the weapon, phaṭ! Aiṃ to the two thumbs; Klīṃ to the two index fingers; Sauḥ to the two middle fingers; Aiṃ to the two ring fingers; Klīṃ to the two little fingers.
*Sauḥ* to the palms and backs of the hands. The visualization (*dhyāna*):
521) Her quarters and the intermediate spaces are colored by networks of ruddy rays; she holds in her hands a rosary, a book, and the gesture of fearlessness.
May that young girl, endowed with excellent other hands, seated upon a full-blown white lotus, and possessing an eternally auspicious form, dwell within my heart.

O Consort of the Lord of the Mountains, he who, though immersed in a state of dullness, mutters at midnight the seed-syllable of Bhavānī in Tripura— that very speech— shall become greater than even Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods; for him, there shall be mastery over speech and other such powers.

O Kāmeśvarī, at the end of the day [or the end of dalliance], one should mutter your three-syllabled King of Mantras, the Kāmarāja. Even Rambhā, abandoning the assembly of Indra, would worship that man on earth who has received the Kula initiation.
He who recites this third seed-syllable before Tripura, the Mother of the Three Worlds,
having performed his sport in the universe, likewise at the end attains the stainless state of Brahman.
He who worships Bālā upon the seat of the Bindu— situated on the earth, consisting of three circles, eight petals, six corners, and a central city— shall become Śiva at the end.

Whoever recites this hymn consisting of mantras to Tripurā at night or at the end of the night shall become on earth the crest-jewel of universal monarchs, and in heaven one equal to Śakra in valor and splendor.
Thus, O Goddess, this supreme hymn of the young girl, consisting of mantra, must not be given to those who are not devotees; it should be guarded like one's own private parts. (8)
Thus ends the hymn to Śrī Bālā Tripurasundarī in the Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra, within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī.
5. The Five-Limbed Ritual Manual (Pañcāṅga) of Śrī Bālā is complete.
Now,
the section on the extraction [of the essence]:
Once, on a mountain peak made of crystal, thickly covered with forests, [he sat].
Pārvatī and Śambhu remained established there, intent upon the protection of the world.
Pārvatī spoke these most beneficial words to the Supreme Lord:
"O God of gods, best among the deities, whose mind possesses the three qualities of compassion! (2)
O God, by whom was the Goddess Bhagavatī Mahātripurasundarī revealed in this manifest world of moving and non-moving beings, which is otherwise cruel? (3)
Śrī Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, for your curiosity I shall declare that which is to be kept secret.
On the highly meritorious bank of the Revā, there is a virtuous city named Śrīgarbhā. || 4 ||
There is [a city] renowned throughout the three worlds, the crest-jewel of all the earth;
in it there was [a place] frequented by the best of Brahmins, gods, and Gandharvas.
p.
523) There was a sacred grove of asceticism, crowded with various trees [the manuscript *g* reads "divine trees"].
In that holy penance-grove, which was even frequented by the lords of the gods, || 6 ||
The sage Dakṣiṇāmūrti, intent upon his worship,
became a vessel for the ocean of various scriptures and a treasury of all the Agamas.
Once, having come to the Revā river, which is endowed with meritorious waters, to bathe,
Tripurasundarī was pleased with him on account of his previous meritorious deeds.
The protectress Mahātripurasundarī resides in the midst of the water;
she has taught the root-mantra of the Goddess, which is pure and of the nature of nectar.
That crest-jewel among the lords of sages [said]: "It bestows fruit quickly and must be kept secret.
From that time forward, meditating upon that mantra and chanting the hymn within his heart, he remained there.
O Great Goddess, by her power he desired to compose this book;
through her grace alone, he was honored by the lords of sages.
Having examined various other texts, O you who are worshipped by the three worlds, he composed the *Mantrasāgara*, known as the *Granthamuddhārakośa*.
From that time onwards, O Goddess of gods, this work known as the *Granthoddhārakośa*, which is determined by all the Āgamas, became famous throughout the circle of the earth. (13)
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, bestower of grace upon devotees,
I wish to hear that which is called the Uddhārakośa, as determined by various scriptures.
"I desire to hear with supreme delight; you ought to speak, O Dhūrjaṭi. Śrī Īśvara said: "Listen, O Goddess, for I shall proclaim the deliverance from Tripura and the rest."
The unsurpassed extraction of the mantras of the ten goddesses, the ten Vidyās. || 15 ||
Listen as I speak of that which is known as the *Granthamuddhārakośa*, determined by all the Āgamas; it is the foremost object of worship among all texts. (p. 524) 16.
By his mere grace, Dakṣiṇāmūrti spoke to his disciple named Akṣobhya concerning the entire collection of liberations.
Listen, O illustrious student, endowed with devotion to the Goddess;
this is a secret of all the worlds, difficult even for the gods to obtain. (18)
O Goddess, at that time, the Lord of Sages, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, spoke this supreme text to his disciple who was so dear to him.
O Maheśvarī, listen as I speak of that which was spoken by him in the past; hear how, through its power, it pertains to the gods and the deities.

First, therein is the extraction of the Tripurā mantra. As it is stated in the Vāmakeśvara Tantra: "Lakṣmī, Parā, joined with Madana, Vāgbhava, and Śakti, followed by Tāra and Bhūti-Kamalā—this is declared to be the Vidya.
When the sequence beginning with Śakti is stated in reverse order, may this auspicious procedure of the sixteen-syllable Śrī-mantra bestow welfare."
Pūrṇa. || 1 ||
Thus it is said in the Uḍḍāmara:
"The ash originates from the Ocean of Milk; Kāma and Vāgbhava likewise; Śakti arises from Praṇava and Lañjā; then Lakṣmī and the rest follow from Śakti. (1)
The sixteen-syllable Vidyā, O Bhadrā, has been declared in its inverted form;
this sixteen-syllable Vidyā is Trikūṭā and Sakalā. (2)
Thus it is said. Also in the Rudrayāmala:
"The deer-eyed one (hariṇākṣī), likewise Māyā, Kāmarāja, and Vāsanā; Śara, the three-eyed one (tryakṣa), as well as Kṣāmā, Lakṣmī, and the rest beginning with Śakti. [Kh: thereafter].
The venerable sixteen-syllabled Vidyā has been taught in its reverse order.
Regarding that, the names of the Lakṣmī-bījas have been stated in the Chinnārahasya:
O beloved, Lakṣmī, Padmā, Hariṇākṣī, Saroruhanivāsinī,
Kamalā, Rukmiṇī, and Nārāyaṇapriyā are one and the same.
There are exactly seven seed-syllables (bījas) of Lakṣmī; the others, however, are artificial.

(The letter *va* joined with fire [the letter *ra*] and adorned with the drop of passion [*bindu*] is declared to be the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, which grants the accomplishment of all desires and aims.
Furthermore, in the *Tripurātilaka*:
These two are *kamalā* and *padmā*, and likewise *harikāntā*;
these five are the seed-syllables of Śrī, while the others are false. (1)

*Śrīṃ* is the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī. Now, the names of the seed-syllables of Parā are as follows (in manuscript *kh*: *hrīṃ*). And it is stated in the *Āgamālaṅkāra*: "Parā, Bhūti, Lajjā, Māyā, Sakalā, and Kṛśā."
Likewise, Samastā, Kṣamā, Devī, Praṇava, and Vīraka [are the six]. (1)
The syllable *va* is the ocean of elephants and the seed-syllable of nectar; however, the others are artificial.

O Maheśānī, the seed-syllable of Śiva, joined with the left eye [the letter *i*] and fire [the letter *ra*], and adorned with the bindu and nāda, is declared to be the seed-syllable of modesty (*lajjā*). (2)

Having extracted the seed-syllable of the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva), adorned with the nasal bindu and the nāda, and having placed the left ear (the letter *u*) all around it, the wise here declare that to be *māyā*;
thus, *hrīṃ* is the supreme seed-syllable (*parābīja*). Next, the names of the seed-syllables of Madana are stated in the Bhairava Tantra:
Kāma, Pañceṣu, Madana, and likewise Manmatha; Māra, Pradyumna, and Kandarpa—these, however, are other [names] that are not true [to his nature]. (1)
*Klīṃ* is the seed-syllable of Madana. Next are the names of the seed-syllables of Vāgbhava, as stated in the *Tripurāsārasarvasva*:
"The Vāgbhava is the upper seed-syllable, Cāraṇa, and Caṇḍakeśvara. [Variant readings: *caṇḍi*; *candri*].
Candra is also Carmavasana, and Vāsanā is likewise. || 1 ||
The limbs are beautiful, yet the skins are unreal and of another nature;
it consists of the twelve vowels and consonants, adorned with the *nāda* and the *bindu*.
The seed-syllable of speech (*vāgbhava*) is said to be for the purification of all utterances.
*Aiṃ* is the seed-syllable of speech. The two seed-syllables of Cārvaṅgī are *aiṃ* and *cchīṃ*. Now, the names of the seed-syllables of Śakti are stated in the *Chinnāśiromaṇi*:
Śakti, Śarma, Vijñeya, and likewise Śaracchaṅka are to be known;
these are the four artificial seed-syllables (bījas) of Śakti, while others are different. || 1 ||
*Sauḥ* (or *saḥ*) is the seed-syllable of Śakti. There are two seed-syllables of Śarman: *sauḥ* and *śāṃ*.
Then, the names of the Tāra-seed syllables are given in that very same place: "The Praṇava, Dhanus, Tāra, Tryakṣa, Tomā, and also Tryambaka."
Trāsa, Tāraka, and these [other] syllables are the seeds of the Praṇava.
Indeed, O Pārvatī, other [mantras] which were previously declared by me as untrue have been taught here in reverse form as the sixteen-syllable Śrī-vidyā. (2)

*Oṃ*—thus is the *tāra* seed-syllable, which is luminous. *Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ sauḥ oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ka e ī la hrīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ sakalahrīṃ sauḥ aiṃ klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*. Thus is the extraction of the mantra of Śrī Tripurā.
Now, the ten Vidyās. It is stated in the *Āgama-laharī*:
Tripurā, Śrī, Vāgdevī, Tārā, Bhuvaneśvarī, Mātaṅgī, Śārikā, Rājñī, Bhīḍā, and likewise Jvālāmukhī. || 1 ||
These ten vidyās were themselves spoken by the one clad in animal skin (Kṛttivāsas).
These same ten, joined with six others, constitute the sixteen-syllable mantra.
Daśavidyā, Bhadrakālī, Turī, Chinnamastakā, Dakṣiṇākālikā, Śyāmā, and Kālarātri, O beautiful one. (3)
This sixteen-syllable Vidyā of Śrī, when joined with their root mantras and the single-syllable mantra, is to be worshipped by the deities beginning with Brahmā. (4)
In the Vāmakeśvara [Tantra], it is said that this is the sixteen-syllable vidyā.
(p. 527) Next follows the extraction of the Lakṣmī mantra. And it is stated in the Rudrayāmala:
The deer-eyed goddess is supreme; this triad of Lakṣmī’s seed-syllables, when recited in reverse order, is said to bestow fruits swiftly.
O best of disciples, even the word *kṣāmā* signifies water; at its end, the word *nīra* is also taught.
Regarding the names for the water-seed (*nīrabīja*) therein, it is stated in the *Uḍḍāmareśvara*:
"Water (*āpaḥ*), forest (*vana*), likewise water (*nīra*), the two *ṭha*s, and milk (*payaḥ*)."
The seeds of water have been described as being indeed unreal, whereas others are supreme.

"svāhā" is the seed-syllable of water. "oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ lakṣmi mahālakṣmi sarvakāmaprade sarvasaubhāgyadāyini abhimataṃ prayaccha sarve sarvagate sarvasvarūpe sarvadurjayavimocini hrīṃsauḥ svāhā" is the root mantra.
In the *Śāradā*: Vāgbhava, Śambhuvanitā, Ramā, Makaraketana,
the third [syllable], and Jagatpārśva, blazing with the seed-syllable of fire (1).
The mantra of Bhṛgu, which begins with *u* and is rich in long vowels, consists of twelve syllables:
*aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ sauḥ jagatprasūtyai namaḥ*. Following that is the extraction of the Sarasvatī mantra, as stated in the Śāradā-paṭala:
Tāra, Lajjā, Vāgbhava, Parā, and Praṇava—these are to be known as the five-headed seed-mantra; at the end, the word "namaḥ" is prescribed. || 1 ||

[Publicly] Oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ hrīṃ oṃ, salutation to Vāgdevī. (In the *Śāradā*: "The syllable Om, Parā, the lower [vowel], the Bindu, Śakti, Om, and Sarasvatī—this eleven-syllabled mantra is declared to end with the feminine suffix -ī and the word 'namas' [in the dative case].")
[The mantra] for the manifestation is: *Oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ hrīṃ oṃ sarasvatyai namaḥ*. The names of the seed-syllables (*namobīja*) are stated in the *Āgamālaṅkāra*:
"Namo, viśvaṃ, likewise stambha, auśmaka, and likewise aśmarī."
The others are indeed artificial, O you who are worshipped by gods and asuras! || 1 ||
Thus [ends the section]. Next is the extraction of the Tārā mantra. And it is said in the *Bhairavasarvasva*:
"The Savior (Tāra), the three pungents (Vyoṣa), likewise the Beloved (Kāntā), Māyā, and the Vāgbhava.
And likewise the *kūrca* [hūṃ], O Maheśānī, at the end, as well as *phaṭ* twice and *ṭha* twice. || 1 ||
Regarding the names of the *vyoṣa* seed, it is stated in the *Āgamasindhu*:
"By joining Skanda, Vyoṣa, and Ḍimba, one obtains Hara;
therefore, 'Hāṃ' is indeed the extraction of the seed, and anything else would be false. (1)
*Hrāṃ* is the seed-syllable of Vyoṣa. Following that are the names of the *kāntā* (beloved) seeds; as it is stated in the *Vāmakeśvara*:
"Kāntā, Kamalākṣī, Priyā, and Paramā, Lambhā, Lalanā, and Lajjā—these indeed are the others, and no other [names] exist. (1)
(The sixteenth consonant [Ṣ], joined with the fire [R] and the left eye [I] and the bindu [Ṃ], mounted upon the seed-syllable of the moon [A]; this is known as the seed-syllable of the Vadhū.
*Strīṃ* is the seed-syllable of the Beloved (*kāntā*). It is also the single-eyed seed-syllable (*ekākṣībīja*). Then, the names of the seed-syllables of the *kūrca* are stated:
In the *Cchinnārahasya*:
"Kūrca, kūla, taṭa, and tīra [mean] 'bank'; others, however, are untrue.
"Hūṃ" is the *kūrca* seed-syllable. Then, the names of the *phaṭ* seed-syllables are given in the *Cchinnārahasya*:
"Haraṃ phaṭ" is the horse-mantra; any other [version] is false, O Maheśvarī.
"Oṃ hrāṃ strīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ hūṃ ugratāre phaṭ svāhā"—thus [it is]. Now follows the extraction of the Bhuvaneśvarī mantra. And it is said in the *Kubjikāsarvasva*:
O Goddess of the Gods, the Praṇava, Māyā, Kamalā, and Manmatha are likewise [the first parts]; the name "Viśva" is indeed said to be in the middle, at the end. 1.
This mantra, known as the "four-syllabled," has been proclaimed by Bhuvaneśvarī.

Regarding the names of the mantra and its seed-syllable (*bīja*), it is stated in the *Svatantre Tripurāṭīkā*: "The wise know that the mantra, the *manu*, the *hara*, and the *hanu* are indeed the *bāla*."
These are the seed-syllables (bīja) of the mantra; however, there are others that are artificial.

The two seed-syllables are *ha* and *ra*, and the mantra is *phaṭ*. The *prakāśa* is: *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ bhuvaneśvaryai namaḥ*. Next is the extraction of the *Mātaṅgī* mantra. For it is said in the *Kulasiddhāsantāna*:
"Tomā, Kālī, Lakṣmī, and likewise the two *vāgurās*."
Indeed, Cāruka and the seed-syllables of the tastes were first proclaimed by Śambhu.
The tongue is the lotus, and modesty is the water-lily; the latent impressions are the mud, and this is declared by the Wielder of the Trident to be the forest. (2)
Thus, regarding the names of the tongue-seed (*jihvā-bīja*) and the extractions of the *Kālī*-seed, it is said in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"Kālī, Kuntī, Rasajñā, Jihvā, and likewise Rasanā;
